questions.q: Arrange the following in the correct order of their reactivity towards nucleophilic addition reactions
questions.solution: The reactivity of a substrate towards nucleophilic addition reactions depends on the groups attached to the carbonyl carbon that affect the charge density on it. III is most reactive due to absence of electron-donating $-\mathrm{CH}_3$ groups that are present on other compounds. II is least reactive due $-\mathrm{CH}_3$ and $-\mathrm{NH}_2$ that greatly increase the charge density on carbonyl carbon, making it least prone to nucleophilic attack. Among $\mathrm{I}$ and IV, I is more reactive due to only one $-\mathrm{CH}_3$ group. Thus, the order will be III > I > IV > II.

questions.q: $NaCl$ is a $FCC$ lattice where ${Na}^{+}$ ions are at corner and face centre positions. Chloride ions are at edge centres and body centre positions. How many $NaCl$ formula units will be in an unit cell
questions.solution:
Here, it is given that& $NaCl$ is a& $FCC$ lattice.

& ${Na}^{+}$ ions occupy corner positions and face centres of the cube and& ${Cl}^{-}$ ions are& located at the centre of the cube.

We know that,

There are& $8$ corners present in a cube and each corner contributes& $\dfrac{1}{8}th$ to the unit cell& and& $6$ faces& present in a cube and each face centre& contributes& $\dfrac{1}{2}th$ to the unit cell.

Number of ${Na}^{+}$ ions corners and face centres =& $1 + 3 = 4$

And for ${Cl}^{-}$,

There are $12$ edge centres in a cube and each contributes& $\dfrac{1}{4}th$ to the unit cell and there is& $1$ body centre present in a cube which fully contributes to unit cell.

Number of& ${Cl}^{-}$ ions& edge centres& and body centre& =& $3 + 1 = 4$

Hence, units of $NaCl = 4$

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The denaturation of proteins can destroy all $1 ° , 2 °$ and $3 °$& protein structures.

Reason (R): Curdling of milk is due to denaturation of proteins.

The correct option among the following is
options: (A) is true, (R) is true and (R) is the correct explanation for (A)
(A) is true, (R) is true but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A)
questions.solution:
Protein found in a biological system with a unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein. When a protein in its native form, is subjected to physical change like change in temperature or chemical change like change in pH, the hydrogen bonds are disturbed. Due to this, globules unfold and helix get uncoiled and protein loses its biological activity. This is called denaturation of protein.

The coagulation of egg white on boiling is a common example of denaturation. Another example is curdling of milk which is caused due to the formation of lactic acid by the bacteria present in milk.

During denaturation secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed but primary structure remains intact.

Hence,(A) is false but (R) is true

questions.q: Identify the correct set of $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_6\right]^{3+}$ ion. (hybridisation of $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$, type of complex, number of unpaired electrons in the complex ion respectively)
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Co}$ in $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_6\right]^{3+}$ is in +3 state as $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is a neutral ligand. Since there are a total of six ligands, the hybridization state will be either $\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{sp}^3$ or $\mathrm{sp}^3 \mathrm{~d}^2$.
Since $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is a strong-field ligand, it pairs the $3 \mathrm{~d}^6$ electrons and two of the $\mathrm{NH}_3$ ligands donate their electron pairs into the inner d-orbitals (3d).
Thus, the complex is an inner-orbital complex with $\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{sp}^3$ hybridization and zero unpaired electrons.

How many of the following species have the bond order $2$ ?
${C}_{2}, {B}_{2}^{2 -}, {N}_{2}^{2 +}, {CN}^{+}, {NO}^{-}, {O}_{2}, {C}_{2}^{+}$

The bond order can be determined by using the formula shown below:&

Bond order $= \dfrac{NumberofBondingelectron - Numberofantibondingelectrons}{2}$

Now,

( {CN}^{+} ) = \dfrac{8 - 4}{2} = 2B. O. \left({NO}^{-}\right) = \dfrac{10 - 6}{2} = 2B. O. ( {B}_{2}^{- 2} ) = \dfrac{8 - 4}{2} = 2$

Therefore, the molecule whose bond order is $2$ are:

${C}_{2}, {B}_{2}^{2 -}, {N}_{2}^{2 +}, {CN}^{+}, {NO}^{-}, {O}_{2}$

Hence, $6$ species show bond order of $2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The compound with more covalent character in the following is
questions.solution:
The magnitude of polarization or increased covalent character depends upon a number of factors. These factors are,

(1) Small size of cation: Smaller the size of cation, greater is its polarizing power i.e. greater will be the covalent nature of the bond.

(2) Large size of anion: Larger the size of anion, greater is its polarizing power i.e. greater will be the covalent nature of the bond.

(3) Large charge on either of the two ions: As the charge on the ion increases, the electrostatic attraction of the cation for the outer electrons of the anion also increases with the result its ability for forming the covalent bond increases.

(4) Electronic configuration of the cation: For the two ions of the same size and charge, one with a pseudo noble gas configuration (i.e. 18 electrons in the outermost shell) will be more polarizing than a cation with noble gas configuration (i.e., 8 electron in the outer most shell).

In VF_{5}& the oxidation state of vanadium is +5.Where as in other compounds given oxidation states of the metal ions are +2 and +3.Hence, due to the greater charge on the cation VF_{5&}has greater covalent character.

How many of the following species are diamagnetic?

$\mathrm{He}}_{2}^{+},  \mathrm{H}$}_{2}, $\mathrm{H}}_{2}^{+},  \mathrm{H}$}_{2}^{-}, $\mathrm{He}$
questions.solution:
According to molecular orbital theory, species with all paired electrons in their electronic configuration are diamagnetic in nature.
$\mathrm{He}_2^{+} \rightarrow$ Has total 3 electrons, thus it contains one unpaired electron and is paramagnetic in nature. $\mathrm{H}_2 \rightarrow$ Has total 2 electrons, thus it contains all paired electrons and is diamagnetic in nature. $\mathrm{H}_2^{+} \rightarrow$ Has only l electron, thus it is paramagnetic in nature.
$\mathrm{H}_2^{-} \rightarrow$ Has total 3 electrons, thus it contains one unpaired electron and is paramagnetic in nature. $\mathrm{He} \rightarrow$ Contains total two (2) electrons and has no unpaired electron, thus is diamagnetic in nature.
Hence, among the given species, we have only two of them which are diamagnetic and thus, option (2) is the correct answer.

$\mathrm{AO}_2(\mathrm{ g})+\mathrm{BO}_2(\mathrm{ g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{AO}_3(\mathrm{ g})+\mathrm{BO}(\mathrm{g})$ is 16. One mole each of reactants and products are taken in a 1 L flask and heated to $T(K)$, and equilibrium is established. What is the equilibrium concentration of BO (in $\mathrm{mol} \mathrmL^{-1}$ )?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{AO}_3\right][\mathrm{BO}]}{\left[\mathrm{AO}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{BO}_2\right]}=16$ Initial concentrations :- $\left[\mathrm{AO}_3\right]=[\mathrm{BO}]=\left[\mathrm{AO}_2\right]=\left[\mathrm{BO}_2\right]=\frac{1.0 \mathrm{ mol}}{1.0 \mathrm{ L}}=10 \mathrm{M} \begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|}\hline$ Conc. & {$\left[\mathrm{AO}_{2}\right]} & {\left[\mathrm{BO}$}_{2}\right]} & {$\left[\mathrm{AO}_{3}\right]} & {[ \mathrm{BO}]} \\\hline Initial & 1.0 & 1.0 & 1.0 & 1.0 \\\hline At equilibrium & 1-\alpha& 1-\alpha& 1+\alpha& 1+\alpha\\\hline\end{array}
\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{(1+\alpha) \times(1+\alpha)}{(1-\alpha)(1-\alpha)}=16 \\ & \frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}=4 \\ & \therefore \quad 1+\alpha=4-4 \alpha$\\ & 5 $\alpha=3 \\ & \alpha=3 / 5=0.6 \end{aligned}\therefore$ Equilibrium concentration of [$\mathrm{BO}$] is $=1+0.6=1.6$.

questions.q:
In which of the following reactions at equilibria, the
position of the equilibrium shifts towards the products, if
the total pressure is increased?
(i) $\mathrm{X}_2(\mathrm{~g})+3 \mathrm{Y}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{XY}_3(\mathrm{~g})$
(ii) $\mathrm{X}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\mathrm{Y}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{XY}(\mathrm{g})$
(iii) $\mathrm{X}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\mathrm{Z}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{XZ}(\mathrm{g})$
(iv) $\mathrm{X}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\mathrm{Y}_4(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{XY}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
questions.solution: According to Le-chatelier's principle; on increasing the pressure, equilibrium shifts towards that direction where number of gaseous moles are minimum. In reaction (i) no. of moles in product side is less. Hence, on increasing pressure, equilibrium shift towards product side.

questions.q: For a reaction $2A ⇌ B + C, {K}_{c}$ is $2 \times {10}^{- 3}.$ At a given time, the reaction mixture has $[ A ] = [ B ] = [ C ] = 3 \times {10}^{- 4}M.$& Which of the following options is correct?
options: The reaction proceeds to the left
The reaction proceeds to the right
questions.solution:
If the value of reaction quotient (Q) is higher than that of equilibrium constant (K), the reaction favour reactants more since the amount of products in the system is higher than that of reactants. Then the reaction tends to form more reactants in order to keep the equilibrium at constant.

If Q is lower than K, the system is composed of more reactants than products. Therefore, the reaction tends to form more products in order to keep the equilibrium.

If Q and K are equal, then the reaction mixture is at an equilibrium.

$Q = \dfrac{\left[B\right]\left[C\right]}{\left[A\right]2} = \dfrac{3 \times {10}^{- 4} \times 3 \times {10}^{- 4}}{\left(3 \times {10}^{- 4}\right)^{2}} = 1 > {K}_{C}$

So, Reaction will proceeds to the left.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the reaction $A\left(g\right) ⇌ B\left(g\right) + C\left(g\right), A$ is $33 %$ dissociated at a total pressure $P.$ The correct relation between $P$ and ${K}_{p}$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

Total pressure$= P$

Degree of dissociation $= 33 % = 0 . 33$

The given equilibrium reaction is,

$\begin{cases} & A ( g ) & ⇌ & B ( g ) & + & C ( g ) \\ att = 0 & 1 & & 0 & & 0 \\ att = {T}_{eq} & 1 - \alpha & & \alpha & & \alpha\end{cases}$

Now, Total number of moles $= 1 - \alpha + \alpha + \alpha = 1 + \alpha$

Partial pressure of& $A = \left(\dfrac{1 - \alpha}{1 + \alpha}\right) \times P$

Partial pressure of $B = \left(\dfrac{α}{1 + \alpha}\right) \times P$

Partial pressure of $C = \left(\dfrac{α}{1 + \alpha}\right) \times P$

The relation between the ${K}_{P}$ and the total pressure is,

${K}_{P} = \dfrac{{P}_{B} \times {P}_{C}}{PA}$

Putting all the values of partial pressure, we get

${K}_{P} = {α}^{2}P \left(1 - {α}^{2}\right)$

${K}_{P} = \left(0 . 33\right)2P \left[1 - \left(0 . 33\right)2\right]$

${K}_{P} = 0 . 122P$

$P = 8 . 19{K}_{P}$

$P \approx8{K}_{P}$

Thus, the relation between $P$ and ${K}_{P}$ is& $P = 8{K}_{P}$

If at any given time the composition of the reaction mixture is $[A]=[B]=[C]=6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{M}$; predict in which direction the reaction will proceed and the correct value for reaction quotient.
questions.solution:
$2 A \rightleftharpoons B+C$
Reaction quotient,
$\begin{aligned}
Q & =\frac{[B][C]}{[A]^2}=\frac{\left(6 \times 10^{-5}\right) \times\left(6 \times 10^{-5}\right)}{\left(6 \times 10^{-5}\right)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad Q & =1>K_{\mathrm{eq}}=2 \times 10^{-3}
\end{aligned}$
So, the reaction will proceed in backward direction. Given, at an instant,
$[A]=[B]=[C]=6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{M}$
and equilibrium constant, $K_{\mathrm{eq}}=2 \times 10^{-3}$

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SO}_2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2 & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SO}_3 \\ K_1 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{1 / 2}} \\ 2 \mathrm{SO}_3 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 \\ \mathrm{ K}_2 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]^2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} K_2 & =\frac{1}{K_1^2} \\ K_2 & =\frac{1}{\left(5 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}=\frac{1}{25 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & =\frac{100 \times 10^2}{25} \\ & =4 \times 10^2 \mathrm{ atm}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following reaction in a $1 \mathrm{~L}$ closed vessel.
$\mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3$

If all the species; $\mathrm{N}_2, \mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ are in $1 \mathrm{~mol}$ in the beginning of the reaction and equilibrium is attained after unreacted $\mathrm{N}_2$ is $0.7 \mathrm{~mol}$. What is the value of equilibrium constant?
questions.solution:
For the given reaction:
$\mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3$
$\begin{array}{llll}\text{ Initial moles } & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}$
At equilibrium $1-x \quad 1-3 x \quad 2 x$
Given, $1-x=0.7 \mathrm{~mol}$
$\therefore \quad x=0.3 \mathrm{~mol}$
Therefore, concentration of $\mathrm{N}_2, \mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ at equilibrium will be
$\begin{aligned}
{\left[\mathrm{N}_2\right] } & =[0.7] \\
{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right] } & =1-(3 \times 0.3)=[0.1] \\
{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right] } & =1+2 x=1+(2 \times 0.3)=[1.6]
\end{aligned}$
According to law of equilibrium constant $\left(K_C\right)$
$\begin{aligned}
K_C & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{~N}^2\right],\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3}=\frac{[\mathrm{l} .6]^2}{[0.7][0.1]^3} \\
K_C & =\frac{(256)}{0.007}=3657.14
\end{aligned}$
Hence, equilibrium constant $\left(K_C\right)=3657.14$ and (b) is the correct option.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the formation of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ from $\mathrm{N}_2$ and $\mathrm{H}_2$ at $500 \mathrm{ K}$, the concentration of $\mathrm{N}_2, \mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{NH}_3$ at equilibrium are $1.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M}, 3.0 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M}$ and $1.2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M}$, respectively. The equilibrium constant for the reverse reaction is
questions.solution:
Given: Concentration of
$\begin{aligned}
{\left[\mathrm{N}_2\right] } & =1.5 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M} \\
{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right] } & =3.0 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M} \\
{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right] } & =1.2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{M}
\end{aligned}$
The reaction for the formation of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ is
$\mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3$
Thus, the reverse reaction will be
$2 \mathrm{NH}_3 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \text{ and }$
equilibrium constant $\left(K_C\right)$ will be
$K_C=\frac{\left[\mathrm{N}_2\right] \cdot\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2}=\frac{\left[1.5 \times 10^{-2}\right]\left[3.0 \times 10^{-2}\right]^3}{\left[1.2 \times 10^{-2}\right]^2}\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{\left(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\right)\left(27.0 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{1.44 \times 10^{-4}}=\frac{40.5}{1.44} \times 10^{-4} \\
& =28.125 \times 10^{-4} \\
\text{or } \quad K_C & =2.81 \times 10^{-3}
\end{aligned}$

Initially, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ and 3 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$ are taken in a $2 \mathrm{~L}$ flask. At equilibrium state if, the number of moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$ is 0.6 , what is the total number of moles of all gases present in the flask?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{N}_2(g)+3 \mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g) \begin{array}{ll}1 \text{ mole } 3 \text{ mole } & 0 \text{ moles (2 L) (initially) } \\ 0.6 \text{ or } \quad(3-3 x) & 2 x \text{ moles } \\ (1-x) \text{ moles moles } & \text{ (at equilibrium) }\end{array}$
Number of moles of $\mathrm{N}_2=0.6=1-x$ \therefore x=1-0.6=0.4$
So, 3-3 x=3-3 \times 0.4=1.8$,
and $2 x=2 \times 0.4=0.8$
Therefore, the total number of moles at equilibrium.
$=(1+x)+(3-3 x)+2 x =0.6+1.8+0.8=3.2 $$\mathrm{ mol}$

\end{aligned}
$$
$\therefore$ Reaction 1:1st order, Reaction 2:2nd order, Reaction $3:$ 3rd order
$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \mathrm{r}_1 & =\mathrm{k}_1[\mathrm{~A}] & & \mathrm{r}_2=\mathrm{k}_2[\mathrm{~A}]^2 \mathrm{r}_3=\mathrm{k}_3[\mathrm{~A}]^3 \\

& =10 \mathrm{r}_2 & & =\frac{1}{10}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{10}=\frac{1}{100}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{100} \\
& =100 \mathrm{r}_3 & & \therefore \mathrm{r}_2=10 \mathrm{r}_3 \therefore \mathrm{r}_1=100 \mathrm{r}_3
\end{aligned}
$$

The order of reaction is equal to the sum of power of concentration of reactants given in the rate law.

Order of reaction = Sum of exponents of the concentration terms in rate law

For a given reaction,

According to the rate law,

questions.q:
Consider the following reaction
$\mathrm{N}_2(g)+3 \mathrm{H}_2(g) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g)$
The rate of this reaction in terms of $\mathrm{N}_2$ at $T \mathrm{~K}$ is $\frac{-d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2\right]}{d t}=0.02 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. What is the value of $-d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right] / d t$ (in units of $\mathrm{mol} \mathrm{L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ ) at the same temperature.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \frac{-d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2\right]}{d t} & =-\frac{1}{3} \frac{d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]}{d t} \\ \frac{-3 d\left[\mathrm{~N}_2\right]}{d t} & =\frac{-d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]}{d t} \\ 3 \times 0.02 & =\frac{d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]}{d t} \\ \therefore \frac{d\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]}{d t} & =0.06 \mathrm{~mol} \mathrm{~L}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Choose the correct order of second ionisation enthalpies Carbon, Nitrogen, Oxygen and Fluorine.
questions.solution:
The corresponding electronic configurations for the given species are:
$\mathrm{C}: 1 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^2, \mathrm{ N}: 1 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^3, \mathrm{O}: 1 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^4$
F : $1 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{ s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^5$.
Since there are three 2 p-orbitals in the 2 p-subshell, it is evident that the loss of a second electron from the valence shell will be most difficult in oxygen as it would disturb the stable half-filled p-subshell.
The removal of second electron will be easiest for carbon as it would give a fully-filled $2 \mathrm{ s}$-subshell.
Thus, the order of second ionization energy will be:Oxygen > Fluorine > Nitrogen > Carbon

A binary compound of oxygen with another element is called oxide

Oxides can be simple (e.g., MgO, Al2O3 ) or mixed (Pb3O4 ,Fe3O4 ). Simple oxides can be classified on the basis of their acidic, basic or amphoteric character. An oxide that combines with water to give an acid is termed acidic oxide (e.g., SO2 ,Cl2O7,CO2 , N2O5 ). For example, SO2 combines with water to give H2SO3 , an acid.

& The oxides which give a base with water are known as basic oxides (e.g., Na2O, CaO, BaO). For example, CaO combines with water to give Ca(OH)2, a base.

Some metallic oxides exhibit a dual behaviour. They show characteristics of both acidic as well as basic oxides. Such oxides are known as amphoteric oxides. They react with acids as well as alkalies. For example, Al2O3 reacts with acids as well as alkalies.

There are some oxides which are neither acidic nor basic. Such oxides are known as neutral oxides. Examples of neutral oxides are CO, NO and N2O.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Which one among the following statements is/are not correct?
I. Ba compounds, generally are more covalent than Be compounds.
II. The electron gain enthalpy of $\mathrm{He}$ is positive.
III. The oxidation state of $\mathrm{O}$ in $\mathrm{OF}_2$ and $\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{O}$ are same.
IV. The radius of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ ion is smaller than that of $\mathrmF^{-}$ ion.
questions.solution:
The explanation of given statements are:
I. Both beryllium ( $\mathrm{Be}$ ) and barium ( $\mathrm{Ba}$ ) belongs to the same group (i.e. group-II) and as we move down the group, size of atom/ion increases while their covalent character decreases. Thus, Ba compounds are generally less covalent than Be compounds.
Therefore, the given statement is not correct.
II. The electron gain enthalpy of $\mathrm{He}$ is positive because of very small size with full-filled electronic configuration. (i.e. $1 s^2$ ). Hence, the given statement is correct.
III. The oxidation state of $\mathrm{O}$ in $\mathrm{OF}_2=+1$ and oxidation state of $\mathrm{O}$ in $\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{O}=-1$. Hence, the given statement is not correct. IV. The radius of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ ion is smaller than $\mathrmF^{-}$ ion because both are isoelectronic species but $\mathrmF^{-}$ has less number of protons (i.e. more number of electrons) [i.e. $\mathrm{F}$ has 9 protons], than, that of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$(has 11 protons).
Hence, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ ion is of smaller in size than that of $\mathrmF^{-}$ ion (due to greater attractive force in sodium.)
Thus, I and III are not the correct statements.
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Assertion (A) $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ are isoelectronic but the magnitude of ionic radius of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is less than that in $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$.
Reason $(R)$ The effective nuclear charge on the outermost electrons in $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is greater than that in $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$. The correct option among the following is
options: $A$ is true, $R$ is true and $R$ is the correct explanation for A.
$A$ is true, $R$ is true but $R$ is not the correct explanation for $A$.
questions.solution:
Higher the electrostatic attraction between nucleus and valence electron, smaller will be the size of the atom/ion.
Electrostatic attraction is given by $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}=Z-S$ where, $Z=$ the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom or ion (the atomic number) and $S=$ shielding from core electrons.
In case of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$, they are isoelectronic species and thus have same number of electrons as $1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6$ isoelectric series of atoms and ions with different numbers of protons (and thus different nuclear attraction, gives) the relative ionic sizes of each atom or ion with respect to atomic number.
Atomic number, $Z_{\mathrm{Al}}=13$ and $Z_{\mathrm{Mg}}=12$.
Thus, $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ has lower ionic radii than $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ due to higher nuclear charge.
Hence, A is true, $\mathrm{R}$ is true and $\mathrm{R}$ is the correct explanation for A.

The electronic configuration of $\mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{Ne}, \mathrm{Mg}$ and $\mathrm{Al}$ after the removal of an electron is as
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Na}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6 \\
& \mathrm{Ne}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^5 \\
& \mathrm{Mg}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^1 \\
& \mathrm{Al}^{+}: 1 s^2, 2 s^2, 2 p^6, 3 s^2
\end{aligned}$
The ionisation energy decreases as the size of the atom/ion increases. Further ionisation energy increases with increase in nuclear charge. Since, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ gives a stable electronic configuration hence its $\mathrm{IE}_2$ is highest among the given species and therefore the correct order of their $\mathrm{IE}_2$ is
$\mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ne} < \mathrm{Na}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q: Which one of the following order is correct for the first ionisation energies of the elements?
questions.solution:
First ionisation energy increases in a period. Thus, the first IE of the elements of the second period should be as follows
$\mathrm{Be} < \mathrm{B} < \mathrm{N} < \mathrm{O}$
But in practice, the elements do not follow the above order. The first IE of these elements is
$\mathrm{B} < \mathrm{Be} < \mathrm{O} < \mathrm{N}$
The lower IE of $\mathrm{B}$ than that of $\mathrm{Be}$ is because in $\mathrm{B}  \left(1 s², 2 s² 2 p¹\right)$, electron is to be removed from $2 p$ which is easy while in $\operatorname{Be}  \left(1 s², 2 s²\right)$, electron is to be removed from $2 s$ which is difficult. The low IE of $\mathrm{O}$ than that of $\mathrm{N}$ is because of the half-filled $2 p$ orbitals in $\mathrm{N}  \left(1 s², 2 s² 2 p³\right).$

The crystal field splitting, ${∆}_{o}$, depends upon the field produced by the ligand and charge on the metal ion. Some ligands are able to produce strong fields in which case, the splitting will be large whereas others produce weak fields and consequently result in small splitting of d orbitals. In general, ligands can be arranged in a series in the order of increasing field strength as given below:$I^{-} < {Br}^{–} < {SCN}^{-} < {Cl}^{-} < S^{2 –} < F^{–} < {OH}^{–} < {C}_{2}{O4}^{2 –} < {H}_{2}O < {NCS}^{–} < {edta}^{4 –} < {NH}_{3} < en < {CN}^{–} < CO$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following is tris (ethane-1,2-diammine) cobalt (III) sulphate?
questions.solution:
The given name is of cation type complex.
Thus, its formula is $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{en})_3\right]_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3$ and is named as tris (ethane 1, 2, diammine) cobalt (III) sulphate. The following rules are used while naming the complex :
(i) The cation is named first (if present outside the coordination sphere).
(ii) Then, the ligands are named in an alphabetical order along with their quantity before the name of central atom/ion. (This procedure is reversed for writing the formula).
(iii) The name of central metal is written along with its oxidation state in roman.
(iv) If, name of ligand includes numerical prefix, then, the terms bis for (2) tris for (3) etc. are used and name of ligand is written in parentheses.
(v) If, anion is present outside the coordination sphere, it named without their quantity.
(vi) If the complex ion is a cation, the metal is named as the name of metal but, if the complex ion is an anion, the name of metal ends with suffix-'ate'.
(vii) The neutral complex molecules are named similar to that of complex cation.
Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

questions.q: The covalency of Al in $\left[AlCl\left({H}_{2}O\right)5\right]2 +$ is:
questions.solution:
The given compound is a coordination compound. In the given compound, $Al$~is the central metal atom and the atoms present in coordination sphere& are bonded to& it.

Here,& $Al$~is bonded to $6$ ligands.~$( 5{H}_{2}O and 1Cl )$

Therefore, the covalency of Al in $\left[AlCl\left({H}_{2}O\right)5\right]2 +$~is& $6$.

questions.q:
Which of the following molecules/ions can exhibit isomerism:

Tetrahedral compounds do not show isomerism because the relative position of the& unidentate ligand attached to the central atom is the& same with respect& to each other. Square planar compounds of type ${Ma}_{2}{b}_{2}$ show geometric isomerism.

Octahedral compounds of type ${Ma}_{3}{b}_{3}$ show geometric isomerism, and those of type $M\left(AA\right)^{3}$ exhibit& optical isomerism.

questions.q: A complex compound of $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ with molecular formula $\mathrm{CoCl}_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot \mathrm{yNH}_3$ gives a total of 3 ions when dissolved in water. How many $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ions satisfy both primary and secondary valencies in this complex?
questions.solution:
As cobalt is present as $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ and co-ordination number of cobalt is 6 , the molecular formula of compound should be $\mathrm{CoCl}_3 \cdot \mathrm{yNH}_3$. Now, as it gives a total of 3 ions when dissolved in water, its structural formula must be $\left[\mathrm{CoCl}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2\left[\mathrm{CoCl}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2 \rightleftharpoons\left[\mathrm{CoCl}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5\right]^{2+}+2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$
Thus only one $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ion is satisfying both primary and secondary valency of $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ in this compound.

questions.q: Choose the correct statement from the following with reference to inert pair effect
options: $\mathrm{Sn}^{+4}$ is reducing agent but $\mathrm{Pb}^{+4}$ is an oxidizing agent
$\mathrm{Sn}^{+4}$ is an oxidizing agent but $\mathrm{Pb}^{+2}$ is a reducing agent
$\mathrm{Sn}^{+2}$ is reducing agent but $\mathrm{Pb}^{+4}$ is an oxidizing agent
$\mathrm{Sn}^{+2}$ is an oxidizing agent but $\mathrm{Pb}^{+4}$ is a reducing agent
questions.solution:
The inert pair effect results in the stabilization of an oxidation state, two units less than the common group oxidation state.
The stability of the oxidation state, two units less than the group oxidation state increases down the group.
Thus, $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$ is much more stable than $\mathrm{Pb}^{4+}$ because of which $\mathrm{Pb}^{4+}$ acts as an oxidizing agent and itself gets reduced to $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$.
$\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}$ acts as a reducing agent and gets oxidized to $\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}$.

(B) The chemical reactivity decreases from $\mathrm{La}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}$.
(C) $\mathrm{La}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is more basic than $\mathrm{Lu}(\mathrm{OH})_3$
(D) Zr and Hf have about the same radius.
(E) Separation of Lanthanides from one another is easy
questions.solution:
The change in ionic radii is Lanthanide series is very small, their chemical properties are small. Thus, the separation of Lanthanide is difficult due to consequence of Lanthanide contraction.
The ionic radii of same positive charge of $\mathrm{La}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}$ decreases. So, the polarizing power towards hydroxyl group increases. Therefore the covalent character increases. Thus, $\mathrm{La}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is more basic than $\mathrm{Lu}(\mathrm{OH})_3$. $\mathrm{Zr}$ and $\mathrm{Hf}$ have the almost same radius as the electrons in the elements after $\mathrm{Zr}$ are added into the deep seated $4 \mathrm{f}$ orbitals which do not take part in the chemical reaction.

and also ${Ce}^{+ 4}$ is less& stable than ${Ce}^{+ 3}$ and thus it will readily accept $e^{-}$ convert into ${Ce}^{+ 3}$ and so it will less basic than ${Ce}^{+ 3}$.

Hence, from all above observations it can be concluded that $Ce{( OH )}_{3}$is most basic among all given options.

questions.q: Salts of $A$ (atomic weight $8$), $B$ (atomic weight $18$) and $C$ (atomic weight $50$) were electrolysed under identical conditions using the same quantity of electricity. It was found that $2. 4g$ of $A$ was deposited, the weight of $B$ and $C$ deposited are $1. 8g$ and $7. 5g$ respectively. The valences of $A, B$ and $C$ are, respectively,
questions.solution:
According to the Faraday's law of electrolysis,

$W = ZQ = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q$

For the compound $A$,

Equivalent mass of $A$ = $\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{8}{x}$

$x$ is the valency factor for compound $A$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{8}{x}}{96500}Qx = \dfrac{7}{2 . 4 \times 96500}Q$

For compound $B$,

Equivalent mass of $B$=$\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{18}{y}$

$y$ is the valency factor for compound $B$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{18}{y}}{96500}Qy = \dfrac{27}{1 . 8 \times 96500}Q$

For compound $C$,

Equivalent mass of $C$ = $\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{50}{z}$

$z$ is the valency factor for compound $C$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{50}{z}}{96500}Qz = \dfrac{50}{7 . 5 \times 96500}Q$

Hence, $x: y: z = \dfrac{8}{2 . 4}: \dfrac{18}{1 . 8}: \dfrac{50}{7 . 5} = 3 . 33: 10: 6 . 66x: y: z = 1: 3: 2$

Hence, the valencies of $A, B$ and $C$ respectively are $1, 3, 2$.

questions.solution:
The amount of oxygen required by bacteria to break down the organic matter present in a certain volume of a sample of water, is called biochemical oxygen demand (BOD).
The amount of BOD in the water is a measure of the amount of organic material in the water, in terms of much oxygen will be required to break it down biologically. Clean water would have BOD value of less than 5 ppm whereas highly polluted water could have a BOD value of 17 ppm or more. It means BOD value less than $5 \mathrm{ppm}$ indicates a water sample to be rich in dissolved oxygen.

questions.solution:

II. In pyridine, lonepair is in a $s p^2$ hybridised orbital but does not get involved in delocalisation. The acidity of unsaturated compounds can be best described by observing the substituted group. The compounds containing the substituted group having strong $- I$ effect or week $+ I$ will be more acidic than the compounds containing the substituted group having week $- I$ effect or strong $+ I$ effect.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following are not aromatic?
questions.solution:
Key Idea Conditions for species to be an aromatic are:
(i) The aromatic structures follows Huckel's mule, i.e. species have $(4 n+2) \pi$-electrons in its structure. where, $n=$ integer $0,1,2,3, \ldots$. so on.
(ii) Should be planar ring structure.
(A) It follows Huckel's rule and has planar structure thus, is an aromatic $(\because n=1$, $\pi e^{-}=6$ ).
(B) It does not follow Huckel's rule ( $\because$ has $8 \pi$ electrons with $n=2$ ).
(C) It follows Huckel's rule and has planar structure. Thus, is an aromatic $(\because n=1$, $\left.\pi e^{-}=6\right)$.
(D) It follows Huckel's rule and has planar structure as it has $n=3 and 14 \pi$ electrons.
(E) It does not follow Huckel's rule, thus is not an aromatic compound $\left(n=1, \pi e^{-}=4\right)$.
(F) It also does not follow Huckel's rule. Thus, is not an aromatic $\left(n=0, \pi e^{-}=4\right.$ )
Hence, species (B), (E) and (F) are not aromatic and option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
(b) Key Idea Acidic strength increases with presence of $E W G$ (i.e. groups show-I effect) and decreases with the presence of EDG (i.e. groups show $+I$ or hyperconjugation effect). More be the number and more close be the EWG to the $-\mathrm{COOH}$ group, more is the acidic strength.
(A) $\stackrel{2}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_3-\stackrel{1}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{OOH}$, has only one EDG, i.e. (by hyperconjugation) one $\mathrm{CH}_3$ group is bonded with $-\mathrm{COOH}$ group.
(B) < smiles>CC(Cl)CC(=O)O < /smiles>
has one EWG
(i.e. $\mathrm{Cl}$ ) at $\mathrm{C}-3$ position and $\mathrm{CH}_3$, i.e. one $\mathrm{EDG}$ (by hyperconjugation) at $\mathrm{C}_3$-position.
(C) $\mathrm{Cl}-\stackrel{2}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_2-\stackrel{1}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{OOH}$, has one EWG (i.e. Cl-atoms) at $\mathrm{C}_2-$ position.
(D) $\mathrm{Cl}_2-\stackrel{2}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}-\stackrel{1}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{OOH}$, has two EWG's (i.e. two $\mathrm{Cl}$-atom) at $\mathrm{C}_2$-position.
Thus, order of acidic strength is
(D) > (C) > (B) > (A) and option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
According to Cahn-Ingold-Prelog sequence rules, the priority of groups is decided by the atomic number of their atoms. When the atom (which is directly attached to the asymmetric carbon atom) of a group has higher atomic number, then the group gets higher priority. Groups with atoms of comparable atomic number having double or triple bond, have high priority than those have single bond.
Hence, the order of priority of groups is -$\mathrm{OH}$>-$\mathrm{COOH}$>-$\mathrm{CHO}$>-$\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{OH}$

questions.q: Which one of the following is used to produce $\mathrm{Al}$ by electrolysis?
options: Molten $\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3+\mathrm{Na}_3 \mathrm{AlF}_6$ electrolyte, carbon coated steel vessel cathode, graphite anode.
Molten $\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3+\mathrm{Na}_3 \mathrm{AlF}_6$ electrolyte, graphite cathode, steel anode
questions.solution:
Molien $\mathrm{Al} \mathrm{O}_3+\mathrm{Na} \mathrm{AlF}_6$ as elecurolyse, carbon
coated steel vessel cathode, graphite anode is used to produce aluminium (Al) by electrolysis. The process is called Hall's process.
In this process, purified alumina is mixed with $\mathrm{Na}_3 \mathrm{AlF}_6$ or $\mathrm{CaF}_2$ (cryolite or fluorspar), which lowers the melting point of alumina and brings conductivity.
In the electrolytic cell, steel cathode and series of graphite anode are used.
The overall reaction is
$2 \mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3+3 \mathrm{C} \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{Al}+3 \mathrm{CO}_2 \uparrow$
The electrolytic reactions are as follows:
$\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Al}^{3+}+3 \mathrmO^{2-}$
At cathode $\quad \mathrm{Al}^{3+}+3 e^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{l})$ At anode $\mathrm{C}(s)+\mathrmO^{2-}($ melt $) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}(g)+2 e^{-}\mathrm{C}(s)+2 \mathrmO^{2-}($ melt $) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(g)+4 e^{-}$
The oxygen liberated at anode reacts with the carbon of anode producing $\mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{CO}_2$. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
Iron is extracted from its ore, (haematite) in a blast furnace. The ore is fed into the top of the furnace along with coke and lime stone.
Carbon monoxide act as reducing agent during the reaction in blast furnace and lime stone decomposes in the hot furnace forming calcium oxide. The molten iron is then tapped from the bottom of the furnace. Further, calcium oxide react with $\mathrm{SiO}_2$ to form a slag.
$\mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{SiO}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CaSiO}_3$ Slag can be used in making roads.

questions.q: What is the role of limestone during the extraction of iron from haematite ore?
questions.solution: During extraction of iron from haematite ore, roasted ore, along with coke and limestone is heated in blast furnance. Here coke behaves as reducing agent and limestone is worked as flux. In this process, in reducing zone $\left(400-900^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)$, spongy iron is obtained. In slag zone $\left(900-1200^{{}^{\circ}}\right)$, limestone reacts with impurity (e.g., silica) to form slag. In the combustion and fusion zone $\left(1200-1600^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)$, all the charge melts and pig iron is obtained which purified further.

questions.q:
The order of reactivity of the following compounds towards dilute aqueous $KOH$ in ${S}_{N}1$ reaction is

$\mathop{{CH}_{3}{CH}_{2}{CH}_{2}{CH}_{2}Br}_{I}\mathop{{H}_{3}{CCH}_{2}{CHBrCH}_{3}}_{II}\mathop{{\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{2}{CHCH}_{2}Br}_{III}\mathop{{\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{3}CBr}_{IV}$
questions.solution:
The ${S}_{N}1$ reaction rate depends on the stability of cabocation formed in the rate determining step.

$\mathop{{CH}_{3}{CH}_{2}{CH}_{2}{{CH}_{2}}^{+}}_{I}\mathop{{H}_{3}{CCH}_{2}{CH}^{+}{CH}_{3}}_{II}\mathop{{\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{2}{{CHCH}_{2}}^{+}}_{III}\mathop{{\left({CH}_{3}\right)}_{3}{C}^{+}}_{IV}$

Tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary and primary. Among the carbocations $IandIII$, $III$ is readily formed than $I$. Hence, the correct reactivity order is $I < III < II < IV$.

questions.q:
The correct order of rates of addition of ${Br}_{2} /$ water to the following alkenes is

[A] ${CH}_{2} = {CH}_{2}$

[B] ${CH}_{2} = CH - {NO}_{2}$

[C] ${CH}_{3} - {CH}_{2} - CH = {CH}_{2}$

[D] ${CH}_{3} - CH\mathop{CH3}_{|} = {CH}_{2}$
questions.solution:
Addition of ${Br}_{2} /$ water to the alkene is example of electrophilic addition reaction. This reaction take place in two steps. In first step electrophile is added to the alkene and intermediate carbocation is formed. This step is also called rate determining step.

So, reactivity of this reaction depends on stability of carbocation formed and as we know for carbocation $3 ° > 2 ° > 1 °$. So, reactivity order will be

[B] ${CH}_{2} = CH - {NO}_{2} < \text{ and } [A] ${CH}_{2} = {CH}_{2}$ < [C] ${CH}_{3} - {CH}_{2} - CH = {CH}_{2}$ < \text{ and } [D] ${CH}_{3} - CH\mathop{CH3}_{|} = {CH}_{2}$

$

This secondary carbocation attack on benzene ring.

Next step is the abstraction of proton from conjugate base

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{CCH}_2 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Cl}$
For isomeric alkyl halides, the boiling points decreases with branching. Branching of the chain makes the molecule more compact and therefore, the surface area decreases. Hence, the intermolecular attractive forces which depend upon the surface area, also become small in magnitude due to branching. Consequently, the boiling points of the branched chain having same molecular formula are less than the straight chain isomers. Higher the molecular weight, higher is the boiling point, but branching reduces boiling point.

Chlorination of ethane takes place by free radical substitution and involves the following steps Step I Initiation step $\mathrm{Cl}_2 \stackrel{h v}{\longrightarrow} 2 \mathrm{Cl}^{\bullet}$ Step II Propagation step

Temporary hardness of water is removed by Clark's Process and in Clark's process, slaked lime $Ca\left(OH\right)^{2}$ is added to hard water.

Insoluble calcium& and magnesium carbonates precipitated out as end products of the reaction and no longer cause& hardness.

Slaked lime is itself a source of calcium ions (and hence hardness) so care must be taken to avoid adding in& excess quantity.

With reference to the redox properties of hydrogen peroxide $\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2\right)$, which of these reactions are feasible?
(i) $2 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+} 2 \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
(ii) $2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}+6 \mathrmH^{+}+5 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}+8 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}+5 \mathrm{O}_2$
(iii) $2 \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
(iv)$2 \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{MnO}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}+3 \mathrm{O}_2+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
questions.solution:
$\because \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$ show oxidising as well as reducing action.
Oxidising nature (i.e. act as oxidising agent)
(i) In acidic solution,
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2+2 \mathrmH^{+}+2 e^{-} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
(ii) In alkaline solution,
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2+2 e^{-} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{OH}^{-}$
Reducing nature (i.e. act as reducing agent)
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{O}_2+2 e^{-}$
(in acidic medium)
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}+\mathrm{O}_2+2 e^{-}$
(in alkaline medium)
Hence, (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) all are possible.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The correct order of reducing abilities of hydrides of V group elements is
questions.solution:
The reducing character of the hydrides of group V elements depends upon the stability of hydrides. With progressive decrease in stability, the reducing character of hydrides increases as we move down the group. Thus, ammonia, being stable, has least reducing
ability. The order of reducing abilities of $\mathrm{V}$ group hydrides is

$\mathrm{NH}_{3} <  \mathrm{PH}$}_{3} < $\mathrm{AsH}_{3} <  \mathrm{SbH}$}_{3} <  $\mathrm{BiH}_{3}
$

' $X$ ' is $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ and ' $Y$ ' is $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}_2 \mathrm{O}_8$. So ' $X$ ' and ' $Y$ ' contains zero and one peroxy bond respectively.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The $pH$ of pure water at $80 ° C$& is
questions.solution:
At ${25}^{°}C$, the value of the ionic product of water is${10}^{- 14}$. The ionic product of water is defined as

${K}_{w} = \left[H^{+}\right]\left[{OH}^{-}\right] ⇒ {10}^{- 14} = \left[H^{+}\right]\left[{OH}^{-}\right]Forpurewater\left[H^{+}\right] = \left[{OH}^{-}\right]So\left[H^{+}\right] = {10}^{- 7}ThusthepH = 7$

Since the degree of ionization is proportional to temperature, the value of the ionic product of water increases with increase in temperature. So, the ionic product will increase at a temperature more than $25 ° C$
Therefore, at $80 ° C$, the ionic product will increase and so the hydrogen ion concentration will increase and thus, the pH will become less than 7.

where, ${K}_{c} =$ equilibrium constant

$C =$concentration

Here, $C = 0. 1M, \alpha = 5 % = 0. 05$

${K}_{c} = {\alpha}^{2} \times C$

${K}_{c} = \left(0. 05\right)^{2} \times 0. 1{K}_{c} = 2. 5 \times {10}^{- 4}M$

Hence, option $C$ is correct.

questions.q: If the molar concentrations of base and its conjugate acid are same, then $pOH$ of the buffer solution is
questions.solution:
According to the& buffer solution the $pOH$ of solution is :-

$pOH = {pK}_{b} + \log \left[Salt\right]\left[base\right]$

If the $molar concentrations of base and its conjugate acid are same then& \left[Salt\right]$ =$\left[Base\right]$

So, the $pOH = {pK}_{b} + log1 = {pK}_{b} + 0 = {pK}_{b}$

Hence, if the molar concentrations of base and its conjugate acid are same, then $pOH$ of the buffer solution is same as ${pK}_{b}$ of base.

questions.solution:
$\because$ (i) Sodium acetate, i.e. $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COONa}\right)$ in water gives $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH} and \mathrm{NaOH}$ as follows :

Also,

$\mathrm{NH}_4^{+} \text{(aqueous) }+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NH}_3+\mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{OH}^{-}$
Hence, $\mathrm{pH} \lt  7$
Hence, the correct answer is, for (i) $\mathrm{pH} \gt 7$ and for (ii) $\mathrm{pH} \lt  7$.

questions.q: The correct order of reducing ability of the following hydrides is
questions.solution:
The reducing character of the hydrides of group V elements depends upon the stability of hydrides. diamond is ionic whereas graphite is covalent
each carbon atom in diamond is chemically bonded to greater number of neighbouring carbon atoms
certain atoms in diamond are smaller in size
questions.solution:
In diamond carbon atom is ${sp}^{3}$& hybridised due to tetrahedral structure. In diamond each carbon atom is present at the same distance to each of its neighbouring carbon atom. In this rigid network atom cannot move that is why diamond are& so hard.

Graphite is layered. Graphite& has planar hexagonal layers of carbon atom held together by weal forces like vanderwaal& forces of attraction. This& allows layers of carbon to slide over each other in graphite, which make graphite soft.

Thus, diamond is hard because diamond is in tetrahedral form while graphite is soft because it is in planar.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the nature of the bonding in anhydrous $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ and hydrated $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ respectively?
questions.solution:
Many simple compounds of elements such as $\mathrm{AlCl}_3, \mathrm{GaCl}_3$ and $\mathrm{InCl}_3$ are covalent while anhydrous but in aqueous solution, these are ionic in nature. In anhydrous condition, the (charge/radius) ratio, i.e. polarisability of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ is high and hence, according to Fajans' rule, $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$ polarises $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ions to large extent, there introducing covalent character in the compound, i.e. $\mathrm{AlCl}_3$ behaves as a covalent compound in anhydrous conditions.
In aqueous medium the ions get hydrated, because the amount of hydration enthalpy released exceeds, the sum total of ionisation enthalpy required.
Since, the (charge/radius ratio of hydrated aluminium ion is much smaller as compared to that of $\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$, the tendency of $\left[\mathrm{Al}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right]^{3+}$ to polarise hydrated $\mathrm{Cl}^{\ominus}$ ion decreases and the resulting hydrated compound is ionic in nature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify the correct statements from the following:

(a) In Orthoboric acid, boron is in planar geometry.&

(b) In ${BCl}_{3} \cdot {NH}_{3}$,& boron has tetrahedral geometry.&

(c) Aqueous solution of borax is acidic.&
questions.solution:
$1.$ In orthoboric acid ${H}_{3}{BO}_{3}$, boron is ${sp}^{2}$ hybridized and thus is in planar geometry.

$2.$ In ${BCl}_{3}. {NH}_{3}$, Boron and Nitrogen $( N )$are both $sp^{3}$ hybridized& and the shape of the adduct& is tetrahedral.

$3.$ Combination of a strong base and a weak acid results in a salt which is basic in nature. Borax is a salt which is formed by the reaction of $NaOH$ (strong base) with ${H}_{3}{BO}_{3}$& (weak acid). Thus, the aqueous solution of borax is basic and not acidic.

questions.solution:
When heating the silicon with methyl chloride at high temperature in the presence of copper, it produces a& mixture of mono,& di and tri-methyl chlorosilanes and tetramethylsilane.

${CH}_{3}Cl + Si\mathop{→}_{573K}^{Cupowder}{CH}_{3}{SiCl}_{3} + \left({CH}_{3}\right)^{2}{SiCl}_{2} + \left({CH}_{3}\right)3SiCl + \left({CH}_{3}\right)4Si$

Out of which,& tetramethylsilane has the minimum yield as to have four bulky methyl groups around silicon is not preferred.

questions.q: Hybridisation of boron in diborane is
questions.solution:
Boron atom in diborane is known to be $s p^3$
hybridised because it has four hybrid-orbitals. Three of these has one electron each and one is an empty orbital. The two electrons of hybrid orbitals in each of boron atom form two bonds with $1 s$ of hydrogen atoms. The two atoms of boron left with that of each unpaired electron orbital and empty orbital forms two bridging $(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B})$ bonds with that of two $1 s$ hydrogen atoms. It is also called banana bond.
Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.q: Among the hydrides of group 16 elements, the hydriae $\mathrm{X}$ has lowest boiling point and the hydride $\mathrm{Y}$ has highest boiling point. $\mathrm{X}$ and $\mathrm{Y}$ respectively are
questions.solution:
On moving down the group from $\mathrm{S}$ to $\mathrm{Te}$, the boiling point of hydrides increases due to increase in van der wal force of attraction. But $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ has highest boiling point due to presence of hydrogen bonding.
Hence, the increasing order of boiling point of group 16 hydrides is given as : $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{ S} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Se} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{Te} < \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ Thus, $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{ S}$ has lowest boiling point while $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ has highest boiling point.

questions.q:
Identify the correct orders from the following with respect to the property associated with
A. $\mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{PH}_3 > \mathrm{AsH}_3 > \mathrm{SbH}_3-$ Bond Angle
B. $\mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{PH}_3 > \mathrm{AsH}_3 > \mathrm{SbH}_3$ - Basic Character
C. $\mathrm{PH}_3 > \mathrm{AsH}_3 > \mathrm{SbH}_3 > \mathrm{NH}_3$ - Thermal stability
D. $\mathrm{SbH}_3 > \mathrm{NH}_3 > \mathrm{AsH}_3 > \mathrm{PH}_3$ - Boiling point
questions.solution:
The order in 'A' is correct as the bond pair- bond pair repulsion increases of the central atom that decreases the bond angle.
The order is ' $\mathrm{B}$ ' is correct as the size of the orbital increases down the group because of which the lone pair accommodation becomes easier.
The order in ' $\mathrm{C}$ ' is incorrect as the correct order is:

$\mathrm{NH}}_{3}> \mathrm{PH}$}_{3}>$\mathrm{AsH}}_{3}> \mathrm{SbH}$}_{3}

This is due to the bond strength which decreases down the group.
The order in ' $\mathrm{D}$ ' is correct due to extensive intermolecular H-bonding in $\mathrm{NH}_3$ and molecular weight of $\mathrm{SbH}_3$.

A free oxygen atom then combines with another oxygen molecule to form a molecule of ozone. $\mathrm{O}_2+h v \underset{\text{ discharge }}{\stackrel{\text{ Electric }}{\longrightarrow}} $2 $\mathrm{O}\mathrm{O}$+$\mathrm{O}_2$ \longrightarrow $\mathrm{O}_3

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the order of relative basic strength of $\mathrm{ClO}_2^{-}, \mathrm{ClO}_3^{-}, \mathrm{ClO}_4^{-} ?$
questions.solution:
More be the oxidation state of central atom
(i.e. $\mathrm{Cl}$-atom), more is the acidic nature of the species and lesser will be the basic strength.
As, oxidation number of :
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Cl} \text{ in } \mathrm{ClO}_2^{-} \rightarrow x-4 & =-1 \\ x & =+3 \\ \mathrm{Cl} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{ClO}_3^{-} \rightarrow x-6 & =-1 \\ x & =+5 \\ \mathrm{C} \mathrm{lin} \mathrm{ClO}_4^{-} \rightarrow x-8 & =-1 \\ x & =+7\end{aligned}$
Thus, order of acidic nature is
$\mathrm{ClO}_4^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_3^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_2^{-}$
and order for basic strength is
$\mathrm{ClO}_2^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_3^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_4^{-}$.
Alternate method
The more be the oxygen atom in the given species, the more is the dispersion of electrons from Cl-atoms, which decreases the basic strength. $\because \mathrm{ClO}_2^{-}$ has only two oxygen atoms while $\mathrm{ClO}_4^{-}$ has four oxygen atoms. Thus, order of basic strength is
$\mathrm{ClO}_2^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_3^{-} > \mathrm{ClO}_4^{-}$
Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
When Pt reacts with a $3: 1$ mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid $(\mathrm{HCl})$ and concentrated nitric acid $\left(\mathrm{HNO}_3\right)$, It forms a solution known as aqua regia. aqua regia is capable of dissolving platinum by forming chlorocomplexes. The reaction typically forms $\mathrm{H}_2 \left[\mathrm{PtCl}_6\right]$ In this complex. The $\mathbf{P t}$ is in the +4 oxidation state. The Balance chemical equation for the reaction is $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Pa}+4 \mathrm{HNO}_2+6 \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{H}_2\left[\mathrm{Pt} \mathrm{Cl}_6\right]+4 \mathrm{NO}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\\ & \mathrm{Ht} \end{aligned}$$
So $\operatorname{In} \mathrm{H}_2 \left[\mathrm{PtCl}_{6}\right]$$ the oxidation state of Pt $$\begin{aligned}& =+2(x-6)=0 \\ & x-4=0 \\ & x=+4 \end{aligned}

From the given reactions identify the disproportionation reaction
i) ${Cl}_{2} ( g ) + 2KI ( aq ) ⟶ 2KCl ( aq ) + {I}_{2} ( s )$
ii) ${Cl}_{2} ( g ) + 2{OH}^{-} ( aq ) ⟶ {ClO}^{-} ( aq ) + {Cl}^{-} ( aq ) + {H}_{2}O ( l )$
iii) $Mg ( s ) + 2HCl ( aq ) ⟶ {MgCl}_{2} ( aq ) + {H}_{2} ( g )$
iv) $2{H}_{2}{O}_{2} ( aq ) ⟶ 2{H}_{2}O ( l ) + {O}_{2} ( g )$
questions.solution:
The reaction in which one reactant gets oxidized, and the same reactant gets reduced is known as disproportionation reaction.

$\overset{0}{Cl}2 ( g ) + 2K\overset{- 1}{I} ( aq ) ⟶ 2K\overset{0}{C}l ( aq ) + \overset{- 1}{I}2 ( s )$

In the above reaction different elements undergoing oxidation and reduction. Hence, It is not a disproportionation reaction.

$\overset{0}{Cl}2 ( g ) + 2{OH}^{-} ( aq ) ⟶ \overset{+ 1}{Cl}{O}^{-} ( aq ) + {Cl}^{-} ( aq ) + {H}_{2}O ( l )$

In the above reaction chlorine is undergoing oxidation as well as reduction. Hence, It is a disproportionation reaction.

$\overset{0}{Mg} ( s ) + 2\overset{+ 1}{H}Cl ( aq ) ⟶ \overset{+ 2}{Mg}{Cl}_{2} ( aq ) + \overset{0}{H}2 ( g )$

In the above reaction magnesium is undergoing oxidation and hydrogen ion undergoing reduction. Hence, It is not a disproportionation reaction.

$2{H}_{2}\overset{- 1}{O}2 ( aq ) ⟶ 2{H}_{2}\overset{- 2}{O} ( l ) + \overset{0}{O}2 ( g )$

In the above reaction peroxide is undergoing oxidation as well as reduction. Hence, It is a disproportionation reaction.

questions.q:
In the balanced equation of the following reaction, the ratio of $a / b$ is

${aCaCO}_{3} + {bH}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {pCa}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2} + {qCO}_{2} + {rH}_{2}O$
questions.solution:
${aCaCO}_{3} + {bH}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {pCa}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2} + {qCO}_{2} + {rH}_{2}O$

First balance the `phosphate group and calcium atom,

So, $3{CaCO}_{3} + 2{H}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {pCa}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2} + {qCO}_{2} + {rH}_{2}O$

After that balance the carbon atom,

$3{CaCO}_{3} + 2{H}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {pCa}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2} + 3{CO}_{2} + {rH}_{2}O$

After that balance the oxygen and hydrogen atoms,

$3{CaCO}_{3} + 2{H}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to 1{Ca}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2} + 3{CO}_{2} + 3{H}_{2}O$

Compare this balanced equation with the given equation. So, the value of $a = 3 \text{ and } b = 2$

Hence, the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}$ is equal to the $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

questions.solution:
Titration of iodine $( {I}_{2} )$ by& thiosulphate solution $( {S}_{2}{O}_{3}^{2 -} )$ follows the reaction:

$2{S}_{2}{O}_{3}^{2 -} + {I}_{2} \to 2I^{-} + {S}_{4}{O}_{6}^{2 -}$

In the presence of starch,& free iodine present in the solution imparts blue colour to the solution.

End point marks the completion of reaction, that is, at this point all the iodine present in the solution is reduced to iodide ions by thiosulphate solution.

So, due to the absence of free iodine in the solution, the solution turns colourless.

Thus, the& end point is indicated by colour change in the solution from blue to colourless.

questions.q: Identify the oxidation states of $\mathrm{Mn}$, when $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}$ ion undergoes disproportionation reaction under acidic medíum.
questions.solution:
The disproportionation reaction for $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}$ occurs as follows :
$3 \stackrel{+6}{\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}}+4 \mathrmH^{+} \longrightarrow \stackrel{+4}{\mathrm{MnO}_2}+2 \stackrel{+7}{\mathrm{M} n} \mathrm{MO}_4^{-}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
Hence, $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}$ is oxidised to $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$ and reduced to $\mathrm{MnO}_2$. Thus, oxidation state of $\mathrm{Mn}$ when $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{2-}$ undergoes disproportionation reaction under acidic medium are +7 and +4.
$\therefore$ Hence option (d) is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the following:
The correct answer is $\begin{array}{llllllll}A & B & C & D & A & B & C & D\end{array}$
questions.solution:
(A) $\mathrm{TiCl}_4(l)+2 \mathrm{Mg}(s) \stackrel{\Delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{Ti}(s)+2 \mathrm{MgCl}_2(s)$
The above reaction is an example of metal displacement reaction in which more reactive metal. (i.e. $\mathrm{Mg}$ ) will displace less reactive metal (i.e. Ti).
Thus, option (II) is related with (A).
(B) $2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2(a q) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(l)+\mathrm{O}_2(g)$
The above reaction is an example of disproportionation reaction in which $\mathrm{O}$-atom of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}_2$ is oxidised as $\left(\mathrm{O}_2\right)$ and also reduced to $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$. Thus, option (I) is related with (B).
(C) $\mathrm{C}(s)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) \stackrel{\Delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathrm{CO}_2(g)$
The above reaction is an example of combination reaction in which carbon(s) combines with $\mathrm{O}_2(g)$ to give $\mathrm{CO}_2(g)$. Thus, option (IV) is related with (C).
(D) $2 \mathrm{NaH}(s) \stackrel{\Delta}{\longrightarrow} 2 \mathrm{Na}(s)+\mathrm{H}_2(g)$
The above reaction is an example of decomposition reaction in which $\mathrm{NaH}$ is decomposes to $\mathrm{Na}(s) and \mathrm{H}_2(g)$. Thus, option (III) is related with (D).
Hence,
$(\mathrm{A}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{II}),(\mathrm{B}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{I}),(\mathrm{C}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{IV}),(\mathrm{D}) \rightarrow(\mathrm{III})$
and option (a) is the correct answer.

The following reaction occurs in acidic medium

What is the equivalent weight of $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ ?

questions.solution:

questions.solution:
Beryllium sulphate has its hydration enthalpy greater than its lattice enthalpy. Hence, it is highly soluble in water. On moving down the group from Be to Ra, the magnitude of hydration enthalpy decreases significantly, due to increase in the atomic radius of alkaline earth metals,& bringing about a decrease in solubility of their sulphates.&

If the magnitude of lattice energy is higher than hydration energy then ionic compound is insoluble in water. Whereas if the magnitude of hydration energy is higher than lattice energy, then ionic compound is soluble in water.&

questions.q:
Predict the feasibility of the given reactions in aqueous solution
(i) $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+2 \mathrm{OH}^{-} \longrightarrow\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right]^{2-}$
(ii) $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+2 \mathrm{H}^{+} \longrightarrow\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right]^{2+}$
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is amphoteric and the basic strength increases down the group. Due to small size and high ionisation enthalpy of $\mathrm{Be}, \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is amphoteric.
Therefore, it dissolves both in acid and bases.
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+2 \mathrm{HCl}+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \longrightarrow\left[\mathrm{Be}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_4\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2 \\
& \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{BeO}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\
& \mathrm{Or} \mathrm{Na}_2\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right] \text{ or Be}(\mathrm{OH})_2+2 \mathrm{O} \mathrm{H} \longrightarrow\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right]^{2-}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, both reaction are feasible.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements are correct for alkali metal compounds?
(i) Superoxides are paramagnetic in nature.
(ii) The basic strengths of hydroxides increases down the group.
(iii) The conductivity of chlorides in their aqueous solutions decreases down the group.
(iv) The basic nature of carbonates in aqueous solutions is due to cationic hydrolysis.

(i) The alkali metal superoxides contain $\mathrm{O}_2^{-}$ ion, which has an unpaired electron, hence they are paramagnetic in nature.
(ii) The basic character of alkali metal hydroxides increases on moving down the group.
(iii) The conductivity of alkali metal chlorides in their aqueous solution increases on moving down the group because in aqueous solution alkali metal chlorides ionise to give alkali metal ions. On moving down the group the size of alkali metal ion increases, thus degree of hydration decreases, due to this reason their conductivity in aqueous solution increases on moving down the group.
(iv)

\begin{aligned}$ \mathrm{M}_{2}  \mathrm{CO}$}_{3} \underset{$\text{ aq solution } }{\stackrel{\text{ Ionisation in }$}{\rightleftharpoons$}} 2 \mathrm{M}^{+}+\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-} \\
& \mathrm{CO}$}_{3}^{2-}+2 $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}$ \longrightarrow $\mathrm{H} }_{2}  \mathrm{CO} }_{3}+2  \mathrm{OH}^{-}
\end{aligned}$ Thus, basic nature of carbonates in aqueous solution is due to anionic hydrolysis.$$

questions.q: The fraction of the total volume occupied by the atoms in a simple cube is
questions.solution:
In a simple cubic structure, the atoms are present at all the corners. The effective number of atoms inside a unit cell is one.

Thus, the volume occupied by the atoms& $= \dfrac{4}{3}{πr}^{3} \left($r = $\text{radius of the atom}\right)

The volume of the cube~$= a^{3} $\left(\text{where}, a = \text{side length}\right)$

The relation between side length and the radius of the atoms$⇒ 2r = a$

Thus, the fraction of total volume occupied by the atoms$= \dfrac{4{πr}^{3}}{3a^{3}} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)3 = \dfrac{π}{6}$

Given,

questions.q: The vapour pressure of a pure liquid $\mathrm{A}$ is 70 torr at 300 $\mathrm{K}$. It forms an ideal solution with another liquid B. The mole fraction of B is 0.2 and total vapour pressure of the solution is 84 torr at the same temperature. The vapour pressure of pure liquid B (in torr) is
questions.solution:
From Raoult's Law;

$\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{P}_{\text{total }}=\mathrm{P}_{1}+ \mathrm{P}_{2}=\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}^{{}^{\circ}}+\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}^{{}^{\circ}}\\
& \text{ We have, } \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}^{{}^{\circ}}=70 \text{ torr }\\
& \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{B}}=0.2 \text{ so } \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{A}}=1-0.2=0.8 \\
& \mathrm{P}_{\text{total }}=84 \text{ torr }\\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{B}^{{}^{\circ}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\text{total }}-\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{A}^{{}^{\circ}}}{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{B}}}\\
& =\frac{84-(0.8 \times 70)}{0.2}=140 \text{ torr }
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution: The given solution of methyl alcohol and acetic acid is a non-ideal solution. When a solution does not obey Raoult’s law over the entire range of concentration, then it is called non-ideal solution. The vapour pressure of such a solution is either higher or lower than that predicted by Raoult’s law. If it is higher, the solution exhibits positive deviation and if it is lower, it exhibits negative deviation from Raoult’s law.& In case of negative deviations from Raoult’s law, the intermolecular attractive forces between A-A and B-B are weaker than those between A-B and leads to decrease in vapour pressure resulting in negative deviations. In the given system, the attraction forces after formation of the solution is greater than before formation of the solution.& Hence, the solution shows negative deviation from raoult's law.

questions.q: Calculate the molal depression constant of a solution, which freezes at $15^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The latent heat of fusion is $180.7 \mathrm{Jg}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
$K_f=\frac{R T_f^2}{1000 \times L_f}$
Where, $\begin{aligned} K_f \text{$ and $} =\text{ molal depression constant }\\
R \text{ and } =\text{ gas constant }=8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}\\
T_f \text{ and } =\text{ freezing point }=273+15=288 \mathrm{ K}\\
L_f \text{ and } =\text{ latent heat of fusion }=180.73 \mathrm{Jg}^{-1}\\
K_f \text{ and } =\frac{8.314 \times(288)^2}{1000 \times 180.7}=\frac{8.314 \times 82944}{1807}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{68959}{18070}=3.81 \mathrm{ K} \mathrm{molal}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$

An ideal solution is the solution which obeys Raoult's law over entire range of concentration. Such solutions are formed by mixing the two components which are similar in molecular size, in structure and have almost identical intermolecular forces.

The characteristics of ideal solutions:

(ii) $60 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ L}^{-1}$ of $\mathrm{NH}_2 \mathrm{CONH}_2$
(iii) $80 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ L}^{-1}$ of glucose
(iv) $58.5 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ L}^{-1}$ of $\mathrm{NaCl}$
questions.solution:
$\because \mathrm{NaCl}$ is an ionic salt and go for complete
ionisation, so has maximum osmotic pressure, while glucose and urea does not ionises. For $\mathrm{NaCl}(i=2)$ and for glucose and urea $(i=1) \because \quad \pi=i C R T$
where, $\pi=$ osmotic pressure
$i=$ van't Hoff factor
$C=$ molarity
$R=$ gas constant
$T=$ temperature in Kelvin
Also,
$\pi=i \frac{n}{V} R T \quad\left[\because C=\frac{n}{V}\right]
and
\pi=i \frac{w}{M \times V} R T$
If $V, R and T$ are same $\pi \propto i \times \frac{W}{M}$
where, $n=$ number of moles of solute
$\begin{aligned} W & =\text{ mass of solute } \\ M & =\text{ molar mass of solute } \\ V & =\text{ volume }\end{aligned}$
Thus, (i) $30 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mL}^{-1}$ of glucose
$\begin{aligned}(w=30, M=180) & \\ & \pi \propto \frac{1 \times 30}{180}=0.166\end{aligned}$
(ii)
$\begin{aligned} 60 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mL}^{-1} & \text{$ of $} \mathrm{NH}_2 \mathrm{CONH}_2 \\ (w=60, M & =60) \\ \pi & \propto \frac{1 \times 60}{60}=1.00\end{aligned}$
(iii) $80 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mL}^{-1}$ of glucose
$\begin{aligned}(w=80, M & =180) \\ \pi & \propto \frac{1 \times 80}{80}=0.44\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Two compounds form an ideal solution at room temperature. Which of the following are correct for this ideal solution?

(B) $\Delta S=(+$ ve) surrounding
(C) $\Delta S=(+v e)$ system
(D) $\Delta_{\max } H=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}

& \mathrm{K}_3\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6\right] \rightleftharpoons \\

questions.q: A solution of 17.1 w\% of sucrose (molar mass $=342 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ mol}^1$ ) is isotonic with a $x$ w\% solution of oxalic acid (molar mass $=90 \mathrm{ g}$ mol ${ }^1$ ). Assume the degree of dissociation of oxalic acid as 0.01. What is $x$ ?
questions.solution:
Given,
Mass of sucrose $\left(w_1\right)=17.1 \mathrm{~g}$
Molar mass of sucrose $\left(M_1\right)=342 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Mass of oxalic acid $\left(w_2\right)=x g$
Molar mass of oxalic acid $\left(M_2\right)=90 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
Degree of dissociation $(\alpha)$ of oxalic acid $=0.01$
Step I To find the value of van't Hoff factor (i)
$i=(1-\alpha)+n \alpha$
where, $n=$ number of parts in which one molecule of oxalic acid dissociates $(=3) \begin{aligned}$& i=(1-0.01)+(3 $\times$0.01) \\
& i=0.99+0.03 \\
& i=1.02
\end{aligned}

Step II$ To find the value of(x)$
For isotonic solutions :
$\pi$ (sucrose $)=\pi$ (oxalic acid)

[\because $\pi=$C R T]

or, Molarity (sucrose) = i Molarity (oxalic acid)

$\begin{aligned}$& $\left.\frac{w_1}{M_1} \text{ (sucrose }\right)=$i $\times\left(\frac{x}{M_2}\right) \text{ (oxalic acid) }$\\
& x=$\frac{w_1}{M_1} \times \frac{M_2}{i}=\frac{171 \times 90}{1.02 \times 342}$\\
& x=$\frac{1539}{348.84}=$4.41 $\mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}$Hence, value of $x=4.41 \mathrm{~g}$
Hence, option (3) is correct.

Melting point of camphor $=176^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ $\left(K_f\right)$ for camphor $=40 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ Mass of hydrocarbon $\left(w_B\right)=0.02 \mathrm{~g}$ Mass of camphor $\left(w_A\right)=0.8 \mathrm{~g}$ Temperature of camphor (at which it melts) $=156.77^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ Thus, $\Delta T_f$ for camphor $=176-156.77$ $=19.23^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=19.23 \mathrm{~K}$ $\therefore$ Depression in freezing point, $\begin{aligned} \Delta T_f & =\frac{K_f \times w_B}{M_B} \times \frac{1000}{W_A} \\ 19.23 & =\frac{40 \times 0.02 \times 1000}{M_B \times 0.8}\end{aligned}$ Molar mass of solute $\left(M_B\right)$ $=\frac{40 \times 0.02 \times 1000}{19.23 \times 0.8}=52$
$\therefore$ Empirical formula $=\mathrm{CH}$ Empirical formula weight $=12+1=13$ Multiple $(n)=\frac{\text{ Molecular weight }}{\text{ Empirical formula weight }}=\frac{52}{13}=4$ Thus, molecular formula $=(\mathrm{CH})_4=\mathrm{C}_4 \mathrm{H}_4$

questions.solution:
Relative lowering of vapour pressure,
$\begin{aligned} \frac{p^{{}^{\circ}}-p_s}{p^{{}^{\circ}}} & =x_A \\ & =\frac{\frac{w_A}{m_A}}{\frac{w_A}{m_A}+\frac{w_B}{m_B}}\end{aligned}$
(where, $w_A and m_A$ are the mass and molar mass of solute and $w_B and m_B$ are the mass and molar mass of water.)
$\therefore \quad \begin{aligned} 0.02 & =\frac{\frac{x}{60}}{\frac{x}{60}+\frac{90}{18}} \\ 0.02 & =\frac{\frac{x}{60}}{\frac{x}{60}+5} \\ \frac{1}{0.02} & =\frac{\frac{x}{60}+5}{\frac{x}{60}} \\ 50 & =1+\frac{5 \times 60}{x} \\ 49 & =\frac{300}{x} \\ x & =\frac{300}{49}=6 \mathrm{ g}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
When a non-volatile solute is added to a volatile solvent, the solute covers up some of the surface of solvent. Thus, less surface area is available for vaporisation of solvent and hence, vapour pressure decreases. As the amount of non-volatile solute increases, vapour pressure decreases accordingly.
$\because$ The order of concentration of $X$ is
$0.01 < 0.10 < 0.25\therefore$ The order of vapour pressure is
$p_3 > p_1 > p_2$

questions.q: Which one of the following is the ratio of the lowering of vapour pressure of $0.1 \mathrm{M}$ aqueous solutions of $\mathrm{BaCl}_2, \mathrm{NaCl}$ and $\mathrm{Al}_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3$ respectively?
questions.solution:
Lowering of vapour pressure is a colligative property. It depends on the number of particles of the solute.
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{BaCl}_2 & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ba}^{2+}+2 \mathrm{Cl}^{-} ; 3 \text{ ions } \\
\mathrm{NaCl} & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Na}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-} ; 2 \text{ ions } \\
\mathrm{Al}_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{Al}^{3+}+3 \mathrm{SO}_4^{3-} ; 5 \text{ ions }
\end{aligned}$
Hence the ratio of lowering of vapour pressure is $3: 2: 5$.

Freezing point of a substance is the temperature at which the solid and the liquid forms of the substance are in equilibrium.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For a given unbalanced reaction, $\mathrm{MnO}_2+\mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$, which is the limiting reagent, if the initial amount for each of the reactant is 100 grams?
[Molar masses : $\mathrm{MnO}_2=86.9 ; \mathrm{HCl}=36.5;  \left.\mathrm{MnCl}_2=125.8 ; \mathrm{Cl}_2=70.9 ; \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=18\right]$
questions.solution: Limiting reagent In a chemical reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant that determine, how much of the products are made. The other reactants are sometimes referred to as being in excess, since there will be some leftover after the limiting reagent is completely used up. Given, unbalanced reaction, $\begin{array}{lcccc} & \mathrm{MnO}_2+ & \mathrm{HCl} & \longrightarrow \mathrm{MnCl}_2+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} \\ \text{ Initial amount } & 100 \mathrm{ g } & 100 \mathrm{ g} & & \\ \text{ of reactant } & & \\ \text{ Molar mass } & 86.9 & 36.5 & 125.8 & 18 \end{array}$ Balancing the reaction, $$ \\ Convert amounts to moles Moles of $\mathrm{MnO}_2=100 \mathrm{ g} \times \frac{1 \mathrm{ mol}}{86.9 \mathrm{ g}}=1.15 \mathrm{ mol}$ of $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ Moles of $\mathrm{HCl}=100 \mathrm{ g} \times \frac{1 \mathrm{ mol}}{36.5 \mathrm{ g}}=2.73 \mathrm{ mol}$ of $\mathrm{HCl}$ Actual ratio (molar ratio) of reactants $=\frac{\text{ Moles of } \mathrm{MnO}_2}{\text{ Moles of } \mathrm{HCl}}=\frac{1.15 \mathrm{ mol}}{2.73 \mathrm{ mol}}=\frac{0.42}{1} \mathrm{ mol}$ The actual ratio tells us that we have 0.42 moles of $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ for every 1 mole of $\mathrm{HCl}$. In comparison, the stoichiometric ratio from our balanced reaction is below : $\text{ Stoichiometric ratio }=\frac{1 \text{ moles of } \mathrm{N}_2}{4 \text{ moles of } \mathrm{HCl}}=\frac{0.25 \text{ moles } \mathrm{MnO}_2}{1 \text{ moles } \mathrm{HCl}}$ This means we need at least 0.25 mole of $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ for every mole of $\mathrm{HCl}$. Since, our actual ratio is greater then our stoichiometric ratio, we have more $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ than we need to react with each mole of $\mathrm{HCl}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{HCl}$ is our limiting reagent and $\mathrm{MnO}_2$ is in excess. Hence, correct option is (b).

Vapour density $=45$
Molecular formula $=$ ?
Empirical formulas show the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound.
Molecular formula show the number of each type of atom in a molecule.
Relation between empirical formula and molecular formula.
Molecular formula $=n$ (empirical formula $)n=\frac{\text{ MM (molar mass) }}{\text{ EFM (empirical formula molar mass) }}$
Molecular weight $=2 \times$ vapour density $=2 \times 45=90$
Let, the molecular forumula be $\mathrm{C}_{2 x} \mathrm{H}_{5 x} \mathrm{O}_x$.
Therefore, $n=\frac{90 \text{ (molecular weight })}{47(\text{ EFM })}=1.47 \approx 2$
Value of $x=2$
Molecular formula $=\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{O}\right)_2=\mathrm{C}_4 \mathrm{H}_{10} \mathrm{O}_2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A polymer contains 50 molecules with molecular mass 5000, 100 molecules with molecular mass 10,000 and 50 molecules with molecular mass 15,000. Calculate number average molecular mass?
questions.solution:
$\because$ Number average molecular mass $(M n)$
=$\frac{N_2 M_2+N_2 M_2+N_3 M_3}{N_2+N_2+N_3}$ where, $N_2, N_2$ and $N_3$ are number of molecules and $M_2, M_2$ and $M_3$ are respectively their molecular masses.
Given, $\begin{aligned}& N_2=50 \text{ and } M_2=5000 \\
& N_2=100 \text{ and } M_2=10,000 \\
& N_3=50 \text{ and } M_3=15,000
\end{aligned} Thus, \begin{aligned} M \bar{n} & =\frac{N_1 M_1+N_2 M_2+N_3 M_3}{N_1+N_2+N_3}\\
& =\frac{(50 \times 5000)+(100 \times 10,000)+(50 \times 15000)}{50+100+50}\\
& =\frac{(25,0000)+(1,000,000)+(75,00,00)}{200}\\
M \bar{n} & =10,000
\end{aligned} Hence, option (3) is the correct answer.$

( molar mass of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}=34 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
$2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}+3 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{SO}_2+2 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$
From balanced equation
3 moles of $\mathrm{O}_2$ reacts with 2 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$
$22.4 \mathrm{~L}$ of $\mathrm{O}_2=1 \mathrm{moI}$
$$
\therefore 15 \mathrm{~L} \text{ of } \mathrm{O}_2=\left(\frac{1}{22.4} \times 15\right) \mathrm{moI}
$$

3 moles of oxygen uses 2 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$.
$\therefore\left(\frac{15}{224}\right)$ moles of $\mathrm{O}_2$ uses $\left(\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{15}{22.4}\right)$ moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$
Molar mass of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}=34 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{moI}$
$\therefore$ Gram of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}=\left(34 \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{15}{224}\right) \mathrm{g}=15.17 \mathrm{~g}$

The number of moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$, which is required to produce 10 moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ in the following reaction is

questions.solution:
The reaction of $\mathrm{H}_2(g)$ with $\mathrm{NO}_2(g)$ occurs as follows:
$7 \mathrm{H}_2(g)+2 \mathrm{NO}_2(g) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(g)+4 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(g)$
$\because 2$ moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ are produced by $=7$ moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$.
$\therefore 10$ moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ are produced by
$=\frac{7 \times 10}{2}$ moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$.
Therefore, moles of $\mathrm{H}_2(g)$ required $=35$ moles Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
The ratio of weight average molecular weight and the number average molecular weight is called poly dispersity index (PDI). $\mathrm{PDI}=\frac{\bar{M}_w}{\bar{M}_n}$ where,

$\bar{M}_n=$ number average molecular weight

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{PV}=\mathrm{nRT}$ or $\mathrm{PV}=\mathrm{RT}$ (for $1 \mathrm{ mole}$ )
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{V}=\frac{\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{(0.0821)(300)}{1}(760 \text{ torr }=1 \mathrm{ atm})=24.63 \mathrm{ L}(of the $mixture)

& \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{d}=24.63 \mathrm{ L} \times 0.543 \mathrm{gL}^{-1} \\
& =13.37 \mathrm{ g}
\end{aligned}$
Mole fraction of $\mathrm{O}_2=\mathrm{x}$
Mole fraction of $\mathrm{He}=1-\mathrm{x}$.
Average molecular weight
$\begin{aligned}
& =\left[\left(\mathrm{x} \times \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{O}_2}\right)+(1-\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{He}}\right] \\
& =[32 \mathrm{x}+(1-\mathrm{x}) 4] \\
& =13.37 \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=0.334 \\
& \Rightarrow \text{ Mass$ of $} \mathrm{O}_2=0.334 \times 32=10.688 \\
& \Rightarrow \text{ Mass } \% \text{ of } \mathrm{O}_2=\frac{10.688}{13.37} \times 100 \\
& \cong 80 \%
\end{aligned}$

${p}_{\text{total}} = 6\text{atm}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressures because the gas molecules
questions.solution: Some attractive forces exist between the molecules of real gases. When a molecule approaches the wall of the container, it experiences an inward pull as a result of attractive forces exerted by the neighbouring molecules inside the vessel. Therefore, the observed pressure is less than the ideal pressure and hence gas deviates from ideal behaviour at high pressure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
According to kinetic molecular theory of gases, which of the following statements are correct?

a) The actual volume of the molecules is negligible in comparison to the empty space between them.

b) Collisions of gas molecules are inelastic.

c) At any particular time, different particles in the gas have the same speed and same kinetic energies.

d) Pressure is exerted by the gas as a result of collision of the particles with the walls of the container.
questions.solution:
According to kinetic molecular theory of gases,

a) The actual volume of the molecules is negligible in comparison to the empty space between them. Means particle size is very, very small (point mass).

b) Collisions of gas molecules are perfectly elastic. So, given statement is wrong.

c) At any particular time, different particles in the gas have different& speed and different kinetic energies. Therefore, average kinetic energy or average speed is calculated. So, given statement is wrong.

d) Pressure is exerted by the gas as a result of collision of the particles with the walls of the container.

So, statement a and d are correct and b, c are incorrect.
