questions.q:
If $\omega$ is a complex cube root of unity, then
$\begin{aligned} & \left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2020}+\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2026} \\ & +\sin \left(\sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \frac{3 \pi}{152}\right)=\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
We have,
$\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}=-\left[\frac{-1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right]=-\omega$ and $\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}=-\left[\frac{-1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right]=-\omega^2\therefore \quad\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2020}+\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2026}\begin{aligned} & =(-\omega)^{2020}+\left(-\omega^2\right)^{2026} \\ & =\omega^{2020}+\omega^{4052}=\omega+\omega^2=-1\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned} & \sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \\ & =\sum_{j=1}^6\left(j^2+j \omega^2+j \omega+\omega^3\right) \\ & =\sum_{j=1}^6\left(j^2-j+1\right)=\sum_{j=1}^6 j^2-\sum_{j=1}^6 j+\sum_{j=1}^6 1 \\ & =\frac{6(6+1)(12+1)}{6}-\frac{6(6+1)}{2}+6 \\ & =7 \times 13-3 \times 7+6=91-21+6=76\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \sin \left(\sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \frac{3 \pi}{152}\right) & =\sin \left(\frac{76 \times 3 \pi}{152}\right) \\ & =\sin \frac{3 \pi}{2}=-1\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2020}+ & \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{3} i}{2}\right)^{2026} \\ & +\sin \left(\sum_{j=1}^6(j+\omega)\left(j+\omega^2\right) \frac{3 \pi}{512}\right) \\ =-1-1 & =-2\end{aligned}$

Given that

Real part of& $\dfrac{\overset{¯}{z} - 1}{z - i} = 2$

here~$z = x + iy$

$⇒ \overset{¯}{z} = x - iy$

$⇒ \dfrac{\overset{¯}{z} - 1}{z - i} = \dfrac{\left(x - iy\right) - 1}{\left(x + iy\right) - i} = \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) - iy}{x + i\left(y - 1\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\overset{¯}{z} - 1}{z - i} = \dfrac{\left\{\left(x - 1\right) - iy\right\} \times \left(x - i\left(y - 1\right)\right)}{x^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\overset{¯}{z} - 1}{z - i} = \dfrac{\left(x^{2} - x - y - y^{2}\right) - i\left(xy - x - y + 1 + xy\right)}{x^{2} + \left(y - 1\right)2}$

Real part$= 2$

$⇒ \left(x^{2} - x + y - y^{2}\right) = 2\left\{x^{2} + 1 + y^{2} - 2y\right\}$

$⇒ x^{2} + 3y^{2} + x - 5y + 2 = 0$

questions.q: The locus of a point on the argand plane represented by the complex number $z$, when $z$ satisfies the condition $\left|\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right|=\left|\operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right)\right|$ is
options: A straight line that does not contain the point $(-1+i)$
A circle that does not contain the point $(-1+i)$
A parabola that does not contain the point $(-1+i)$
A hyperbola that does not contain the point $(-1+i)$
questions.solution:
Given condition is
$\left|\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right|=\left|\operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right)\right|, z \neq-1+i$
Let $z=x+i y$, then
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}=\frac{(x-1)+i(y+1)}{(x+1)+i(y-1)} \times \frac{(x+1)-i(y-1)}{(x+1)-i(y-1)} \\ & =\frac{\left[\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right]+i[(x+1)(y+1)-(x-1)}{(x+1)^2+(y-1)^2}\end{aligned}$
So, $\left|\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right|=\sqrt{\frac{\left[\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right]^2+(2(x+y))^2}{\left((x+1)^2+(y-1)^2\right)^2}}$ and $\left|\operatorname{Re}\left(\frac{z-1+i}{z+1-i}\right)\right|=\frac{\left|\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right|}{(x+1)^2+(y-1)^2}$
Now, according to given condition
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{\sqrt{\left(\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right)^2+(2(x+y))^2}}{(x+1)^2+(y-1)^2} \\ & =\frac{\left|\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right|}{(x+1)^2+(y-1)^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad\left(\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right)^2+4(x+y)^2 \\ & =\left(\left(x^2-1\right)+\left(y^2-1\right)\right)^2\end{aligned}\Rightarrow x+y=0$ is a straight line, but as $z \neq-1+i$ so locus of $z$ is a straight line that does not contain the point $(-1+i)$.
Hence, option (a) is correct.

questions.q: If $P$ is a complex number whose modulus is one, then the equation $\left(\frac{1+i z}{1-i z}\right)^4=P$ has
options: two real and two complex roots
questions.solution:
We have,

$\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & $\left(\frac{1+i z}{1-i z}\right)^$4 & =P \\
\Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{i-z}{i+z}\right)^$4 & =P \\
\Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{z-i}{z+i}\right)^$4 & =P \\
\Rightarrow & & $\left|\frac{z-i}{z+i}\right|^$4 & =|P| \\
\Rightarrow & & $\left|\frac{z-i}{z+i}\right|^$4 & =1 \\
\Rightarrow & & |z-i|^4 & =|z+i|^4 \\
\Rightarrow & & |z-i| & =|z+i|
\end{array}

$\therefore z$ lies on perpendicular bisector of $i$ and $-i$.
$\therefore z$ lies on $y$-axis.
$\therefore z$ has all complex roots.

questions.solution: Given, $\quad x=p+q, \quad y+p \omega+q \omega^2 \quad$ and $z=p \omega^2+q \omega\begin{aligned} \therefore x y z= & (p+q)\left(p \omega+q \omega^2\right)\left(p \omega^2+q \omega\right) \\ = & (p+q)\left(p^2 \omega^3+p q \omega^2+p q \omega^4+q^2 \omega^3\right) \\ = & (p+q)\left(p^2+p q \omega^2+p q \omega+q^2\right) \\ & \quad\left(\because \omega^3=1\right) \\ = & (p+q)\left(p^2+p q\left(\omega+\omega^2\right)+q^2\right) \\ = & (p+q)\left(p^2-p q+q^2\right)=p^3+q^3 \\ & \quad\left(\because 1+\omega+\omega^2=-1\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If a complex number $z$ satisfies $\left|z^2-1\right|=|z|^2+1$, then $z$ lies on
questions.solution:
Given, $\quad\left|z^2-1\right|=|z|^2+1$
Let z=x+i y $\begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \quad\left|( x+i y)^2-1\right|=|x+i y|^2+1 \\
& \Rightarrow\left| x^2-y²+2 i x y-1\right|=\left( x^2+y²\right)+1 \\
& \Rightarrow\left|\left( x^2-y²-1\right)+2 i x y\right|=\left( x^2+y²+1\right) \\
& \Rightarrow \sqrt{\left(x^2-y^2-1\right)^2+4 x^2 y^2}= x^2+y²+1 \\
& \Rightarrow\left( x^2-y²\right)^2+1-2\left( x^2-y²\right)+4 x² y² \\
& =\left( x^2+y²+1\right)^2 \\
& =x⁴+y⁴+2 x² y²+1+2 x²+2 y² \\
& \Rightarrow-2 x² y²-2 x²+4 x² y²=2 x² y²+2 x² \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-2 x²=2 x² \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 4 x²=0 \Rightarrow x=0 \\
& \therefore \quad z=x+i y=0+i y \\
& \Rightarrow \quad z=i y \quad \Rightarrow \quad(x, y)=(0, y) \\
&
\end{aligned} Hence, $ z$ lies on the imaginary axis.$

questions.solution:
Since, $\alpha$ is a non-real root of the equation $x^6-1=0$.
$\begin{array}{lc}\therefore & \alpha^6-1=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \alpha^6-1=0 \times \alpha-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{\alpha^6-1}{\alpha-1}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\alpha^3+\alpha^4+\alpha^5=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (1+\alpha)+\alpha^2(1+\alpha)+\alpha^4(1+\alpha)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (1+\alpha)\left(1+\alpha^2+\alpha^4\right)=0\end{array} \begin{aligned}& \therefore \frac{\alpha^2+\alpha^3+\alpha^4+\alpha^5}{\alpha+1}=\frac{\alpha^2(\alpha+1)+\alpha^4(\alpha+1)}{\alpha+1}\\ & \quad=\frac{(\alpha+1)\left(\alpha^2+\alpha^4\right)}{\alpha+1}\\ & =\alpha^2+\alpha^4=-1 \quad \text{ [from Eq. (i)] }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of the equation $x^2-4 x+8=0$, then for any $n \in \mathbb{N}, \alpha^{2 n}+\beta^{2 n}$ equals
questions.solution:
Since, $\alpha, \beta$ are the roots of the equation $\begin{aligned} x²-4 x+8 & =0 \\
\therefore \quad \alpha, \beta& =\frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16-32}}{2}=\frac{4 \pm 4 i}{2}=2 \pm2 i \\
\Rightarrow \quad \alpha, \beta& =2 \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \pmi \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\\
& =2 \sqrt{2} \left(\cos \frac{\pi}{4} \pmi \sin \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\
\text{ Now, } \alpha^{2 n}& =(2 \sqrt{2})^{2 n}\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{4}+i \sin \frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2 n},n \in N \\
& =(2 \sqrt{2})^{2 n}\left(\cos \frac{n \pi}{2}+i \sin \frac{n \pi}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}Similarly, \beta^{2 n}=(2 \sqrt{2})^{2 n} \left(\cos \frac{n \pi}{2}-i \sin \frac{n \pi}{2}\right)
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \alpha^{2 n}+\beta^{2 n}& =(2 \sqrt{2})^{2 n} \cdot2 \cos \frac{n \pi}{2}\\
& =\left(2^{3 / 2}\right)^{2 n} \cdot2 \cos \frac{n \pi}{2}\\
\Rightarrow \quad \alpha^{2 n}+\beta^{2 n}& =2^{3 n+1} \cos \frac{n \pi}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $z=1+i \sqrt{3}$ then $|\operatorname{Arg} z|+|\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}|$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$z=1+i \sqrt{3}$
Let $1+i \sqrt{3}=r(\cos \theta+i \sin \theta)$
Then, $\quad r \cos \theta=1\ldots$ (i)
$r \sin \theta=\sqrt{3}\ldots$ (ii)
Eq. (i) + Eq. (ii), we get $r^2\left(\sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta\right)=3+1\left(\because \sin ^2 \theta+\cos ^2 \theta=1\right)r^2=4r=2$
Eq. (ii) \div Eq. (i), we get
$\tan \theta=\sqrt{3}\Rightarrow \quad \tan \theta=\tan \frac{\pi}{3}\Rightarrow \quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$
So, $z=(1+i \sqrt{3})=2\left\{\cos \frac{\pi}{3}+i \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\right\}$
Then $\bar{z}=(1-i \sqrt{3})=2\left\{\cos \frac{\pi}{3}-i \sin \frac{\pi}{3}\right\}=2\left\{\cos \left(\frac{-\pi}{3}\right)+i \sin \left(\frac{-\pi}{3}\right)\right\}$
So, $\quad \operatorname{Arg} z=\frac{\pi}{3}\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}=-\frac{\pi}{3}|\operatorname{Arg} z|+|\operatorname{Arg} \bar{z}|=\left|\frac{\pi}{3}\right|+\left|\frac{-\pi}{3}\right|=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2 \pi}{3}$

questions.q: Consider the following statements Statement I If $a_0+\frac{a_1}{2}+\frac{a_2}{3}+\ldots .+\frac{a_n}{n+1}=0$, where $a_0, a_1, \ldots ., a_n$ are real numbers, then the polynomial $a_0+a_1 x+a_2 x^2+\ldots .+a_n x^n$ has a zero in the interval $(0,1)$.Statement II If $f:[a, b] \rightarrow \mathbf{R}$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f$ is differentiable in $(a, b)$, where $a > 0$ and if $\frac{f(a)}{a}=\frac{f(b)}{b}$, then there exists $c \in(a, b)$, such that $c f^{\prime}(c)=f(c)$. Which one of the following options is true?
questions.solution:
Let a polynomial function
$f(x)=a_0 x+a_1 \frac{x^2}{2}+a_2 \frac{x^3}{3}+\ldots \ldots+a_n \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}$
Now, as $f(x)$ is a polynomial so it is continuous and differentiable in $R$.
and as $f(0)=0$ and
$f(1)=a_0+\frac{a_1}{2}+\frac{a_3}{3}+\ldots+\frac{9 n}{n+1}=0$(given)
So, according to Rolle's theorem $f^{\prime}(x)=0$ for at least one value of $x \in(0,1)$.
Therefore, Statement (I) is true.
It is given that $[f: a, b] \rightarrow R$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable in $(a, b)$, where $a > 0$ and
$\frac{f(a)}{a}=\frac{f(b)}{b} \Rightarrow f(b)=\frac{b}{a} f(a)$
Now, according to By Lagrange's mean value theorem (L.M.V.T), we have
$f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\frac{\frac{b}{a} f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=\frac{f(a)}{a}=\frac{f(b)}{b}\therefore f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(c)}{c} \Rightarrow c f^{\prime}(c)=f(c)$
Therefore, Statement II is also correct.

questions.solution:
We have,
$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{\sqrt{1+a x}-\sqrt{1-a x}}{x}, & -1 \leq x < 0 \\
\frac{x^2+2}{x-2}, & 0 \leq x \leq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$
Since, $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \therefore f(x) \text{ is continuous at } x=0 \\
& \therefore \text{ LHL (at } x=0)=\text{ RHL (at } x=0) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sqrt{1+a x}-\sqrt{1-a x}}{x}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x^2+2}{x-2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1+a x)-(1-a x)}{x[\sqrt{1+a x}+\sqrt{1-a x}]}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x^2+2}{x-2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{2 a}{\sqrt{1+a x}+\sqrt{1-a x}}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{x^2+2}{x-2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a=-1
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.solution:
We know that,
$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
x-(n-1) & \text{ for }-1 < x < n \\

$$

Now, we check the continuity at $x=n$
$$

f(n-0) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow n^{-}}[x-(n-1)] \\

& =1 \\
f(n+0) & =\lim _{x \rightarrow n^{+}}[x-n] \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}(n+h-n)=0
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
f(n)=0
$$
$\Rightarrow f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=n$
$\therefore$ Set of discontinuous of $f$ is $z$

on $R$, then $(a, b)=$
questions.solution:
We have,
$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}
a x+b, & x \leq-1 \\
2 x^2+2 b x-\frac{a}{2}, & -1 < x < 1 \\
7, & x \geq 1
\end{array}\right.
$$
$f(x)$ is continuous on $R$.
$\therefore f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$ and $x=1$ at $x=-1$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \lim _{x \rightarrow-1^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow-1^{+}} f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a(-1)+b=2(-1)^2+2 b(-1)-\frac{a}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad-a+b=2-2 b-\frac{a}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{a}{2}+3 b=2 \\
& \text { at } \quad x=1 \\
& \lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{-}} f(x)=\lim _{x \rightarrow 1^{+}} f(x) \\
& \Rightarrow 2(1)^2+2 b(1)-\frac{a}{2}=7 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{a}{2}+2 b=5
\end{aligned}
$$

From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$$
b=-3
$$

Substitute value of $b$ in Eq. (i)
$$
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{a}{2}+3(-3) & =2 \quad-\frac{a}{2}=11 \\
a & =-22
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\quad(a, b)=(-22,-3)$

questions.q: If $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{2}lncosx}{\ln\left(1 + x^{2}\right)} & , x \ne 0 \\ 0 & , x = 0\end{cases}\right$, then $f  \left(x\right) is$
options: continuous but not differentiable at zero
not continuous and not differentiable at zero
questions.solution:
${f}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(0 + h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(h\right)}{h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{lncosh}{ln\left(1 + {h}^{2}\right)} \times \dfrac{{h}^{2}}{{h}^{2}} . . . . \left(1\right)$   {Multiplying Numerator & denominator by $h$}

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{h}^{2}}{ln\left(1 + {h}^{2}\right)} \times \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{lncos h}{{h}^{2}}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{h}^{2}}{ln\left(1 + {h}^{2}\right)} \times \lim_{h \to 0} - \dfrac{tan h}{2h}$      {Using L'Hospital's Rule}
 $= 1 \times - \dfrac{1}{2}$
$= - \dfrac{1}{2}$

and   ${f}^{'}\left({0}^{-}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(0 - h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{- h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(- h\right)}{- h}$

$= - \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{- hln cos \left(- h\right)}{ln\left(1 + {\left(- h\right)}^{2}\right)\left(- h\right)}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{logcos h}{log\left(1 + {h}^{2}\right)}$

$= - \dfrac{1}{2}$                                 {from Eq. $\left(1\right)$}

$∴ {f}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right)$ = {f}^{'}$\left({0}^{-}\right)$

$∴$ $f\left(x\right) is differentiable$ and hence continuous at x = 0$.

$

questions.solution:
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{rr}\frac{1+3 x^2-\cos 2 x}{x^2}, & \text{ for } x \neq 0 \\ k, & \text{ for } x=0\end{array}\right.$
RHL
$f(0+h)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3(0+h)^2-\cos 2(0+h)}{(0+h)^2}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3 h^2-\cos 2 h}{h^2}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3 h^2-\left(1-2 \sin ^2 h\right)}{h^2}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3 h^2-1+2 \sin ^2 h}{h^2}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left\{3+2\left(\frac{\sin ^2 h}{h^2}\right)\right\}=3+2 \cdot \lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{\sin h}{h}\right)^2=3+2 \cdot(1)^2 \quad\left\{\because \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}=1\right\}=3+2=5$
LHL
$f(0-h)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3(0-h)^2-\cos 2(0-h)}{(0-h)^2}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+3 h^2-\cos 2 h}{h^2}=5$
Since, the function is continuous at $x=0$, then LHL $=$ RHL $=f(0) \because f(0)=k \Rightarrow k=5$

If $f: R \rightarrow R$ is defined by
$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ccc}
\frac{x+2}{x^2+3 x+2} & \text{ if } & x \in \mathbb{R}-\{-1,-2\} \\
-1 & \text{ if } & x=-2 \\
0 & \text{ if } & x=-1
\end{array}\right.$
then $f$ is continuous on the set
questions.solution:
Given that
$f(x)=\left\{$\begin{array}{ccc}
$\frac{x+2}{x^2+3 x+2}$, & $\text{$ if } & x \in R-\{-1,-2\} \\
-1, & $\text{$ if } & x=-2 \\
0, & $\text{$ if } & x=-1
\end{array}$\right.$
Now, we have to check the continuity
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{ at } x= \\
& \text{ at } x=-2,-1 \\
& \begin{aligned}
\text{ LHL } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(-2-h)+2}{(-2-h)^2+3(-2-h)+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-h}{4+h^2+4 h-6-3 h+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-h}{h^2+h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-1}{h+1}=-1
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
\text{ RHL } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(-2+h)+2}{(-2+h)^2+3(-2+h)+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h}{4+h^2-4 h-6+3 h+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h}{h^2-h} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{h-1}=-1 \\
\Rightarrow \text{ LHL } & =\text{ RHL }=f(-2)
\end{aligned}\therefore$ It is continuous at $x=-2$
Now, check for $x=-1\begin{aligned}
\text{ LHL } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(-1-h)+2}{(-1-h)^2+3(-1-h)+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-h}{1^2+h^2+2 h-3-3 h+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-h}{h^2-h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-1}{2 h-1}=1 \\
\text{ RHL } & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(-1+h)+2}{(-1+h)^2+3(-1+h)+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+h}{1+h^2-2 h-3+3 h+2} \\
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{1+h}{h^2+h}=1
\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \mathrm{LHL}=\mathrm{RHL} \neq f(-1)\therefore$ It is not continuous at $x=-1$
The required function is continuous in $R-\{-1\}$.

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ Let } I=\int_0^\pi x f(\sin x) d x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad I=\int_0^\pi(\pi-x) f[\sin (\pi-x)] d x\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad I=\int_0^\pi \pi f(\sin x) d x-\int_0^\pi x f(\sin x) d x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 2 I=\pi \int_0^\pi f(\sin x) d x \Rightarrow 2 I=\pi \int_0^{\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \times 2} f(\sin x) d x \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 2 I=2 \pi \int_0^{\pi / 2} f(\sin x) d x \\ & \quad \quad\left[\because \text{ if } f(2 a-x)=f(x), \operatorname{then} \int_0^{2 a} f(x) d x=2 \int_0^a f(x) d x\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \quad I=\pi \int_0^{\pi / 2} f(\sin x) d x\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Let $l = \lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}log\left(\dfrac{\left(2n\right) !}{{n}^{n}n !}\right)$

Note: Assume base of logarithm as $e$

$l = \lim_{n \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}log\left(\dfrac{\left(n + 1\right)\left(n + 2\right) . . . . . \left(n + n\right)}{{n}^{n}}\right)$

$⇒ l = \lim_{x \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}log\left(\dfrac{n + r}{n}\right)$

$⇒ l = \lim_{x \to \infty}\dfrac{1}{n}\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}log\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{n}\right)$

$⇒ l = {∫}_{0}^{1}log\left(1 + x\right)dx$

put $x + 1 = t$

$⇒ dx = dt$

$⇒ l = {∫}_{1}^{2}logtdt = {∫}_{1}^{2}logxdx$

Comparing with ${∫}_{1}^{2}f\left(x\right)dx$, we get

$f\left(x\right) = logx$

questions.q: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ If } \int x^4(\log x)^3 d x=x^5\left[A(\log x)^3+B(\log x)^2+C \log x+D\right] \\ & +k, \text{ then } A+B+C+5 D=\end{aligned}$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \int x_{\text{II }^4(\log x)^3 d x \\ = & (\log x)^3 \cdot \int x^4 d x-\int\left(3(\log x)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} \cdot \int x^4 d x\right) d x \\ = & \frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{5} \int(\log x)^2 x^4 d x \\ = & \frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{5}\left[(\log x)^2 \cdot \frac{x^5}{5}-\int 2(\log x) \cdot \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{x^5}{5} d x\right] \\ = & \frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{5}\left[\frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^2-\frac{2}{5} \int(\log x) \cdot x^4 d x\right] \\ = & \frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{25} x^5(\log x)^2+\frac{6}{25}\left[\frac{x^5}{5} \log x-\int \frac{1}{x} \cdot \frac{x^5}{5} d x\right] \\ = & \frac{x^5}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{25} x^5(\log x)^2+\frac{6}{125} x^5 \log x-\frac{6 x^5}{625}+K \\ = & x^5\left[\frac{1}{5}(\log x)^3-\frac{3}{25}(\log x)^2+\frac{6}{125} \log x-\frac{6}{625}\right]+K \\ A & \frac{1}{5}, B=\frac{-3}{25}, C=\frac{6}{125}, D=\frac{-6}{625} \\ A+B+C+5 D=\frac{1}{5}-\frac{3}{25}+\frac{6}{125}-\frac{6}{125} & \\ = & \frac{25-15+6-6}{125}=\frac{10}{125}=\frac{2}{25} .\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Assertion
$\int_{-a}^a f(x) d x=\int_0^a(f(x)+f(-x)) d x$
Reason (R) $\int_a^b f(x) d x=\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(g(u)) g^{\prime}(u) d u$
The correct option among the following is
options: (A) is true, $(R)$ is true and $(R)$ is the correct explanation for (A)
$(A)$ is true, $(R)$ is true but $(R)$ is not the correct explanation for $(A)$
questions.solution:
We have, $A=\int_{-a}^a f(x) d x=\int_0^a(f(x)+f(-x)) d x$
A is true, $\quad R=\int_a^b f(x) d x=\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f\left(g(u) g^{\prime}(u) d u\right.$
Put, $x=g(u), d x=g(u) d u$
at $x=a=g(u)$ and $x=b \quad u=g^{-1}(b) \Rightarrow u=g^{-1}(a)\therefore \quad \int_a^b f(x) d x=\int_{g^{-1}(a)}^{g^{-1}(b)} f\left(g(x) g^{\prime}(x) d x\right.\therefore \mathrm{R}$ is false.

questions.q:
If $f(x)=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1+\sin x+\sin 2 x+\sin 3 x & \frac{3+\sin 2 x}{2} & \frac{-2+\sin 3 x}{3} \\3+4 \sin x & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{4}{3} \sin x \\1+\sin x & \frac{1}{2} \sin x & \frac{1}{3}\end{array}\right|$
then $\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)\right) d x=$
questions.solution:
Given that,
$f(x)=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1+\sin x+\sin 2 x+\sin 3 x & \frac{3+\sin 2 x}{2} & \frac{-2+\sin 3 x}{3} \\ 3+4 \sin x & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{4}{3} \sin x \\ 1+\sin x & \frac{1}{2} \sin x & \frac{1}{3}\end{array}\right|$
$C_1 \rightarrow C_1-2 C_2-3 C_3$
$f(x)=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\sin x & \frac{3+\sin 2 x}{2} & \frac{-2+\sin 3 x}{3} \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{4}{3} \sin x \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \sin x & \frac{1}{3}\end{array}\right|$
On expanding, we get
$f(x)=\sin x\left|\begin{array}{cc}\frac{3}{2} & \frac{4}{3} \sin x \\ \frac{1}{2} \sin x & \frac{1}{3}\end{array}\right|+0+0$
$=\sin x\left(\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{1}{3}-\frac{4}{3} \sin x \times \frac{1}{2} \sin x\right)$
$=\sin x\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{2}{3} \sin ^2 x\right)$
$f(x)=\frac{1}{6}\left(3 \sin x-4 \sin ^3 x\right)$
$f(x)=\frac{\sin 3 x}{6} \quad\left[\because \sin 3 x=3 \sin x-4 \sin ^3 x\right]$
Differentiating on both sides w.r.t. ' $x$ ', we get
$f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{\sin 3 x}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{6} \cdot \cos 3 x \cdot 3$
$f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{\cos 3 x}{2}$
Let $\quad I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(f(x)+f^{\prime}(x)\right) d x$
$I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\sin 3 x}{6}+\frac{\cos 3 x}{2}\right) d x$ $\ldots$ (i)
or $\quad I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\sin 3\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{6}+\frac{\cos 3\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)}{2}\right) d x$
$=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\sin \left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}-3 x\right)}{6}+\frac{\cos \left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}-3 x\right)}{2}\right) d x$
$I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(-\frac{\cos 3 x}{6}-\frac{\sin 3 x}{2}\right) d x$ $\ldots$ (ii)
Adding Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$2 I=\int_0^{\pi / 2}\left(\frac{\cos 3 x}{2}-\frac{\cos 3 x}{6}+\frac{\sin 3 x}{6}-\frac{\sin 3 x}{2}\right) d x$
$2 I=\frac{1}{3} \int_0^{\pi / 2}(\cos 3 x-\sin 3 x) d x$
or $2 I=\frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{\sin 3 x}{3}+\frac{\cos 3 x}{3}\right]_0^{\pi / 2}$
$=\frac{1}{9}\left[\sin 3 \times \frac{\pi}{2}+\cos 3 \times \frac{\pi}{2}-\sin 3 \times 0-\cos 3 \times 0\right]$
$=\frac{1}{9}[-1+0-0-1]=-\frac{2}{9}$ or $I=-\frac{1}{9}$

questions.q: If $I_n=\int_0^a \frac{x^n}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} d x$, then $\frac{I_8}{I_4}=$
questions.solution:
We have,
$I_n=\int_0^a \frac{x^n}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} d x$
Put, $x=a \sin \theta \Rightarrow d x=a \cos \theta d \theta$ When $x=0 \Rightarrow \theta=0$ and $x=a \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\therefore \quad I_n=\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{a^n \sin ^n \theta}{a \cos \theta} \cdot a \cos \theta d \theta=a^n \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^n \theta d \theta$
Now, $\begin{aligned} I_8 & =a^8 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^8 \theta d \theta \\ & =a^8 \times \frac{7}{8} \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\end{aligned}$ and $I_4=a^4 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \sin ^4 \theta d \theta=a^4 \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\therefore \quad \frac{l_8}{l_4}=a^4 \times \frac{7}{8} \times \frac{5}{6}=\frac{35}{48} a^4$

questions.q: $\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{d x}{4+5 \sin x}$
questions.solution:
We have, $\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{d x}{4+5 \sin x}=\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{d x}{4+5\left(\frac{2 \tan \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}\right)}=\int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\left(1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}\right)}{4+4 \tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}+10 \tan \frac{x}{2}} d x=\frac{1}{4} \int_0^{\pi / 2} \frac{\sec ^2 \frac{x}{2}}{\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}+\frac{5}{2} \tan \frac{x}{2}+1} d x$
let $\tan \frac{x}{2}=t\Rightarrow \quad \sec ^2 \frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) d x=d t\Rightarrow \sec ^2 \frac{x}{2} d x=2 d t$ at $x=0, t=0$
and $\quad x=\frac{\pi}{2}, t=1=\frac{2}{4} \int_0^1-\frac{1}{t^2+\frac{5}{2} t+1} d t=\frac{1}{2} \int_0^1 \frac{d t}{t^2+\frac{5}{2} t+1+\frac{25}{16}-\frac{25}{16}}=\frac{1}{2} \int_0^1 \frac{d t}{\left(t+\frac{5}{4}\right)^2-\frac{9}{16}}=\frac{1}{2} \int_0^1 \frac{d t}{\left(t+\frac{5}{4}\right)^2-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{2 \times\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)} \log \left|\frac{t+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{3}{4}}{t+\frac{5}{4}+\frac{3}{4}}\right|\right]_0^1=\frac{1}{3}\left[\log \left|\frac{t+\frac{1}{2}}{t+2}\right|\right]_0^1=\frac{1}{3}\left[\log \left(\frac{3 / 2}{3}\right)-\log \left(\frac{1 / 2}{2}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{3}\left[\log \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\log \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{3}\left[\log \left(\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{4}}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{3} \log 2$

$\Delta_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & a^2 & b c \\ 1 & b^2 & c a \\ 1 & c^2 & a b\end{array}\right|$
$\text{Applying } R_2 \rightarrow R_2-R_1 ; R_3 \rightarrow R_3-R_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & a^2 & b c \\ 0 & (b-a)(b+a) & c(a-b) \\ 0 & (c-a)(c+a) & b(a-c) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & a^2 & b c \\ 0 & -(a+b) & c \\ 0 & (a+c) & -b \end{array}\right|\text{Applying } R_3 \rightarrow R_3+R_2=(a-b)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & a^2 & b c \\ 0 & -(b+a) & c \\ 0 & (c-b) & (c-b) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & a^2 & b c \\ 0 & -(b+a) & c \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c)\Delta_2=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \\ a^3 & b^3 & c^3 \end{array}\right|\text{Applying } C_2 \rightarrow C_2-C_1 ; C_3 \rightarrow C_3-C_1=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a^2 & (b-a)(b+a) & (c-a)(c+a) \\ a^3 & (b-a)\left(a^2+b^2+a b\right) & (c-a)\left(a^2+c^2+a c\right) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a^2 & (b-a)(b+a) & (c-a)(c+a) \\ a^3 & (b-a)\left(a^2+b^2+a b\right) & (c-a)\left(a^2+c^2+a c\right) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a^2 & -(b+a) & c+a \\ a^3 & -\left(a^2+b^2+a b\right) & a^2+c^2+a c \end{array}\right|$
Applying $C_3 \rightarrow C_3+C_2=(2-\mathrm{b})(\mathrm{c}-\mathrm{a})\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a^2 & -(b+a) & c-b \\ a^3 & -\left(a^2+b^2+a b\right) & (c-b)(a+b+c) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a^2 & -(b+a) & -1 \\ a^3 & -\left(a^2+b^2+a b\right) & -(a+b+c) \end{array}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a b+b c+c a)$
Now, $\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta_2}=\frac{6}{11} \Rightarrow \frac{a+b+c}{a b+b c+c a}=\frac{6}{11}\Rightarrow 11(a+b+c)=6(a b+b c+c a) .$

questions.solution:
Given, det.$\left({A}^{T}BA\right) = 27$

$⇒ \left|{A}^{T}\right|\left|B\right|\left|A\right| = 27$

$⇒ {\left|A\right|}^{2}\left|B\right| = 27 . . . . . \left(i\right)$

Also, det$\left|A{B}^{- 1}\right| = 8$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left|A\right|}{\left|B\right|} = 8$

$⇒ \left|B\right| = \dfrac{\left|A\right|}{8} . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

From $\left(i\right)$

$⇒ {\left|A\right|}^{2}\dfrac{\left|A\right|}{8} = 27$

$⇒ \left|A\right| = 6$

From $\left(ii\right)$,

$\left|B\right| = \dfrac{\left|A\right|}{8} = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

det$\left({B}^{T}{A}^{- 1}B\right)$

$= \left|{B}^{T}\right|\left|{A}^{- 1}\right|\left|B\right|$

$= \dfrac{{\left|B\right|}^{2}}{\left|A\right|} = \dfrac{{\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}}{6}$

$= \dfrac{9}{\left(16\right)\left(6\right)} = \dfrac{3}{32}$

questions.solution:
Given the system of equations& $2x + 9y + 5z = 8, 2x + 3y - z = - 4$~and& $x - 2z = - 5$~have an infinite number of solutions given by$x = - 5 + at, y = 2 + bt, z = ct, t \in R$~then $x, y, z$~will satisfy the given equations.

Thus, we have& $2\left(- 5 + at\right) + 9\left(2 + bt\right) + 5\left(ct\right) = 8, 2\left(- 5 + at\right) + 3\left(2 + bt\right) - \left(ct\right) = - 4$~and& $\left(- 5 + at\right) - 2\left(ct\right) = - 5$

$⇒ - 10 + 2at + 18 + 9bt + 5ct = 8, - 10 + 2at + 6 + 3bt - ct = - 4$~and& $- 5 + at - 2ct = - 5$

$⇒ 2at + 9bt + 5ct = 0, 2at + 3bt - ct = 0$~and& $at - 2ct = 0$

$⇒ 2a + 9b + 5c = 0, 2a + 3b - c = 0$~and& $a - 2c = 0 .

From the third equation, we get~$a = 2c,$~put this value in any of the first two equations, to get

$2 \times 2c + 9b + 5c = 0$

$⇒ b = - c .

Thus, we have~$a: b: c = 2c: - c: c$

$⇒ a: b: c = 2: - 1: 1 .

Hence, the solution can be~$a = 2, b = - 1, c = 1 .

questions.q: $A$ and $C$ lie in $\left[0, \dfrac{π}{2}\right)$ and $B$ lies in $\left[0, 2\pi\right] .$~If $tanA + 3cosB + 6sinC = 1;$~$3tanA + cosB + 4sinC = 4; 5tanA + 3cosB - 8sinC = - 2,$~then $B - 2A - C =$
questions.solution:
Given $tanA + 3cosB + 6sinC = 1;$ $3tanA + cosB + 4sinC = 4$ and $5tanA + 3cosB - 8sinC = - 2 .$

Let $tanA = x, cosB = y \text{ and } sinC = z,$ then the given equations become

$x + 3y + 6z = 1 . . . \left(i\right)$

$3x + y + 4z = 4 . . . \left(ii\right)$ and

$5x + 3y - 8z = - 2 . . . \left(iii\right)$

Let $P = \left[\begin{cases}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 3 & - 8\end{cases}\right], X = \left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right]$ and $Q = \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 4 \\ - 2\end{array}\right] .$

Then, the system of equations can be written as $PX = Q .$

Hence, we have $X = {P}^{- 1}Q .$

Now $\left|P\right| = \left|\begin{cases}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 3 & - 8\end{cases}\right|$

$⇒ \left|P\right| = 1\left(- 8 - 12\right) - 3\left(- 24 - 20\right) + 6\left(9 - 5\right)$

$⇒ \left|P\right| = - 20 + 132 + 24 = 136 .$

The cofactors of the elements of the matrix $P$ are

${A}_{11} = - 8 - 12 = - 20, {A}_{12} = - \left(- 24 - 20\right) = 44, {A}_{13} = 9 - 5 = 4,$

${A}_{21} = - \left(- 24 - 18\right) = 42, {A}_{22} = - 8 - 30 = - 38, {A}_{23} = - \left(3 - 15\right) = 12,$

${A}_{31} = 12 - 6 = 6, {A}_{32} = - \left(4 - 18\right) = 14, {A}_{33} = 1 - 9 = - 8 .$Thus, the adjoint matrix of $P$ is

$adjP = \left[\begin{cases}- 20 & 42 & 6 \\ 44 & - 38 & 14 \\ 4 & 12 & - 8\end{cases}\right] .$

And ${P}^{- 1} = \dfrac{adjP}{\left|P\right|},$

$⇒ {P}^{- 1} = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{cases}- 20 & 42 & 6 \\ 44 & - 38 & 14 \\ 4 & 12 & - 8\end{cases}\right] .$

The solution of the given system is

$\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{cases}- 20 & 42 & 6 \\ 44 & - 38 & 14 \\ 4 & 12 & - 8\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 4 \\ - 2\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{array}{ll}- 20 \times 1 + 42 \times 4 + 6 \times \left(- 2\right) \\ 44 \times 1 + \left(- 38\right) \times 4 + 14 \times \left(- 2\right) \\ 4 \times 1 + 12 \times 4 + \left(- 8\right) \times \left(- 2\right)\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{array}{ll}136 \\ 136 \\ 68\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ x = tanA = 1, y = cosB = - 1$ and $z = sinC = \dfrac{1}{2} .$

Also, $A$ and $C$ lie in $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $B$ lies in $\left[0, 2\pi\right] .$

Thus $tanA = 1, ⇒ A = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, cosB = - 1, ⇒ B = \pi$ and $sinC = \dfrac{1}{2}, C = \dfrac{\pi}{6} .$

Now $B - 2A - C = \pi - 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} .$

now $(A B-C)^{-1}=D=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{array}\right]$
Statement $1: \operatorname\det(\mathrm{BA})=\operatorname\det(\mathrm{BA}-\mathrm{C}) \operatorname\det(\mathrm{BDA})\Rightarrow 0=-1 \times 0 \Rightarrow 0=0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $Consider the following system of equations in matrix form& \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 2 \\ \lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \lambda\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = 0$.& Then which one of the following statements is true?
options: $∀ \lambda \in \left(- \infty , \infty\right),$& the given system has non-trivial solution
$∀ \lambda \in \left(- \infty , \infty\right),$& the& given system has only trivial solution
For $\lambda \ne 0,$& the given system does not have any solution
For $\lambda = 0,$& the given system is inconsistent
questions.solution:
Given system of equations& $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 2 \\ \lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \lambda\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] =$0$

$⇒ $\left[\begin{cases}1 \times 1 & 1 \times 2 & 1 \times \lambda \\ 2 \times 1 & 2 \times 2 & 2 \times \lambda \\ \lambda \times 1 & \lambda \times 2 & \lambda \times \lambda\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] =$0$

$⇒ $\left[\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \lambda \\ 2 & 4 & 2\lambda \\ \lambda & 2\lambda & {λ}^{2}\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] =$0$

Now, \left|\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \lambda \\ 2 & 4 & 2\lambda \\ \lambda & 2\lambda & {λ}^{2}\end{cases}\right| = \left(1\right)\left\{\left(4\right)\left({λ}^{2}\right) - \left(2\lambda\right)\left(2\lambda\right)\right\} - 2\left\{\left(2\right)\left({λ}^{2}\right) - \left(\lambda\right)\left(2\lambda\right)\right\} + \lambda\left\{\left(2\right)\left(2\lambda\right) - \left(\lambda\right)\left(4\right)\right\} = 0$

Here, the determinant is zero, so the given system of equations has infinitely many solutions.

We know that for a system of equations of form $AX = 0$, it has non-trivial solution if $\left|A\right| =$0$.

So, the given system of equations \left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 2 \\ \lambda\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & 2 & \lambda\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = 0$ has non-trivial solution for any real value of $\lambda$.

i.e. $∀ \lambda \in \left(- \infty , \infty\right),$& the given system has non-trivial solution.

\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $A$ be the set of all $3 \times 3$ determinants with entries 0 or 1 only and $B$ be the subset of $A$ consisting of all determinants with value 1. If $C$ is the subset of $A$ consisting of all determinants with value -1 , then
questions.solution:
We know that the interchange of two adjacent rows (columns) changes the value of a determinant only in sign but not in magnitude.
Hence, corresponding to every element $\Delta$ at $B$ there is an element $\Delta^{\prime}$ in $C$ obtained by inter changing two adjacent rows (columns) in $\Delta$. It follows that $n(B) \leq n(c)$, i.e. the number of elements in $B$ is less than an equal to the number of elements in $C$.
Similarly, $\quad n(C) \leq n(B)$
Hence, $\quad n(B)=n(C)$
i.e. $B$ has an many elements as $C$.

questions.q: If $af\left(x\right) + bf\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = x + 1$, and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}f\left(x\right)\right) = 2x^{2} + 2x + \dfrac{1}{3}$, then $a - b =$
questions.solution:
Given $af\left(x\right) + bf\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) = x + 1 . . . \left(i\right)$

Replacing $x \to \dfrac{1}{x}$, we get

$af\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + bf\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{x} + 1 . . . \left(ii\right)$

$a \times \left(i\right) - b \times \left(ii\right)$, we get

$\left[{a}^{2}f\left(x\right) + abf\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\right] - \left[abf\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + {b}^{2}f\left(x\right)\right] = ax + a - \dfrac{b}{x} - b$

$\left({a}^{2} - {b}^{2}\right)f\left(x\right) = ax - \dfrac{b}{x} + a - b$

$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{ax - \dfrac{b}{x}}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{a + b}$

Now, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left({x}^{2}f\left(x\right)\right) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left({x}^{2}\left(\dfrac{ax - \dfrac{b}{x}}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{a + b}\right)\right)$

$= \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\left(\dfrac{a{x}^{3} - bx}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} + \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{a + b}\right)\right) = \dfrac{3a{x}^{2} - b}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} + \dfrac{2x}{a + b}$

Given, $\dfrac{3a{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} + \dfrac{2x}{a + b} - \dfrac{b}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} = 2{x}^{2} + 2x + \dfrac{1}{3}$

i.e. $\dfrac{3a}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} = 2$,

$\dfrac{1}{a + b} = 1$ and 

$- \dfrac{b}{{a}^{2} - {b}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

So, $\dfrac{a}{a - b} = \dfrac{2}{3} \text{ and } - \dfrac{b}{a - b} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

i.e. $a = - 2b ⇒ b = - 1, a = 2$

Hence, $a - b = 3$

questions.q: If $f\left(x\right) = \log_{\mathrm{e}}\left(e^{2x}\left(\dfrac{3x + 5}{5 - 3x}\right)\dfrac{2}{3}\right), x \ne \dfrac{- 5}{3}, \dfrac{5}{3}$, then the value of $\dfrac{df}{dx}$ at $x = 1$, is
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = {\log}_{e}\left({e}^{2x}\left(\dfrac{3x + 5}{5 - 3x}\right)\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = {\log}_{e}{e}^{2x} + {\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{3x + 5}{5 - 3x}\right)\dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 2x + \dfrac{2}{3}{\log}_{e}\left(\dfrac{3x + 5}{5 - 3x}\right)$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 2x + \dfrac{2}{3}\left({\log}_{e}\left(3x + 5\right) - {\log}_{e}\left(5 - 3x\right)\right)$

Now differentiating the function with respect to $x$ we get,

$\dfrac{df}{dx} = 2 + \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{3x + 5} \times 3 - \dfrac{1}{5 - 3x} \times \left(- 3\right)\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{df}{dx} = 2 + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3x + 5} + \dfrac{1}{5 - 3x}\right)$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{df}{dx}\right)}_{x = 1} = 2 + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{3 + 5} + \dfrac{1}{5 - 3}\right) = 2 + 2 \times \dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{13}{4}$

questions.q: If $x = cosec \theta - sin\theta, y = {cosec}^{2022}\theta - {sin}^{2022}\theta$~and $\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)2 = \dfrac{k\left(y^{2} + 4\right)}{g\left(x\right)}$~where $k \in \mathbb{R}$, then~$10 + k - g\left(2022\right) =$
questions.solution:
Given,

$x = cosec \theta - sin\theta$

So, $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta} = - \text{c}osec\theta\text{cot \theta} - cos\theta = - \text{cot}\theta\left(cos\text{ec}\theta + sin\theta\right) . . . . \left(1\right)$

$y = {cosec}^{2022}\theta - {sin}^{2022}\theta$

So, $\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = - 2022{cosec}^{2021}\theta cosec \thetaco\text{t}\theta - 2022{sin}^{2021}\thetacos\theta$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = - 2022co\text{t}\theta\left({cosec}^{2022}\theta + {sin}^{2022}\theta\right) . . . . . . . \left(2\right)$

Now squaring $y = {cosec}^{2022}\theta - {sin}^{2022}\theta$ we get,

${y}^{2} = {\left({cosec}^{2022}\theta - {sin}^{2022}\theta\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ {y}^{2} + 4 = {\left({cosec}^{2022}\theta + {sin}^{2022}\theta\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ \sqrt{{y}^{2} + 4} = \left({cosec}^{2022}\theta + {sin}^{2022}\theta\right)$ so putting in equation $\left(2\right)$ we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = - 2022co\text{t}\theta\left(\sqrt{{y}^{2} + 4}\right) . . . . . . . \left(3\right)$

Similarly we get $\sqrt{{x}^{2} + 4} = cosec \theta + sin\theta$ putting in equation $\left(1\right)$

We get $\dfrac{dx}{d\theta} = - \text{cot}\theta\left(\sqrt{{x}^{2} + 4}\right) . . . . \left(4\right)$

Now dividing equation $\left(3\right) \text{ and } \left(4\right)$ we get,

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2022 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{{y}^{2} + 4}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2} + 4}}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}^{2} = {\left(2022\right)}^{2} \times \dfrac{{y}^{2} + 4}{{x}^{2} + 4}$

Now on comparing with ${\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{k\left({y}^{2} + 4\right)}{g\left(x\right)}$ 

We get $g\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} + 4 \text{ and } k = {\left(2022\right)}^{2}$

Now putting the value in $10 + k - g\left(2022\right)$ we get,

$10 + k - g\left(2022\right) = 10 + {\left(2022\right)}^{2} - {\left(2022\right)}^{2} - 4 = 6$

questions.q: If $\left(a + bx\right)e\dfrac{y}{x} = x$, then $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} =$
questions.solution:
Given, $\left(a + bx\right)e\dfrac{y}{x} = x$

$⇒ e\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{x}{\left(a + bx\right)}$

$⇒ log\left(e\dfrac{y}{x}\right) = log\left(\dfrac{x}{a + bx}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{y}{x} = logx - log\left(a + bx\right)$

$⇒ y = xlogx - xlog\left(a + bx\right)$

Differentiate both sides

$y ' = \dfrac{x}{x} + logx - \dfrac{bx}{a + bx} - log\left(a + bx\right)$

$y ' = x\left[\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{b}{a + bx}\right] + \left[logx - log\left(a + bx\right)\right]$

$y ' = x\left[\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{b}{a + bx}\right] + \dfrac{y}{x}$

$xy ' = {x}^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{b}{a + bx}\right] + y$

$xy ' = {x}^{2}\left[\dfrac{a + bx - bx}{x\left(a + bx\right)}\right] + y$

$xy ' = \left[\dfrac{ax}{\left(a + bx\right)}\right] + y$

$x\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d {x}^{2}} + y ' = a\left[\dfrac{\left(a + bx\right) \cdot 1 - x \cdot b}{{\left(a + bx\right)}^{2}}\right] + y '$

${x}^{3}\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d {x}^{2}} = \left[\dfrac{{a}^{2}{x}^{2}}{{\left(a + bx\right)}^{2}}\right]$

${x}^{3}\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d {x}^{2}} = {\left[\dfrac{ax}{\left(a + bx\right)}\right]}^{2}$

${x}^{3}\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d {x}^{2}} = {\left[xy ' - y\right]}^{2}$

$\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d {x}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{{x}^{3}}{\left[xy ' - y\right]}^{2}$

questions.q: If $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\cos^{2}x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}$, then $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - 3f^{'}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) =$
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\cos^{2}x}{1 + \sin^{2}x} ⇒ f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}{1 + \sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{1}{3}... ( 1 )$

$⇒ \ln\left(f\left(x\right)\right) = \ln\left(\dfrac{\cos^{2}x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}\right) = 2\ln\left|cosx\right| - \ln\left|1 + \sin^{2}x\right|$

Differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$,

$⇒ \dfrac{f^{'}\left(x\right)}{f\left(x\right)} = \dfrac{- 2sinx}{cosx} - \dfrac{2sinxcosx}{1 + \sin^{2}x} = - 2tanx - \dfrac{sin2x}{1 + \sin^{2}x}$

Putting $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$,

$⇒ \dfrac{f^{'}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}{f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} = - 2 - \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{- 8}{3}$

$⇒ f^{'}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{- 8}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{- 8}{9}$

So, $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - 3f^{'}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} + 3 \times \dfrac{8}{9} = 3$

questions.q: If $f(x)=\frac{x-1}{e^x}$, then $f^{\prime}(0)+f^{\prime \prime}(0)=$
questions.solution:
Given that, $f(x)=\frac{x-1}{e^x}\ldots(\mathrm{i})$
Differentiating Eq. (i) w.r.t. $x$ on both sides, we get
$f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{e^x \frac{d}{d x}(x-1)-(x-1) \frac{d}{d x}\left(e^x\right)}{\left(e^x\right)^2}\left[\because \frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=\frac{v \frac{d}{d x} u-u \frac{d v}{d x}}{v^2}\right]=\frac{e^x \cdot 1-(x-1) e^x}{e^{2 x}}f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2-x}{e^x}\ldots(\mathrm{ii})$
Putting $x=0$ in Eq. (ii), we get
$f^{\prime}(0)=\frac{2-0}{e^0}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(0)=2\ldots(\mathrm{iii})$
Now, differentiating Eq. (ii) w.r.t. $x$ on both sides, we get
$f^{\prime \prime}(x)=\frac{e^x \frac{d}{d x}(2-x)-(2-x) \frac{d}{d x}\left(e^x\right)}{\left(e^x\right)^2}=\frac{e^x(-1)-(2-x) e^x}{e^{2 x}}f^{\prime \prime}(x)=\frac{(x-3)}{e^x}\ldots(\mathrm{iv})$
Putting $x=0$, in Eq. (iv), we get
$f^{\prime \prime}(0)=\frac{0-3}{e^0}=\frac{-3}{1} \Rightarrow f^{\prime \prime}(0)=-3\ldots(\mathrm{v})$
Adding Eq. (iii) and Eq. (v), we get
$f^{\prime}(0)+f^{\prime \prime}(0)=2+(-3) \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(0)+f^{\prime \prime}(0)=-1$

questions.q: If $\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)}$ and $\frac{d^2 x}{d y^2}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^3+\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=k$, then $e^{k f(x)}-k f(x)=$
questions.solution:
Given that, $\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)}$ or $\frac{d y}{d x}=\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)^{-1} \ldots$(i)
Differentiating Eq. (i) on both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)^{-2}\left\{\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)\right\}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)^{-2}\left\{\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right) \frac{d y}{d x}\right\}$ [from chain rule]
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)^{-2}\left\{\frac{d^2 x}{d y^2} \cdot \frac{d x}{d y}\right\}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=-\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2 \frac{d^2 x}{d y^2} \Rightarrow \frac{d^2 x}{d y^2}+\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^3 \frac{d^2 x}{d y^2}=0$
Comparing with given expression, we get
$k=0$
Now, $e^{k f(x)}-k f(x)=e^{0 \times f(x)}-0 \times f(x)e^{k f(x)}-k f(x)=e^0-0=1 \quad   \left[\becausee^0=1\right]$

questions.q: If $p(x)$ be a polynomial satisfying $p(2 x)=p^{\prime}(x) \cdot p^{\prime \prime}(x)$, then $\sum_{x=1}^5 p(x)=$
questions.solution:
It is given a polynomial satisfying
$p(2 x)=p^{\prime}(x) p^{\prime \prime}(x)$
Let the degree of polynomial is $n$, then degree of $p^{\prime}(x)$ and $p^{\prime \prime}(x)$ are $n-1$ and $n-2$ respectively, so
$n=n-1+n-2 \Rightarrow n=3$
Now, let the polynomial $p(x)=a x^3\therefore \quad p(2 x)=p^{\prime}(x) \cdot p^{\prime \prime}(x) \Rightarrow 8 a x^3=\left(3 a x^2\right) \cdot(6 a x)\Rightarrow \quad a=\frac{4}{9}\therefore$ The required polynomial is $p(x) \frac{4}{9} x^3$
Therefore $\sum_{x=1}^5 p(x)=\frac{4}{9}\left[1^3+2^3+3^3+4^3+5^3\right]=\frac{4}{9}\left(\frac{5 \times 6}{2}\right)^2=100$

Reason: For $x < 0, | x | = - x$
options: Assertion is false but Reason is true.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
questions.solution:
Note: Assuming base of logarithm as& $e$.

Given

Assertion:& for& $x < 0, \dfrac{d2}{dx^{2}}\left(log | x |\right) = \dfrac{1}{| x{|}^{2}}$

Reason: for& $x < 0, | x | = - x$

So, let $f ( x ) = log ( | x | )$

For $x < 0$

$y = f ( x ) = log ( - x )$

Now, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{( - x )}\left(- 1\right) = \dfrac{1}{x}$

$\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx} = - \dfrac{1}{x2}$

So, Assertion is wrong but reason is true.

questions.q: If $ax^{2} + 2hxy + by^{2} = 0,$ then $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} =$
questions.solution:
Given, $a{x}^{2} + 2hxy + b{y}^{2} = 0$

Now, differentiating both the sides with respect to $x$

$⇒ 2ax + 2h ( y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} ) + 2by\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$

$⇒ 2hx\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2by\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2ax + 2hy = 0$

$⇒ 2\dfrac{dy}{dx} ( hx + by ) = - 2 ( ax + hy )$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = - \dfrac{\left(ax + hy\right)}{hx + by} . . . \left(1\right)$

Now, again differentiating with respect to $x$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - \left[\dfrac{\left(a + h\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) ( hx + by ) - \left(h + b\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right) ( ax + hy )}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - \dfrac{\left[\left(ahx + {h}^{2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}x + aby + bh\dfrac{dy}{dx}y\right) - \left(ahx + ab\dfrac{dy}{dx}x + {h}^{2}y + hby\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)\right]}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - \left[\dfrac{( ab - {h}^{2} ) y + ( {h}^{2} - ab ) x\dfrac{dy}{dx}}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - ( ab - {h}^{2} ) \left[\dfrac{y - x\dfrac{dy}{dx}}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}\right]$

Now, put $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = - \dfrac{\left(ax + hy\right)}{( hx + by )}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - \left(ab - {h}^{2}\right)\left[\dfrac{y - x\left(- \dfrac{\left(ax + hy\right)}{( hx + by )}\right)}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}\right]$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = - \left(ab - {h}^{2}\right)\left[\dfrac{a{x}^{2} + 2hxy + b{y}^{2}}{( hx + by{)}^{2}}\right]$

As given $a{x}^{2} + 2hxy + b{y}^{2} = 0$

So, $\dfrac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}} = 0$

questions.q: If $\sqrt{x+y}-\sqrt{x-y}=$c$, then \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=$
questions.solution:
It is given that
$\sqrt{x+y}-\sqrt{x-y}=c$
On squaring both sides, we get
$(x+y)+(x-y)-2 \sqrt{x^2-y^2}=c^22 x-c^2=2 \sqrt{x^2-y^2}$
Again on squaring both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned} & & 4 x^2+c^4-4 x c^2 & =4 x^2-4 y^2 \\ \Rightarrow & & c^4-4 x c^2 & =-4 y^2 \\ \Rightarrow & & 4 y^2 & =4 x c^2-c^4\end{aligned}$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned} & 8 y \frac{d y}{d x}=4 c^2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 y \frac{d y}{d x} & =c^2\end{aligned}$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t. $x$, we get
$2\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2+2 y \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=0\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2} & =-\frac{\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2}{y}=-\frac{\left(\frac{c^2}{2 y}\right)^2}{y} \quad \text{ [From Eq. (i)] } \\ & =-\frac{c^4}{4 y^3}\end{aligned}$
Hence, option (b) is correct.

options: $\frac{\left(a x y+h x^2+b y x\right)}{(a x+b y)^2}$
questions.solution:
We have, a x²+2 h x y+b y²=3 On differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $\begin{aligned}& 2 a x+2 h x \frac{d y}{d x}+2 h y+2 b y \frac{d y}{d x}=0 \\
& \frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{(a x+h y)}{(b y+h x)}
\end{aligned}$ Again differentiating with respect to $x$, we get $\begin{aligned}& 2 a+2 h x \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}+2 h \frac{d y}{d x}+2 h \frac{d y}{d x}+2 b\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2 \\
&+2 b y \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=0
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}( h x+b y)=-\left( a+2 h \frac{d y}{d x}+ b\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)^2\right) \\
& \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}( h x+b y)= \\
&-\left( a+2 h\left(\frac{-a x-h y}{h x+b y}\right)+ b\left(\frac{-a x-h y}{h x+b y}\right)^2\right)
\end{aligned} \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}(h x+b y)=-\left[\frac{a(h x+b y)^2-2 h(a x+h y)(h x+b y)+b(a x+h y)^2}{(h x+b y)^2}\right] \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\frac{3\left(h^2-a b\right)}{(h x+b y)^3}$

questions.q: If $x^{2} + xy + y^{2} = k,$ then $\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} =$
questions.solution:
Given& $x^{2} + xy + y^{2} = k$

Differentiating the above function,

$2x + y + x\dfrac{d y}{d x} + 2y\dfrac{d y}{d x} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{d y}{d x} = - \left(y + 2x\right)x + 2y$

Differentiating the above function,

$\dfrac{d^{2}y}{d x^{2}} = \dfrac{- \left(x + 2y\right)\left(\dfrac{d y}{d x} + 2\right) + \left(1 + 2\dfrac{d y}{d x}\right)\left(y + 2x\right)}{\left(x + 2y\right)2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{d^{2}y}{d x^{2}} = \dfrac{- 3y + \left(- 3x\right)\left(y + 2x\right)\left(x + 2y\right)}{\left(x + 2y\right)2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{d^{2}y}{d x^{2}} = \dfrac{- 3xy - 6y^{2} - 3xy - 6x^{2}}{\left(x + 2y\right)3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{d^{2}y}{d x^{2}} = \dfrac{- 6 ( x^{2} + y^{2} + xy )}{\left(x + 2y\right)3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{d^{2}y}{d x^{2}} = \dfrac{- 6k}{\left(x + 2y\right)3}$

questions.q: $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{x+5}{(x+1)^2(x+2)}\right)=$

Let $\frac{x+5}{(x+1)^2(x+4)}=\frac{A}{(x+1)}+\frac{B}{(x+1)^2}+\frac{C}{(x+4)} \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow x+5=A(x+1)(x+2)+B(x+2)+c(x+1)^2 \\
& \Rightarrow x+5=x²(A+C)+x(3 A+B+2 C)+2 A+2 B+C .
\end{aligned} On comparing$ the coefficients of like power of x$, we get \begin{aligned} A+C & =0, \\
3 A+B+2 C & =1 \text{ and }2 A+2 B+C=5
\end{aligned} On substituting$ A=-C in $last two equations, we get \begin{aligned} B-C & =1 \\
2 B-C & =5
\end{aligned} and 2 B-C=5 On subtracting Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get B=4 \Rightarrow C=3 [from Eq. (ii)]
and hence$ A=-3$
Now, \frac{(x+5)}{(x+1)^2(x+2)}=\frac{-3}{(x+1)}+\frac{4}{(x+1)^2}+\frac{3}{(x+2)}$
On differentiating both sides w.r.t $x$, we get. $\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{(x+5)}{(x+1)^2(x+4)}\right)=\frac{3}{(x+1)^2}-\frac{8}{(x+1)^3}-\frac{3}{(x+2)^2}$

& =-a² x\left(2 y^{\prime}\right) \quad[\because \text{$ from $Eq. (i) }]\\
\Rightarrow\left(1+a² x²\right) y^{\prime \prime} & +2 a² x y^{\prime}=0

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $x=a\left\{\cos \theta+\log \tan \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right\}$ and $y=a \sin \theta$, then $\frac{d y}{d x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given that,

x=a$\left(\cos \theta+\log \tan \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right) \text{$ and }$y=a \sin $\thetaOn differentiating w.r.t. $\theta$ respectively, we get

$\begin{aligned}\frac{d x}{d \theta}& =a\left(-\sin \theta+\frac{1}{\tan   \left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} \cdot \sec ^2 \frac{\theta}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\right)\\
& =a\left(-\sin \theta+\frac{1}{\sin \theta}\right)=\frac{a \cos ^2 \theta}{\sin \theta}
\end{aligned}$ and $\frac{d y}{d \theta}= a \cos$\theta
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \frac{d y}{d x}& =\frac{d y / d \theta}{d x / d \theta}=\frac{a \cos \theta}{a \cos ^2 \theta / \sin \theta}\\
& =\tan \theta
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: $y=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x} \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}-(2 n+1) x y_{n+1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $\quad y=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x}$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& y_1=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x} a \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & y_1 \sqrt{1-x^2}=a y \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \left(1-x^2\right) y_1^2=a^2 y^2
\end{aligned}$
Again, differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
\left(1-x^2\right) 2 y_1 y_2-2 x y_1^2 & =a^2 2 y y_1 \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(1-x^2\right) y_2-x y_1-a^2 y & =0
\end{aligned}$
Using Leibnitz's rule,
$\begin{aligned}
& \left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}+{ }^n C_1 y_{n+1}(-2 x)+{ }^n C_2 y_n(-2) \\
& -x y_{n+1}-{ }^n C_1 y_n-a^2 y_n=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}+x y_{n+1}(-2 n-1) \\
& +y_n\left[-n(n-1)-n-a^2\right]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}-(2 n+1) x y_{n+1}=\left(n^2+a^2\right) y_n \\
&
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $y=\sin  \left(\log _ e$ x\right)$, then $x^2 $\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}+x \frac{d y}{d x}is equal to$
questions.solution:
Given that,

y=\sin $\left(\log _$ e x\right)$ On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get

\frac{d y}{d x}=\cos \left(\log _$ e x\right)$\cdot \frac{1}{x}$ Again differentiating, we get

$\begin{aligned}\frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}& =\frac{-x \cdot \sin \left(\log _e x\right) \cdot \frac{1}{x}-\cos \left(\log _e x\right) \cdot 1}{x^2}\\
& =\frac{-\sin \left(\log _e x\right)-\cos \left(\log _e x\right)}{x^2}
\end{aligned}$ Now, $\quad x^2 \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}+x \frac{d y}{d x} \begin{aligned}& =\frac{x^2\left[-\sin \left(\log _e x\right)-\cos \left(\log _e x\right)\right]}{x^2}\\
& =-\sin \left(\log _e x\right) \\
& =-y \quad \text{ [from Eq. (i)] }
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $2 x^2-3 x y+y^2+x+2 y-8=0$, then $\frac{d y}{d x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have, $2 x^2-3 x y+y^2+x+2 y-8=0$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get

questions.q: If $z=\log (\tan x+\tan y)$, then $(\sin 2 x) \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+(\sin 2 y) \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$z=\log (\tan x+\tan y)$
On differentiating partially w.r.t. $x and y$, we get
and $\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} & =\frac{1 \cdot \sec ^2 x}{\tan x+\tan y} \\ \text{$ and $} \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} & =\frac{\sec ^2 y}{\tan x+\tan y}\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned} & \sin 2 x \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\sin 2 y \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \\ & =\frac{\sin 2 x \sec ^2 x+\sin 2 y \sec ^2 y}{\tan x+\tan y} \\ & =\frac{2 \sin x \cos x \cdot \frac{1}{\cos ^2 x}+2 \sin y \cos y \cdot \frac{1}{\cos ^2 y}}{\tan x+\tan y} \\ & =\frac{2[\tan x+\tan y]}{\tan x+\tan y} \\ & =2\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $x=\cos \theta, y=\sin 5 \theta \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}-x \frac{d y}{d x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $x=\cos \theta, y=\sin 5 \theta\frac{d x}{d \theta}=-\sin \theta, \frac{d y}{d \theta}=5 \cos 5 \theta\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d y / d \theta}{d x / d \theta}=-\frac{5 \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}=\frac{d}{d x}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)=\frac{d}{d \theta}\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right) \cdot \frac{d \theta}{d x} \\ & =\frac{d}{d \theta}\left(\frac{-5 \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{-\sin \theta} \\ & =\left(\frac{\sin \theta \sin 5 \theta \cdot 25+5 \cos 5 \theta \cos \theta}{\sin ^2 \theta}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{-\sin \theta} \\ & =-\frac{25 \sin 5 \theta}{\sin ^2 \theta}-\frac{5 \cos 5 \theta \cos \theta}{\sin ^3 \theta}\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned} &\left(1-x^2\right) \frac{d^2 y}{d x^2}-x \frac{d y}{d x} \\ &=\left(1-\cos ^2 \theta\right)\left(\frac{-25 \sin 5 \theta}{\sin ^2 \theta}-\frac{5 \cos 5 \theta \cos \theta}{\sin ^3 \theta}\right) \\ &-\cos \theta\left(\frac{-5 \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta}\right) \\ &= \sin ^2 \theta\left(\frac{-25 \sin 5 \theta}{\sin ^2 \theta}-\frac{5 \cos \theta \cos 5 \theta}{\sin ^3 \theta}\right) \\ &+\frac{5 \cos \theta \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta} \\ &=-25 \sin 5 \theta-\frac{5 \cos \theta \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta}+\frac{5 \cos \theta \cos 5 \theta}{\sin \theta} \\ &=-25 \sin 5 \theta \\ &=-25 y\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $u=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}\right)$ then $x \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+y \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}$ equal to :
questions.solution:
$u=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}\right)$
Here $u$ is not a homogeneous function. But $f(x, y)=\sin u=\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}$ is a homogeneous function of degree one. Here by Euler's theorem
$x \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}+y \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=f$
$\Rightarrow \quad x \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(\sin u)+y \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(\sin u)=\sin u$
$\Rightarrow \quad x \cos u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+y \cos u \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\sin u$
$\Rightarrow \quad x \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+y \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\tan u$

questions.q:
Observe the following statements
I. $f(x)=a x^{41}+b x^{-40} \Rightarrow \frac{f^{\prime \prime}(x)}{f(x)}=1640 x^{-2}$
II. $\frac{d}{d x} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 x}{1-x^2}\right)=\frac{1}{1+x^2}$
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both I and II are true
Neither I nor II is true
I is false, but II is true
questions.solution:
I.
$\begin{aligned}
& f(x)=a x^{41}+b x^{-40} \\
& f^{\prime}(x)=41 a x^{40}-40 b x^{-41} \\
& f^{\prime \prime}(x)=1640 a x^{39}+1640 b x^{-42}
\end{aligned}$
Now, $\frac{f^{\prime \prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{1640\left(a x^{39}+b x^{-42}\right)}{a x^{41}+b x^{-40}}=1640 x^{-2}$
II.
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{d}{d x} \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 x}{1-x^2}\right) \\
& =\frac{d}{d x} \tan ^{-1}(\tan 2 x) \\
& =\frac{d}{d x} 2 x \\
& =2
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Statement I is true, but II is false.

questions.q: If $f(x)\left\{\begin{array}{cc}\frac{x-1}{2 x^2-7 x+5}, & \text{ for } x \neq 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & , \text{ for } x=1\end{array}\right.$, then $f^{\prime}(1)$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
We have,
$f(x)=\frac{x-1}{2 x^2-7 x+5}, x \neq 1=\frac{(x-1)}{2 x^2-2 x-5 x+5}=\frac{x-1}{2 x(x-1)-5(x-1)}=\frac{1}{2 x-5}f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{2 x-5}, & x \neq 1 \\ -\frac{1}{3}, & x=1\end{array}\right.$
Now, $\quad f^{\prime}(1)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(1+h)-f(1)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2(1+h)-5}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2 h-3}+\frac{1}{3}}{h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{3+2 h-3}{3 h(2 h-3)}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{2}{3(2 h-3)}=-\frac{2}{9}$

questions.q: If $f(x)=(\cos x)(\cos 2 x) \ldots(\cos n x)$ then $f^{\prime}(x)+\sum_{r=1}^n(r \tan r x) f(x)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$f(x)=(\cos x)(\cos 2 x) \ldots(\cos n x)f^{\prime}(x)=-\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x+\cos x \frac{d}{d x}\{\cos 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x\}f^{\prime}(x)=-\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x+\cos x[-2 \sin 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x\left.+\cos 2 x \frac{d}{d x} \cos 3 x \cdot \cos 4 x \ldots \cos n x\right]f^{\prime}(x) \Rightarrow-(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x)+\cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \frac{d}{d x}(\cos 3 x \cdot \cos 4 x \cdot \cos n x)f^{\prime}(x) \Rightarrow-(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(3 \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \cdot \sin 3 x \ldots \cos n x)-(n \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \sin n x)$
So,
$\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)+\sum_{r=1}^n(r \tan r x) f(x)=f^{\prime}(x)+\{\tan x+2 \tan 2 x+3 \tan 3 x+\ldots+n \tan n x\} f(x)=f^{\prime}(x)+f(x) \tan x+2 f(x) \tan 2 x+\ldots+n f(x) \tan n x=f^{\prime}(x)+[(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)+(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \ldots \cos n x)+\ldots+(n \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \sin n x)]=f^{\prime}(x)-f^{\prime}(x)\Rightarrow 0$
Hence, $f^{\prime}(x)+\sum_{r=1}^n(r \tan r x) f(x)=0$

questions.q: If $u(x, y)=y \log x+x \log y$, then $u_x u_y-u_x \log x-u_y \log y+\log x \log y$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
We have,
$u(x, y)=y \log x+x \log y$
On differentiating partially w.r.t. $x$ and $y$ respectively,
$u_x=\frac{y}{x}+\log y, u_y=\log x+\frac{x}{y}$
Now, $u_x u_y-u_x \log x-u_y \log y+\log x \log y=\left(\frac{y}{x}+\log y\right)\left(\log x+\frac{x}{y}\right)-\left(\frac{y}{x}+\log y\right) \log x-\left(\log x+\frac{x}{y}\right) \log y+\log x \log y=1+\frac{y}{x} \log x+\frac{x}{y} \log y+\log x \log y-\frac{y}{x} \log x-\log x \log y-\log x \log y-\frac{x}{y} \log y+\log x \log y=1$

questions.q: $P\left({\theta}_{1}\right)$ and $Q\left({\theta}_{2}\right)$ are two points on the ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$ with eccentricity $e$. If $PSQ$ is a focal chord and $tan\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1}}{2}\right)tan\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{2}}{2}\right) = - \left(2\sqrt{2} + 3\right)$, then $e$ and $S$ are
questions.solution:
Here, $S ≡ \left(ae, 0\right)$.

Let $P\left(acos{\theta}_{1}, bsin{\theta}_{1}\right)$ and $Q\left(acos{\theta}_{2}, bsin{\theta}_{2}\right)$ are two points on the ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$, so

Slope of $PS =$Slope of $QS$

$⇒ \dfrac{0 - bsin{\theta}_{1}}{ae - acos{\theta}_{1}} = \dfrac{0 - bsin{\theta}_{2}}{ae - acos{\theta}_{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{sin{\theta}_{1}}{e - cos{\theta}_{1}} = \dfrac{sin{\theta}_{2}}{e - cos{\theta}_{2}}$

$⇒ sin{\theta}_{1}\left(e - cos{\theta}_{2}\right) = sin{\theta}_{2}\left(e - cos{\theta}_{1}\right)$

$⇒ esin{\theta}_{1} - sin{\theta}_{1}cos{\theta}_{2} = esin{\theta}_{2} - sin{\theta}_{2}cos{\theta}_{1}$

$⇒ e\left(sin{\theta}_{1} - sin{\theta}_{2}\right) = sin{\theta}_{1}cos{\theta}_{2} - sin{\theta}_{2}cos{\theta}_{1}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{sin\left({\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}\right)}{sin{\theta}_{1} - sin{\theta}_{2}}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{2sin\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}{2cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)sin\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}{cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{e + 1}{e - 1} = \dfrac{cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right) + cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}{cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} - {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right) - cos\left(\dfrac{{\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2}}{2}\right)}$

$⇒ \dfrac{e + 1}{e - 1} = \dfrac{2cos{\theta}_{1}cos{\theta}_{2}}{2sin{\theta}_{1}sin{\theta}_{2}}$

$⇒ tan\left({\theta}_{1}\right)tan\left({\theta}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{e - 1}{e + 1}$

$⇒ \dfrac{e - 1}{e + 1} = - \left(2\sqrt{2} + 3\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1 - e}{1 + e} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 3}{1}$

Applying Componendo and Dividendo rule,

$\dfrac{2}{2e} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 4}{- 2 - 2\sqrt{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{e} = - \sqrt{2}$

$⇒ e = - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Since, eccentricty of ellipse is always positive so $e = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Hence, $S ≡ \left(\pm \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}, 0\right)$.

questions.q: If $\frac{\pi}{3}, \theta$ are the eccentric angles of the ends of a focal chord of the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{12}=1$, then $\tan \theta=$
questions.solution:
Given ellipse, $\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{12}=1$
Let eccentricity of ellipse be ' $e$ ' Then
$b^2=a^2\left(1-e^2\right)$
Here, $\quad b^2=12, a^2=16$
$\therefore \quad 12=16\left(1-e^2\right)$
$1-e^2=\frac{3}{4}$
or $e^2=1-\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4} \text{ or } e=\frac{1}{2}$
If $\alpha, \beta$ are the eccentric angles of the ends of a focal chord of the ellipse, then eccentricity is given by
$e=\frac{\cos \left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)}{\cos \left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)}$
Here, $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}, \beta=\theta$, and $e=\frac{1}{2}$
$\frac{1}{2}=\frac{\cos \left(\frac{\pi / 3-\theta}{2}\right)}{\cos \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right)}$
Multiplying in $N^r$ and $D^r$ by $2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right)$
$\frac{1}{2}=\frac{2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{\pi / 3-\theta}{2}\right)}{2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right)}$
$=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta+\pi / 3-\theta}{2}\right)+\sin \left(\frac{\pi / 3+\theta-\pi / 3+\theta}{2}\right)}{\sin (\pi / 3+\theta)}$
$\left\{\because 2 \sin A \cos B=\sin \left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)+\sin \left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)\right.$ and $2 \sin A \cos A=\sin 2 A\}$
$\frac{1}{2}=\frac{\sin \frac{\pi}{3}+\sin \theta}{\sin \frac{\pi}{3} \cos \theta+\cos \frac{\pi}{3} \sin \theta}$
$\sin \frac{\pi}{3} \cos \theta+\cos \frac{\pi}{3} \sin \theta=2\left(\sin \frac{\pi}{3}+\sin \theta\right)$
$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \theta+\frac{1}{2} \sin \theta=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\sin \theta\right)$
$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \theta+\frac{1}{2} \sin \theta=\sqrt{3}+2 \sin \theta$
or $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \cos \theta=\frac{3}{2} \sin \theta+\sqrt{3}$
$\cos \theta=\sqrt{3} \sin \theta+2$ or $\frac{1}{2} \cos \theta-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \sin \theta=1$
or $\quad \cos \frac{\pi}{3} \cos \theta-\sin \frac{\pi}{3} \sin \theta=1$
or $\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3}+\theta\right)=1$ or $\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3}+\theta\right)=\cos 0^{\circ}$
On comparing both sides, we get
$\frac{\pi}{3}+\theta=0^{\circ} \text{ or } \theta=-\frac{\pi}{3} \quad \therefore \quad \tan \theta=\tan \left(\frac{-\pi}{3}\right)$
$\tan \theta=-\sqrt{3}$

$\Rightarrow \quad a^2-b^2=96\ldots$ (iii)
and $\quad a b=20 \ldots$ (iv) [from Eq. (ii)]

Therefore, equation of required ellipse is
$\frac{x^2}{100}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$

questions.q: $P$ is a point on the conic $a^{2}x^{2} + b^{2}y^{2} = a^{2}  \left(a^{2} + b^{2} - y^{2}\right)$ and $S$ is a focus of that conic. $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ on to a directrix of that conic nearer to $S$. If $PM = KSP$, then $K =$
questions.solution:
Given, equation of conic

$a^{2}x^{2} + b^{2}y^{2} = a^{2} \left(a^{2} + b^{2} - y^{2}\right)

$⇒ a^{2}x^{2} + b^{2}y^{2} + a^{2}y^{2} = a^{2} $\left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{a^{2}x^{2}}{a^{2}\left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right)} + \dfrac{y^{2}\left(b^{2} + a^{2}\right)}{a^{2}\left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right)} =1$

$⇒ x^{2} \left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right) + \dfrac{y2}{a2} =1 \ldots \left(i\right)$

$∴$Equation $\left( i\right)$ represents an ellipse whose eccentricity is given by&

$e = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{a2}{a^{2} + b^{2}}} = \dfrac{b}{a^{2} + b^{2}}$

Also, we know that in a conic,

Distance of a moving point $P$ from focus $S = e \timesPerpendicular distance of a point $ P from $directrix \left( PM\right)

$⇒ SP = ePM$

$⇒ PM = $\dfrac{1}{e} SP = KSP$

$∴ K = \dfrac{1}{e} =\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{b}$

questions.q: A line perpendicular to the $X$-axis cuts the circle $x^2+y^2=9$ at $A$ and the ellipse $4 x^2+9 y^2=36$ at $B$ such that $A$ and $B$ lie in the same quadrant. If $\theta$ is the greatest acute angle between the tangents drawn to the curves at $A$ and $B$, then $\tan \theta=$
questions.solution:
Let the equation of line perpendicular to $X$-axis cut the circle $x^2+y^2=9$ at A$ is $(3 \cos \alpha, 3 \sin \alpha)$
Equation of tangent at A$ is $x \cos \alpha+y \sin \alpha=3$
Slope $=-\cot \alpha$
Similarly, cut the ellipse $4 x^2+9 y^2=36$ at $B$ is $(3 \cos \alpha, 2 \sin \alpha$ )
Equation of tangent at $B
\begin{aligned}2 \cos \alpha+3 \sin \alpha$& =6 \\
$\text{ Slope }$& =-$\frac{2}{3}$ \cot \alpha
\end{aligned}$ Angle between tangents is \theta$, then

\tan $\theta=\frac{\left(-\frac{2}{3}+1\right) \cot \alpha}{1+\frac{2}{3} \cot ^2 \alpha}=\frac{\cot \alpha}{3+2 \cot ^2 \alpha}$ Let $\quad \tan \theta=z \Rightarrow z=\frac{\cot \alpha}{3+2 \cot ^2 \alpha}
\because \frac{d z}{d \alpha}=-\left[\frac{\left(3+2 \cot ^2 \alpha\right)\left(\operatorname{cosec}{ }^2 \alpha\right)-\cot \alpha   \left(4 \cot \alpha \operatorname{cosec}^2 \alpha\r$rright)}{$\left(3+2 \cot ^2 \alpha\right)$}\right] For $maxima or minima \frac{d z}{d \alpha}=0\therefore 3 \operatorname{cosec}^2 \alpha+2 \cot ^2 \alpha \operatorname{cosec}^2 \alpha-4 \cot ^2 \alpha \operatorname{cosec}^2 \alpha=0
\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow \cos ^2 $\alpha=\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow \cot \alpha=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\\
& \because \tan \theta=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}}{3+2 \times \frac{3}{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \times \frac{1}{6}=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{6}}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Greatest acute angle when, $\tan \theta=\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{6}}.$

Equation of tangent at $(3 \sqrt{3} \cos \theta, \sin \theta)$ on the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{27}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$ is $\begin{aligned}& \frac{3 \sqrt{3} x \cos \theta}{27}+\frac{y \sin \theta}{1}=1 \\
& \frac{x}{3 \sqrt{3}} \cos \theta+\frac{y \sin \theta}{1}=1

i.e. L=3 $\sqrt{3} \sec \theta+\operatorname{cosec}$ \theta\because $\frac{d L}{d \theta}=3 \sqrt{3} \sec \theta \tan \theta-\operatorname{cosec}$\theta \cot \theta For $maxima or minima \frac{d L}{d \theta}=03 \sqrt{3} \sec \theta \tan \theta-\operatorname{cosec} \theta \cot \theta=0\tan ^3 \theta=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{3}} \Rightarrow \tan \theta=1 \sqrt{3} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$
Minimum at $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$

questions.q: The locus of the midpoints of the portion of the tangents of the ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{1} = 1$ intercepted between the coordinate axes is
questions.solution:
Given: ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{1} = 1$

We know that equation of tangent in parametric form is given by $\dfrac{x}{a}cos\theta + \dfrac{y}{b}sin\theta = 1$

So here $\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2}}cos\theta + \dfrac{y}{1}sin\theta = 1$

Let $A \text{ and } B$ are intersection points of the tangents on the coordinates axes

So $A\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{cos\theta}, 0\right) \text{ and } B\left(0, \dfrac{1}{sin\theta}\right)$

Now let the midpoint of $AB$ is $C\left(h, k\right)$

So using midpoint formula $2h = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{cos\theta}, 2k = \dfrac{1}{sin\theta} . . . \left(i\right)$

Now we have ${sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta = 1$

Using Equation $\left(i\right)$

${\left(\dfrac{1}{2k}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2h}\right)}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4{k}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2{h}^{2}} = 1$

So the required locus $\dfrac{1}{4{y}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2{x}^{2}} = 1$

questions.q: If the normal drawn at one end of the latus rectum of the ellipse $b^{2}x^{2} + a^{2}y^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$ with eccentricity '$e$'& passes through one end of the minor axis, then
questions.solution:
$b^{2}x^{2} + a^{2}y^{2} = a^{2}b^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$

Equation of the normal to $\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$ at $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ is, $\dfrac{a^{2}x}{x1} - \dfrac{b^{2}y}{y1} = a^{2} - b^{2}$

$⇒$ Normal at $\left(ae, \dfrac{b2}{a}\right)$ to one end of latus rectum is

$\dfrac{a^{2}x}{ae} - \dfrac{b^{2}y}{b^{2}a} = a^{2} - b^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{ax}{e} - ay = a^{2} - b^{2}$

$⇒ ab = a^{2} - b^{2}$

$⇒ ab = a^{2} - a^{2} \left(1 - e^{2}\right)$ = a^{2} $\left(1 - 1 + e^{2}\right)$

$⇒ b = ae^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{b}{a} =e^{2}$

$⇒ e^{4} = \dfrac{b2}{a2} =1 - e^{2}$

$∴ e^{4} + e^{2} = 1$

questions.q: A variable tangent to the ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$ makes intercepts on both the axes. The locus of the middle point of the portion of the tangent between the coordinate axes is
questions.solution:
Given:
The equation of ellipse is $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$.

Equation of tangent is $\dfrac{x}{a}cos\theta + \dfrac{y}{b}sin\theta = 1$.

The tangent meets the axes at $A\left(\dfrac{a}{cos\theta}, 0\right)$ and $B\left(0, \dfrac{b}{sin\theta}\right)$.

Let $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ be the midpoint of $AB$.

$\begin{array}{ll}\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{a}{cos\theta} + 0}{2}, \dfrac{0 + \dfrac{b}{sin\theta}}{2}\right) = \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll}⇒ \dfrac{a}{cos\theta} = 2{x}_{1} ⇒ cos\theta = \dfrac{a}{2{x}_{1}}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll}⇒ \dfrac{b}{sin\theta} = 2{y}_{1} ⇒ sin\theta = \dfrac{b}{2{y}_{1}}\end{array}$

Now, ${sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta = 1$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{b}{2{y}_{1}}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{a}{2{x}_{1}}\right)}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{4{y}_{1}^{2}} + \dfrac{{a}^{2}}{4{x}_{1}^{2}} = 1$

$⇒ {a}^{2}{x}_{1}^{2} + {b}^{2}{y}_{1}^{2} = 4$
$∴$ Locus of mid-point is $\dfrac{{a}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} + \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} = 4$.

questions.q: For $k > 0$, the shortest distance from a point $P(1, k)$ on the ellipse $9 x^2+4 y^2-18 x+16 y-11=0$ to one of its directrix is
questions.solution:
We, have, $P(1, k)$ lies on ellipse
$\begin{aligned} & 9 x^2+4 y^2-18 x+16 y-11=0 \\ & \therefore \quad 9+4 k^2-18+16 k-11=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 4 k^2+16 k-20=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad k^2+4 k-5=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad(k+5)(k-1)=0 \Rightarrow k=-5,1 \\ & \end{aligned}\therefore P$ is either $(1,-5)$ or $(1,1)$
Again, equation of ellipse is
$\begin{aligned} & & 9 x^2+4 y^2-18 x+16 y-11 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & & 9(x-1)^2+4(y+2)^2 & =36 \\ \Rightarrow & & \frac{(x-1)^2}{4}+\frac{(y+2)^2}{9} & =0\end{aligned}\therefore$ Eccentricity, $e=\sqrt{1-\frac{a^2}{b^2}}=\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{9}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\therefore$ Equation of directrices are
$\begin{aligned} y+2 & = \pm \frac{b}{e} \Rightarrow y+2= \pm \frac{9}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \Rightarrow y+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}} & =0 \text{ or } y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0\end{aligned}$
Now, distance of $(1,-5)$ from $y+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is
$\left|-5+2+\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}-3$.

Distance of $(1,-5)$ from $y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is $\left|-5+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}+3$

and distance of $(1,1)$ from $y+2-\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}=0$ is
$\left|1+2-\frac{9}{2 \sqrt{5}}\right|=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}-3\therefore$ Shortest distance $=\frac{9}{\sqrt{5}}-3$

questions.q:
Assertion (A) If the tangent and normal to the ellipse $9 x^2+16 y^2=144$ at the point $p \left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) on it meet the major axis in $Q$ and $R$ respectively, then $Q R=$\frac{57}{8}.
Reason (R) If the tangent and normal to the ellipse \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ at the point $P($\theta) on it meet the major axis in $ Q$ and $R$ respectively, then $Q R=\left|\frac{a^2 \sin ^2 \theta-b² \cos ^2 \theta}{a \cos \theta}\right|$The correct answer is
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of $(A)$.
Both $(A)$ and $(R)$ are true but $(R)$ is not the correct explanation of $(A)$.
questions.solution:
Equation of tangent of ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ at $(a \cos \theta, b \sin \theta)$ is
$$
\frac{x \cos \theta}{a}+\frac{y \sin \theta}{b}=1
$$
It cuts the major axis at $Q\left(\frac{a}{\cos \theta}, 0\right)$
Equation of normal of ellipse at $(a \cos \theta, b \sin \theta)$ is
$$
\frac{a x}{\cos \theta}-\frac{b y}{\sin \theta}=a^2-b^2
$$
It cuts the major axis at $R\left(\frac{\left(a^2-b^2\right) \cos \theta}{a}, 0\right)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \text{ Distance } Q R & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{a}{\cos \theta}-\frac{\left(a^2-b^2\right) \cos \theta}{a}\right)^2} \\
& =\left|\frac{a^2-\left(a^2-b^2\right) \cos ^2 \theta}{a \cos \theta}\right| \\
& =\left|\frac{a^2-a^2 \cos ^2 \theta+b^2 \cos ^2 \theta}{a \cos \theta}\right| \\
& =\left|\frac{a^2 \sin ^2 \theta+b^2 \cos ^2 \theta}{a \cos \theta}\right|
\end{aligned}
$$
Put $a=4, b=3, \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$, we get
$$
Q R=\frac{16 \times \frac{3}{4}+9 \times \frac{1}{4}}{4 \times \frac{1}{2}}=\frac{48+9}{8}=\frac{57}{8}
$$
Hence, $\mathrm{A}$ is true, $\mathrm{R}$ is false.

Now, $\frac{d^2 y}{d \theta^2}$ <$0$ for $\cos $\theta=$1-2 a$
Thus, distance $P Q$ is maximum, when $\cos $\theta=1-2 a and $\sin ^2$\theta=-$4 a²+4 a$
Now, required longest distance is
=\sqrt{$\frac{1}{2}+$a²-a+$\left(\frac{1}{2}-a$\right)$(1-2 a)+\frac{1}{4}\left(-4 a²+4 a\right)}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}$+$a²-a+\frac{1}{2}-a$-a+2 a²-a²+a}=\sqrt{2 a²-2 a+1}=\sqrt{1-2 a+2 a²}

& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{196}{q^2}=\frac{\frac{256}{q^2} \times\left(\frac{33 \times 7}{8}\right)^2}{\frac{33 \times 8 q^2+33 \times 256}{8 q^2}}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{196}{q^2}=\frac{32 \times 33 \times 33 \times 7 \times 7}{8 \times 33\left[q^2+32\right]}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{q^2}=\frac{33}{q^2+32}\\
& \Rightarrow q²+32=33 q² \Rightarrow q²=1 \\

&

questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of all real numbers.

Statement I : The function $f: \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = secx + tanx$ is a one - one function.

Statement II : The function $f: [ 0, \infty ) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = x^{2}$ is a one-one function.

Which of the above statements is(are) true?
options: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement II is true, but Statement I is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.solution:
Given,

$\mathbb{R}$ be the set of all real numbers.

Now solving statement I : The function $f: \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = secx + tanx$

Now differentiating the function with respect to $x$ we get,

$f^{'} \left(x\right) = secx \left( secx + tanx\right)$

Now we know that $secx$ is always positive in given domain and& $secx + tanx$ will also be positive as& $tanx$ is negative in& $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$ but& $secx ≥ tanx$ in& $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$

So, $f^{'}\left(x\right) ≥ 0$ hence it is& a one - one function.

Now solving statement II : The function $f: [ 0, \infty ) \to \mathbb{R}$defined by

$f\left(x\right) = x^{2}$

Differentiating the function we get,

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 2x$

$⇒ f^{'}\left(x\right) ≥ 0 ∀ x \in [ 0, \infty )$

Hence it is also a& one-one function.

So both are true.

On putting $x+1=03(-1)+2=A\left[2(-1)^2+3\right]\Rightarrow \quad-3+2=A(5)\Rightarrow \quad A=-\frac{1}{5}$
Now on comparing the coefficients of like power of $x$
Coefficient of $x^20=2 A+B\Rightarrow \quad B=\frac{2}{5}$

We have, $\begin{aligned}& f(x)=3 x-4=y \\

& \Rightarrow \quad f^{-1}(y)=\frac{y+4}{3}\\
& \text{$ and $} \quad g(x)=2+3 x=z \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 x=z-2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{z-2}{3}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad g^{-1}(z)=\frac{z-2}{3}\\
& \therefore \quad g^{-1}\left( f^{-1}(5)\right)=g^{-1}\left[\frac{5+4}{3}\right]= g^{-1}[3] \\
& =\frac{3-2}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\\
&

questions.solution:
Given that $\begin{gathered} \frac{x^3}{(2 x-1)(x+2)(x-3)}= \\ A+\frac{B}{2 x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2}+\frac{D}{x-3} \end{gathered}$ Let $\begin{aligned} f(x) & =\frac{x^3}{(2 x-1)(x+2)(x-3)} \\ & =\frac{x^3}{(2 x-1)\left(x^2-x-6\right)} \\ & =\frac{x^3}{2 x^3-3 x^2-11 x+6} \end{aligned}$ Here we see that the power of $x$ will be same in Nr and Dr. $\therefore$ First we divide the numerator by denominator
$\begin{array}{cc}\Rightarrow & \frac{x^3}{(2 x-1)(x+2)(x-3)} \\ = & \frac{1}{2}+\frac{\frac{3}{2} x^2+\frac{11}{2} x-3}{(2 x-1)(x+2)(x-3)} \\ \Rightarrow & A=\frac{1}{2}\end{array}$

We have,

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
The function $f: R \rightarrow R$ is defined by $f(x)=3^{-x}$. Observe the following statements of it
I. $f$ is one-one
II. $f$ is onto
III. $f$ is a decreasing function
Out of these, true statement are
questions.solution:
Since, $f: R \rightarrow R$ such that $f(x)=3^{-x}$.
Let $y_1 and y_2$ be two elements of $f(x)$ such that $\begin{aligned} \text{$ and $} y_1=y_2 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \quad 3^{-x_1}=3^{-x_2} \Rightarrow x_1=x_2 \\ \text{ and } \end{aligned} Since, if two images are equal, then their elements are equal, therefore it is one-one function
Let y=3^{-x} On differentiating w.r.t.$ x$, we get
\frac{d y}{d x}=-3^{-x} \log 3 < 0$ for every value of $x\therefore$ It is decreasing function
$\therefore$ Statement I and II are true.

questions.q: If $\quad e^{f(x)}=\frac{10+x}{10-x}, x \in(-10,10) \quad$ and $f(x)=k f \left(\frac{200 x}{100+x^2}\right), then $k$ is equal to$
questions.solution:
We have,
$e^{f(x)}=\frac{10+x}{10-x}f(x)=\log \frac{10+x}{10-x}$
Given that $f(x)=k f\left(\frac{200 x}{100+x^2}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \log \frac{10+x}{10-x}=k \cdot \log \left\{\frac{10+\frac{200 x}{100+x^2}}{10-\frac{200 x}{100+x^2}}\right\}=k \log \left\{\frac{1000+10 x^2+200 x}{1000+10 x^2-200 x}\right\}=k \log \left\{\frac{x^2+100+20 x}{x^2+100-20 x}\right\}=k \log \left\{\frac{(x+10)^2}{(10-x)^2}\right\}=2 k \log \frac{10+x}{10-x}\Rightarrow \quad \log \frac{10+x}{10-x}=2 k \log \frac{10+x}{10-x}\therefore \quad 2 k=1 \Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{2}=0.5$
