questions.q: Two small conducting balls of identical mass $20 \mathrm{ g}$ and identical charge $10^{-10} \mathrm{C}$ hang from non-conducting threads of length, $L=300 \mathrm{ cm}$. If the equilibrium separation of balls is $x$ and $x \ll L$ then the magnitude of $x$ is (Assume, $4 \pi \in_0=\frac{1}{9 \times 10^9} \mathrm{ F} / \mathrm{m}$ and $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution: Given, mass of each spherical ball, m=20 $\mathrm{ g}=2 \times10^{-2} \mathrm{ kg},$ g=10 $\mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}^2 charge on each spherical ball, q_1=q_2=q=10^{-10} \mathrm{C}$ and length of thread, L=300 $\mathrm{ cm}=3 \mathrm{ m}$ According to the question, $$ \\ Equilibrium at point $B$, $\begin{aligned} T \cos \theta& =m g \\ T \sin \theta& =F \\ T \sin \theta& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q^2}{x^2} \end{aligned} ($ From Coulomb's law) From Eqn. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{T \sin \theta}{T \cos \theta}=\frac{\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q^2}{x^2}}{m g} \left[\text{ Given, }4 \pi \varepsilon_0=\frac{1}{9 \times 10^9} \mathrm{C}^2$/ $\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{m}^2\right]\therefore m g \tan \theta=9 \times10^9 \cdot \frac{q^2}{x^2}$ From $\triangle A B M$, $\tan \theta=\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{\sqrt{L^2-\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2}}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{4 L^2-x^2}}=\frac{x}{2 L} \quad(\becauseL > x)\therefore$ From Eq. (iii), we get m g $\cdot \frac{x}{2 L}=\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times q^2}{x^2}$ Putting the given values, we get $\begin{array}{rlrl}2 \times10^{-2} \times10 \times \frac{x}{2 \times 3}& =\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 10^{-20}}{x^2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad x³ & =\frac{27}{10^{10}} \mathrm{ m}\\ \Rightarrow \quad x & \quad \frac{3}{10^3 \times 10^{1 / 3}}& =\frac{3}{10^{1 / 3}} \mathrm{ mm} \end{array}$ Therefore, magnitude of equilibrium separation distance of balls is $\frac{3}{10^{1 / 3}} \mathrm{ mm}.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The space between the two large parallel plates is filled with a material of uniform charge density $\rho$. Assume that one of the plate is kept at $x=0$. The potential at any point $x$ between these plates is given by (A$ and $B$ are constants).
$
questions.solution:
According to the question, the space between the two large parallel plates is filled with a material of uniform charge density pi.e., It is a homogeneous medium, therefore the potential at any point between these plates is calculated by Poisson's equation as given below,

\nabla^2 V=-$\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$Since, we have to calculate the potential at any point along $x$-direction, hence the derivative of the potential along $y and z$ directions is zero.
Hence, from Eq. (i), we get

$\frac{d^2 V}{d x^2}=-\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}Integrate on both the $sides, we get

\Rightarrow$\int \frac{d^2 V}{d x^2}$d x=-$\int \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$d x \Rightarrow $\frac{d V}{d x}=\frac{-\rho x}{\varepsilon_0}-A

Integrate on both sides again, we get

$\begin{array}{rlrl}
\Rightarrow& $\int\frac{d V}{d x}d$x & =$\int\frac{-\rho x}{\varepsilon_0}d x-\intA d x \\
V & =\frac{-\rho x^2}{2 \varepsilon_0}-A$ x-B \\
\therefore & V & =-$\left(\frac{+\rho x^2}{2 \varepsilon_0}+A$ x+B\right)$
\end{array}
$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Choose the incorrect statement from the following.
options: The electric field in electrostatics obey principle of superposition
The electric field inside a perfect conductor is zero
The electric dipole will try to orient in a direction opposite to the external electric field
The electric flux passing through any closed surface enclosing the charges remains constant
questions.solution: Third statement is incorrect because electric dipole will always try to orient in the direction of electric field in order to achieve minimum potential energy and maximum stability.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin spherical shell encloses a concentric solid sphere. The radius of the shell is $(0.060)^{\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{ m}$ and its surface charge density is $-10^{-5} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{m}^2$.The radius of the solid sphere is $(0.01)^{\frac{1}{3}} \mathrm{ m}$ and its volumetric charge density is $3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{m}^3. \varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space in $\mathrm{C}^2 / \mathrm{Nm}^2$. The electric flux through a spherical surface concentric with the spherical shell and of radius greater than that of the shell in V-m is
questions.solution:
Electric flux through spherical surface $\begin{aligned}& =\frac{q_{\text{net enclosed }}}{\varepsilon_0}\\
& =\frac{\text{ Charge of sheII }+ \text{ Charge of sphere }}{\varepsilon_0}\\
& =\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\left[\begin{array}{l}4 \pi\left(0.06^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^2\times(-10)^{-6} \\
+\frac{4}{3} \pi\left(0.01^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3\times3 \times10^{-5}
\end{array}\right]
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& =\frac{\pi}{\varepsilon_0}\left\{-0.24 \times10^{-6}+0.39 \times10^{-6}\right\} \\
& =\frac{1.6 \pi \times 10^{-7}}{\varepsilon_0} \mathrm{ V}-\mathrm{m}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting sphere $S_1$ of radius $r_1$ is connected by a conducting wire to another conducting sphere $S_2$ of radius $r_2$, where $r_1=3 \mathrm{ cm}$ and $r_2=2\mathrm{cm}$. Before they are connected, $s_1$ carries charge of 10 units. The electric potential at the point which is at a distance $4 \mathrm{ cm}$ from the centre of $S_1$ and a distance $3 \mathrm{ cm}$ from the centre of $S_2$ is
questions.solution:
When spheres are connected, charges are redistributed such that potential on their surfaces are same.
So, we have $\begin{aligned} q_1+q_2 & =10 \\ \frac{k q_1}{r_1}& =\frac{k q_2}{r_2} \Rightarrow \frac{q_1}{3}=\frac{q_2}{2} \end{aligned}$ and $\frac{k q_1}{r_1}=\frac{k q_2}{r_2} \Rightarrow \frac{q_1}{3}=\frac{q_2}{2}$ Hence, $q_1=6$ units and $q_2=4$ units. Now, potential at some point $P$ distant $4 \mathrm{ cm}$ from $s_1 and 3 \mathrm{ cm}$ from $s_2$ is $\begin{aligned} V & =\frac{k q_1}{r_1}+\frac{k q_2}{r_2}= k \frac{6}{4}+ k \frac{4}{3}\\ & =k\left(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{4}{3}\right)= k \frac{17}{6} V=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{17}{6} V \end{aligned} $

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of radius $r_1=1 \mathrm{ cm}$ carries charge distributed uniformly over it with density $\rho_1=-3 \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{cm}^3$. It is surrounded by a concentric spherical shell of radius $r_2=2 \mathrm{ cm}$ carrying uniform charge density $\rho_2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{cm}^2$. If $E_d$ denotes the magnitude of the electric field at distance $d$ from the common centre of the spheres, then
questions.solution:
Electric field at a point inside inner sphere is only due to charge enclosed.

We use Gauss' law to get,

E=$\left(\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R^3}\right)$ r=$\frac{\rho_R}{3 \varepsilon_0}$ Here,

\rho=-3$\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{cm}^3}\right)$ So,

E=$\frac{-d}{\varepsilon_0} \text{$ or $}|\mathbf{E}|=\frac{d}{\varepsilon_0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two isolated, concentric, conducting spherical shells have radii $R and 2 R$ and uniform charges $q and 2 q$ respectively. If $V_1 and V_2$ are potentials at points located at distances 3 R and $\frac{R}{2}$, respectively, from the centre of shells.
Then the ratio of $\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$ will be
questions.solution:
For point, $r=\frac{R}{2}V_1=$ Potential of surface radius $R+$ Potential of surface radius $2 R$
=$\frac{k q}{R}+\frac{k 2 q}{2 R}=\frac{2 k q}{R}$ For point $\quad r=3 R$,
$V_2=$ Potential due to charges $q$ and $2 q$ assumed to be concentrated at centre $=\frac{k(3 q)}{3 R}=\frac{k q}{R}$
So, ratio $\quad \frac{V_1}{V_2}=2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion (A) Electromagnetic force is enormously strong as compared to gravitational force. Yet, gravity dominates in the large-scale phenomena (e.g. formation of galaxies).
Reason $(R)$ Existence of positive and negative charges make matter mostly electrically neutral.
Which of the following is true?
options: Both $(A)$ and $(R)$ are true and $(R)$ is the correct explanation of $(A)$
Both $(A)$ and $(R)$ are true, but $(R)$ is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Both A and $\mathrm{R}$ true and $\mathrm{R}$ is the correct explanation of A.
"Although the electromagnetic force is far stronger than gravity, it tends to cancel itself out within large objects, so over the largest distances (on the scale of planets and galaxies), gravity is the dominant force."

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The volume charge density in a spherical ball of radius $R$ varies with distance $r$ from the centre as $\rho(r)=\rho_0 \left[1- \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^3\right], where, \rho_0$ is a constant. The radius at which the field would be maximum is
questions.solution:
Given, $\quad \rho(r)=\rho_0  \left[1- \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^3\right]
So, effective charge at $ r$ is q(r)=\int \rho(r) \cdot$ V$
=\$rho_0\lleft[1- $\$left($\frac{r}{R}\right)^3\right]\frac{4}{3} \pir^3$ For maximum value of field,

$\begin{array}{rlrl}& \frac{d q(r)}{d r} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{4}{3} \pi \rho_0 \left[3  r^2\ lleft(1-\frac{r^3}{R^3}\rright)+ r³\left(-\frac{3 r²}{R^3}\right)\right]& =0 \\
\Rightarrow & & 3  r^2-\frac{3 r⁵}{R^3}-\frac{3 r⁵}{R^3} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & r³   =\frac{R^3}{2} \Rightarrowr =\frac{R}{2^{1 / 3}}
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The potential $\phi(x, y)$ of an electrostatic field $\mathbf{E}=a(\hat{y}+x \hat{\mathbf{j}})$ is [a is a constant and $\hat{\mathbf{i}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{j}}$ are unit vectors along $X$ and $Y$ axes]
options: $-2 a x y+c$ (c is a constant)
questions.solution:
(No option is matching)
Using,

\begin{aligned}
\phi$& =-\int \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{d r}\\
\phi & =-\int$ a(y \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{j}$})(d x $\cdot \hat{\mathbf{i}}+$ d y $\cdot \hat{\mathbf{j}})\\
& =-a\left(\int(y d x+x d y)=-a \int$ d(x y)\right. \\
& =-a x y+C

we get
$\therefore$ Potential, $\phi(x, y)=-a x y+C$

questions.q: A point charge of $50\muC$ is placed in the $XY$ plane at a location with radius vector~$\overset{→}{r}0 = 2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}m$ The electric field strength and its magnitude at a point with radius vector~$\overset{→}{r} = 8\overset{^}{i} - 5\overset{^}{j}m$ is $\left({ε}_{o} = 8 . 85 \times {10}^{- 12}C^{2}N - m^{- 2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Separation vector, $= \overset{→}{r} - \overset{→}{r0}$

$= \left(8\overset{^}{i} - 5\overset{^}{j}\right) - \left(2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j}\right)$

$\left|\overset{→}{r} - \overset{→}{r}0\right| =\sqrt{\left(6\right)$^{2} + $\left(- 8\right)$^{2}} =$10$

Electric field strength,

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\left(\dfrac{q}{r2}\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{4 \times \pi \times 8. 85 \times {10}^{- 12}} \times \dfrac{50 \times {10}^{- 6}}{100}$

$= 4495. 9$

$= 4. 495 \times {10}^{3} \approx 4. 5kVm^{- 1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charged identical metal spheres $A$ and $B$ repel each other with a force of $3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ N}$. Another identical wncharged sphere $C$ is touched with sphere $A$ and then it is placed mid-way between $A$ and $B$. Then, the magnitude of net force on $C$ is
questions.solution:
Spheres $A and B$ have the same charge of same nature. When uncharged sphere $C$ is touched with sphere $A$, then charge is transferred to $C$ and this charge is equally divided between two spheres.
Let initially the charge on spheres $A and B$ is $q$. Initially, the repelling force between charged spheres $A and B=3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ N}$ When, sphere $C$, is placed between charged spheres $A and B$, then the force between $A and C$, F_{A C}=$\frac{k \frac{q}{2} \times q / 2}{(r / 2)^2}$ Similarly, between $B and C$ F_{B C}=$\frac{k q \times q / 2}{(r / 2)^2}$ The magnitude of net force on $C, F^{\prime}=F_{B C}-F_{A C}$ Also F=$\frac{k q \times q}{r^2}=3 \times10^{-5} \mathrm{ N}$ So, $\frac{F}{F_{B C}-F_{A C}}=\frac{\left(k q^2 / r^2\right)}{k\left[\frac{q \times q / 2}{(r / 2)^2}-\frac{q / 2 \times q / 2}{(r / 2)^2}\right]}$ Here, $\quad F=3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ N}, F_{B C}-F_{A C}=F^{\prime} \begin{aligned}$& $\frac{3 \times 10^{-5}}{F^{\prime}}$& =$\frac{1}{2-1}=\frac{1}{1}=1 \\ \therefore \quad \text{$ and $} F^{\prime} \text{ and } =3 \times10^{-5} \mathrm{ N} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The electrostatic potential inside a charged sphere is given as $V=A r^2+B$, where $r$ is the distance from the centre of the sphere, $A$ and $B$ are constants. Then, the charge density in the sphere is
questions.solution:
Let the volume charge density be $\rho$. The electric field inside the charged sphere,
E=$\frac{K q r}{R^3}$ where, $R=$ Radius of charged sphere $r=$ Distance of the point $(P)$ inside the sphere As volume charge density is $\rho$, then in terms of charge density, $\begin{aligned} E & =\frac{\rho r}{3 \varepsilon_0}\\ \quad \quad \quad \rho & =\frac{3 E \varepsilon_0}{r} \end{aligned}$ Now, electric field, $E=-\frac{d V}{d r}$ Here, $V=A r^2+B $\begin{array}{ll} \therefore& E=-$\frac{d V}{d r}=$-2 A r+0=-2 A r \\ \therefore & \rho=$\frac{3 E \varepsilon_0}{r}$ \end{array}$ =\frac{3\left(-2 A r \cdot \varepsilon_0\right)}{r}=-6 A \varepsilon_0 $

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Charges $Q$ are placed at the ends of a diagonal of a square and charges $q$ are placed at the other two corners. The condition for the net electric force on $Q$ to be zero is
questions.solution:
Net force on $D$ due to $A and B=\frac{K \sqrt{2} Q q}{a^2}$
Force on $D$ due to $B=\frac{K Q^2}{2 a^2}$ For net electric field on $D$ to be zero $\begin{aligned}$K$\left[\frac{Q^2}{2 a^2}+\frac{\sqrt{2} Q q}{a^2}\right]$& =0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad $\frac{Q}{2}+\sqrt{2}$q & =0 \\ Q & =-2 $\sqrt{2}$q \end{aligned} $\therefore q$ should be negative.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is divided into two charges $q$ and $Q-q$. The value of $q$ such that the force between them is maximum, is
questions.solution:
By Coulomb's law,
When charge $Q$ is divided into two charges $q and Q-q$
F=$\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q \cdot(Q-q)}{r^2}$ The value of $q$
F_{\max }=$\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\frac{Q}{2}\left(Q-\frac{Q}{2}\right)}{r^2} ($ Putting $q=\frac{Q}{0}$ for the maximum force) $\begin{aligned}& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\frac{Q}{2}\left(\frac{Q}{2}\right)}{r^2}\\
& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\frac{Q^2}{4}}{r^2}\\
& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Q^2}{4 r^2}\\
& =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{\left(\frac{Q}{2}\right)^2}{r^2}
\end{aligned}$ So, option (3) is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two concentric hollow spherical shells have radii $r$ and $R(R \gg r)$. A charge $Q$ is distributed on them such that the surface charge densities are equal. The electric potential at the centre is
questions.solution:
We know that, the surface charge densities is $\sigma=\frac{Q}{4 \pi\left(r^2+R^2\right)}$The electric potential at the centre $\begin{aligned} V \text{ and } =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \left[\frac{\sigma \times 4 \pi r^2}{r}+\frac{\sigma \times 4 \pi R^2}{R}\right]\\ \text{ and } =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \times \sigma \times4 \pi \left[\frac{r^2}{r}+\frac{R^2}{R}\right]\\ \text{ and } =\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}(r+R)
\end{aligned} and $\quad $ V=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 \cdot 4 \pi\left(r^2+R^2\right)} \cdot(r+R)$
\Rightarrow \quad $V=\frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{(r+R)}{\left(r²+R²\right)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two small spheres each having equal positive charge $Q$ (Coulomb) on each are suspended by two insulating strings of equal length $L$ (metre) from a rigid hook (shown in figure). The whole set up is taken into satellite where there is no gravity. The two balls are now held by electrostatic forces in horizontal position, the tension in each string is then
questions.solution:
In this case, tension will be equal to force The tension in $each string
\begin{aligned} T & =F \\ & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{Q^2}{(2 L)^2} \\ & =\frac{Q^2}{16 \pi \varepsilon_0 L^2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A proton, a deutron and an $\alpha$-particle having the same momentum, enters a region of uniform electric field between the parallel plates of a capacitor. The electric field is perpendicular to the initial path of the particles. Then the ratio of deflections suffered by them is
questions.solution:
The deflection suffered by charged particle in an electric field is
$y=\frac{q E L D}{m \mu^2}=\frac{q E L D}{p^2 / m} \quad(p=m u)\Rightarrow \quad y \propto \frac{q m}{p^2}\Rightarrow y_p: y_d: y_\alpha=\frac{q_p m_p}{p_p^2}: \frac{q_d m_d}{p_d^2}: \frac{q_\alpha m_\alpha}{p_a^2}$
Since, $\quad p_\alpha=p_d=p_p \quad$ (given)
$m_p: m_d: m_\alpha=1: 2: 4$
and $\quad q_1: q_d: q_\alpha=1: 1: 2\Rightarrow \quad y_b: y_d: y_\alpha=1 \times 1: 1 \times 2: 2 \times 4=1: 2: 8$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point charges $-q$ and $+q$ are located at points $(0,0,-a)$ and $(0,0, a)$ respectively. The electric potential at a point $(0,0, z)$, where $z > a$ is
questions.solution:
Potential at $P$ due to $(+q)$ charge $V_1=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q}{(z-a)}$
Potential at $P$ due to $(-q)$ charge $V_2=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{-q}{(z+a)}$ Total potential at $P$ due to $(A B)$ electric dipole $\begin{aligned} V & =V_1+V_2 \\ & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q}{(z-a)}-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{(z+a)} \\ & =\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{(z+a-z+a)}{(z-a)(z+a)} \end{aligned}\Rightarrow \quad V=\frac{2 q a}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0\left(z^2-a^2\right)}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge of $1 \mu \mathrm{C}$ is divided into two parts such that their charges are in the ratio of $2: 3$. These two charges are kept at a distance $1 \mathrm{ m}$ apart in vacuum. Then, the electric force between them $($ in $N)$ is
questions.solution:
Ratio of charges $=2: 3$
\therefore q_1=$\frac{2}{5} \times1 \mu \mathrm{C} \text{$ and } q_2=$\frac{3}{5} \times1 \mu \mathrm{C}$ Electrostatic force between the two charges $\begin{aligned} F & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\\
& =\frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 3 \times 10^{-6}}{5 \times 5 \times(1)^2}\\
& =2.16 \times10^{-3} \mathrm{ N}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Along the $x$-axis, three charges $\frac{q}{2},-q$ and $\frac{q}{2}$ are placed at $x=0, x=a and x=2 a$ respectively. The resultant electric potential at a point $P$ located at a distance $r$ from the charge $-q(a \lt  r)$ is $\left(\varepsilon_0\right.$ is the permittivity of free space)
questions.solution: As $r \gg a$, so $r > 2 a$ So, potential at point $P \begin{aligned} V & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{q / 2}{r+a}-\frac{q}{r}+\frac{q / 2}{r-a}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q}{2}\left[\frac{1}{r+a}-\frac{2}{r}+\frac{1}{r-a}\right] \\ & =\frac{q}{8 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{r(r-a)-2\left(r^2-a^2\right)+r(r+a)}{r\left(r^2-a^2\right)}\right] \\ & =\frac{q}{8 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{2 a^2}{r\left(r^2-a^2\right)} \\ & =\frac{q a^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^3}(\text{ as } r > a)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two unit negative charges are placed on a straight line. A positive charge $q$ is placed exactly at the mid point between these unit charges. If the system of these three charges is in equilibrium, the value of $q$ (in $\mathrm{C}$ ) is
questions.solution:
For equilibrium, we have
$F_{A B}+F_{A C}=0$ or $\quad \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q}{(d / 2)^2}+\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \times \frac{q_1 q_2}{d^2}=0$ Given, $\quad q_1=q_2=-1 \mu \mathrm{C}$ So, $\quad-\frac{q}{(d / 2)^2}+\frac{1}{d^2}=0q=\frac{1}{4}=0.25 \mathrm{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Along the X-axis, three charges $\frac{q}{2},-q$ and $\frac{q}{2}$ are placed at $x=0, x=a$ and $x=2 a$ respectively. The resultant electric potential at $x=a+r$ (if $a< < r)$ is : ( $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space)
questions.solution:
We have to find the electric potential at point $P$.
$V_P=\left[\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{q / 2}{(r+a)}-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q}{r}+\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{q / 2}{(r-a)}\right]=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{2(r+a)}-\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{2(r-a)}\right]=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{r(r-a)-2\left(r^2-a^2\right)+(r+a) r}{2 r\left(r^2-a^2\right)}\right]=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{r^2-a r-2 r^2+2 a^2+r^2+a r}{2 r\left(r^2-a^2\right)}\right]=\frac{q a^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r\left(r^2-a^2\right)}$ Since, $r > > a$, so we have $r^2-a^2 \approx r^2\therefore \quad V_P=\frac{q a^2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two charges $2 \mathrm{C}$ and $6 \mathrm{C}$ are separated by a finite distance. If a charge of $-4 \mathrm{C}$ is added to each of them, the initial force of $12 \times 10^3 \mathrm{ N}$ will change to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Initial force, } F=k \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \\

questions.q:
An infinite number of electric charges each equal to 5 nano-coulomb (magnitude) are placed along $X$-axis at $x=1 \mathrm{~cm}, x=2 \mathrm{~cm}$, $x=4 \mathrm{~cm}, x=8 \mathrm{~cm} . . .$. and so on. In this set up if the consecutive charges have opposite sign, then the electric field in newton/coulomb at $x=0$ is :
$\left(\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}=9 \times 10^9 \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m}^2 / \mathrm{C}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Electric field intensity due to a point charge. $E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Q}{r^2}$
The consecutive charges are of opposite signs. $\therefore$ Net electric field at $x=0$, is $E=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{Q}{r_1^2}-\frac{Q}{r_2^2}+\frac{Q}{r_3^2}-\frac{Q}{r_4^2} \ldots . . \infty\right]=\frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{r_1^2}-\frac{1}{r_2^2}+\frac{1}{r_3^2}-\frac{1}{r_4^2}+\ldots . \infty\right\rceil=9 \times 10^9 \times 5 \times 10^{-9}\left[\frac{1}{\left(1 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}+\frac{1}{\left(4 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}+\ldots \infty\right\rfloor=\frac{45}{10^{-4}}\left[\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{8^2}+\ldots . \infty\right]=45 \times 10^4\left[\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{8^2} \ldots \infty\right]\left\lceil\frac{1}{1^2}-\frac{1}{2^2}+\frac{1}{4^2}-\frac{1}{8^2} \ldots \infty\right\rfloor=\frac{\frac{1}{1^2}}{1-\left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)^2}\left[\right.$ Sum of infinite GP, $\left.\mathrm{S}_{\infty}=\frac{a}{1-r}\right]=\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{4}{5}\therefore \quad E=45 \times 10^4 \times \frac{4}{5}=36 \times 10^4 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{C}$

29 main scale division $($ MSD $)=30$ vernier scale division (VSD)

$\begin{aligned}

& =0.5^{{}^{\circ}}-\left(\frac{29}{60}\right)^{{}^{\circ}}=\left(\frac{30-29}{60}\right)^{{}^{\circ}}=\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& =1 \min \quad\left[\because 1 \min =\frac{1}{60} \text{ degree }\right]
\end{aligned}$

As the particles move& under gravitational influence, the gravitational force will provide the centripetal force required.&

Gravitational force between two bodies of masses& ${m}_{1} and {m}_{2}$ separated by distance $d$ is given by,~$G\dfrac{{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{d2}$, where~$G$~is the universal gravitational constant.

Net force on the particle& at $A$~due to& particles at $B$~and $C$~is,

$\overset{→}{F}net = \overset{→}{F}AC + \overset{→}{F}AB$

$\overset{→}{F}net = G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\overset{^}{AC} + G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\overset{^}{AB}$.

Here,~$\overset{^}{AB}$~and $\overset{^}{AC}$~are unit vectors along $AB and AC$.

On simplifying vector addition$\left(\text{taking}F = G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\right)$, we get,

${F}_{net} = 2Fcos\left(30 °\right) = 2G\dfrac{M2}{L2}\dfrac{3}{2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M2}{L2}$

From geometry, radius of circle,~$R = \dfrac{L}{3}$.

Since the~force ${F}_{net}$~provides the centripetal force required, so,

$⇒ \dfrac{Mv^{2}}{R} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M2}{L2}$

$⇒ v^{2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{MR}{L2} = \sqrt{3}G\dfrac{M\left(\dfrac{L}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}{L2} = \dfrac{GM}{L}$

$⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{L}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match the following columns.

Codes
$\begin{array}{llll}A & B & C & D\end{array}$
questions.solution:
The potential energy of satellite at distance $r$ from earth is U=$\frac{-G M m}{r}$ So, it is always negative as it is due to attractive gravitation force of earth's field. The kinetic energy of satellite is K=$\frac{G M m}{2 r}$ It is always positive.
The total energy of satellite is $\begin{aligned}\mathrm{TE}$& =K+U=$\frac{G M m}{2 r}-\frac{G M m}{r}$\\
& =-$\frac{G M m}{2 r}
\end{aligned}$ which is negative.
The gravitation potential energy of satellite at infinity is U=-$\frac{G M m}{r}=-\frac{G M m}{\infty}=0 So, the correct match is \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{II}, \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{II}, \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}, \mathrm{D} \rightarrow$ III.
No option is correct.

questions.q: A satellite revolving around the earth at a certain height experiences acceleration due to gravity equal to $\frac{16}{49} g_0$, where $g_0$ is the acceleration due to gravity on the earth's surface. If $R$ is the radius of earth, then the square of time period of the satellite's revolution is equal to $K \left[\frac{\pi^2 R^3}{G M}\right]. The value of $K$ is$
questions.solution: Acceleration due to gravity at height $h$ from the surface of earth, $\begin{aligned} g & =g_0\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2=\frac{16}{49} g_0 \\ \frac{R}{R+h}& =\frac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$ \\ Now, orbital velocity of satellite, $v_0=\sqrt{G M / r}$ \\ Now, time period of revolution, $\begin{aligned} T & =\frac{2 \pi r}{\sqrt{\frac{G M}{r}}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{G M}}\\ T² & =\frac{4 \pi^2 r^3}{G M}=\frac{4 \pi^2}{G M}\left(\frac{7 R}{4}\right)^3\left[\because r=R+h=R+\frac{3 R}{4}=\frac{7 R}{4}\right] \end{aligned}$ \\ $$ \\ Comparing Eqs. (ii) and (iii), we get K=$\frac{343}{16}$

questions.q: A simple harmonic oscillator has an amplitude of $0. 5m$ and a time period of $2$ seconds. What is the magnitude of acceleration when it is displaced from the mean position by $0. 25m ?$
questions.solution:
Magnitude of acceleration in terms of displacement is given by, $a = {ω}^{2}x$
$⇒ a = \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)2x$
$⇒ a = \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{2}\right)^{2} \times 0. 25 = \dfrac{\pi2}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three bodies a ring, a solid cylinder and a solid sphere roll down an inclined plane without slipping. They start from rest. Which of the bodies reaches bottom of plane with minimum velocity?
questions.solution:
Say, the radius of gyration of the body is $K$.
The mass is $m$.
The height is $h$.
The radius of the body is $R$.
According to the conservation of mechanical energy,$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} \left(1 + \dfrac{K2}{R2}\right)or $v^{2} = $\left(\dfrac{2gh}{1 + \dfrac{K2}{R2}}\right)$
Note: It is independent of the mass of the rolling body.
For a ring, $K^{2} = R^{2}$
So, the speed of the ring becomes,${v}_{ring} = $\sqrt{$\dfrac{2gh}{1 + 1}} = \sqrt{gh}$
For a solid cylinder, $K^{2} = \dfrac{R^{2}}{2}$
${v}_{cylinder} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + \dfrac{1}{2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4gh}{3}}$
For a solid sphere, $K^{2} = \dfrac{2}{5} R^{2}$
${v}_{sphere} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + \dfrac{2}{5}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10gh}{7}}$
Among the given three bodies, the solid sphere has the greatest and the ring has the least velocity at the bottom of the inclined plane.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the earth shrinks to $\dfrac{1}{8} of its original volume, while maintaining the same mass, then the duration of the day will be$
questions.solution:
Use the concept of conservation of angular momentum the initial& angular momentum of the earth should be same as final momentum of the earth,& it means,&
${J}_{1} = {J}_{2} ⇒ {I}_{1}{ω}_{1} = {I}_{2}{ω}_{2}$, here the value of the moment of inertia for the solid sphere is, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^{2}$ and, the value of& $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$,

$⇒ \dfrac{2}{5}m\left({R}_{1}\right)2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T1}\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}m\left({R}_{2}\right)2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T2}\right) ⇒ \dfrac{\left({R}_{1}\right)2}{\left({R}_{2}\right)2} = \dfrac{T1}{T2}$

When the original volume becomes one by eight of its original volume then, $\dfrac{1}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left({R}_{1}\right)3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi\left({R}_{2}\right)3 ⇒ {R}_{1} = 2{R}_{2}$,
$⇒ \dfrac{\left(2{R}_{2}\right)2}{\left({R}_{2}\right)2} = \dfrac{24}{T2} ⇒ {T}_{2} = 6h$.&

questions.q: A small disc of mass $500gm$ and radius $5$ cm rolls down an inclined plane without slipping. Speed of its center of mass when it reaches the bottom of the incline plane depends on

The loss in gravitational potential energy is equal to the gain in translational kinetic energy and rotational kinetic energy for the case of maximum velocity of sphere when it reaches ground.&

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}I{ω}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, here the relation, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r}$ and $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^{2}$, it means,

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{5}mr^{2} \times \dfrac{v}{r2}2 + \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}mv^{2} + mv^{2}\right) ⇒ gh = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{7}{5}v^{2}\right) ⇒ v = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}gh}$

Only depends on height and acceleration due to gravity.&

questions.q: A mass $M$ is split into two parts $m_0$ and $M-m_0$. These two masses are then separated by a distance $D$. If the gravitational force between the parts is maximum, then the ratio $\frac{m_0}{M}$ is
questions.solution:
According to given situation,
Again, $m_0$ and $M-m_0$ are kept at a distance $D$ gravitational force,
$F=\frac{G m_0\left(M-m_0\right)}{D^2}F$ will be maximum, when $\frac{d F}{d m_0}=0\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow & \frac{d}{d m_0} \frac{G m_0\left(M-m_0\right)}{D^2}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{d}{d m_0}\left(\frac{G m_0 M-G m_0^2}{D^2}\right)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{G M-2 G m_0}{D^2}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & G M-2 G m_0=0 \Rightarrow M-2 m_0=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 m_0=M \Rightarrow \frac{m_0}{M}=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the escape velocity on earth is $11.2 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{s}$, its value for a planet having double the radius and 8 time the mass of earth is
questions.solution:
Escape velocity of an object on a planetary body,
$v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} \Rightarrow v_e \propto \sqrt{\frac{M}{R}}$
So, $\begin{aligned} \frac{\left(v_e\right)_1}{\left(v_e\right)_2} & =\frac{\sqrt{\frac{M_1}{R_1}}}{\sqrt{\frac{M_2}{R_2}}} \Rightarrow \frac{\left(v_e\right)_1}{\left(v_e\right)_2}=\sqrt{\frac{M_1}{M_2} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1}} \\ \frac{11.2}{\left(v_e\right)_2} & =\sqrt{\frac{M}{8 M} \times \frac{2 R}{R}} \Rightarrow \frac{11.2}{\left(v_e\right)_2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \Rightarrow \frac{11.2}{\left(v_e\right)_2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \left(v_e\right)_2 & =2 \times 11.2 \Rightarrow\left(v_e\right)_2=22.4 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the radius of the earth shrinks by $1 \%$, its mass remaining the same, then the acceleration due to gravity on the earth surface would
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity,
$g_1=\frac{G M}{R_1^2}$
As, $M$ remain constant and $R$ becomes
$R_2=R_1-1 \% \text{ of } R_1=R_1-\frac{R_1}{100}=\frac{99}{100} R_1$
Therefore, the new gravitational acceleration becomes,
$g_2=\frac{G M}{R_2^2}=\frac{G M \times(100)^2}{(99)^2 R_1^2}=\frac{(100)^2}{(99)^2} g_1=1.02 g_1$
Change in the gravitational acceleration,
$g_2-g_1=1.02 g_1-g_1=0.02 g_1$
Hence, the percentage increase is
$\frac{g_2-g_1}{g_1} \times 100=0.02 \times 100=2 \%$
So, if the radius of earth shrinks by $1 \%$, the value of $g$ would increase by $2 \%$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A planet is moving in an elliptical orbit around the sun. The work done on the planet by the gravitational force of the sun
(i) is zero in no part of the motion.
(ii) is zero in some parts of the orbit.
(iii) is zero in one complete revolution.
(iv) is zero in any small part of the orbit.
Which of the following is true?
questions.solution:
Gravitational force is a conservative force, hence work done in a complete cycle will be zero due to zero displacement.
Again, since, work done, $W=\mathbf{F} \cdot d \mathbf{r}=m \mathbf{a} \cdot d \mathbf{r}$ If $\mathbf{a} \perp d \mathbf{r}$, then $W=0$
Clearly, the moments when displacement vector makes $90^{{}^{\circ}}$ angle with acceleration, work done will be zero.

questions.q: Choose the correct statement.
options: Acceleration due to gravity increases with increasing altitude.
Acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass of earth.
A geostationary satellite can have a time period less than 24 h.
Acceleration due to gravity decreases with increasing depth assuming earth to be a sphere of uniform density.
questions.solution:
Acceleration due to gravity at altitude $h$ is
$g_h=\frac{G M}{(R+h)^2}\therefore g_h$ decreases with altitude.
$g=\frac{G M}{R^2}, g \propto M$
Geostationary satellite has a time period of $24 \mathrm{ h}$. $g$ at depth $d$ is

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Find the acceleration of our galaxy, due to the nearest comparably sized galaxy. The approximate masses of each galaxy is $8 \times 10^{11}$ solar mass and they are separated by 2 million light-years. Each galaxy has a diameter of 100000 light year.
(Assume, 1 light year $\approx 10^{16} \mathrm{ m}$, gravitational constant, $G \approx 10^{-10} \left(\frac{\mathrm{Nm}^2}{\mathrm{ kg}^2}\right)$ and mass of sun $=2.0 $\times$10^{30}  \mathrm{ kg} )$
questions.solution:
Here, masses of each galaxy are
$\begin{aligned} m_1 & =m_2=8 \times 10^{11} \text{ solar mass } \\ & =8 \times 10^{11} \times 2 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{ kg} \\ & =16 \times 10^{41} \mathrm{ kg}\end{aligned}$
Distance between galaxies is
$\begin{aligned} d & =2 \times 10^6 \text{ light year } \\ & =2 \times 10^6 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{ m}=2 \times 10^{22} \mathrm{ m}\end{aligned}$
Force of gravitational pull on each of galaxy is
$F=\frac{G m_1 m_2}{d^2}=\frac{10^{-10} \times\left(16 \times 10^{41}\right)^2}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2}$
Acceleration of galaxy is
$\begin{aligned} a & =\frac{F}{m}=\frac{10^{-10} \times\left(16 \times 10^{41}\right)^2}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2 \times 16 \times 10^{41}} \\ & =\frac{10^{-10} \times 16 \times 10^{41}}{\left(2 \times 10^{22}\right)^2}=4 \times 10^{-13} \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of mass $M$ moving with a speed of $2ms^{- 1}$ hits another ball of mass $1$ kg moving in the same direction with a speed of $1ms^{- 1}$. If the kinetic energy of center of mass is $\dfrac{4}{3}Joule$, then the magnitude of $M$ is
questions.solution:
Given: Kinetic energy of the centre of mass $K . E = \dfrac{4}{3}Joule$

The velocity~of centre of mass& ${v}_{cm}$ is equal to the summation of the momentum of each ball to the total mass of the system.

${v}_{cm} = \dfrac{2 \times M + 1 \times 1}{M + 1} = \dfrac{2M + 1}{M + 1}$

Now kinetic energy of the centre of mass is~$K . E = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$~

$K . E = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(M + 1\right)\left(\dfrac{2M + 1}{M + 1}\right)2 = \dfrac{4}{3}$

$\left(2M + 1\right)2 = \dfrac{8 ( M + 1 )}{3}$

$3\left(2M + 1\right)2 = 8\left(M + 1\right)$

$12M^{2} + 4M - 5 = 0$

$M = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0 . 5kg$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet of mass $m$ moves around the Sun along an elliptical path with a period of revolution $T$. During the motion, the planet's maximum and minimum distance from Sun is $R$ and $\frac{R}{3}$ respectively. If $T^2=\alpha R^3$, then the magnitude of constant $\alpha$ will be
questions.solution:
Given, mass of planet $=\mathrm{m}$
Maximum and minimum distance of the planet from Sun is $R and \frac{R}{3}$, respectively.
$\therefore$ Semi-major axis of elliptical path of planet around the Sun,
$a=\frac{R+\frac{R}{3}}{2}=\frac{2 R}{3}\therefore$ Time period of planet is given by
$\begin{aligned} & T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{G m}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\left(\frac{2 R}{3}\right)^3}{G m}} \\ & T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{8 R^3}{27 G m}}\end{aligned}$
Square on the both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned} T^2 & =4 \pi^2 \cdot \frac{8 R^3}{27 G m} \\ T^2 & =\frac{32 \pi^2}{27 G m} \cdot R^3=\alpha R^3 \\ \therefore \quad \alpha & =\frac{32 \pi^2}{27 G m}\end{aligned}$
Hence, the magnitude of constant $\alpha$ will be $\frac{32}{27} \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{G m}$

questions.q: If a planet of mass $6.4 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{ kg}$ can be compressed into a sphere such that the escape velocity from its surface is $8 \times 10^4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$, then what showld be the radius of the sphere? (Gravitational constant, $G=6.6 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{Nm}^2 \mathrm{ kg}^2$ )
questions.solution:
As, we know, the escape velocity of a planet is given as
or $\begin{aligned} \text{ and } v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}}\\ \text{ and } v_e^2=\frac{2 G M}{R}
\end{aligned}$ Radius of sphere $=\frac{2 G M}{v_e^2}$
where, $M=6.4 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{Kg}, v_e=8 \times 10^4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$
and $G=6.6 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{ N}-\mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{ kg}^{-2}$
So, $R=\frac{2 \times 6.6 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.4 \times 10^{23}}{64 \times 10^8}=13.2 \times 10^3\Rightarrow R=13.2 \mathrm{ km}$
Hence, option (2) is correct.

If the initial phase is $45 ° ,$ the equation of its motion is (Assume, $x  \left(t\right)$ as the position of the particle at time $t)$

$x \left(t\right) = 0. 1sin \left(4t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a spherical planet which is rotating about its axis such that the speed of a point on its equator is $v$ and the effective acceleration due to gravity on the equator is $\frac{1}{3}$ of its value at the poles. What is the escape velocity for a particle at the pole of this planet.
questions.solution:
We know that the escape velocity of a particle from the surface of a planet is given by

$\begin{aligned}$v_e & =$\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 g R^2}{R}} \quad\left[\because$G M=g R²\right] \\
& =$\sqrt{2 g R}
\end{aligned}$where, $g=$ acceleration due to gravity, and $R=$ radius of the planet
Given, the velocity at equator, $v_E=V$ and acceleration due to gravity at equator,

$\begin{aligned}$g_E & =$\frac{1}{3}$g_P \\
\therefore \quad g_P & =3 g_E
\end{aligned}$ The escape velocity of a particle at equator,

v_E=\sqrt{2 g_E R}$and at poles,

$\begin{aligned}$v_P & =$\sqrt{2 g_P R}$\\
& =$\sqrt{2 \times 3 g_E R}=\sqrt{3} \sqrt{2 g_E R}$\\
& =$\sqrt{3}$v_E \\
& =$\sqrt{3} \mathrm{v}
\end{aligned}

[$From Eq. (i)]
[From Eq. (ii)]

$\left[\because$v_E=V\right]

Hence, $\sqrt{3} v$ is the escape velocity for a particle at the pole of this planet.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An artificial satellite of mass $m$ revolves around the earth at a height $h$ with a speed $v$. How much power (energy per second) will it require to keep itself moving with constant speed in the orbit of radius $r$ ?
questions.solution:
Speed of satellite is constant, so by workenergy theorem, $\begin{aligned}$& W=K_f-K_{\dot{i}} \\
& W=$\frac{1}{2}$ m v²-$\frac{1}{2}$ m v² \\
& W=0
\end{aligned} As, work on satellite is zero, so power required will also be zero, i.e. $ P=\frac{W}{t}=0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The mass density inside a solid sphere of radius $r$ varies as $\rho(r)=\rho_0\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^\beta$, where $\rho_0$ and $\beta$ are constants and $r$ is the distance from the centre. Let $E_1$ and $E_2$ be gravitational fields due to sphere at distance $\frac{R}{2}$ and $2 R$ from the centre of sphere. If $\frac{E_2}{E_1}=4$, the value of $\beta$ is
questions.solution:
$\text{ Mass enclosed$ in a sphere of radius } r $\text{ is }$ \\ $\begin{aligned} M_p & =\int \rho d V=\int_0^\rho \rho_0\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^\beta \cdot4 \pi r^2 d r \\
& =\left[\frac{4 \pi \rho_0}{R^\beta} \cdot \frac{r^{\beta+3}}{\beta+3}\right]_0^r
\end{aligned} So, mass enclosed$ in $a sphere of radius \frac{R}{2}$ is M_1=$\frac{4 \pi \rho_0}{R^\beta} \frac{\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^{\beta+3}}{(\beta+3)}=\frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3)} \times \frac{1}{2^{\beta+3}}$ and mass enclosed in radius $R$ is M_2=$\frac{4 \pi \rho_0}{R^\beta} \cdot \frac{R^{\beta+3}}{\beta+3}=\frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3}$ So, gravitational field intensities are E_1=$\frac{G M_1}{\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2}=\frac{4 G}{R^2} \times \frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3} \times \frac{1}{2^{\beta+3}}$ and $E_2=\frac{G M_2}{(2 R)^2}=\frac{G}{4 R^2} \times \frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3}$ As $\frac{E_2}{E_1}=4$ we get $\begin{array}{cc}& \frac{\frac{G}{4 R^2} \times \frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3}}{\frac{4 G}{R^2} \times \frac{4 \pi \rho_0 R^3}{\beta+3} \times \frac{1}{2^{\beta+3}}}=4 \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \frac{2^{\beta+3}}{16}=4 \Rightarrow 2^{\beta+3}=64 \\
2^\beta .2^3=2^6 \Rightarrow 2^\beta=8 \Rightarrow 2^\beta=2^3 \Rightarrow \beta=3
\end{array} $

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the pole of the earth, a body of mass $m$ is imparted a velocity $v_0$ directed vertically up. If $M$ is the mass of the earth, $R$ its radius and $g$ is the free-fall acceleration on its surface, then the height $h$ to which the body will ascent is (neglect air resistance)
questions.solution:
If body moves up to height $h$, then by conservation of energy, we get $\begin{gathered} \Delta(\mathrm{KE})=\Delta(\mathrm{PE})$\\
0-$\frac{1}{2}$ m $v_0^2=\frac{-G M m}{R}-  \left(-\frac{G M m}{R+h}\right)$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{v_0^2}{2 G m}=\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{R+h} \Rightarrow \frac{R(R+h)}{h}=\frac{2 g R²}{v_0^2}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad $h=\frac{R}{\left(\frac{2 g R}{v_0^2}-1\right)} \text{ or }}}h=\frac{ R v_0^2}{2 g R-v_0^2}
\end{gathered}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The density of a solid sphere of radius $R$ is $\rho(r)=20 \frac{r^2}{R^2}$ where, $r$ is the distance from its centre. If the gravitational field due to this sphere at a distance $4 R$ from its centre is $E$ and $G$ is the gravitational constant, then the ratio of $\frac{B}{G R}$ is
questions.solution:
Volume of a spherical shell of thickness $d r$ and of radius $r$ is $d V=4 \pi r^2 d r
So, mass of $this sheIl is d M=\rho d V=$\frac{20 r^2}{R^2} \cdot4 \pi$ r^2 $\cdot$ d r Total mass of complete solid sphere is $\begin{aligned}& M=\int_0^R d M=\int_0^R \frac{80 \pi r^4}{R^2} d r \\ \Rightarrow \quad & M=\frac{80 \pi R^5}{5 R^2}=16 \pi R^3 \end{aligned} Due to this mass $ M$, gravitational field intensity at a distance 4 R$ from its' centre is $\begin{array}{cc}& B=\frac{G M}{(4 R)^2}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & E=$\frac{G \cdot 16 \pi R^3}{(4)^2 R^2}\\ \Rightarrow \quad & B=G \pi R \Rightarrow \frac{B}{G R}$=\pi \end{array}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet of mass $m$ moves in a elliptical orbit around an unknown star of mass $M$ such that its maximum and minimum distances from the star are equal to $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively. The angular momentum of the planet relative to the centre of the star is
questions.solution: According to the law of conservation of angular momentum, $\begin{aligned} m v_1 r_1 & =m v_2 r_2 \\ \Rightarrow \quad v_2 & =\frac{v_1 r_1}{r_2} \end{aligned}$ From the law of conservation of total mechanical energy. $\frac{-G M m}{r_1}+\frac{1}{2}$ m v_1^2=-$\frac{G M m}{r_2}+\frac{1}{2}$ m v_2^2 From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get v_1=$\sqrt{\frac{2 G M r_2}{\left(r_1+r_2\right) r_1}}$ Angular momentum, $\begin{aligned}& L=m v_1 r_1=m\left(\sqrt{\frac{2 G M r_2}{\left(r_1+r_2\right) r_1}}\right) \times r_1 \\ & L=m \sqrt{\frac{2 G M r_1 r_2}{r_1+r_2}} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The bodies of masses $100 \mathrm{~kg}$ and $8100 \mathrm{~kg}$ are held at a distance of $1 \mathrm{~m}$. The gravitational field at a point on the line joining them is zero. The gravitational potential at that point in $\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kg}$ is $\left(G=6.67 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{Nm}^2 / \mathrm{kg}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Mass of first body $\left(m_1\right)=100 \mathrm{~kg}$
Mass of second body $\left(m_2\right)=8100 \mathrm{~kg}$
Distance between two bodies $=1 \mathrm{~m}$
Distance of null point from $100 \mathrm{~kg} \begin{aligned}$& x=$\frac{d}{\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}+1}$\\
& x=$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{8100}{100}}+1}
\end{aligned}$or,

x=$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{8100}{100}}+1}$or,

$\begin{aligned}$x & =$\frac{1}{9+1}=\frac{1}{10}$\\
& =0.1 $\mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}$The gravitational potential at that point is given by

$\begin{aligned}$& =-G$\left(\frac{m_1}{0.1}+\frac{m_2}{0.9}\right)$\\
& =-6.67 $\times$10^{-11}$\left(\frac{100}{10^{-1}}+\frac{8100}{9 \times 10^{-1}}\right)$\\
& =-6.67 $\times$10^{-11}(1000+9000) \\
& =-6.67 $\times$10^{-7} $\mathrm{~J}$/ $\mathrm{kg}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is revolving very close to a planet of density $\rho$. The period of revolution of satellite is
questions.solution:
We know that,
Period of revolution
Let, $T$ be the time of one revolution of the satellite.
Then,

$\begin{aligned}T & =\frac{2 \pi r}{v_0}=\frac{2 \pi\left(R_p+h\right)}{v_0}\\
T & =\frac{2 \pi\left(R_p+h\right)}{\left[G M_{\ominus} /\left(R_\rho+h\right)\right]^{1 / 2}}\\
\because \quad v_0 & =\sqrt{\frac{G M_\rho}{\left(R_p+h\right)}}\\
T & =2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\left(R_p+h\right)^3}{G M_p}}
\end{aligned}$ Again, $\quad G M_e=g R_e^2\therefore \quad T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\left(R_p+h\right)^3}{g R_\rho^2}}$
If the planet is supposed to be a sphere of mean density $\rho$, then the mass of the planet is given by

$\begin{aligned}M_\rho & =\text{ volume } \times \text{ density }\\
& =\frac{4}{3} \pir_\rho^3 \cdot \rho
\end{aligned}So,

T=\sqrt{\frac{3 \pi\left(R_p+h\right)^3$}{G \rho R_p^3}}If a satellite is orbiting very close$ to the planet's surface \left(h \ll R_p\right), then putting$h=0 in $eq. (iii), we have

\begin{aligned}T & =\sqrt{\frac{3 \pi R_\rho^3}{G \rho R_\rho^3}}\\
\Rightarrow \quad T & =\sqrt{\frac{3 \pi}{G \rho}$}$\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The gravitational force acting on a particle, due to a solid sphere of uniform density and radius $R$, at a distance of $3 R$ from the centre of the sphere is $F_1$. A spherical hole of radius $(R / 2)$ is now made in the sphere as shown in the figure. The sphere with hole now exerts a force $F_2$ on the same particle. Ratio of $F_1$ and $F_2$ is
questions.solution: Gravitational force due to solid sphere is F_1=$\frac{G M m}{(3 R)^2}=\frac{G M m}{9 R^2}$ \\ where, $M and m$ are mass of solid sphere and particle respectively. Gravitational force on particle due to sphere with cavity $\begin{aligned}F_2 & =\frac{G M m}{9 R^2}-\frac{G \left(\frac{M}{8}\right)m}{(5 R / 2)^2}\\ & =\frac{G M m}{R^2} \left[\frac{1}{9}-\frac{4}{8 \times 25}\right]\\ & =\frac{G M m}{R^2}\left[\frac{41}{50 \times 9}\right]\\ \therefore \quad \frac{F_1}{F_2}& =\frac{50}{41} \end{aligned}$

If a particle of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is moved from the origin to the point $(12 \mathrm{ m}, 5 \mathrm{ m})$ in this region, the change in gravitational potential energy is

We have,
$\begin{aligned} d V & =-E \cdot d r=-(5 \mathbf{i}+12 \mathbf{j}) \cdot(12 \mathbf{i}+15 \mathbf{j}) \\ & =(60+60)=-120\end{aligned}$
The change in gravitational potential energy
$U=m d V=2 \times(-120)=-240 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A launching vehicle carrying an artificial satellite of mass $m$ is set for launch on the surface of the earth of mass $M$ and radius $R$. If the satellite is intended to move in a circular orbit of radius $7 R$, the minimum energy required to be spent by the launching vehicle on the satellite is
$($ Gravitational constant $=G$ )
questions.solution:
The energy of artificial satellite at the surface of the earth
$E_1=-\frac{G M m}{R}$
When the satellite is intended to move in a circular orbit of radius $7 R$, then energy of artificial satellite
$E_2=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{G M m}{7 R}$
The minimum energy required
$E=E_1-E_2=-\frac{G M m}{R}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{G M m}{7 R}\right)=\frac{-14 G M m+G M m}{14 R}=-\frac{13 G M m}{14 R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards from the surface of the earth with a velocity equal to half the escape velocity. If $R$ is the radius of the earth, maximum height attained by the body from the surface of the earth is
questions.solution:
Maximum height attained by a projectile

Velocity of body $=$ half the escape velocity
$v=\frac{v_e}{2}\begin{aligned}
\text{or} \quad v=\frac{\sqrt{2 g R}}{2} \Rightarrow v^2=\frac{2 g R}{4} \\
\text{or} \quad v^2=\left(\frac{g R}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}$
Now, putting value of $v^2$ in Eq. (i), we get
$\begin{aligned}
h & =\frac{\frac{g R}{2} \cdot R}{2 g R-\frac{g R}{2}}=\frac{g R^2 / 2}{3 g R / 2} \\
\text{ or } \quad h & =\frac{R}{3}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The escape velocity of a body on the earth's surface is $v_e$.A body is thrown up with a speed $\sqrt{5}$v_e$.Assuming that the sun and planets do not influence the motion of the body, velocity of the body at infinite distance, is :$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In planetary motion the areal velocity of position vector of a planet depends on angular velocity $\omega$ and the distance of the planet from sun $r$. The correct relation for areal velocity is
questions.solution:
Areal velocity $\frac{d A}{d t}$ depends on angular velocity $(\omega)$ and distance of the planet from sun.
$\frac{d A}{d t} \propto w^a r^b \Rightarrow \frac{d A}{d t}=K \omega^a r^b$
Writing the dimensional formula on both sides,
$\left[\mathrm{L}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]=k\left[\mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]^a[\mathrm{~L}]^b$
On comparing, $-a=-1 \Rightarrow a=1b=2\therefore \quad \frac{d A}{d t} \propto \omega r^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is launched into a circular orbit of radius $R$ around earth while a second satellite is launched into a orbit of radius $1.02 R$. The percentage difference in the time periods of the two satellites is :
questions.solution:
From Kepler's law,
$T^2 \propto R^3 \Rightarrow \frac{T_1^2}{T_2^2}=\frac{R_1^3}{R_2^3}\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right)^{3 / 2}=\left(\frac{R}{1.02 R}\right)^{3 / 2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\left(\frac{50}{51}\right)^{3 / 2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{50}{51}\left(\frac{50}{51}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{50}{51} \times 0.99\frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{0.97}{1} \Rightarrow T_1=0.97 x, T_2=x$
Difference $=T_2-T_1=x-0.97 x=0.03 x\%$ difference $=\frac{0.03 x}{x} \times 100=3 \%$

questions.q: A body is projected up with a velocity equal to $\frac{3}{4}$ th of the escape velocity from the surface of the earth. The height it reaches is (Radius of the earth $=R$ )
questions.solution:
Velocity of projection $v=\frac{3}{4} v_e$
where, $v_e=$ escape velocity $=\sqrt{2 g R}$
Maximum height attained by the body $\begin{aligned} h \text{ and } =\frac{v^2 R}{2 g R-v^2}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{\left(\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{2 g R}\right)^2 \times R}{2 g \mathbb{R} - \left(\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{2 g R}\right)^2}=\frac{\frac{9}{16} \times 2 g R \times R}{2 g R-\frac{9}{16} \times 2 g R}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{\frac{9}{16} \times 2 g R^2}{2 g R\left(1-\frac{9}{16}\right)}=\frac{\frac{9}{16} R}{\frac{7}{16}}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{9}{7}$ R
\end{aligned}

questions.q: Mass $M$ is divided into two parts $x m$ and $(1-x) m$. For a given separation the value of $x$ for which the gravitational attraction between the two pieces becomes maximum is

Force of gravitation $F \propto m_1 m_2\begin{aligned} & F=k m_1 m_2 \\ & F=k(x m)(1-x) \times m\end{aligned}$
For $F$ to be maximum $\frac{d F}{d x}=0\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{d x}[k(x m)(1-x) \times m] & =0 \\ m^2-2 x m^2 & =0 \\ \therefore \quad x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the temperature of a gas is increased from $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $159^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, the increase in the rms speed of the gas molecules is
questions.solution: RMS speed of gas, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}}}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad V_{\mathrm{mss}} \alpha \sqrt{\mathrm{T}} \\ & \text{ Initial temperature, } \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{i}}=27+273=300 \mathrm{k} \\ & \text{ Final temperature, } \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{f}}=159+273=432 \mathrm{k} \\ & \% \text{ increase$ in $RMS speed }=\frac{\sqrt{432}-\sqrt{300}}{\sqrt{300}} \times 100 \\ & =\frac{20.78-17.32}{17.32} \times 100 \\ & =19.78 \approx 20\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
$V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}}}$ At $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=27+273=300 \mathrm{ K}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{R}(300)}{\mathrm{M}}} \text{$ and $} \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_2}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{R}(432)}{\mathrm{M}}} \\ & \text{ at } \mathrmT^{\prime}=159+273=432\end{aligned}\therefore$ Percentage increase in the $\mathrm{r} \mathrm{ms}$ speed
$=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{mms}_2}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}}{\mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{rms}_1}}\right) \times 100=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{3 R}{M}}(\sqrt{432}-\sqrt{300})}{\sqrt{\frac{3 R}{M}}(\sqrt{300})} \times 100=\left(\frac{20.78-17.32}{17.32}\right) \times 100 \approx 20 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\mathrm{N}$ molecules each of mass $\mathrm{m}$ of gas $\mathrm{A}$ and $2 \mathrm{ N}$ molecules each of mass $2 \mathrm{ m}$ of gas $\mathrm{B}$ are contained in a vessel which is maintained at temperature $T$. The mean square velocity of the molecules of gas B is denoted by $V_2^2$ and the mean square of the $\mathrm{X}$-component velocity of the molecules of gas $A$ is denoted by $V_1^2$, then $\frac{V_1}{V_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The mean square velocity of gas molecule is given by
$\begin{aligned} & v^2=\frac{3 K T}{m} \\ & \text{$ for $gas A, } \\ & v_A^2=\frac{3 K T}{m} \\ & v^2=v_x^2+v_y^2+v_z^2 \quad\left(\because v_x^2=v_y^2=v_z^2\right) \\ & v^2=3 v_x^2 \Rightarrow v_x^2=\frac{v^2}{3} \\ & v_1^2=v_x^2=\frac{3 K T}{3 m}=\frac{\dot{K} T}{m}\end{aligned}\mathrm{v}_1=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{KT}}{\mathrm{m}}}$...(1)
For gas B, $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}} \mathrm{v}_2^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}} ; \mathrm{v}_2=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}}}$...(2)
Divide equation (1) by ( 2 ), we have $\frac{\mathrm{v}_1}{\mathrm{v}_2}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{KT}}{\mathrm{m}}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{KT}}{2 \mathrm{ m}}}}$

questions.q: Air is filled at $60^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ in a vessel of open mouth. The vessel is heated to a temperature $t^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ so that $\frac{1}{4}$ th of the air is escaped from the vessel. Assuming air as ideal gas and the volume of the vessel remaining constant, then the value of ' $t$ ' is
questions.solution:
Initial temperature, $T_1=60^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=60+273=333 \mathrm{ K}$ Mass of the air left in the vessel, $M_2=M-\frac{M}{4}$
=$\frac{3 \mathrm{M}}{4}$ Here pressure and volume remain constant from ideal gas equation $\begin{aligned}& P V=n R T \\
& P V=\left(\frac{M}{m}\right) R T
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \mathrm{MT}=\text{ constant }\\
& \mathrm{M}_{1} \mathrm{ T}_{1}-\mathrm{M}_{2} \mathrm{ T}_{2} \\
& \mathrm{ T}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{M}_1 \mathrm{ T}_1}{\mathrm{M}_2}=\frac{\mathrm{M} \times 333}{3 \mathrm{M}} \times4 \\
& =444 \mathrm{ K}\\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{T}_{2}=171^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas at $127^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is compressed suddenly to $\frac{8}{27}$ of its initial volume. If $\gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ for an ideal gas, then rise in its temperature is
questions.solution:
The condition for adiabatic process is $\mathrm{TV}^{\gamma-1}=$ constant

Before compression, $\mathrm{T}_1 \mathrm{ V}_1^{\gamma-1}=$ const.
After compression, $\mathrm{T}_2 \mathrm{ V}_2^{\gamma-1}=$ const.
Dividing (ii) by (i):

\begin{aligned}$ \mathrm{T}_{2}  \mathrm{ V}$_{{2}}$^{\gamma-$1}=$\mathrm{T}_{1} \mathrm{ V}_{1}$^{\gamma-$1} \\
& \frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{ T}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{ V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}\\
 \mathrm{ T}_{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V}_1}{\mathrm{ V}_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}\left(\mathrm{ T}$_{{1}}$\right) \\
 \mathrm{T}_{2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{V} \times 27}{8 \mathrm{ V}}\right)^{\frac{5}{3}-1}[400]=\frac{9}{4}$ \times400 \\
& =900 $\mathrm{ K}$.
\end{aligned}Change$ in $temperature,

\begin{aligned}
& \Delta$\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{T}_{2}- \mathrm{T}_{1}=900-400 \\
 \Delta \mathrm{T}$=$500  \mathrm{ K}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An insulating cylinder contains 4 moles of an ideal diatomic gas. When a heat $\mathrm{Q}$ is supplied, to it, 2 moles of the gas molecules dissociate. If the temperature of the gas remains constant, then the value of $Q$ is $\text{ ( } \mathbf{R} $$\text{ - universal gas constant) }$
questions.solution:
Heat supplied " $Q$ " is given by: $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}\\
& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{Initial}_{\text{Internal Energy }}\\
& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}=\text{ Final Internal Energy }
\end{aligned}$ Initially cylinder contains 4 moles of diatomic gas, $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{n} \left(\frac{\mathrm{f}}{2} \mathrm{RT}\right)\\
& \mathrm{U}=4[- \mathrm{RT}]=10 \mathrm{RT}
\end{aligned}2 moles of diatomic gas dissociate into monoatomic gas. Hence there are 4 moles of monoatomic gas and 2 moles of diatomic gas. Final Internal Energy is given by: \begin{aligned}
& U_f=n\left(\frac{f}{2}R T\right)+n^{\prime}\left(\frac{f^{\prime}}{2}-R T\right) \\
& =4\left(\frac{3}{2}R T\right)+2\left(\frac{5}{2}R T\right) \\
& =11 R T
\end{aligned} Thus Heat supplied is, \begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}\\
& =11 \mathrm{RT}-10 \mathrm{RT}=\mathrm{RT}\\
& \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{RT} .
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Statement (I) : Gas thermometers are less sensitive than liquid thermometers.

Statement (II) : The ratio of universal gas constant and avagadro's number is called Boltzman's constant.

Statement (III) : The density of a given mass of a gas at constant pressure is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature.

The correct option among the following is
options: Statements I, II, III are true.
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false.
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false.
Statements I, II, III are false.
questions.solution:
Thermal expansion in gases is more than thermal expansion in liquids. Therefore, gas thermometers are more sensitive than liquid thermometers.

The ratio of universal gas constant and avagadro's number is called Boltzman's constant. $k = \dfrac{R}{NA}$

At constant pressure, $V ∝ T$& therefore, the density of a given mass of a gas at constant pressure is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature.

The rms speed of gas molecules at a temperature $T$ is given by,

${v}_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}} ⇒ \dfrac{vHe}{v{N}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M{N}_{2}}{MHe}} ⇒ {v}_{He} = 100\sqrt{7}ms^{- 1}$.

questions.q: A cylinder consists of a gas mixture of helium and oxygen. If the mass of helium is $4 \mathrm{~g}$ and the mass of oxygen is $32 \mathrm{~g}$, then the ratio of specific heat of the mixture $\left(C_p / C_V\right)$
questions.solution:
Mass of helium, $m_{\mathrm{He}}=4 \mathrm{ g}$
Mass of oxygen, $m_{\mathrm{O}}=32 \mathrm{ g}$
Helium is a monoatomic gas.
$\therefore$ Degrees of freedom, $f_1=3$
Oxygen is a diatomic gas.
$\therefore$ Degrees of freedom, $f_2=54 \mathrm{ g}$ helium contains $N_1=N_A=6.023 \times 10^{23}$ number of molecules
$32 \mathrm{ g}$ oxygen contains $N_2=N_A$ number of molecules.
(As atomic mass of oxygen is $16 \mathrm{ g}$ ) $\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad\frac{C_p}{C_V}$& =$\gamma\\ \text{$ and $} =\frac{N_1\left(2+f_1\right)+N_2\left(2+f_2\right)}{N_1 f_1+N_2 f_2}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{N_A(2+3)+N_A(2+5)}{3 N_A+5 N_A}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{5+7}{3+5}=\frac{12}{8}=\frac{3}{2}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature at which the rms speed of molecules in hydrogen gas will be double of its initial value at $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
The rms speed of molecules in hydrogen gas is

$v_{\mathrm{rms}$}=$\sqrt{\frac{3 k_B T}{m}}$where,
$m=$ mass of hydrogen,
$k_B=$ Boltzmann's constant
and $T=temperature in $kelvin.

\therefore \quad v_${\text{rms }}$ \propto$\sqrt{T}$Initial temperature, $T_1=(27+273 \mathrm{~K})=300 \mathrm{~K}$
If initial rms speed be $v_1$.
Final rms speed, $v_2=2 v_1$ at temperature $T_2$.

$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore & $\frac{v_1}{v_2}$& =$\sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}}$\\
& \Rightarrow & $\left(\frac{v_1}{2 v_1}\right)^$2= & $\frac{T_1}{T_2}$\\
& \Rightarrow & T_2 & =4 T_1=4 $\times$300 $\mathrm{~K}=$1200 $\mathrm{~K}$\\
& \therefore & T_2 & =(1200-273)^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}=$927^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A molecule is travelling in air at $300 \mathrm{ K}$ and $1 \mathrm{ atm}$, and the radius of the molecule is $0.6 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$. Calculate the approx. mean free path of the molecule. (The number density is $2.44 \times 10^{25}$ molecules $/ \mathrm{m}^3$ )
questions.solution:
Given that, temperature, $T=300 \mathrm{ K}$
Pressure, $p=1$ atm $=1.01 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$
Radius, $r=0.6 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$, diameter $d=1.2 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{ m}$
Number density, $\rho=2.44 \times 10^{25}$ molecules $/ \mathrm{m}^3$
Boltzmann constant, $K=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{JK}^{-1}$
Now, mean free path, $\lambda=\frac{K T}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 p} \begin{aligned}
\lambda$& =$\frac{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.414 \pi \times\left(1.2 \times 10^{-10}\right)^2 \times 1.01 \times 10^5}$\\
& =$\frac{0.2}{\pi} \times10^{-5} \mathrm{ m}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The following figure shows a Carnot engine that works between temperatures ${T}_{1} = 400K$ and ${T}_{2} = 200K$ and drives a Carnot refrigeration that works between temperatures ${T}_{3} = 350K$ and ${T}_{4} = 250K .$ The quantity $\dfrac{Q3}{Q1}$ will be
questions.solution:
Efficiency of Carnot engine is given by, $η = \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}\right) . . . \left(1\right)$
$⇒ 1 - \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} = 1 - \dfrac{200}{400}, \left(∵ W = {Q}_{1} - {Q}_{2}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} = \dfrac{200}{400} = \dfrac{1}{2} . . . \left(2\right)$

For refrigerator, $COP$ is given by, $COP = \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{W} = \dfrac{{T}_{4}}{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}} . . . \left(3\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{\left({Q}_{3} - {Q}_{4}\right)}{{Q}_{4}} = \dfrac{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}}{{T}_{4}}$
$⇒ \left(\dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{4}} - 1\right) = \left(\dfrac{{T}_{3}}{{T}_{4}} - 1\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{4}} = \dfrac{{T}_{3}}{{T}_{4}} = \dfrac{350}{250} = \dfrac{7}{5} . . . \left(4\right)$

On multiplying $\left(1\right) \text{ and } \left(3\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{W}{{Q}_{1}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{W} = \left(\dfrac{{T}_{1} - {T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{{T}_{4}}{{T}_{3} - {T}_{4}}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{400 - 200}{400}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{250}{350 - 250}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{1}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{4} . . . \left(5\right)$

On multiplying $\left(2\right) \text{ and } \left(4\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{1}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{4}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{7} = \dfrac{5}{14}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} \times \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{5}{7}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{2}{7} . . . \left(6\right)$

On multiplying $\left(6\right)\text{by}\left(1\right)$, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{2}}{{Q}_{3}} \times \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{{Q}_{2}} = \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{1}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{1}}{{Q}_{3}} = \dfrac{4}{7}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{Q}_{3}}{{Q}_{1}} = \dfrac{7}{4} = 1 . 75$

questions.q: A body cools from $70 ° C$ to $40 ° C$ in $5min.$ Calculate the time it takes to cool from $60 ° C$ to $40 ° C.$ The temperature of the surrounding is $20 ° C.$
questions.solution:
In the first case, the average temperature of the liquid

$= \dfrac{70 + 40}{2} = 55 ° C$.~
Excess temperature $= 55 - 20 = 35 ° C$

$\dfrac{d{θ}_{1}}{dt} = \dfrac{40 - 70}{5} = - 6 ° C{minutes}^{- 1}$

$- 6 = K \times 35$~...$\left(1\right)$

In the second case, the average temperature of liquid, $= \dfrac{60 + 40}{2} = {50}^{o}C$ .
Excess temperature $= 50 - 20 = 30 ° C$.
Rate of fall in temperature$⇒ \dfrac{d{θ}_{2}}{dt}$
$\dfrac{d{θ}_{2}}{dt} = - \dfrac{60 - 40}{tmin}$
$- \dfrac{20}{tmin} = K \times 30$ ...$\left(2\right)$
Divide $\left(1\right)$~by& $\left(2\right)$,~
$\dfrac{- 6}{\dfrac{- 20}{tmin}} = \dfrac{K \times 35}{K \times 30} ⇒ \dfrac{7}{6} = \dfrac{3 \times {t}_{min}}{10} ⇒ {t}_{min} = 3 . 89min$

Recall the formula of efficiency of Carnot's engine in terms of source and sink temperature,& $η = 1 - \dfrac{T2}{T1}$, here ${T}_{2} = 500K$, it means,
$0 . 5 = 1 - \dfrac{500}{T1} . . . . . \left(1\right)$ when the efficiency becomes,& $0 . 8$ then,&

from the equation one and two,

questions.q: Consider a two stage Carnot engine. In the first stage heat ${Q}_{1}$ is absorbed at temperature $T$ and heat ${Q}_{2}$ is expelled at temperature $\alphaT$ (where $\alpha < 1$). In the second stage heat ${Q}_{2}$ is absorbed at temperature $\alphaT$ and heat ${Q}_{3}$ is expelled at temperature $\betaT ( \beta < \alpha ).$& The efficiency of the Carnot engine will be
questions.solution:
The formula of efficiency of Carnot's engine in terms of sink temperature and source temperature is, $η = 1 - \dfrac{TSink}{TSource}$, in the two-stage Carnot's engine the source temperature is initial one and sink temperature will be the final one, it means, ${T}_{Sink} = \betat \text{ and } {T}_{Source} = T$
$⇒ η = 1 - \dfrac{\betaT}{T} = 1 - \beta$.&

questions.q: All gases deviate from gas laws at
questions.solution: At high pressure, the volume occupied by gas molecules does not approach to zero and at low temperature, the contribution of intermolecular forces becomes significant. Hence, at high pressure and low temperature, all gases deviate from gas laws.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Mean free path of molecules in a polyatomic gas is independent of
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \text{ Mean free path } & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 n_V} \\ & =\frac{\mathbf{v} t}{\sqrt{2}\left(\pi d^2 \mathbf{v} t\right) n_V}=\frac{\mathbf{v} t}{\sqrt{2}(V) n_V}\end{aligned}$
where, $d=$ size (diameter) of a molecule,
$n_V=$ number of molecules per unit volume,
$=$ number density of the molecules,
$\mathbf{v}=$ average velocity of gas molecules,
$t=$ time interval between two successive collisions
and $\quad V=$ volume of the molecule.
So clearly, mean free path depends on number density of the molecules, volume of the molecule, temperature of the gas (as average velocity of gas molecules depend on temperature of the gas).
But mean free path doesn't depend on gas constant $R$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If a gas has $n$ degrees of freedom, then the ratio of $\frac{C_p}{C_V}$ is
questions.solution:
For a gas with $n$ degree of freedom,
$\begin{aligned}
C_p & =\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right) \cdot R \quad \text{ and } C_V=\frac{n}{2} R \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{C_p}{C_V} & =\frac{\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right) R}{\frac{n}{2} \cdot R}=\left(\frac{n+2}{n}\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an ideal gas, if the masses of all molecules are doubled and their speeds are halved, then the ratio of initial and final pressures of the gas is
questions.solution:
Pressure of an ideal gas is given by
$p=\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}\left(\mathbf{v}^2\right)$
When mass of molecule is doubled and speed is halved, pressure becomes
$p^{\prime}=\frac{1}{3} \frac{(2 m) N}{V} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{v}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2}\left\{\frac{1}{3} \frac{m N}{V}(\mathbf{v})^2\right\}$
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} p^{\prime} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{p}{p^{\prime}}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow p: p^{\prime}=2: 1\end{aligned}$

Mass of water, $m = 100kg$ and temperature of vapour $T = 100 ° C$.

The relation of heat and latent heat of vaporization is given as,$Q = m{L}_{v}$

$Q = 100 \times 22. 6 \times {10}^{5} = 22. 6 \times {10}^{7}J$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider an ideal gas at pressure $p$, volume $V$ and temperature $T$. The mean free path for molecules of the gas is $L$. If the radius of gas molecules, as well as pressure, volume and temperature of the gas are doubled, then the mean free path will be
questions.solution:
Given, initial values of pressure, volume,
temperature, radius of molecule of gas and mean free path are $P p, V, T, r and L$, respectively.
$\therefore$ Mean free path,
$\begin{aligned} \lambda & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p} \\ \therefore \quad L & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p}\end{aligned}$
According to question if the radius of gas molecules, as well as pressure, volume and temperature of gas are doubled then
$\begin{aligned} \lambda^{\prime} & =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} R \cdot 2 T}{\pi \times 4 r^2 \times N \times 2 p} \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2 \sqrt{2} R T}{\pi r^2 N p}=\frac{L}{4}\end{aligned}$
(From Eq. (i))
Hence, the mean free path will be $\frac{L}{4}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel of volume $V$ contains ideal gas having mass density $\rho$ at temperature $T$ and pressure $p$. After a portion of the gas is let out, the pressure in the vessel is decreased by $\Delta p$. The mass of the released gas is
questions.solution:
Given, initial value of volume, pressure and temperature of an ideal gas in vessel, V_1=V, p_1=p $\text{$ and } T_1=T and density of gas $=\rho$
When, $\Delta V$ volume of gas is let out, hence pressure of gas is decreased to $\Delta p$.
Then, $\begin{aligned}& V_2=V-\Delta V \\
& p_2=p-\Delta p \\
& T_2=T_1
\end{aligned} By an ideal gas equation, $\begin{array}{rlr}$\frac{p_1 V_1}{T_1}$& =$\frac{p_2 V_2}{T_2}$& \\
$\frac{p_1}{p_2}$& =$\frac{V_2}{V_1}$& {$\left[\because T_1=T_2\right]$} \\
$\frac{p}{p-\Delta p}$& =$\frac{V-\Delta V}{V}=$1-$\frac{\Delta V}{V}$& \\
$\frac{\Delta V}{V}$& =1-$\frac{p}{p-\Delta p}$& \\
& =$\frac{p-\Delta p-p}{p-\Delta p}$& \\
\Delta V & =$\frac{-\Delta p V}{p-\Delta p}$&
\end{array}$ \therefore$ Mass of released gas $=\rho \Delta V=\frac{\rho \Delta p V}{p-\Delta p}$ \approx $\frac{\rho \Delta p V}{p}$

30 & =$\sqrt{300 T}$\\

T & =3 $\mathrm{ K}

atomic mass of molecules of gas A, m_A=4 u$
and temperature of gas, $T_A=27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$
For diatomic gas $B$,
atomic mass of molecules of gas $B$,
$m_B=2 \times 20 \mathrm{u}=40 \mathrm{u}$
Temperature of gas, $B=\mathrm{T}_B$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A polyatomic gas has $f$ vibrational degrees of freedom, then the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure to that at constant volume will be
questions.solution:
For a polyatomic atom value of specific heat at constant volume, $C_V=(3+f) R$ where, $f=$ vibration degree of freedom and $R=$ gas constant.
Now, $\begin{aligned}& C_p=C_V+R \\
& C_p=(3+f) R+R \\
& C_p=(4+f) R
\end{aligned} Now, ratio$ of  C_p and C_V$\frac{C_p}{C_V}=\frac{4+f}{3+f}$

As $V$ and $T$ are same for both gases, we can write

$\left.\begin{array}{rl}$p_1 V & =n_1 R T \\

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Uranium has two isotopes of masses 235 and 238 wits. If both of them are present in wranium hexafluoride gas, find the percentage ratio of difference in rms velocities of two isotopes to the rms velocity of heavier isotope.
questions.solution:
Given,
Mass of first uranium isotope $=238$ units
Mass of second uranium isotope $=235$ units
We know that, $\begin{aligned}& v_{\text{rms }} & =\sqrt{\frac{\gamma R T}{M}}\\
\Rightarrow & v_{\text{rms }} & \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}
\end{aligned}$ So, the percentage ratio of difference in rms velocity of isotopes is given by $\begin{aligned}& \frac{V_{\mathrm{rms}_2}-V_{\mathrm{rms}_1}}{V_{\mathrm{rms}_2}} \times100 \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{M_1}-\sqrt{M_2}}{\sqrt{M_1}} \times100 \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{238}-\sqrt{235}}{\sqrt{238}} \times100
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& =\frac{15.427-15.329}{15.427} \times100=\frac{0.097}{15.427} \times100 \\
& =6.34 \times10^{-3} \times100=0.634 \approx0.64
\end{aligned}
$

questions.q: A block is kept on a rough horizontal surface. The acceleration of the block increases from $6 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ to $11 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ when the horizontal force acting on it increases from 20 N to 30 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the surface is (Acceleration due to gravity $=10\mathrm{ms}^{-2}$ )
questions.solution:
Acceleration of the block, $\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{F}-\mathrm{fi}}{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}-\mu \mathrm{img}}{\mathrm{m}}$

$\therefore a_1=\frac{F_1-\mu m g}{m} \Rightarrow \sigma=\frac{20-\mu m g}{m}$...(i) Also, $a_2=\frac{F_2-\mu \mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{m}} \Rightarrow 11=\frac{30-\mu \mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{m}}$..(ii) From eq (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{6}{11}=\frac{20-\mu \mathrm{mg}}{30-\mu \mathrm{mg}} \Rightarrow \mu=\frac{8}{\mathrm{mg}}=\frac{8}{\left(\frac{30-20}{11-6}\right) \times 10}=0.4$

questions.q: A 20 ton truck is travelling along a curved path of radius 240 m. If the center of gravity of the truck above the ground is 2 m and the distance between its wheels is 1.5 m , the maximum speed of the truck with which it can travel without toppling over is (Acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ )
questions.solution:
Let the maximum speed of the truck with which it can travel without toppling $=V_{\max }=$ ?
Here $\frac{m V_{\max }^2 \mathrm{ h}}{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{mg} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$ where $\mathrm{h}=$ height of centre of gravity of truck above the ground, $R=$ radius of curved path, $d=$ distance between the wheels of truck
$\therefore \mathrm{V}_{\max }^2=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Rgd}}{2 \mathrm{ h}}}=\sqrt{\frac{240 \times 10 \times 1.5}{2 \times 2}}=\sqrt{60 \times 15}=30 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$

questions.q: A car is moving on circular track banked at an angle of $45^{{}^{\circ}}$. If the maximum permissible speed of the car to avoid slipping is twice the optimum speed of the car to avoid the wear and tear of the tyres, then the coefficient of static friction between the wheels of the car and the road is
questions.solution:
Maximum speed $V_{\max }=\sqrt{\frac{r g(\mu+\tan \theta)}{1-\mu \tan \theta}}$
and optimum speed $V_{\mathrm{o}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{rg} \tan \theta}$
Given $\theta=45^{{}^{\circ}}$ and $V_{\max }=2 V_0\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{rg}(\mu+\tan \theta)}{1-\mu \tan \theta}}=2 \sqrt{\operatorname{rg} \tan \theta}$
Squaring both sides $\frac{(\mu+\tan \theta)}{(1-\mu \tan \theta)}=4 \tan \theta\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \frac{\mu+\tan 45^{{}^{\circ}}}{1-\mu \tan 45^{{}^{\circ}}}=4 \tan 45^{{}^{\circ}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mu+1}{1-\mu}=4 \\
& \Rightarrow \mu+1=4-4 \mu \Rightarrow 5 \mu=3 \therefore \mu=\frac{3}{5}=0.6
\end{aligned}$

or, $\frac{\mathrm{v}-0}{4}=\frac{5-(0.2 \times 0.5 \times 10)}{0.5} \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}=\frac{5-1}{0.5} \times 4=32 \mathrm{ m} / $$\mathrm{s}$$ Therefore kinetic energy of the block in a time of 4 s $=$\frac{1}{2}$ m v^2=$\frac{1}{2}$ \times 0.5 \times(32)^2=256 $\mathrm{ J}$

questions.q: Two blocks of masses $W_1$ and $W_2$ are suspended from the ends of a light string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. If the pulley is pulled up with an acceleration ' $\mathrm{g}$ ', then the tension in the string will be
questions.solution: For mass $\mathrm{W}_1 \begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{a}-\mathrm{W}_{1}$ a_0=$\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T}\\ & \mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{a}-\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}=\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T}$\\ & $\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{a}=2 \mathrm{~W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T} \end{aligned}$For mass $\mathrm{W}_2 \begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{o}}=\mathrm{T}-\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{~g}\\ & \mathrm{~W}_{2} \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{~g}=\mathrm{T}-\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{~g}$\\ & $\mathrm{~W}_{2} \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{T}-2 \mathrm{~W}_{2} \mathrm{~g} \end{aligned}$Adding equation (i) and (ii), We have $\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{W}_{1} \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{W}_{2} \mathrm{a}=$2 $\mathrm{~W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-2 \mathrm{~W}_{2} \mathrm{~g}$\\ & $\mathrm{a}=\frac{2 \mathrm{~g}\left(\mathrm{~W}_1-\mathrm{W}_2\right)}{\mathrm{W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2} \end{aligned}$Put this value in equation (i) $\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{W}_{1} \times \frac{2 \mathrm{~g}\left(\mathrm{~W}_1-\mathrm{W}_2\right)}{\mathrm{W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}=2 \mathrm{~W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T}$\\ & $\frac{2 \mathrm{gW}_1^2}{\mathrm{~W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}-\frac{2 \mathrm{gW}_1 \mathrm{~W}_2}{\mathrm{~W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}=$2 $\mathrm{~W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T}\\ & \mathrm{T}=2 \mathrm{~W}_{1} \mathrm{~g}-\frac{2 \mathrm{gW}_1^2}{\mathrm{~W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}+\frac{2 \mathrm{gW}_1 \mathrm{~W}_2}{\mathrm{~W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}$\\ & =$\frac{2 \mathrm{~g}\left[\mathrm{~W}_1^2+\mathrm{W}_1 \mathrm{~W}_2-\mathrm{W}_1^2+\mathrm{W}_1 \mathrm{~W}_2\right]}{\mathrm{W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2}$\\ & =$\frac{4 \mathrm{~W}_1 \mathrm{~W}_2 \mathrm{~g}}{\mathrm{~W}_1+\mathrm{W}_2} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: A person initially at rest, starts walking towards east without slipping or skidding. What is the type of friction acting on the person from the ground and in which direction the frictional force acts?
questions.solution:
When the person starts walking towards East, he pushes the ground in the backward direction [i.e., West]. Since friction acts in opposite direction so the frictional force will act in East direction. Since the person is walking kinetic friction will act.
Hence option (4) is the correct answer.

The block will& start slipping when the slope of the curve will be equal to $tan\theta$ where $\theta$ is angle of repose.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of masses $1$ kg and $2$ kg connected by a light rod and the system is slipping down a rough incline angle $45 °$ with the horizontal. The frictional coefficient at both the contacts is $0. 4$. If the acceleration of the system is $\alpha\sqrt{2}$, the value of $\alpha$ is (Use $g = 10ms^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
Frictional& force acting on both the block will be kinetic in nature.

Therefore,

${f}_{1} = \mu{m}_{1}gcos45 ° = 0. 4 \times 1 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\sqrt{2}N$

Similarly,

${f}_{2} = \mu{m}_{2}gcos45 ° = 0. 4 \times 1 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 4\sqrt{2}N$

Now, net force along the incline in the downward direction will provide the required acceleration,

${m}_{1}gsin45 ° + {m}_{2}gsin45 ° - {f}_{1} - {f}_{2} = \left({m}_{1} + {m}_{2}\right) \times \left(\alpha\sqrt{2}\right) ⇒ 5\sqrt{2} + 10\sqrt{2} - 2\sqrt{2} - 4\sqrt{2} = 3\left(\alpha\sqrt{2}\right) ⇒ \alpha = 3$
