(i) and (ii), we have $K_{\mathrm{rot}}=\frac{1}{24} \times A L \rho \times L^2 \omega^2=\frac{1}{24} A L^3 \rho \omega^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere and a solid cylinder, each of mass $M$ and radius $R$ are rolling with a linear speed on a flat surface without slipping. Let $L_1$ be magnitude of the angular momentum of the sphere with respect to a fixed point along the path of the sphere. Likewise $L_2$ be the magnitude of angular momentum of the cylinder with respect to the same fixed point along its path. The ratio $\frac{L_1}{L_2}$ is
questions.solution:
We take origin as fixed point.

Now, angular momentum about origin $O=$ angular momentum due to linear motion of centre of mass + angular momentum due to rotation of body about its' centre of mass
$\therefore \quad L_O=L_{\text{linear motion }}+L_{\text{rotational motion }}=m v R+I \omega=m R^2 \omega+I \omega \quad[\therefore v=R \omega]=\left(m R^2+I\right) \omega$
For solid sphere, $I=\frac{2}{5} m R^2$
and for solid cylinder, $I=\frac{1}{2} m R^2$
So, $\left(L_{\text{sphere }}\right)_{\text{about ' } O \text{ ' }}=\left(m R^2+\frac{2}{5} m R^2\right) \omega=\frac{7}{5} m R^2 \omega$ and $\left(L_{\text{sphere }}\right)_{\text{about ' } O}=\left(m R^2+\frac{1}{2} m R^2\right) \omega=\frac{3}{2} m R^2 \omega$
So, ratio of $\frac{L_{\text{sphere }}}{L_{\text{cylinder }}}=\frac{\frac{7}{5} m R^2 \omega}{\frac{3}{2} m R^2 \omega} \Rightarrow \frac{L_1}{L_2}=\frac{14}{15}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A planet is moving in a circular orbit. It completes $2$ revolutions in $360days$. What is its angular frequency?
questions.solution:
Given: The planet completes $2$ revolutions& in $360$ days.

One rotation of the planet& moves $2\piradians$ angle.

Thus, angular frequency $\omega = \dfrac{θ}{t}$, where $\theta$ represents the angle moved by the object and $t$ represents the time taken by the object to travel through $\theta$.

$\omega = \dfrac{2 \times 2\pi}{360} = 0. 0348 = 3. 5 \times {10}^{- 2}rad{day}^{- 1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular disc of mass $12 \mathrm{ kg}$ and radius $0.5 \mathrm{ m}$ rotates with an angular velocity of $100 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. The rotational kinetic energy of the disc is
questions.solution:
Given, mass of a circular disc, $M=12 \mathrm{ kg}$,
radius, $R=0.5 \mathrm{ m}$,
angular velocity, $\omega=100 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}\therefore$ Rotational kinetic energy of the disc,
$\begin{aligned} & K=\frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 \\ = & \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} M R^2 \cdot \omega^2 \quad\left[\because I=\frac{1}{2} M R^2\right]\end{aligned}$
Putting the given values in the above relation,
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{4} \times 12 \times(0.5)^2 \times 100 \times 100 \\ & =7500 \mathrm{ J}=7.5 \times 10^3 5 \mathrm{ J}=7.5 \mathrm{ kJ}\end{aligned}$
Hence, the rotational kinetic energy of the disc is $7.5 \mathrm{ kJ}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The distance between Sun and Earth is $1.6 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{ m}$ and the radius of Earth is $6.4 \times 10^6 \mathrm{ m}$. The ratio of the angular momentum of Earth around the Sun to the angular momentum around its own axis is approximately (Assume Earth as a solid sphere with uniform mass density and rotates around the Sun in a circular path.)
questions.solution:
Given, the distance between the Sun and
Earth, $r_1=1.6 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{ m}$
Radius of earth, $R_e=6.4 \times 10^6 \mathrm{ m}$
Angular momentum of Earth around the Sun,
$L_1=M_e v_1 r_1=M_e \cdot \frac{2 \pi r_1}{T_1} \cdot r_1L_1=2 \times 3.14 \times 6.0 \times 10^{24} \times \frac{\left(1.6 \times 10^{11}\right)^2}{365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60}\left(\because\right.$ Mass of earth, $M_e=6.0 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{ kg} and T_1=365$
days)
$L_1=3.06 \times 10^{40} \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}^2 / \mathrm{s}$
Angular momentum of Earth about its own axis, where, moment $L_2=I \omega$ of inertia of Earth (uniform solid sphere) around its own axis, $I=\frac{2}{5} M_e R_e^2$.
or $\begin{aligned} I & =\frac{2}{5} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24} \times\left(6.4 \times 10^6\right)^2 \\ & \simeq 9.8 \times 10^{37} \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}^2\end{aligned}$
The earth's angular velocity, $\omega=\frac{2 \pi}{1 \text{ day }}=\frac{2 \pi}{24 \times 60 \times 10}=7.3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}\therefore \quad L_2=9.8 \times 10^{37} \times 7.3 \times 10^{-5} \approx 7.2 \times 10^{33} \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{L_1}{L_2}=\frac{3.06 \times 10^{40}}{7.2 \times 10^{33}}=4.3 \times 10^6$
The ratio of angular momentum of Earth around the Sun to the angular momentum around its own axis is $4.3 \times 10^6$ approximately. Hence, the correct option is (c).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform sphere of radius $R$ and mass $m$ is placed on an inclined plane which makes an angle $45^{{}^{\circ}}$ to the horizontal. For which of the following value of coefficient of friction, the sphere rolls without slipping. Select incorrect option.
questions.solution: Given, radius of sphere $=R$ mass of sphere $=m$ and the angle of inclination in inclined plane, $\theta=45^{{}^{\circ}}$. $\text{ The linear acceleration of solid sphere is given by }$ \\ $\begin{array}{ll}$a=$\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\frac{I}{M R^2}}=\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\frac{2}{5} M R^2}$& {$\left[\because$I=$\frac{2}{5}$M R²\right]} \\ a=$\frac{5}{7}$g \sin $\theta$& \end{array} Applying Newton's second law of motion for linear motion of the centre of mass, $m g \sin \theta-f=m a$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow$f=m g \sin $\theta-$m a & =m g \sin $\theta-$m $\frac{5}{7} \cdot$g \sin $\theta$\\ & =$\frac{2}{7}$m g \sin $\theta \end{aligned}\therefore$ Coefficient of friction $\left(\mu_s\right)=\frac{f}{N}=\frac{\frac{2}{7} m g \sin \theta}{m g \cos \theta}$ =$\frac{2}{7} \tan \theta$To prevent slipping, $\mu_s \geq \frac{2}{7} \tan \theta$ \mu_s \geq $\frac{2}{7} \quad\left[\because \tan$45^{{}^{\circ}}=1\right] Hence, $\frac{3}{7}, \frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{5}{8}$ are all greater than $\frac{2}{7}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A circular ring of mass $10 \mathrm{ kg}$ rolls along a horizontal floor. The center of mass of the ring has a speed $1.5 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. The work required to stop the ring is
questions.solution:
Given,
mass of a circular ring, $m=10 \mathrm{~kg}$
speed of centre of mass of the ring

Here, I=m R^2 and $\omega=\frac{v}{R}\begin{aligned}$& =$\frac{1}{2}$m R²$\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^$2+$\frac{1}{2}$m v²=$\frac{1}{2}$m v²+$\frac{1}{2}$m v²=m v² \\
& =10 $\times($1.5)^2=22.5 $\mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}$According to work-energy theorem, work required to stop the ring.
$\omega=$ change in kinetic energy

=K_f-K_i=0-22.5=-22.5 $\mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere of mass $5 \mathrm{ kg}$ rolls on a plane surfaces. Find its kinetic energy at an instant when its centre moves with speed $4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$.
questions.solution:
As we know, the rotational kinetic energy of a body is given by,

$\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2}$m v²$\left[$1+$\frac{k^2}{R^2}\right]$where,$k=$ radius of gyration
Given, $m=5 \mathrm{~kg}, v=4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} and k=\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} R$
Hence, $\mathrm{KE}=\frac{5}{2} \times 4^2\left[1+\frac{2}{5}\right] \Rightarrow \mathrm{KE}=40 \times \frac{7}{5}=56 \mathrm{~J}$
Hence, the correct option is (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid spherical ball rolls on a horizontal surface at $10ms^{- 1}$ and continues to roll up on an inclined surface as shown in the figure. If the mass of the ball is $11$ kg and frictional losses are negligible, the value of $h$, where the ball stops and starts rolling down the inclination is (Assume $g = 10ms^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
Given,

Initial velocity of solid spherical ball is $v = 10m{s}^{- 1}$

Mass of ball rolling on the surface is $m = 11kg$

Applying work energy theorem,

$W = ∆ KE$

${W}_{g} = K{E}_{f} - K{E}_{i} . . . \left(1\right)$

Now, initial kinetic energy of spherical ball is ${K}_{i} = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}\right)$

And final kinetic energy is given by

${K}_{f} = 0$

Work done due to gravity is 

${W}_{g} = - mgh$

Substitute the values in equation (1) we get

$⇒ - mgh = 0 - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 11 \times {10}^{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{2}{5}\right)$

Where, $\dfrac{{k}^{2}}{{R}^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{350}{50} = 7m$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three bodies, a ring, a solid disc and a solid sphere roll down the same inclined plane without slipping. The radii of the bodies are Identical and they start from rest. If $V_S, V_R$ and $V_D$ are the speeds of the sphere, ring and disc, respectively when they reach the bottom, then the correct option is
questions.solution:
Given, radii of ring, solid disc and solid sphere are identical, say $R$
When a body of mass $m$ starting from rest rolls down an incined plane, then the velocity of body when it reaches at the ground is given by v=$\sqrt{\frac{2 g h}{1+\frac{k^2}{R^2}}}$ where, $h=$ height of inclined plane,
$R=$ radius of body,
and $k=$ radius of gyration
For a ring, $k^2=R^2\therefore$ Speed of the ring, $v_R=\sqrt{\frac{2 g h}{1+\frac{R^2}{R^2}}}=\sqrt{g h}$
For a solid sphere, $k^2=\frac{2 R^2}{5}$
\therefore $\text{ Speed of the solid sphere, }$ v_s=$\sqrt{\frac{2 g h}{1+\frac{2}{5}}}$ From Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), it is clear that V_S>V_D>V_R $\text{. }$

The density of material of the sphere is $\rho=A r^\alpha$, where $r$ is the radial distance, $\alpha$ and $A$ are constants. questions.q: A solid sphere is rolling without slipping on a semi-circular track of radius $10 \mathrm{ m}$ as shown in the figure. To what maximum angle $\theta$ from the vertical will the sphere travel before it comes back down? Neglect the rolling friction between the sphere and the track. (Take, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )

As there is no slip, energy is conserved.
So, mechanical energy of ball at bottom $=$ mechanical energy of ball at top
$\Rightarrow \quad m g r+\frac{1}{2} m v_{\mathrm{COM}}^2+\frac{1}{2} I_{\mathrm{COM}} \omega^2=m g h$
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{3}{4} v^2=g(h-r) \quad\left[\therefore I=\frac{m r^2}{2}\right.$ and $\left.v=r \omega\right]$
and $r$ can be neglected.
So,
$$
h=\frac{3 v^2}{4 g}
$$
Also, $h=R(1-\cos \theta) \Rightarrow \frac{3 v^2}{4 g}=R(1-\cos \theta)$
With values, we get
$$
\cos \theta=\frac{3}{10} \Rightarrow \theta=\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)
$$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
For a system to follow the law of conservation of linear momentum during a collision, the condition is :
(1) total external force acting on the system is zero.
(2) total external force acting on the system is finite and time of collision is negligible.
(3) total internal force acting on the system is zero.
questions.solution:
From Newton's second law,
$F=\frac{d p}{d t}$
If $F=0$, then $\frac{d p}{d t}=0\Rightarrow \quad p=$ constant
Thus, if total external force acting on the system is zero, then linear momentum of the system remains conserved.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $8 a$ and mass $6 m$ lies on a smooth horizontal surface. Two point masses $m$ and $2 m$ moving in the same plane with speed $2 v$ and $v$ respectively strike the rod perpendicularly at distances $a$ and $2 a$ from the mid point of the rod in the opposite directions and stick to the rod. The angular velocity of the system immediately after the collision is :
questions.solution:
Applying conservation of angular momentum about point $O$,
$m(a)(2 v)+2 m(2 a)(v)=I \omega$ or $\omega=\frac{6 m a v}{I}$...(i) Now, $\quad I=\frac{6 m(8 a)^2}{12}+m\left(a^2\right)+2 m(2 a)^2=32 m a^2+m a^2+8 m a^2=41 \mathrm{ma}^2$ Hence, from Eq. (i) $\omega-=\frac{6 m a v}{41 m a^2}=\frac{6 v}{41 a}$

The percentage increase in moment of inertia of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to the circular face : (linear coefficient of expansion $\left.=11 \times 10^{-6} /{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)$
questions.solution:
Increase in area of disc
$\Delta A=A(2 \alpha) \Delta t=\pi(0.5)^2\left(2 \times 11 \times 10^{-6}\right) \times 10=0.000055 \pi$
New area of the disc,
$A^{\prime}=A+\Delta A\therefore \quad A^{\prime}=\pi(0.5)^2+0.000055 \pi$
or $\quad \pi r^{\prime 2}=0.250055 \pi \mathrm{m}^2$
or $\quad r^{\prime}=0.500055 \mathrm{ m}$
Increase in moment of inertia.
$\frac{I^{\prime}-I}{I}=\frac{(0.500055)^2-(0.5)^2}{(0.5)^2}=0.00022=0.022 \%$

The moment of inertia of a solid sphere about the axis along its diameter is

$\begin{array}{rlrl}I & =\frac{2}{5}m R² \Rightarrow I \propto R² \\

(Breadth of the scale is negligible)
questions.solution:
$m=0.6 \mathrm{ kg}$
Mass per unit length $=\frac{0.6}{100} \mathrm{ kg} / \mathrm{cm}$ Mass of part $A B, m_1=\frac{0.6}{100} \times 20=\frac{0.6}{5} \mathrm{ kg}$ Mass of part $B C, m_2=\frac{0.6}{100} \times 80=\frac{0.6 \times 4}{5}=\frac{2.4}{5} \mathrm{ kg}$ Moment of inertia, $I=m_1\left(\frac{A B}{2}\right)^2+m_2 \frac{(B C)^2}{2}=\frac{0.6}{5} \times\left(\frac{20}{2} \times 10^{-2}\right)^2+\frac{2.4}{5} \times\left(\frac{80}{2} \times 10^{-2}\right)^2=\frac{0.6}{5} \times 10^{-2}+\frac{2.4}{5} \times\left(4 \times 10^{-1}\right)^2=\frac{0.6}{5} \times 10^{-2}+\frac{2.4}{5} \times 16 \times 10^{-2}=\left(\frac{0.6+38.4}{5}\right) \times 10^{-2}=7.8 \times 10^{-2}=0.078 \mathrm{ kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$

questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of a disc,
$I=\frac{1}{2} M R^2$
Disc is melted and recasted into a solid sphere.

$\frac{4}{3} \pi R_1^3=\pi R^2 \times \frac{R}{6} \Rightarrow \frac{4}{3} R_1^3=\frac{R^3}{6}R_1^3=\frac{R^3}{8} \Rightarrow R_1=\frac{R}{2}\therefore \quad$ Moment of inertia of sphere,
$I^{\prime}=\frac{2}{5} M R_1^2=\frac{2}{5} M\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2=\frac{2}{5} \frac{M R^2}{4}=\frac{1}{5}\left(\frac{1}{2} M R^2\right)=\frac{I}{5}$

questions.q:
A uniform metal rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ is rotating about an axis passing through one of the ends and perpendicular to the rod with angular speed $\omega$. If the temperature increases by $t^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, then the change in its angular velocity is proportional to which of the following?
(Coefficient of linear expansion of rod $=\alpha$ )
questions.solution:
From law of conservation of angular momentum
$L=$ constant
$\begin{aligned} I_1 \omega_1 & =I_2 \omega_2=L \\ \omega_1 & =\frac{L}{I_1}, \omega_2=\frac{L}{I_2}\end{aligned}$
Change in angular velocity
$\begin{aligned} \Delta \omega & =\omega_2-\omega_1=\frac{L}{I_2}-\frac{L}{I_1}=L\left(\frac{1}{I_2}-\frac{1}{I_1}\right) \\ & =L\left(\frac{I_1-I_2}{I_1 I_2}\right)=\frac{L}{I_1}\left(\frac{I_1}{I_2}-1\right) \\ & =\omega_1\left(\frac{I_1}{I_2}-1\right) \\ \Delta \omega & \propto \omega_1 \\ \Delta \omega & \propto \omega\end{aligned}$

Moment of inertia of circular loop,
$I=m r^2$
Given,
$\begin{aligned} I_Q & =8 I_D \\ m r_Q^3 & =8 m_p r_D^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} m_p \times\left(n r_p\right)^2 & =8 m_p \times r_p^2 \\ n^2 & =8 \Rightarrow n=2 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A zener diode of zener voltage 30 V is connected in a circuit as shown in the figure. The maximum current through the zener diode is
questions.solution:
Current through Load Resistor $\left(I_L\right)$ Since the zener diode regulates the voltage at 30 V , the voltage across the load resistor ( $R_L=6 \mathrm{k} \Omega$ ) will also be 30 V .
The current through the load resistor, $I_L$, is: $I_L=\frac{V_Z}{R_L}=\frac{30 \mathrm{~V}}{6 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=5 \mathrm{~mA}$ Total Current in the Circuit ( $I_{\text{total }}$ ) The total current supplied by the source, $I_{\text{total, }}$, is given by: $I_{\text{total }}=\frac{V_{\text{in }}-V_Z}{R_{\text{total }}}$ where $R_{\text{total }}=5 k \Omega+2 k \Omega=7 k \Omega$. For maximum $I_{\text{total, }}$, we use the maximum input voltage $V_{\text{in }}=100 \mathrm{~V}$ : $I_{\text{total }}=\frac{100 \mathrm{~V}-30 \mathrm{~V}}{7 k \Omega}=\frac{70 \mathrm{~V}}{7 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=10 \mathrm{~mA}$ Maximum Zener Diode Current ( $I_{Z \max }$ ) The zener diode current $I_Z$ is the difference between the total current and the load current: $I_{Z \max }=I_{\text{total }}-I_L=10 m A-5 m A=5 m A$ Final Answer The maximum current through the zener diode is: $5 m A$

questions.q:
What is the binding energy of $S 1429 i$ whose atomic mass is $28. 976495u$

Mass of proton $= 1. 007276u$

Mass of neutron $= 1. 008664u$

(Neglect the electron mass) (Assume $1u = 931. 5MeV$)
questions.solution:
Given: Atomic mass of $S 1429 i$ is $28. 976495u$.

Mass of proton $= 1. 007276u$

Mass of neutron $= 1. 008664u$

The binding energy for $S 1429 i$ can& be calculated& from the mass defect.

$B. E = ∆ mc^{2}$, where $∆ m$ is the change in mass and $c$ is the speed of light.

In $S 1429 i$ number of neutrons are $29 - 14 = 15$ and the number of protons is $14$.

Hence, change in mass is

$∆ m = \left(1. 007276 \times 14\right) + \left(1. 008664 \times 15\right) - 28. 976495 = 0. 255359u$

Thus, the binding energy is

$B. E = 0. 255359 \times 931. 5MeV = 237. 86MeV$

Differentiating $I_D$ w.r.t. $V_D$, we get

$\begin{gathered}\frac{d}{d V_D}\left($ I_D\right)=$\frac{d}{d V_D}\left(7.8 \times10^{-5} e^{6.9 V_D}\right) \\
=7.8 \times10^{-5} \times6.9 \times$ e^{6.9 V_D} \\
=I_D $\times6.9
\end{gathered}

Dynamic resistance is \frac{d}{d I_D}   \left(V_D\right)$

\begin{aligned}
\frac{d V_D}{d I_D}$& $$=\frac{1}{6.9 \times 4 \times 10^{-3}} \\
& =36.23 \Omega
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ Dynamic resistance $=36.23 \Omega$

Input voltage, $V_i=30 \mathrm{mV}$
Change in base current,

Change in collector current,
$\Delta I_c=3 \mathrm{~mA}=3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~A}$

questions.q: Determine $V_{C E}$ in the following silicon based transistor circuit
questions.solution: Using KVL to CE circuit, $\begin{array}{rlrl} V_{C C} & =i_C R_C+V_{C E}+i_E R_E & \\ & =i_C R_C+V_{C E}+i_C R_E & \left(\because i_E \approx i_C\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad V_{C E} & =V_{C C}-i_C\left( R_C+R_E\right) & & \ldots(\mathrm{i}) \end{array}$ By Ohm's law, current $i_1$ is; i_1=$\frac{V_{C C}}{R_1+R_2}=\frac{10 \mathrm{ V}}{15 \mathrm{k} \Omega}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{ mA}$ Now, $\begin{aligned} V_2 & =i_1 R_2 \\ & =\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{ mA} \times5 \mathrm{k} \Omega=\frac{10}{3}\\ V_2 & =3.3 \mathrm{ V} \end{aligned}$ KVL to base circuit gives, $V_2=V_{B E}+i_E R_E$ For silicon transistor, $\begin{aligned} V_{B E} & =0.7 \mathrm{ V} \Rightarrow i_E=\frac{V_2-V_{B E}}{R_E}\\ & =\frac{3.3-0.7}{526} \approx5 \mathrm{ mA} \end{aligned}$ So, $\quad i_C \approx i_E=5 \mathrm{ mA}$ Hence, from $\mathrm{Eq}$ (i) $V_{C E}$ is $\begin{aligned} V_{C E} & =V_{C C}-i_C\left( R_C+R_E\right) \\ & =10-5 \mathrm{ mA}(1 \mathrm{k} \Omega+526 \Omega) \\ & \approx2.4 \mathrm{ V} \end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{Q}=\frac{\mathrm{K} A \Delta \mathrm{ T}}{\Delta \mathrm{x}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{ K}=\frac{\mathrm{Q} \Delta \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{ A} \mathrm{\Delta T}}\therefore$ Thermal conductivity, $K=\frac{42 \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-4} \times 14}=30 \mathrm{ W} \mathrm{ m}^{-1} \mathrmk^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of the specific heat capacities of a gas is 1.5. When the gas undergoes an adiabatic process, its volume is doubled and pressure becomes $P_1$. When the gas undergoes isothermal process, its volume is doubled and pressure becomes $P_2$. If $P_1=P_2$, the ratio of the initial pressures of the gas when it undergoes adiabatic and isothermal processes is
questions.solution:
For a gas, $\gamma=1.5$
For adiabatic Process, $\mathrm{V}_{f}=2 \mathrm{V}_{i}, \mathrm{P}_{f}=\mathrm{P} 1\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}^\gamma=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{f}^\gamma \Rightarrow \mathrm{piVi}^{1.5}=\mathrm{P}_1\left(2 \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)^{1.5} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{Pi}_{\text{,ad }}=(2)^{1.5} \mathrm{P}_1
\end{aligned}$For isothermal process, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{f}}=2 \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{P}_2\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{f}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}=\left(\mathrm{P}_2\right)\left(2 \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}\right) \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{Pi}_{\text{iso }}=2 \mathrm{P}_2 \\
& \therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{Pi}_{\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{ad}}}}{\mathrm{Pi}_{\text{iso }}}=\frac{(2)^{1.5} \mathrm{P}_1}{2 \mathrm{P}_2}=\sqrt{2}: 1
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Steam of mass 60 g at a temperature $100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is mixed with water of mass 360 g at a temperature $40^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The ratio of the masses of steam and water in equilibrium is (Latent heat of steam is $540 \mathrm{cal} \mathrmg^{-1}$ and specific heat capacity of water is $1 \mathrm{cal} \mathrmg^{-1}{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrmC^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
For water, $\mathrm{m}_1=360 \mathrm{ g}, \mathrm{ T}_1=40^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \mathrm{T}_2=100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\therefore$ Heat required, $\mathrm{H}_1=\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{C}_1\left(\mathrm{ T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1\right)=360 \times 1 \times(100-40)=21600 \mathrm{cal}$ At equilibrium, Heat released by steam = Heat required by water $\therefore$ Mass of steam converted into water, $\mathrm{m}_2=\frac{\mathrm{H}_1}{\mathrm{ L}}=\frac{21600}{540}=40 \mathrm{ g}$
$\therefore$ Mass of steam let, $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{s}}=60-40=20 \mathrm{ g}$ Mass of water, $m_w=360+40=400 \mathrm{ g}\therefore \frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{s}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{W}}}=\frac{20}{400}=1: 20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature difference between the ends of two cylindrical rods $A$ and $B$ of the same material is $2: 3$. In steady state the ratio of the rates of flow of heat through the rods $A$ and $B$ is $5: 9$. If the radii of the rods $A$ and $B$ are in the ratio $1: 2$, then the ratio of lengths of the rods $A$ and $B$ is
questions.solution:
For two cylindrical rods A and B, $\theta_1: \theta_2=2: 3, H_1: H_2=5: 9, r_1: r_2=1: 2\therefore \quad$ At steady state, $\mathrm{H}=\frac{\mathbb{k}\left(\pi \mathrm{r}^2\right)^8}{\ell} \propto \frac{\mathrm{r}^2 \theta}{\ell}\therefore \frac{\mathrm{H}_1}{\mathrm{H}_2}= \left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2\left(\frac{\theta_1}{\theta_2}\right)\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right)
⇒ \frac{5}{9}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \cdot\left(\frac{\ell_2}{\ell_1}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2}=3: 10$

questions.q: The thickness of a uniform rectangular metal plate is 5 mm and the area of each surface is $5 \mathrm{ cm}^2$. In steady state, the temperature difference between the two surfaces of the plate is $14^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere at a temperature $\mathbf{T K}$ is cut in to two hemispheres. The ratio of energies radiated by one hemisphere to the whole sphere per second is
questions.solution:
From Stefan's law
$\mathrm{E} \propto \mathrm{A}$
Initial area of hemisphere, $\mathrm{A}_1=4 \pi \mathrm{r}^2$
Final area of hemisphere, $A_2=2 \pi \mathrm{r}^2+\pi \mathrm{r}^2=3 \pi \mathrm{r}^2\therefore \frac{E_2}{E_1}=\frac{3 \pi r^2}{4 \pi r^2}=\frac{3}{4}$

questions.solution:

Given $F=2 C$ or $C=F / 2\therefore \mathrm{F}=\frac{9}{5} \times \frac{\mathrm{F}}{2}+32 \Rightarrow \mathrm{ F}-0.9 \mathrm{ F}=32 \therefore \mathrm{ F}=320^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperatures of equal masses of three different liquids $A, B$ and $C$ are $15^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, 24^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and $30^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ respectively. The resultant temperature when liquids $A$ and $B$ are mixed is $20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and when liquids $B$ and $C$ are mixed is $26^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. Then the ratio of specific heat capacities of the liquids $A, B$ and $C$ is
questions.solution:
Temperature of mixture of liquids of same mass
$T_{A B}=\frac{T_A C_A+T_B C_B}{C_A+C_B}$
when liquids A and B mixed
$20=\frac{15 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{A}}+24 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}} \Rightarrow 20 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{A}}+20 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}=15 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{A}}+24 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}$
or, $5 C_A=4 C_B\qquad...\mathrm{(i)}$
Similarly when liquids B and C are mixed
$26=\frac{24 C_B+30 C_C}{C_B+C_C} \Rightarrow 26 \mathrm{C}_B+26 C_C=24 C_B+30 \mathrm{C}_C$
or, $2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}=4 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{C}}\therefore \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}=2 \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{C}}\qquad...\mathrm{(ii)}$
From eq. (i) and (ii)
$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{A}}: \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{B}}: \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{C}}=8: 10: 5$

questions.q:
Steam at $100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is added to $150 \mathrm{ g}$ water to increase its temperature from $20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $40^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The total mass of the water at $40^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is
(specific heat capacity of water $=1 \mathrm{cal} \mathrmg^{-1}{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrmC^{-1}$ and latent heat of steam $=540 \mathrm{cal} \mathrmg^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
Heat gain by water $=$ Heat lost by steam
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{ms}(\Delta \theta)=\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{L}+\mathrm{ms}(\Delta \theta) \\ & 150 \times 1 \times(40-20)=\mathrm{m}[(540+1 \times(100-40)] \\ & \Rightarrow 150 \times 20=\mathrm{m}(540+60) \\ & \therefore \mathrm{m}=\frac{150 \times 20}{600}=5 \mathrm{ g} \\ & \therefore \text{ Total mass$ of $water }=150+5=155 \mathrm{ g} .\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the ratio of densities of two substances is $5: 6$ and the ratio of their specific heat capacities is $3: 5$, then the ratio of heat energies required per unit volume so that the two substances can have same temperature rise is
questions.solution:
Ratio of densities of two substance, $\frac{\mathrm{d}_1}{\mathrm{ d}_2}=\frac{5}{6}$
Ratio of their specific heat capacities, $\frac{c_1}{c_2}=\frac{3}{5} \begin{aligned}$& $\Delta$ Q=m c $\Delta$ T=d c $\Delta$ T \\
& $\Delta$ Q_1=d_1 c_1 $\Delta$ T \\
& $\Delta$ Q_2=d_2 c_2 $\Delta$ T \\
& $\frac{\Delta Q_1}{\Delta Q_2}=\frac{d_1 c_1}{d_2 c_2}=\frac{5}{6} \times \frac{3}{5}=\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}$

mixed in a calorimeter. Total internal energy of the two
bodies remains conserved.

Statement I is true, but statements II and III are false

The time required to raise the temperature of 3 litre of water from $0^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $80^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ by a heater operated under $200 \mathrm{ V}$ having resistance of $50 \Omega$ is
[specific heat capacity of water is $4200 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ kg}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$ ] [density of water $=1000 \mathrm{ kg} / \mathrm{m}^3$ ]

Heat absorbed by water
$\Delta \mathrm{Q}_1=\mathrm{mS} \Delta \mathrm{T}=(3 \times 4200 \times 80) \mathrm{J} \quad[\because \mathrm{m}=\mathrm{V} \rho]$
Also, heat generated by heater
$\Delta \mathrm{Q}_2=800 \times \mathrm{t} \quad\left[\because \mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{200^2}{50}=800\right.$ watt $]$
So, $3 \times 4200 \times 80=800 \mathrm{t}\mathrm{t}=1260 \mathrm\sec=21 \mathrm{ min}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An object cools from $100 ° C$ to $40 ° C$ in $10$ minutes, when the surrounding temperature is $10 ° C$. Then the time taken by the object to cool from $70 ° C$ to $20 ° C$ is
[Take $ln2 = 0. 7, ln3 = 1. 1, ln6 = 1. 8$]
questions.solution:
According to Newton's cooling law, rate of cooling is

$\dfrac{d \theta}{d t} ∝ \left(\theta - {θ}_{0}\right)

Here, \theta =the temperature$ of the body

{θ}_{0} =$ Room temperature(constant)

Let $kbe the $proportionality constant and& \theta be the& temperature.
Therefore,&

\dfrac{d \theta}{d t} = -$ k$\left(\theta - {θ}_{0}\right)$⇒ {∫}_{\theta1}^{\theta2}d $\theta\left(\theta - {θ}_{0}\right) = -$ k{∫}_{0}^{t} d t ⇒ ln$\left(\dfrac{{θ}_{2} - {θ}_{0}}{{θ}_{1} - {θ}_{0}}\right) =$ kt$

Taking ratios,

\dfrac{ln\left(\dfrac{40 - 10}{100 - 10}\right)}{ln\left(\dfrac{20 - 10}{70 - 10}\right)} = \dfrac{10}{t2}$⇒ {t}_{2} = 10 $\times \dfrac{ln6}{ln3} =16 . 3min$

A wooden block of density $0. 5g / cc$ is tied to a string. The other end of the string is fixed to the bottom of a tank. The tank is filled with a liquid of density $1g / cc.$ If the tension of the string is $20N,$ then the mass of the block is

At equilibrium, tension in the string must be equal to apparent weight of the block in liquid, $T = {W}_{Apparent}$

questions.q:
Match the columns I and II
& Column I & Column II
A Stoke's law I Pressure and energy
B Turbulence II Hydraulic lift

D Pascal's law IV Reynold's number

The correct match is
questions.solution:
Stokes law is also known as& the frictional force& also called drag force exerted on spherical objects with very small Reynolds numbers in a viscous fluid.&
The turbulence or turbulent flow is fluid motion characterised by chaotic changes in pressure and flow velocity. It is in contrast to a laminar flow, which occurs when a fluid flows in parallel layers, with no disruption between those layers.
In fluid dynamics, Bernoulli's principle states that an increase in the speed of a fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in static pressure or a decrease in the fluid's potential energy.&
Pascal's law is a principle in fluid mechanics,& that states that a pressure change at any point in a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted throughout the fluid such that the same change occurs everywhere. The example of Pascal law is Hydraulics lift.&

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal ball initially at pressure of ${10}^{5}{P}_{a}$ is heated from $20 ° C$ to $127 ° C$ keeping its volume constant. The coefficient of linear expansion of metal is ${10}^{- 5}  \left(° C^{- 1}\right)$ and bulk modulus of metal is $2 \times {10}^{11}Nm^{- 2}. The pressure inside the ball becomes$
questions.solution:
The ball tries to expand its volume. But it is kept in the same volume. So it is kept at a constant volume. So the stress that arises is defined as:
$B = \dfrac{P}{\dfrac{∆ V}{V}}$, now we know that change in volume due to thermal expansion,
$∆ V = V\gamma ∆ T ⇒ \dfrac{∆ V}{V} = \gamma ∆ T = 3\alpha ∆ T$,
$⇒ B = \dfrac{P}{3\alpha ∆ T} ⇒ P = 3\alpha ∆ T \times B = 3 \times {10}^{- 5} \times 107 \times 2 \times {10}^{11} ⇒ P = 6. 42 \times {10}^{8}Pa \approx 6 \times {10}^{8}Pa$

$⇒ P = Avρgh = \pi{10}^{- 4} \times 10 \times 1000 \times 10 \times 3 = 30\piW$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion A thermos bottle consists of a double walled glass vessel with the space between the two walls evacuated, so that the heat transfer between the contents of the bottle and outside is minimised. Reason The vacuum between the two walls inhibits the heat transfer by radiation mechanism.
Which of the following is correct?
options: Assertion is true, Reason is true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true, Reason is true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
The space between the two walls of a thermos bottle is evacuated, so that the heat transfer due to conduction and convection can be prevented. But heat can travel through vacuum. So this evacuated space cannot prevent the heat transfer due to radiation.
Hence, Assertion is true, but Reason is false.

c=4.2 \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{g} \times{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}}=4.2 \frac{\mathrm{J}}{10^{-3} \mathrm{ kg} \times{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}} \\
=4.2 \times 10^3 \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg} \times{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}}=4200 \frac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{kg} \times{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}} \\
T_1=20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, T_2=100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \Delta Q=?

If the power is switched Off, then approximate time taken by the element to cool down to 126^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C} will be (neglect radiation)$
questions.solution:
Given, power absorbed by element, $P=100 \mathrm{ W}$
Mass of element, $m=100 \mathrm{ g}=0.1 \mathrm{ kg}$
Change in temperature,
$\Delta T=(127-126)^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=1{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$
Specific heat of heating element,

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of radius $r_1=2.5 \mathrm{ cm}$, length $l_1=5.0 \mathrm{ cm}$ and temperature $40^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is suspended in an environment of temperature $60^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The thermal radiation transfer rate for cylinder is $1.0 \mathrm{ W}$. If the cylinder is stretched until its radius becomes $r_2=0.50 \mathrm{ cm}$, the thermal radiation transfer rate is changed to
questions.solution:
Keeping nature of surface and temperature of body and surroundings same, rate of heat transfer by radiation depends on area of body,
\Rightarrow Rate of heat transfer $\propto$ Surface area of body
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}=\frac{S_2}{S_1} \Rightarrow Q_2=Q_1 \times \frac{S_2}{S_1}\ldots(i)$
Now, volume remains same in stretching, so
$\pi r_1^2 l_1=\pi r_2^2 l_2\Rightarrow \quad l_2=\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2} \cdot l_1=\frac{(2.5)^2}{(0.5)^2} \times 5=125 \mathrm{ cm}$
So, area before stretching, $S_1=2 \pi r_1  \left(l_1+r_1\right)$ and area after stretching, $S_2=2 \pir_2  \left(l_2+r_2\right)$ Hence by Eq. (i), we get
$Q_2=Q_1 \times \frac{S_2}{S_1}=Q_1 \times \frac{2 \pi r_2\left(l_2+r_2\right)}{2 \pi r_1\left(l_1+r_1\right)}=Q_1 \times \frac{r_2\left(l_2+r_2\right)}{r_1\left(l_1+r_1\right)}=\frac{1 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-2}(125+0.5) \times 10^{-2}}{2.5 \times 10^{-2}(5+2.5) \times 10^{-2}}=3.346=3.35 \mathrm{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A composite slab is prepared with two different materials $A$ and $B$. The relation between their coefficient of thermal conductivity and thickness is given as $K_A=\frac{K_B}{2}$ and $X_A=2 X_B$, respectively. If the temperature of faces of $A$ and $B$ are $75^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and $50^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ respectively, what will be the temperature of common surface?
questions.solution:
The given situation is shown below
In steady state, heat flow rate through $A$ and $B$ must be equal. If $T=$ temperature of common surface, then $\begin{gathered} Q_A=Q_B \\ \frac{K_A\left(75^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-T\right)}{X_A}=\frac{K_B\left(T-50^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)}{X_B} \end{gathered}$ here, $K_A=\frac{K_B}{2}$ and $X_A=2 X_B\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{K_B\left(75^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-T\right)}{2 \times 2 X_B}=\frac{K_B\left(T-50^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)}{X_B} \\ \Rightarrow & 75^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-T=4 T-200^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C} \\ \Rightarrow & 5 T=275^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C} \Rightarrow T=55^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Newton's law of cooling is a special case of
questions.solution:
According to Stefan's law heat energy
absorbed is given by
$\frac{d Q}{d t}=\varepsilon \sigma A\left(T^4-T_0^4\right)$
where, $T=$ temperature of body
and $T_0=$ temperature of surroundings.
If $m$ be the mass of body and $c$ be the specific heat, then heat loss at temperature $T$ is
$\frac{d Q}{d t}=-m c \frac{d T}{d t}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}-m c \frac{d T}{d t} & =\varepsilon \sigma A\left(T^4-T_0^4\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c}\left(T^4-T_0^4\right)\end{aligned}$
Here, $T=T_0+\Delta T$
$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c}\left[\left(T_0+\Delta T\right)^4-T_0^4\right] \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c} T_0^4\left[\left(1+\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\right)^4-1\right] \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A}{m c} T_0^4\left[1+\frac{4 \Delta T}{T_0}-1\right] \quad\left(\because \Delta T \ll T_0\right) \\ & =\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A 4 T_0^3}{m c} \Delta T \\ \Rightarrow \quad-\frac{d T}{d t} & =k \Delta T\end{aligned}$
where, $\quad k=\frac{\varepsilon \sigma A 4 T_0^3}{m c}$
$\therefore \quad \frac{d T}{d t}=-k\left(T-T_0\right)$
This is Newton's law of cooling.
Hence, Newton's law of cooling is a special case of Stefan's law.

questions.q:
How much thermal energy is required to change a $40 \mathrm{~g}$ ice cube from solid at $-10^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to steam at $110^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ ?
[Assume, latent heat of fusion for water $=80 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}$, specific heat of water $=1 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, specific heat of ice $=0.5 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, specific heat of steam $=0.48 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, latent heat of vaporisation of water $\left.=540 \mathrm{kcal} / \mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right]$
questions.solution:
Following changes occur in given conversion
process

So, required thermal energy
$\begin{gathered}=m\left\{c_{\text{ice }}\left(0^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-\left(-10^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)\right)+\right. \\ L_{\text{fusion }}+c_{\text{water }}\left(100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-0^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right) \\ +L_{\text{vapnorisation }} \\ \left.+c_{\text{steam }}\left(110^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}-100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}\right)\right\}\end{gathered}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{400}{1000}\{0.5 \times 10+80+1 \times 100+540+0.48 \times 10\} \\ & =29.192 \mathrm{kcal}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of a body is increased from $T_1=127^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $T_2=227^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The ambient temperature is $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The energies emitted per second by the body at $T_1$ and $T_2$ are $E_1$ and $E_2$ respectively. The ratio of $\frac{E_2}{E_1}$ is
questions.solution:
Given, temperature of body increases from
$T_1=127^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $T_2=227^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$
and ambient temperature,
$T_0=27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$
By Stefan-Boltzman's law, energy emitted per second is given by
i.c.,
$E=\varepsilon \sigma   \left(T⁴-T_0^4\right)$
i.c., $\quad E \$ propto$\left[T^4-T_0^4\right]\frac{E_2}{E_1}=\frac{\left(T_2^4-T_0^4\right)$}{$\left(T_1^2-T_0^4\right)$}$Putting the given values, we get
$=$\frac{(227)^4-(27)^4}{(127)^4-(27)^4}=\frac{2654706400}{259613200}  Hence, the ratio \frac{E_2}{E_1}$ is 10.22. So, no option is correct.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two thin metallic spherical shells of radii $20 \mathrm{ cm}$ and $30 \mathrm{ cm}$, respectively are placed with their centres coinciding. A material of thermal conductivity $\alpha$ is filled in the space between the shells. The inner shell is maintained at $300 \mathrm{ K}$ and the outer shell at $310 \mathrm{ K}$. If the rate at which heat flows radially through the material is $40 \mathrm{ W}$, find the value of $\alpha$ (in units of $\mathrm{J} \mathrms^{-1} \mathrm{ m}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$ ).
questions.solution:
Given, radius of two thin metallic spherical
shells,
$\begin{aligned} & r_1=20 \mathrm{ cm}=0.2 \mathrm{ m} \\ & r_2=30 \mathrm{ cm}=0.3 \mathrm{ m}\end{aligned}$
temperature of inner shell, $T_1=300 \mathrm{ K}$, temperature of outer shell, $T_2=310 \mathrm{ K}$, and rate of heat flow, $H=40 \mathrm{ W}$.
Radial rate of flow of heat through the shell in the steady state,
$\begin{aligned} H & =\frac{d Q}{d t}=\alpha A \frac{d T}{d r}=\alpha\left(4 \pi r^2\right) \frac{d T}{d r} \\ \frac{d r}{r^2} & =\frac{4 \pi \alpha}{H} \cdot d T\end{aligned}$
Integrate on both sides, we get
$\begin{array}{rlrl}\Rightarrow & \quad \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{d r}{r^2}$ & =$\frac{4 \pi \alpha}{H} \int_{T_1}^{T_2} d T \\ \frac{r_2-r_1}{r_1 r_2}$ & =$\frac{4 \pi \alpha}{H}\left(T_2-T_1\right) \\ \therefore \quad & \alpha & =\frac{H \left(r_2-r_1\right)}{4 \pi r_1 r_2 \left(T_2-T_1\right)}\end{array}$
Putting the given values, we get
$\alpha=\frac{40(0.3-0.2)}{4 \pi(0.3)(0.2)(310-300)}=\frac{4}{2.4 \pi}$=$\frac{5}{3 \pi}
H$ence, the $value of\alpha=\frac{5}{3 \pi}\mathrm{Js}^{-1}\mathrm{ m}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cup of coffee cools from $150^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$ to $144^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$ in $1 \mathrm{ min}$ in a room temperature at $72^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$. How much time with the coffee take to cool from $110^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$ to $104^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$ in the same room?
questions.solution:
Given, in first case, $T_1=150^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}, T_2=144^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}, t_1=1 \mathrm{~min}$ and room temperature, $T_0=72^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$
According to Newton's law of cooling,

$\begin{aligned}$& m c $\frac{\left(T_1-T_2\right)}{t_1}=$K$\left(\frac{T_1+T_2}{2}-$T_0\right) \\
& m c$\left(\frac{150-144}{1}\right)=$K$\left(\frac{150+144}{2}-$72\right) \\
& 6 m c=75 K
\end{aligned}$ In second case,T^{\prime}{ }_1=110^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}, T^{\prime}{ }_2=104^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{F}$ Time $=t_2=$ ?
By Newton's law of cooling, we have

$\begin{aligned}$m c$\left(\frac{110-104}{t_2}\right)$& =K$\left(\frac{110+104}{2}-$72\right) \\
$\frac{6 m c}{t_2}$& =35 $\mathrm{~K}
\end{aligned}$From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get,

$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{6 m c}{\left(\frac{6 m c}{t_2}\right)}=\frac{75 K}{35 K}$\\
\Rightarrow \quad t_2=$\frac{15}{7}$& =2.14 $\mathrm{~min} .
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of the radiation emitted by a black body is $1 \mathrm{ mm}$ and Wien's constant is $3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{mK}$. Then the temperature of the black body will be
questions.solution:
As we know temperature of a black body is given by,

\lambda T=b \quad $\text{ (Wien's displacement law) }$Where, wavelength of the radiation,

\lambda=1 $\mathrm{~mm}=$1 $\times$10^{-3} $\mathrm{~m}$Wien's constant, $\mathrm{b}=3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{mK}$
\Rightarrow \quad T=$\frac{b}{\lambda}=\frac{3 \times 10^{-3}}{1 \times 10^{-3}}=$3 $\mathrm{~K}$So, the correct option is (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hot body placed in air cools down to a lower temperature. The rate of decrease of temperature is proportional to the temperature difference from the surrounding. The body loses $60 \%$ and $80 \%$ of maximum heat it can loose in time $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. The ratio $t_2 / t_1$ will be
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling,
$$
-\frac{d T}{d t} \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T} \text { or } \frac{d T}{d t}=-K \Delta \mathrm{T}
$$
Solved the above Eq., we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
T(t) & =T_0+\left(T_1-T_0\right) e^{-k t} \Rightarrow e^{-k t}=\frac{T(t)-T_0}{T_1-T_0} \\
\text { or } \quad t & =\frac{1}{k} \ln \frac{T_1-T_0}{T(t)-T_0}
\end{aligned}
$$
Where, $T_1=$ temperature of body at $t=0$
$T_0=$ temperature of surrounding.
Let $T_1=0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$
So, $t=\frac{1}{k} \ln \frac{-T_0}{T(t)-T_0}=\frac{1}{k} \ln \frac{-Q_0}{Q(t)-Q_0}[\because Q(t)=m c T(t)]$
According to the question, the body loses $60 \%$ and $80 \%$ of maximum heat in time $t_1$ and $t_2$


$$
\text { then } \quad \begin{aligned}
t_1 & =\frac{1}{k} \ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{\frac{60}{100} Q_0-Q_0}\right) \\
t_2 & =\frac{1}{k} \ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{\frac{80}{100} Q_0-Q_0}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
Divide Eqs. (ii) by (i), we get
$$
\frac{t_2}{t_1}=\frac{\frac{1}{k} \ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{\frac{80}{100} Q_0-Q_0}\right)}{\frac{1}{k} \ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{100-Q_0}\right)}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \frac{t_2}{t_1}=\frac{\ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{\left.\frac{80 Q_0-100 Q_0}{100}\right)}\right.}{\ln \left(\frac{-Q_0}{\left.\frac{60 Q_0-100 Q_0}{100}\right)}\right.}=\frac{\ln \left(\frac{-Q_0 \times 100}{-20 Q_0}\right)}{\ln \left(\frac{Q_0 \times 5}{2 Q_0}\right)}
$$
Hence, the correct option is (4).

Statement $A:$ Convection involves flow of matter within a fluid due to unequal temperatures of its parts.

Statement $B:$ A hot bar placed under a running tap water loses heat due to effect of convection within water.

Statement.$C:$& Heat transfer always involves temperature difference between two systems.

According to the definition of convection, convection involves flow of matter within a fluid due to unequal temperatures of its parts.

Given, area of a circular copper coin increases by $0.4 \%$.
i.e., $\quad \frac{\Delta A}{A}=0.004$

questions.q: A $210 \mathrm{ W}$ heater is used to heat $100 \mathrm{ g}$ water. The time required to raise the temperature of this water from $25^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is (specific heat capacity of water $=4200 \mathrm{ J} / \mathrm{Kg} \cdot{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
Given, specific heat of water, W=4200 $\mathrm{ J}$/ $\mathrm{Kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}=42 \times10^3 \mathrm{ J}$/ $\mathrm{Kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ change in temperature of water, $\Delta$ T=T_2-r_2=100-25=75^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}$ mass of water, $m=100 \mathrm{ g}=10^{-1} \mathrm{ kg}$
and power of heater, $H=\frac{Q}{t}=210 \mathrm{ W}$
\Rightarrow \quad Q=210 $\mathrm{t}$ Where $Q$ is amount of heat required to raise the temperature of water which is given by $\begin{aligned} Q & =m c \Delta r \\
210 t & =m c \Delta r \quad \quad \quad \text{ From Eqs. (i)] }\\
210 t & =10^{-2} \times42 \times10^3 \times75 \\
t & =\frac{10^{-2} \times 42 \times 10^3 \times 75}{210}=150 \mathrm{ s}
\end{aligned} [$ From Eqs. (i)]
Therefore, the time required to raise the temperature of water is $150 \mathrm{ s}$.

How much ice should be added to obtain the final temperature of $0^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ with all ice melted, if the initial temperature of ice is $-10^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. Neglect heat capacity of glass.
[Take, $C_{\text{water }}=4190 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$,

C_{$\text{ice }$}=2100 $\mathrm{~J}$/ $\mathrm{kg}^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C},$L_F=3.34 $\times$10^5 $\mathrm{~J}$/ $\mathrm{kg} \text{ ] }$
questions.solution:
Heat lost by carbonated water $=$ Heat gained by ice
Let, $m_{\hat{i}}=$ mass of ice melted and $m_w=$ initial mass of carbonated water. $\begin{aligned}& m_w c_w(20-0) & =m_i L_f+m_i\left( c_i\right)[0-(-10)] \\
\Rightarrow \quad & & 200 \times10^{-3} \times4190 \times20 \\
& = & m_i\left(3.34 \times10^5+2100 \times10\right) \\
\Rightarrow & & m_i=47 \times10^{-3} \mathrm{ kg} \text{ or } m_i=47 \mathrm{ g}
\end{aligned}$

If the rate of heat loss by convection is equal to the rate of heat loss by radiation, the emissivity of the body surface is

Given, rate of heat lost by convection = Rate of heat lost by radiation

$\begin{array}{lc}
\Rightarrow& h A \left(T-T_0\right)$=e A \sigma $\left(T^4-T_0^4\right) \\
\Rightarrow & 20 \times370=e \times5.67 \times10^{-8}\left[(400)^4-(30)^4\right]$ \\
\Rightarrow & e=$\frac{59}{90} \approx0.66
\end{array}
$

questions.q: An electric heater with constant heat supply rate is used to convert a certain amount of liquid ammonia to saturated vapour at high pressure. The heater takes 14 minutes to bring the liquid at $15^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to the boiling point of $50{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ and 92 minutes to convert the liquid at the boiling point wholly to vapour. If the specific heat capacity of liquid ammonia is $4.9 \mathrm{ kJ} / \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{K}$, the latent heat of vaporisation of ammonia in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{kg}$ is
questions.solution:
Let mass of liquid ammonia taken is $m$ and rate of heat supplied is $r$.
Then, as per given condition, $r \times 14=m \times 4.9 \times(50-15)$ and $r \times 92=mL$
Dividing these, we get $\begin{aligned}\frac{92}{14}& =\frac{L}{4.9 \times(50-15)} \text{$ or $} L=\frac{92 \times 4.9 \times 35}{14}\\
& =1127 \mathrm{ kJ}/ \mathrm{kg}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An aluminium rod of length $1 \mathrm{ m}$ and a steel rod of length $2 \mathrm{ m}$ both having same cross-sectional area, are soldered together end-to-end. The thermal conductivity of aluminium rod and steel rod is $200 \mathrm{Js}^{-1} \mathrm{ m}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$ and $50 \mathrm{Js}^{-1} \mathrm{ m}^{-1} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}$ respectively. The temperatures of the free ends are maintained at $300 \mathrm{ K}$ and $500 \mathrm{ K}$. What is the temperature of the junction?
questions.solution:
Let junction temperature is $T K$, then in steady state heat flow rate is same through both rods.
So, using, $\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{k A\left(T_2-T_1\right)}{l}$, we have, $\frac{Q}{t}=\frac{k_s A_s(500-T)}{2}=\frac{k_{\mathrm{Al}} A_{\mathrm{Al}}(T-300)}{1}$ As areas of both rods is same, so $\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & $\frac{k_s(500-T)}{2}$& =$\frac{k_{\mathrm{Al}}(T-300)}{1}$\\ \Rightarrow & & $\frac{50(500-T)}{2}$& =$\frac{200(T-300)}{1}$\\ \Rightarrow & 25 $\times500-25 T \text{ and } =200 T-200 \times300 \\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \text{ and } 225 T \text{ and } =12500+60000 \\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \text{ and } T \text{ and } =\frac{72500}{225}=322.2 $\approx$322 \mathrm{ K} \end{array}$

m C\left[\frac{100-70}{300}\right]& =k\left[\frac{100+70}{2}-30\right] \\
m C\left[\frac{30}{300}\right]& =k\left[\frac{170}{2}-30\right] \\
m C\left[\frac{1}{10}\right]& =k[85-30] \\

$\mathrm{T}_{2}=$80^{{}^{\circ}} $\mathrm{C}$ & $\text{ time, }$ t_2=t^{\prime} \min =t^{\prime \prime} $\mathrm{s}$

m C $\left[\frac{100-80}{t^{\prime \prime}}\right]$& =k $\left[\frac{100+80}{2}$-$30\right]$ \\
m C $\left[\frac{20}{t^{\prime \prime}}\right]$& =k[90-30] \\

questions.q: A very small hole in an electric furnace is used for heating metals. The hole nearly acts as a black body. The area of the hole is $200 \mathrm{~mm}^2$. questions.solution:
By Stefan's law
If the absolute temperature of a black body is $T$, then the energy $E$ emitted per second per unit surface area of the body

$\begin{aligned}& E \propto T⁴ \\
& E=\sigma \cdotA T⁴
\end{aligned}

Given,

\begin{aligned}\sigma& =5.67 \times10^{-8} \mathrm{ W}/ \mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{ K}^4 \\
T & =727+273=1000 \mathrm{ K}\\
A & =200 \times10^{-6} \mathrm{ m}\\
E & =5.67 \times10^{-8} \times \left(200 \times10^{-6}\right)\times(1000)^4 \\
& =5.67 \times2 \times10^{-12} \times10^{12} \\
& =11.34 \mathrm{ J}/  \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$

\Rightarrow & T_2=$\left(\frac{e_1}{e_2}T_1$^4\right)^{1 / 4}$=\left(\frac{1}{81} \times(5802)^4\right)^{1 / 4}$ \\
\Rightarrow & T_B=1934 $\mathrm{~K}$
\end{array}$From Wein's law, $\lambda_{A T_A}=\lambda_B T_B$\begin{array}{llrl}\Rightarrow & \frac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} & =\frac{T_B}{T_A} \\ \Rightarrow & \frac{\lambda_B-\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} & =\frac{T_B-T_B}{T_A} \\ \Rightarrow & \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_B} & =\frac{5802-1934}{5802}=\frac{3968}{5802} \\ \Rightarrow & \lambda_B & =\frac{3}{2} \mu \mathrm{m}\end{array}$

questions.q:
One junction of a certain thermoelectric couple is at a fixed temperature $T_r$ and the other junction is at temperature $T$. The thermo-electromotive force for this is
expressed by $E=k\left(T-T_r\right)\left[T_0-\frac{1}{2}\left(T+T_r\right)\right]$. At temperature $T=\frac{1}{2} T_0$, the thermoelectric power is
questions.solution:
We know that thermoelectric power
$$
S=\frac{d E}{d T}
$$
Given, $E=K\left(T-T_r\right)\left[T_0-\frac{1}{2}\left(T+T_r\right)\right]$
By differentiating the above equation w.r.t. $T$ and putting $T=\frac{1}{2} T_0$, we get $S=\frac{1}{2} k T_0$

questions.q: The heat evolved for the rise of water when one end of the capillary tube of radius $r$ is immersed vertically into water is (Assume surface tension $=T$ and density of water to be p)
questions.solution:
Water rise to height, $h=\frac{2 T}{\rho g r}$
Potential energy of water column,
$U=\frac{m g h}{2}=\frac{2 \pi T^2}{\rho g}$
The work performed by force of surface tension is
$W=2 \pi r T h=\frac{4 \pi T^2}{\rho g}$
From conservation of energy the heat evolved,
$Q=W-U=\frac{2 \pi T^2}{\rho g}$

Energy radiated per unit time
$E=\sigma A T^4$
where $\sigma=$ Stefan's constant

According to question,
$E_{\text{star }}=10000 E_{\text{sun }}\sigma A_{\text{star }} \times T_{\text{star }}^4=10000 \times \sigma A_{\text{sun }} \times T_{\text{sun }}^4\pi R_{\text{star }}^2 T_{\text{star }}^4=10000 \times \pi R_n^2 \times T_{\text{sun }}^4\left(\frac{R_{\text{star }}}{R_{\text{sun }}}\right)^2=10000\left(\frac{T_{\text{sun }}}{T_{\text{star }}}\right)^4=10000\left(\frac{6000}{2000}\right)^4\Rightarrow \quad \frac{R_{\text{star }}}{R_{\text{sun }}}=\sqrt{10000 \times(3)^4}=100 \times 3^2=900R_{\text{star }}: R_{\text{sun }}=900: 1$

Density at $0^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \rho_0=1.0127$
Density at $100^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \rho_{100}=1$
Coefficient of real expansion of liquid,
$\gamma_{\text{real }}=\frac{\rho_0-\rho_{100}}{\rho_{100} \times \Delta t}=\frac{1.0127-1}{1 \times 100}=0.0127 \times 10^{-2}=1.27 \times 10^{-4}\gamma_{\text{real }}=\gamma_{\text{app }}+\gamma_g\gamma_g=$ coefficient of volume expansion of glass $=3 \alpha\therefore \quad 1.27 \times 10^{-4}=\gamma_{\mathrm{app}}+3 \alpha1.27 \times 10^{-4}=\gamma_{\text{app }}+3 \times 9 \times 10^{-6}\gamma_{\mathrm{app}}=1.27 \times 10^{-4}-27 \times 10^{-6}=1.27 \times 10^{-4}-0.27 \times 10^{-4}=1 \times 10^{-4}\therefore \quad \gamma_{\text{app }}=\frac{\text{ mass expelled }}{\text{ remaining mass } \times \Delta t}1 \times 10^{-4}=\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_2 \times 100}\left(\frac{m_1}{m_2}-1\right)=1 \times 10^{-4} \times 100=10^{-2}\frac{m_1}{m_2}=1+10^{-2}=1.01m_2=\frac{m_1}{1.01}=\frac{300}{1.01}$
Mass expelled $=m_1-m_2=300-\frac{300}{1.01}=\frac{3}{1.01}$

questions.q: When $Q_1$ amount of heat is supplied to a monatomic gas, the work done by the gas is $W$. When $Q_2$ amount of heat is supplied to a diatomic gas, the work done by the gas is $2 W$. Then $Q_1: Q_2=$
questions.solution:
At constant pressure,
$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{V}=\mathbf{n R} \Delta \mathrm{T} \Rightarrow \mathbf{W} \propto \Delta \mathrm{T}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{W}_2}{\mathrm{ W}_1}=\frac{(\Delta \mathrm{T})_2}{(\Delta \mathrm{ T})_1} \Rightarrow \frac{2 \mathrm{ W}}{\mathrm{ W}}=\frac{(\Delta \mathrm{T})_2}{(\Delta \mathrm{ T})_1} \\ & \therefore(\Delta \mathrm{ T})_2=2(\Delta \mathrm{ T})_1\end{aligned}$
For monoatomic gas, $f_1=3\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{Q}_1=(\Delta \mathrm{U})_1+\mathrm{W}_1=\frac{\mathrm{f}_1}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1+\mathrm{W} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{Q}_1=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1+\mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1=\frac{5}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1\end{aligned}$
For diatomic gas, $\mathrm{f}_2=5\begin{aligned} & \therefore Q_2=(\Delta U)_2+W_2=\frac{f_2}{2} n R(\Delta T)_2+2 W \\ & \Rightarrow Q_2=\frac{5}{2} n R \times 2(\Delta T)_1+2 n R(\Delta T)_1\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{Q}_2=\frac{14}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1 \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{Q}_2}=\frac{\frac{5}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1}{\frac{14}{2} \mathrm{nR}(\Delta \mathrm{T})_1}=5: 14\end{aligned}$

& \therefore \quad \mathrm{Pi}_{\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{ad}}}=(2)^{1.5} \mathrm{P}_1
\end{aligned}$For isothermal process, $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{f}}=2 \mathrm{ V}_{\mathrm{i}}, \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathrm{P}_2\begin{aligned}

& \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{2}{3}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}}}{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{m}}}=\frac{2}{3}\\
& \frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{2}{3}\\

&

According to the first law of thermodynamics, heat given to a system is equal to the work done by the gas plus change in internal energy. Therefore,

Work done for isobaric process is given by,

questions.solution:
According to the& first law of thermodynamics,

$∆ Q = ∆ U + W ⇒ ∆ U = ∆ Q - W$

The heat given for the phase change of water is $∆ Q = mL = 2000kJ$.

The change in the volume during phase change is $∆ V = 2. 001 - 0. 001 = 2m^{3}$.

Work done by the steam will be $W = P ∆ V = 1 \times {10}^{5} \times 2 = 200kJ$.

$⇒ ∆ U = ∆ Q - W = 2000 - 200 = 1800kJ$.

& T_2=\text{ exhaust temperature, }

Now, $\eta_1=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}\frac{50}{100}=1-\frac{T_2}{500} \Rightarrow$ T_2=250 $\mathrm{ K}$ and $\begin{aligned}& \eta_2=\frac{60}{100}=\frac{6}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{6}{10}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1{ }^{\prime}}\\
& \frac{T_2}{T_1{ }^{\prime}}=1-\frac{6}{10}=\frac{4}{10} \Rightarrow T_1{ }^{\prime}=\frac{10}{4} T_2 \\
& T_1{ }^{\prime}=\frac{10}{4} \times250=625 \mathrm{ K}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A metal sheet $4m$ on a side and of negligible thickness is attached to a balance and inserted into container fluid. The balance to which metal sheet is attached reads $0. 50N$ and the contact angle is found to be zero. A small amount of oil is then spread over the metal sheet. The contact angle now becomes $180 °$ and the balance now reads $0. 49N.$& The surface tension of the fluid is
questions.solution:
In the first case, when the contact angle is zero, the liquid will apply a force on the metal sheet in the downwards direction.

Net force equation can be written as $0. 50 = mg + T \left(4 \times2\right).... \left(1\right)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas undergoes an adiabatic process. If the pressure of the gas is reduced by $0. 1 %$ then the volume is changed by (Given $r = \dfrac{Cp}{Cv} = \dfrac{5}{3}$)
questions.solution:
The relation between pressure and volume in the case of the adiabatic process,& $PV^{γ} = K$, now for two different conditions,
${P}_{1}{V1}^{γ} = {P}_{2}{V2}^{γ}$, here ${P}_{2} = \dfrac{{P}_{1} \times 0 . 1}{100}$, put the values in the above expression,
$\dfrac{{P}_{1} \times 100}{{P}_{1} \times 0 . 1} = \left(\dfrac{V2}{V1}\right)\dfrac{5}{3} ⇒ \left(\dfrac{V2}{V1}\right)\dfrac{5}{3} = 1000 ⇒ \dfrac{V2}{V1} = \left(1000\right)\dfrac{3}{5} ⇒ {V}_{2} = 0 . 6 % {V}_{1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two spheres of same material and radii $5m$ and $2m$ are at temperature $200K$ and $250K$ respectively. The ratio of energies radiated by them per second is
questions.solution:
By Stefan's Law: The formula of power radiated in terms of cross-section area and temperature of the body,&
$P = \sigmaeAT^{4}$, here $\sigma$ is the constant given by Stefans' and& $e$ is the emissivity power,&
$\dfrac{P1}{P2} = \dfrac{\sigmae{A}_{1}{T1}^{4}}{\sigmae{A}_{2}{T2}^{4}} = \dfrac{\left({r}_{1}\right)2{T1}^{4}}{\left({r}_{2}\right)2{T2}^{4}} = \dfrac{\left(5\right)2\left(200\right)4}{\left(2\right)2\left(250\right)4} = \dfrac{25 \times 160000}{4 \times 625 \times 625} ⇒ \dfrac{P1}{P2} = \dfrac{40000}{25 \times 625} = \dfrac{64}{25}$

questions.q: $500g$ of water is heated from $30 ° C$ to $90 ° C.$ What is the change in its internal energy? (Specific heat of water is $4184J{kg}^{- 1}K^{- 1}$)
questions.solution:
The formula of change in internal energy in terms of molar specific heat at constant volume and, change in temperature,& $dU = m{C}_{V} \left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right), given,
$ dU = $\dfrac{500}{1000} \times4184\left(90 ° - 30 °\right) = 125520J$. So the change in internal energy,
$dU = 1 . 25 \times {10}^{5}$ J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A tyre pumped to a pressure of $2$~atmosphere, suddenly bursts. If the temperature of air before expansion is $T$ then the air temperature after the tyre busts is
(Assume the expansion is adiabatic and adiabatic constant $\left\gamma = \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$
questions.solution:
The above process belongs to the thermodynamic process known as the adiabatic process and the relation between pressure and volume in the adiabatic process is, $PV^{γ} = K$, now use ideal gas equation, $⇒ P\left[\left(nRT\right)\left(P\right)\right]\gamma = K ⇒ \dfrac{T\gamma}{P\gamma - 1} = K$

$⇒ \dfrac{{T}_{1}\gamma}{{P}_{1}\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{{T}_{2}\gamma}{{P}_{2}\gamma - 1} ⇒ \dfrac{T\gamma}{2\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{{T}_{2}\gamma}{1\gamma - 1} ⇒ \dfrac{T\dfrac{3}{2}}{2\dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{{T}_{2}\dfrac{3}{2}}{1} ⇒ \left({T}_{2}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times T^{3} ⇒ \left({T}_{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{1} / 3T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of linear expansivity to the co-efficient of a real expansion of a rectangular sheet of a solid is

Let us suppose that the length of the rod is, $l$, then on the increasing temperature the relation between change in length and coefficient of linear expansion, $\alpha$ is,&
$∆ l = l \left(1 + \alpha∆ T\right)$ and the relationship between change in area and coefficient of superficial expansion, $\beta,$ is,
$∆ A = A \left(1 + \alpha∆ T\right)$, let us suppose that the length of the sides are one meter then,

$∆ l = 1 \times \left(1 + \alpha∆ T\right)$ and $∆ A = 1 \times \left(1 + \beta∆ T\right)$
$⇒ ∆ A = ∆ l \times∆ l = 1 \times \left(1 + \beta∆ T\right) = \left(1 + \alpha∆ T\right)^{2} ⇒ \left(1 + \beta∆ T\right) = \left(1 + \alpha∆ T\right)^{2} = \left(1 + 2\alpha∆ T\right) ⇒ \beta =$=2\alpha⇒ $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta} =0. 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two rods whose lengths are ${l}_{1}$ and ${l}_{2}$ with heat conductivity co-efficients ${k}_{1}$ and ${k}_{2}$ are placed end to end. The heat conductivity coefficient of a uniform rod of length ${l}_{1} + {l}_{2}$ whose conductivity is same as that of the system of these two rods is
questions.solution:
When two rods are connected in series then the heat flow per unit time is the same across each rod, it means,& $H = {H}_{1} = {H}_{2}$,

$⇒ \dfrac{kA\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{2}\right)}{{l}_{1} + {l}_{2}} = \dfrac{{k}_{1}A\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{J}\right)}{l1} = \dfrac{{k}_{2}A\left({T}_{J} - {T}_{2}\right)}{l2}$, first, calculate the junction temperature by the idea, ${H}_{1} = {H}_{2} = \dfrac{{k}_{1}A\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{J}\right)}{l1} = \dfrac{{k}_{2}A\left({T}_{J} - {T}_{2}\right)}{l2} ⇒ {T}_{J} = \dfrac{\dfrac{{k}_{1}{T}_{1}}{l1} + \dfrac{{k}_{2}{T}_{2}}{l2}}{\dfrac{k1}{l1} + \dfrac{k2}{l2}}$

it means,
$\dfrac{k\left({T}_{1} - {T}_{2}\right)}{{l}_{1} + {l}_{2}} = \dfrac{{k}_{1}\left({T}_{1} - \dfrac{\dfrac{{k}_{1}{T}_{1}}{l1} + \dfrac{{k}_{2}{T}_{2}}{l2}}{\dfrac{k1}{l1} + \dfrac{k2}{l2}}\right)}{l1} ⇒ k = \dfrac{\left({l}_{1} + {l}_{2}\right){k}_{1}{k}_{2}}{{k}_{2}{l}_{1} + {k}_{1}{l}_{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the name of ideal-gas process in which no heat is transferred?
questions.solution: The ideal-gas process in which no heat or mass is transferred between a thermodynamic system and its surroundings is called as adiabatic process.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gas is at constant pressure $4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$. When a heat energy of $2000 \mathrm{ J}$ is supplied to the gas, its volume changes by $3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^3$. What is the increase in its internal energy?
questions.solution:
Given, pressure, $p=4 \times 10^5 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2, \Delta Q=2000 \mathrm{ J}$
Change in volume, $\Delta V=3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ m}^3$
Now, the work done to change volume is
$\Delta W=p \Delta V=4 \times 10^5 \times 3 \times 10^{-3}=12 \times 10^2=1200 \mathrm{ J}$
According to first law of thermodynamics, So, change in internal energy,
$\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W=2000-1200=800 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Certain amount of heat supplied to an ideal gas under isothermal condition will result in
options: an increase in the internal energy of the gas
external work done and a change in temperature
external work done by the system
questions.solution:
For isothermal process, $\Delta T=$ constant As we know that, from first law of thermodynamics,
$\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W=n C_V \Delta T+\Delta W\Rightarrow \quad \Delta Q=\Delta W \quad[\because \Delta T=0]$
Hence, heat supplied to an ideal gas under isothermal condition will result in external work done by the system.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An ideal gas at temperature $T$, pressure $p$ occupies a volume $V$. If its temperature is halved and pressure doubled, what is its new volume?
questions.solution:
Given, initial temperature, pressure and volume of ideal gas,
$T_1=T, p_1=p, V_1=V$
Final temperature, pressure and volume of gas is given as
$T_2=\frac{T_1}{2}=\frac{T}{2}p_2=2 p_1=2 pV_2=?$
According to ideal gas equation,
$\frac{p_1 V_1}{T_1}=\frac{p_2 V_2}{T_2}\Rightarrow \quad V_2=\frac{p_1 V_1 T_2}{T_1 p_2}=\frac{p \times V \times T / 2}{T \times 2 p} \Rightarrow V_2=\frac{V}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot engine whose efficiency is $40 \%$, receives heat at $500 \mathrm{ K}$. If the efficiency is to be $50 \%$, the source temperature for the same exhaust temperature is
questions.solution:
We know that, efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by
$\eta= \left(1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)
Given, $\eta_1=0.4$ and $T_1=500 $\mathrm{ K} (temperature of source)
So, 0.4=1-\frac{T_2}{500} \Rightarrow \frac{T_2}{500}=1-0.4=0.6\Rightarrow \quad T_2=0.6 \times500=300 \mathrm{ K} (temperature of sink)
Now, in the second gas,
$\eta=0.5 $\text{ and }$ T_2=300 $\mathrm{ K}\therefore \quad0.5=\left(1-\frac{300}{T_1}\right)\Rightarrow \quad \frac{300}{T_1}=1-0.5=0.5 \Rightarrow T_1=\frac{300}{0.5}=600 $$\mathrm{ K}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A system goes from $A$ and $B$ via two processes I and II as shown in figure. If $\Delta U_1$ and $\Delta U_2$ are the changes in internal energies in the processes I and II respectively, then the relation between $\Delta U_1$ and $\Delta U_2$ is
questions.solution:
Internal energy is a state function, i.e. it depends upon initial and final state.
Hence, it does not depend upon the path chosen.
Since, initial and final states are same, so
$\Delta U_1=\Delta U_2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid of $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ mass absorbs $50 \mathrm{ kJ}$ when its temperature is raised from $20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ to $70^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The specific heat capacity of this solid in unit of $\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{kg}{ }^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
Heat absorbed by a solid is given by
$\Delta Q=m s \Delta T$
where, $s=$ specific heat of solid.
$\therefore \quad s=\frac{\Delta Q}{m \cdot \Delta T}=\frac{50 \times 1000}{2 \times\left(70^{{}^{\circ}}-20^{{}^{\circ}}\right) \mathrm{C}}[\because \Delta Q=50 \mathrm{ kJ}=50 \times 1000 \mathrm{ J}]=500 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ kg}^{-1 {}^{\circ}} \mathrmC^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Five moles of an ideal gas has pressure $p_0$ volume $V_0$ and temperature $T_0$. The gas is expanded to volume $3 V_0$ along a path, so that the pressure $p$ is changed as function of volume $V$ as $p=p_0  \left(V / V_0\right)$. The pressure is then reduced to $p_0$ maintaining the volume constant. The gas undergoes an isobaric compression till the volume and temperature become $V_0$ and $T_0, respectively. The total work done by the gas during the entire process is$
questions.solution:
The given situation is shown in the following diagram

Work done in expansion (process I)
$=\int_{V_i}^{V_f} p d V=\int_{V_0}^{3 V_0} \frac{p_0 V}{V_0} \cdot d V=\frac{p_0}{V_0}\left[\frac{V^2}{2}\right]_{V_0}^{3 V_0}=\frac{p_0}{2 V_0}\left(9 V_0^2-V_0^2\right)=4 p_0 V_0$
In process $\mathrm{II}$, there is no work done as $V=$ constant.
In process III, work done is given as
$W=p_0 \int_{V_i}^{V_f} d V=p_0 \int_{3 V_0}^{V_0} d V=p_0\left(V_0-3 V_0\right)=-2 p_0 V_0$
So, total work done in entire process is
$W_{\text{Total }}=4 p_0 V_0+\left(-2 p_0 V_0\right)=2 p_0 V_0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Work done on heating one mole of monoatomic gas adiabatically through $20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$ is $W$. Then, the work done on heating 6 moles of rigid diatomic gas through the same change in temperature
questions.solution:
Work done in an adiabatic expansion is $\Delta W=\frac{\mu R \Delta T}{\gamma-1}$ For 1 mole of monoatomic gas, $\Delta T=20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \gamma=\frac{5}{3}$
For 6 moles of rigid diatomic gas, $\begin{aligned} \Delta T & =20^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}, \gamma=\frac{7}{5} \\ \Delta W^{\prime} & =\frac{6 \times R \times 20}{\left(\frac{7}{5}-1\right)}=\frac{5 \times 6 \times R \times 20}{2} \end{aligned}=10 \times 30 R=10 \mathrm{ W} \quad$ [from Eq. (i)]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A steel rod at $25 ° C$ is observed to be $1m$ long when measured by another metal scale which is correct at $0 ° C$. The exact length of steel rod at $0 ° C$ is~$\left({α}_{steel} = 12 \times {10}^{- 6} ° C^{- 1}, {α}_{metal} = 20 \times {10}^{- 6} ° C^{- 1}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given: Length of steel rod at $25 ° C$ is $1m$.

The actual length measured by another metal scale at $25 ° C$ is $L = 1 \left(1 + {\alpha}_{m} ∆ T\right)$

$L = 1 \left(1 + 25 \times20 \times {10}^{- 6}\right)$⇒ L = 1. 0005m$ this is the actual length measured by the other metal scale.

Now, the steel rod has the length 1. 0005m$ at the temperature of $25 ° C$.

Let ${L}_{0}$ be the length of the steel rod at $0 ° C$, then

$L = {L}_{0} \left(1 + {\alpha}_{s} ∆ T\right)$

Putting the values in the above equation, we get

$1. 0005 = {L}_{0} \left(1 + 12 \times {10}^{- 6} \times25\right)$

${L}_{0} = \dfrac{1. 0005}{1. 0003} =1. 00019 \approx1. 0002m$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Carnot engine with efficiency $\eta$ operates between two heat reservoirs with temperatures $T_1$ and $T_{2^{\prime}}$ where $T_1 > T_2$. If only $T_1$ is changed by $0.4 \%$, the change in efficiency is $\Delta \eta_1$, whereas if only $T_2$ is changed by $0.2 \%$, the efficiency is changed by $\Delta \eta_2$. The ratio $\frac{\Delta \eta_1}{\Delta \eta_2}$ is approximately,
questions.solution:
Key Idea Efficiency of Carnot engine, \eta=1-$\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ Where, $T_1=$ source temperature and $T_2=\sin k$ temperature
If $T_1$ is changed by $0.4 \%$, then $\frac{\Delta \eta}{\eta}=\frac{\Delta T_1}{T_1}+\frac{\Delta T_2}{T_2} ($ From combination of the error) \Rightarrow $\frac{\Delta \eta_1}{\eta}=\frac{0.4}{100}+0 Similarly, $ T_2$ is changed by 0.2 \%$, then $\frac{\Delta \eta_2}{\eta}=0+\frac{0.2}{100}$ So, from Eq. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{\Delta \eta_1}{\Delta \eta_2}=\frac{0.4}{0.2}=2 Hence, option (1) is correct.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body cools from $70 ° C$ to $40 ° C$ in $5$ minutes. Calculate the time it takes to cool from $60 ° C$ to $30 ° C$. The temperature of the surroundings is $20 ° C$.
questions.solution:
According to Newton's law of cooling, Rate of cooling is directly proportional to the temperature difference between body and surrounding.

$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = K \left(T - {T}_{0}\right) = K \left(\dfrac{{T}_{i} + {T}_{f}}{2} - {T}_{0}\right)

Where, $ T = $\dfrac{{T}_{i} + {T}_{f}}{2} is average temperature$ of body.

The substitute the value as per first condition

⇒ $\dfrac{70 - 40}{5} =$ K $\left(\dfrac{70 + 40}{2} -20\right)$

$∴ K = \dfrac{6}{35}
As per$ the $second condition,

\dfrac{60 - 30}{t} = \dfrac{6}{35}\left(\dfrac{60 + 30}{2} -20\right)$

The time required is given to cool the body from $60 °$ to& $30 °$ is given& by

$⇒ t = \dfrac{30 \times 35}{25 \times 6} =7min$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of ideal gas goes through a process& $PV^{3} =$ constant, where $P and V$~are pressure and volume respectively. Let $W$ be the work done by the gas as its temperature is increased by $\Delta T$. The value of $\left|W\right|$ is ($R$ is the universal gas constant)
questions.solution:
Given,

One mole of ideal gas& $\left(n = 1\right)$ goes through a process is given by

~$PV^{3} =$ constant

Where,~$P and V$~are pressure and volume respectively.

This equation can be compared with the equation of adiabatic process,&

$PV^{γ} =$~constant

We get,& $\gamma = 3$

Work done in adiabatic process is given by

$W = \dfrac{{p}_{1}{V}_{1} - {p}_{2}{V}_{2}}{\gamma - 1}$

Using~$pV = nRT$

$W = \dfrac{nR{T}_{1} - nR{T}_{2}}{3 - 1}$

$⇒ W = \dfrac{R ∆ T}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One mole of nitrogen gas being initially at a temperature of $T_0=300 \mathrm{ K}$ is adiabatically compressed to increase its pressure 10 times. The final gas temperature after compression is (Assume, nitrogen gas molecules as rigid diatomic and $100^{1 / 7}=1.9$ )
questions.solution:
Given, initial temperature of 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ gas r_0=300 $\mathrm{ K}$ initial pressure of gas, $p_1=p$
and final pressure of gas, $p_2=10 p$
By adiabatic process relation between $p and T$, $\begin{aligned} p_1^{1-\gamma} T_1^\gamma& =p_2^{1-\gamma} \cdot \mathrm{T}_{2}^\gamma\\
\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{1-\gamma}& =\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{ T}_1}\right)^\ gamma \Rightarrow\left(\frac{p}{10 p}\right)^{1-\gamma}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{300}\right)^\ gamma\\
10^{\gamma-1}& =\frac{\mathrm{T}_2^\gamma}{300^\gamma} \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{2}^\gamma=10^{\gamma-1} \times300^\gamma\\
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{T}_{2} & =10^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}} \t times300=10^{1-\frac{1}{\gamma}} \times300 \\
& =10^{1-\frac{1}{7 / 5}} \ttimes300 \left[\because \text{$ For $diatomic, } \ gamma=\frac{7}{5}\right] \\
& =10^{2 / 7} \times300=(100)^{1 / 7} \times300 \\
& =1.9 \times300 \\
& =570 \mathrm{ K} \end{aligned}$ Therefore, the final gas temperature after compression is 570 $\mathrm{ K}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vessel of volume $V$ contains a mixture of ideal gases at temperature $T$. The gas mixture contains $n_1, n_2$ and $n_3$ moles of three gases. Assuming ideal gas system, the pressure of the mixture is
questions.solution:
By Dalton's law of partial pressure, pressure of mixture of three gases, p=p_1+p_2+p_3 According to the ideal gas equation, $\begin{gathered}$ p V=n R T \\
p=$\frac{n R T}{V}
\end{gathered}$ Temperature $T$ and volume $V$ are same for all three gases, but number of moles are different, i.e.
$n_1, n_2$ and $n_3$.
So, p=$\frac{n_1 R T}{V}+\frac{n_2 R T}{V}+\frac{n_3 R T}{V}$ p=$\frac{\left(n_1+n_2+n_3\right) R T}{V}$

If the gas is compressed adiabatically 8 times to its initial volume, the mean kinetic energy of gas molecules changes to $\left\langle E_2\right\rangle$. The ratio $\frac{\left\langle E_2\right\rangle}{\left\langle E_1\right\rangle}$ is

In adiabatic process,

T V^{$\gamma-1}=\text{ constant }In given conditions,

V_1=V\left(\text{ say), so })$ V_2=$\left(\frac{V}{8}\right)\right.$ and $\gamma=\frac{5}{3}$ (gas is monoatomic)

T_{\max }=$\frac{p_0 V_0}{R(4 \alpha)^{1 / 3}}-\frac{\alpha p_0 V_0^4}{V_0^3 R(4 \alpha)^{4 / 3}}=\frac{p_0 V_0}{R(4 \alpha)^{1 / 3}}-\frac{p_0 V_0}{R 4^{4 / 3} \alpha^{1 / 3}}$Substituting, $T_{\max }=\frac{3 p_0 V_0}{4 R}$, we get

$\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4^{1 / 3} \alpha^{1 / 3}}-\frac{1}{4^{4 / 3} \alpha^{1 / 3}}$Now from options, we can check that only $\alpha=\frac{1}{4}$, balances the equation.
So, $\quad \alpha=\frac{1}{4}$

questions.q: An ideal gas has molar heat capacity $C_V$ at constant volume. The gas undergoes a process where in the temperature changes as $T=T_0\left(1+\alpha V^2\right)$, where, $T$ and $V$ are temperature and volume respectively, $T_0$ and $\alpha$ are positive constants. The molar heat capacity $C$ of the gas is given as $C=C_V+R f(V)$, where, $f(V)$ is a function of volume. The expression for $f(V)$ is
questions.solution:
Given, $T=T_0\left(1+\alpha V^2\right)$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d T}{d V}=\mathrm{T}_0 \cdot 2 \alpha V \\
& \Rightarrow \quad d V=\frac{d \mathrm{~T}}{\mathrm{~T}_0 \cdot 2 \alpha V}
\end{aligned}
$$
From first law of thermodynamics,
$$
\begin{array}{cc} 
& d Q=d U+d W \\
\Rightarrow & n C \cdot d T=n C_V \cdot d T+p d V \\
\Rightarrow & n C \cdot d T+n C_V \cdot d T+p\left(\frac{d T}{T_0 \cdot 2 \alpha V}\right) \\
\Rightarrow & C=C_V+\left(\frac{p}{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{T_0 2 \alpha V}\right)
\end{array}
$$
Now as gas is ideal,
or
$$
\begin{aligned}
& p V=n R T \\
& \frac{p}{n}=\frac{R T}{V}=\frac{R\left[T_0\left(1+\alpha V^2\right)\right]}{V}
\end{aligned}
$$
substituting in Eq. (ii), we get,
$$
C=C_V+R \cdot\left(\frac{1+\alpha V^2}{\partial \alpha V^2}\right)
$$

questions.q: The efficiency of carnot engine is& $η$ when its hot and cold reservoirs are maintained at temperature ${T}_{1} and {T}_{2}$, respectively. To increase the efficiency to $1 . 5η$, the increase in temperature $\left(\Delta T\right)$ of the hot reservoir by keeping the cold one constant at ${T}_{2}$ is
questions.solution:
The efficiency of Carnot engine is 

$η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{{T}_{1}} ⇒ \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - η}$

The efficiency has to be increased to $1 . 5η$ by maintaining ${T}_{2}$ constant.

$∴ 1 . 5η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{\left({T}_{1} + ∆ T\right)} ⇒ 1 . 5η = 1 - \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{\left({T}_{1} + ∆ T\right)}$

$∴ \dfrac{{T}_{2}}{\left({T}_{1} + ∆ T\right)} = 1 - 1 . 5η$

$∴ \dfrac{\left({T}_{1} + ∆ T\right)}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - 1 . 5η}$

$∴ \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} + \dfrac{∆ T}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - 1 . 5η} ⇒ \dfrac{1}{1 - η} + \dfrac{∆ T}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - 1 . 5η}$

$∴ \dfrac{∆ T}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - 1 . 5η} - \dfrac{1}{1 - η}$

$∴ ∆ T = \dfrac{0 . 5{T}_{2}η}{\left(1 - 1 . 5η\right)\left(1 - η\right)}$

In $P$ - $V$ diagrams process $A B$ is isobaric process in which pressure remains constant i.e, $P=$ constant at all temperatures.
Process $B C$ is isothermal process in which, temperature remains constant i.e., $T=$ constant.
Process $C D$ is isochoric process in which volume remains constant i.e., $P-T$ diagram $C D$ is a straight line passing through origin.
Process $A D$ is adiabatic process which corresponds to process $A D$ in $P$ - $T$ diagram
Hence, the correct $P-T$ diagram is shown in option (a).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The ratio of specific heats of a gas is $\gamma$. The change in internal energy of one mole of the gas, when the volume changes from $V$ to $2 V$ at constant pressure $p$ is
questions.solution:
Change in internal energy,
$d U=d Q-d W$
At constant pressure,
$\begin{aligned}
d U & =C_p d T-p d V \\
& =C_p d T-R d T \\
& =\left(C_p-R\right) d T=C_V d T \\
& =\frac{R}{\gamma-1} d T \\
& =\frac{R}{\gamma-1} \times \frac{p V}{R} \\
& =\frac{p V}{\gamma-1}
\end{aligned}$

5 moles of Hydrogen $\left(\gamma=\frac{7}{5}\right)$ initially at S.T.P. are compressed adiabatically so that its temperature becomes $400^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. The increase in the internal energy of the gas in kilo-joules is

questions.solution:
$\gamma=\frac{7}{5}$
For adiabatic process $P V^\gamma=$ constant where,
$V=$ volume
$\therefore \quad P d^{-7}=$ constant
$\left(\because v \propto \frac{1}{d}\right)$
where $d=$ density
$\begin{aligned} P_1 d_1^{-7} & =P_2 d_2^{-\gamma} \\ \frac{P_1}{P_2} & =\left(\frac{d_2}{d_1}\right)^{-\gamma} \Rightarrow \frac{P_1}{P_2}=\left(\frac{d_1}{d_2}\right)^\gamma \\ \frac{P}{P^{\prime}} & =\left(\frac{d}{d^{\prime}}\right)^{7 / 5} \Rightarrow \frac{P^{\prime}}{P}=\left(\frac{d^{\prime}}{d}\right)^{7 / 5} \\ & =(32)^{7 / 5} \\ & =\left(2^5\right)^{7 / 5}=2^7=128\end{aligned}$
