questions.q: The efficiency of an engine is given by $\eta=\frac{\alpha \beta}{\sin \theta} \cdot \log _{\mathrm{e}} \frac{\beta \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{kT}}$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants. If $T$ is the absolute temperature, $k$ - Boltzmann constant, $\theta$-angular displacement and $\mathbf{x}$ is distance, then the incorrect statement is
options: Dimensions of $\beta$ are same as that of force
Dimensions of $\alpha^{-1} \mathrm{x}$ are same as that of energy
Dimensions of $\eta^{-1} \sin \theta$ are same as that of $\alpha \beta$
Dimensions of $\alpha$ are same as that of $\beta$
questions.solution:
The efficiency of an engine is given by
$\begin{aligned} \\ & \eta=\frac{\alpha \beta}{\sin \theta} \log _{\mathrm{e}} \frac{\beta \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{kT}} \\ \\ & {[\alpha \beta]=[\eta]=[\sin \theta]=\text{ Dimension less }} \\ \\ & {\left[\eta^{-1} \sin \theta\right]=[\alpha \cdot \beta]=\text{ Dimension less }} \\ \\ & \frac{\beta \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{kt}}=1 \\ \\ & \beta=\frac{\mathrm{kT}}{\mathrm{x}} \\ \end{aligned}$
Here, Boltzmann constant, $\mathrm{K}= \left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{ T}^{-2} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}\right]
\begin{aligned}$\\ & $\beta=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{ T}^{-2} \mathrm{ K}^{-1}\right][\mathrm{K}]}{[\mathrm{L}]}$\\ \\ & =$\left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right]$\\ \end{aligned}$
Force, \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{ma}=\mathrm{m} \frac{\mathrm{dv}}{\mathrm{dt}}
Force, \mathrm{F}= \left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right]
Hence, Dimension$ of $\beta are same as that of force.
\begin{aligned}$\\ & $\beta=\alpha^{-1}= \left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right]\\ \\ & \alpha^{-1} \mathrm{x}= \left[\mathrm{ML} \mathrm{T}^{-2}\right][\mathrm{L}]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{ T}^{-2}\right]\\ \end{aligned}$
Energy, $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{mc}^2=\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{ T}^{-2}$
Hence, dimension of $\alpha^{-1} \mathrm{x}$ are same as that of energy.

& a=\frac{v}{t} \\
& \frac{a_2}{a_1}=\frac{v_2}{t_2} \times \frac{t_1}{v_1} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{m n}=\frac{n}{m^2} \times \frac{t_1}{t_2} \\
& t_2=\frac{n^2}{m} t_1 \\

\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
If $E$ and ${E}_{0}$ denote energies at time $t$ and ${t}_{0}$ respectively, and $L$ and ${L}_{0}$ distance from some point at $t$ and ${t}_{0}$ respectively, then which of the following equations can be declared to be incorrect on dimensional grounds

(B) $E = {E}_{0}e^{- \dfrac{2L}{L0}}$

(C) $E = 2Le\dfrac{- L}{E0}$

(D) $E = 2\left(\dfrac{E0}{L0}\right) \times e\dfrac{- L}{L0}$
questions.solution:
Dimensions of energy $= \left[E\right] = \left[{E}_{0}\right] = \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

Dimensions of length

$= \left[L\right] = \left[{L}_{0}\right] = \left[M^{0}L^{1}T^{0}\right]$

For A:

LHS $= \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

RHS $= \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right] \left[L\$ right]$\left[L\right] =\left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

In this case, LHS=RHS

For B:

Exponent should be dimensionless. As we can see

$\left[\dfrac{- 2L}{L0}\right] =\left[\dfrac{L}{L}\right] = \left[M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}\right]$

and LHS $= \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

and RHS $= \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

So in this case, LHS=RHS

For C:

Exponent should be dimensionless but here

$\left[\dfrac{- {L}_{0}}{E0}\right] =\left[M^{0}L^{1}T^{0}\right]\left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right] =\left[M^{- 1}L^{- 1}T^{2}\right]$

is not dimensionless therefore it is wrong.

For D:

Exponent should be dimensionless. Here

\$left[\dfrac{- L}{L0}\right] =\left[M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}\right] \left[M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}\right]$ =$\left[M^{0}L^{0}T^{0}\right]$

Now, LHS $= \left[E\right] =\left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right]$

and RHS $= \left[ML^{2}T^{- 2}\right] \left[L\right] = \left[ML^{1}T^{- 2}\right]$

As in this case, LHS& ≠ RHS, hence it is wrong.

questions.q: The dimension of $\frac{E^2}{\mu_0}$ in mass $(M)$, length $(L)$ and time $(T)$ is ( $E=$ electric field, $\mu_0=$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
We know that,
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ Electric field intensity }=\frac{\text{ Electrostatic force }}{\text{ Electric charge }} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad E=\frac{F}{q}\end{aligned}$

Permeability of Free Space $\left(\mu_0\right)$ Dimension Calculation Magnetic field intensity in at a point in space due to an infinitely long current carrying conducting wire
Now, the magnetic force experienced by a current carrying conductor, when placed in a uniform external magnetic field is given by
$F=I L B \sin (\theta) \Rightarrow B=\frac{F}{I L \sin (\theta)}$
Put this value of $B$ into Eq. (ii) to get
$\begin{aligned}
& \mu_0= \frac{2 \pi r\left[\frac{F}{I L \sin (\theta)}\right]}{I}=\frac{2 \pi r F}{I^2 L \sin (\theta)} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left[\mu_0\right]=\frac{[2 \pi][r][F]}{\left[I^2\right][L][\sin (\theta)]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{ L}^0 \mathrm{ T}^0\right]\left[\mathrm{L}^1\right]\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{ L}^1 \mathrm{ T}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{A}^2\right]\left[\mathrm{L}^1\right]\left[\mathrm{M}^0 \mathrm{ L}^0 \mathrm{ T}^0\right]}
\end{aligned}$
So, now $\left[\frac{E^2}{\mu_0}\right]=\frac{[E]^2}{\left[\mu_0\right]}$
On putting the values from Eqs. (i) and (iii), we will get
$\begin{aligned}
{\left[\frac{E^2}{\mu_0}\right] } & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{ L}^1 \mathrm{ T}^{-3} \mathrm{ A}^{-1}\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{ L}^1 \mathrm{ T}^{-2} \mathrm{ A}^{-2}\right]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{M}^2 \mathrm{ L}^2 \mathrm{ T}^{-6} \mathrm{ A}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{ L}^1 \mathrm{ T}^{-2} \mathrm{ A}^{-2}\right]} \\
& =\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{ L}^1 \mathrm{ T}^{-4}\right]=\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-4}\right]
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: When Young's double slit experiment is performed in air, the Y-coordinates of central maxima and $10^{\text{th }}$ maxima are $2 \mathrm{ cm}  and $5 $\mathrm{ cm}$ respectively. If the apparatus is immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.5 , the corresponding Y-coordinates will be
questions.solution:
For YDSE apparatus in air
For central maxima
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{y_0 d}{D}-d \sin \theta=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{y_0}{D}=\frac{2}{D} ... (i)
\end{aligned}$
For $10^{\text{th }}$ maxima
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{y}_{10} \mathrm{ d}}{\mathrm{D}}-\mathrm{d} \sin \theta=10 \lambda \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{5 \mathrm{ d}}{\mathrm{D}}-\mathrm{d} \sin \theta=10 \lambda
\end{aligned}$
From equation (i), we have
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{5 d}{D}-\frac{2 d}{D}=10 \lambda \\
& \Rightarrow 10 \lambda=\frac{3 d}{D} \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{3 d}{10 D}
\end{aligned}$
Now, when the YDSE apparatus is immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.5 , then it's wave length $\lambda^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda}{1.5}$
As the y coordinate of central maximum doesn't depend upon wavelength, therefore it will remain same as in air, $\mathrm{y}_0^{\prime}=\mathrm{y}_0=2 \mathrm{ cm}$
For $10^{\text{th }}$ maxina
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{y}_{10}^{\prime} \mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{D}}-\mathrm{d} \sin \theta=10 \lambda^{\prime} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{y}_{10}^{\prime} \mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{D}}-\frac{\mathrm{d} \times 2}{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{10 \times 3 \mathrm{ d}}{1.510 \mathrm{D}} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{y}_{10}^{\prime}=4 \mathrm{ cm}
\end{aligned}$

$

Fringe width in Young's double slit experiment is given as

$\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & \frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1}=\frac{d_1}{d_2} \times \frac{D_2}{D_1} \\

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Choose the incorrect statement.
options: The fringe width in a Young's double slit experiment reduces when the width between the two slits increases.
The central fringe observed for in a single slit diffraction experiment is a bright fringe.
The resolving power of the microscope is reciprocal to the maximum separation of two points seen as distinct.
Polarisation phenomenon is observed only for transverse waves.
questions.solution:
(a) In Young's double slit experiment, the
fringe width is given by
$\beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d} \Rightarrow \beta \propto \frac{1}{d}$
So, if width between two slit $(d)$ increases, the fringe width reduces.
(b) In diffraction due to single slit, the path difference between rays reaching centre of screen is zero, so its intensity at centre is maximum i.e., bright fringe is observed at centre.
(c) The resolving power of microscope is
$=\frac{1}{d_{\min }}=\frac{2 n \sin \beta}{1.22 \lambda}$
So, it is the reciprocal of the minimum separation $\left(d_{\min }\right)$ of two points seen as distinct.
(d) The polarisation is possible only in those waves, that have vibrations in different direction, which is in case of transverse waves. Hence, only statement given in option (c) is incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The $P - V$ diagram shown below indicates two paths along which a sample of gas can be taken from state $A$ to state $B$. The energy equal to $5PV$ in the form of heat is required to be transferred if the Path-$1$ is chosen. How much energy in the form of heat should be transferred if Path-$2$ is chosen?
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics

$Q = ∆ U + W$, where $Q$ is the heat transfer to the system, $∆ U$ is the change in the internal energy, and $W$ is the work done by the system.

Applying for the Path $1$, putting the value from the given figure

$5PV = \dfrac{f}{2}\left(nR ∆ T\right) + W$

$5PV = \dfrac{f}{2}2PV + 2PV$

$f = 3$

Now applying for Path $2$,

$Q = ∆ U + W$

$Q = \dfrac{3}{2}\left(\dfrac{PV}{2}\right) + \dfrac{3}{2}\left(\dfrac{3PV}{2}\right) + \left(\dfrac{PV}{2}\right) + 2PV$

$Q = \dfrac{11}{2}PV$

questions.q: Light consisting of a plane waves of wavelength, $\lambda_1=8 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ cm}$ and $\lambda_2=6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ cm}$ generates an interference pattern in Young's double slit experiment. If $n_1$ denotes the $n_1$ th dark fringe due to light of wavelength $\lambda_1$ which coincides with $n_2$ th bright fringe due to light of wavelength $\lambda_2$, then
questions.solution:
Given, $\lambda_1=8 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ cm}$ and $\lambda_2=6 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ cm}$
Position $n^{\text{h }}$, dark fringe (due to light of wavelength $\lambda_1$ ) is given by,
$x_{n_1}=\left(2 n_1 \times 1\right) \frac{D \lambda_1}{2 d}$
Position of $n_2{ }^{\text{th }}$ bright fringe due to light of wavelength $\lambda_2$ is given by
$x_{n_2}=\frac{n_2 D \lambda_2}{d}$
Since both the fringes are coincide to each other. Hence,
$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n_1+1\right)\frac{D \lambda_1}{2 d} \text{ and } =\frac{n_2 D \lambda_2}{d} \\ \frac{2 n_1+1}{n_2} \text{ and } =\frac{2 \lambda_2}{\lambda_1}=\frac{2 \times 6 \times 10^{-5}}{8 \times 10^{-5}} \\ \frac{2 n_1+1}{n_2} \text{ and } =\frac{3}{2} \\ 4 n_1+2 \text{ and } =3 n_2 \\ 4 n_1-3 n_2 \text{ and } =-2 \\ 4 n_1-3 n_2 \text{ and } =-2\end{aligned}$
when $n_1=1 and n_2=2$, then Eq. (i) is satisfied. Hence, for $n_1=1 and n_2=2$, given fringes coincide to each other.

questions.q: The pass-axes of two polarisers were kept such that the incident unpolarised beam of intensity $I_0$, gets completely blocked. Another polariser was introduced in between these two polarisers with its pass-axis $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ with respect to the pass-axis of the first one. The output intensity would then become
questions.solution:
Since, the pass axes of two polarisers $P_1 and P_2$ were kept such that the incident unpolarised beam of intensity $I_0$ gets completely blocked.
This means that both polarisers were kept cross (perpendicular of their pass axes) to each other. When third polariser $P_3$ is introduced between $P_1 and P_2$ such that the angle between the pass axes of $P_1 and P_3$ is $60^{{}^{\circ}}$, i.e. $\theta_1=60^{{}^{\circ}}$.
intensity of polarised light emerging from first polaroid, $I_1=\frac{I_0}{2}$
Intensity of polarised light $\left(I_3\right)$ emerging from polaroid $P_3$ is given by law of Malus, i.e.,

$\begin{aligned}$I_3 & =I_1 \cos ^2 $\theta,$\\
& =$\frac{I_0}{2} \cos ^$2 60=$\frac{I_0}{2} \frac{1}{4}$\\
I_3 & =$\frac{I_0}{8}
\end{aligned}$Now, the angle between pass axis of $P_3 and P_2$, $\theta_2=90^{{}^{\circ}}-60^{{}^{\circ}}=30^{{}^{\circ}}\therefore$ Intensity of polarised light emerging from lost (second) polaroid $P_2$.

I_2=I_3 \cos ^2 30^{{}^{\circ}}=$\frac{I_0}{8} \cdot \frac{3}{4}=\frac{3 I_0}{32}$

questions.q: Two coherent point sources $S_1$ and $S_2$ vibrating in phase emit light of wavelength $\lambda$. The separation between them is $2 \lambda$ as shown in figure. The first bright fringe is formed at $P$ due to interference on a screen placed at a distance $D$ from $S_1(D > > \lambda)$, then $O P$ is
questions.solution:
From the figure,

$\begin{aligned} & \left(S_1 P\right)^2=D^2+x^2 \\ & \text{$ and $} \\ & \left(S_2 P\right)^2=(D-2 \lambda)^2+x^2 \\ & \text{ So, }\left(S_1 P\right)^2-\left(S_2 P\right)^2=D^2+x^2 \\ & -\left[D^2+4 \lambda^2-4 D \lambda+x^2\right] \\ & =4 D \lambda-4 \lambda^2 \\ & \left(S_1 P+S_2 P\right)\left(S_1 P-S_2 P\right)=4 D \lambda-4 \lambda^2 \\ & {[D > > \lambda]} \\ & \text{ Since, }[D > > \lambda] \\ & \therefore \quad S_1 P=S_2 P \\ & \end{aligned}$
and neglecting higher power of $\lambda\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad 2 S_1 P\left(S_1 P-S_2 P\right)=4 D \lambda \\ & 2\left(S_1 P\right)(\lambda)=4 D \lambda \\ & \text{$ or $} \quad S_1 P=2 D \\ & \sqrt{D^2+x^2}=2 D \\ & x^2=3 D^2 \\ & x=\sqrt{3} D \\ & \end{aligned}$
Alternative
$\begin{gathered}2 \lambda \cos \theta=\lambda \\ \Rightarrow \quad \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=60^{{}^{\circ}}, \tan \theta=\frac{x}{D} \\ \sqrt{3}=\frac{x}{D} \Rightarrow x=\sqrt{3} D\end{gathered}$

questions.q: A boy standing on a platform observes the frequency of a train horn as it passes by. The change in the frequency noticed as the train approaches and recedes him with a velocity of 108 kmph is (speed of sound in air $=330 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
Using Doppler's effect formula:
1) Approaching Train:
$\begin{aligned}
& f_{\text{approach }}=f_0 \times \frac{v}{v-v_0} \\
& F_{\text{recede }}=f_0 \times \frac{v}{v+v_0} \\
\therefore \Delta f & =f_{\text{app }}-f_{r e c e d e} \\
& =f_0\left(\frac{v}{v-v_0}-\frac{v}{v+v_0}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \Delta f & =f_0\left(\frac{\left(v+v_0\right)-\left(v-v_0\right)}{\left(v+v_0\right)\left(v-v_0\right)}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \Delta f & =f_0\left(\frac{2 v_0}{v^2-v_s{ }^2}\right) \cdot v \\
v & =330 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s} \\
v_s & =108 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{hr}=\frac{108}{1} \times \frac{5}{18}=30 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s} \\
\Rightarrow \Delta f & =f_0 .330 . \frac{2 \times 30}{330^2-30^2} \\
\Delta f & =f_0 \times 330 \times \frac{60}{108000}
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \Delta f & =f_0 \cdot \frac{19800}{108000}=f_0 \cdot \frac{11}{60} \\
\% \text{ Change } & =\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} \times 100 \\
& =\frac{11}{60} \times 100=18.33 \%
\end{aligned}\therefore$ ANS: $(A) \%$ Change $=18.33 \%$

$V=a \omega=a \times 2 \pi(n)=1.9 \times 2 \pi \times \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{10-1.9}{6.9 \times 10^{-3}}}\begin{aligned} & =1.9 \times 3.42 \times 10 \\ & \therefore \mathrm{V} \cong 72 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}.\end{aligned}$

A source and an observer move away from each other with same velocity of $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ with respect to ground. If the observer finds the frequency of sound coming from the source as $1980 \mathrm{ Hz}$, then actual frequency of the source is
(speed of sound in air $=340 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
By Doppler effect formula

f=f_o$\left(\frac{v-v_0}{v+v_s}\right)$Here $\mathrm{f}=1980 \mathrm{~Hz}$
Speed of sound in air, $v=340 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \begin{aligned}$& v_o=10 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$\\
& v_s=10 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$\\
& 1980=$\mathrm{f}_$o$\left(\frac{340-10}{340+10}\right)$\\
& 1980=$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}} \times \frac{330}{350}$\\
& $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}=\frac{1980 \times 35}{33}=$2100 $\mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two waves of amplitudes ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ respectively are superimposed. The ratio between the maximum and minimum intensities of the resultant waves is $9: 4$. The value of $\dfrac{A2}{{A}_{1}}$ is [Assume ${A}_{1} > {A}_{2}$]
questions.solution:
Intensity of a wave& $I$ is related with the amplitude of a wave as,

$I ∝ A^{2}$.

The ratio of maximum to minimum intensity will be,

$\dfrac{Imax}{Imin} = \left(\dfrac{{A}_{1} + {A}_{2}}{{A}_{1} - {A}_{2}}\right)2 ⇒ \dfrac{{A}_{1} + {A}_{2}}{{A}_{1} - {A}_{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2} ⇒ \dfrac{A2}{A1} = \dfrac{1}{5} = 0 . 2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical wires have a fundamental frequency $f_0$ when kept under the same tension $T$. If the tension of one wire is increased by $\Delta T$, then the $N$ beats occur when both wires oscillate simultaneously.
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency of the wire, f_0=$\frac{v}{2 L}, \text{$ where }$ v=\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}$}$\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & f_0=\frac{1}{2 L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} \\ \Rightarrow & f_0 \propto \sqrt{T}\end{array}$

Dividing Eq. (ii) by Eq. (i), we get $\begin{aligned}\frac{\left(f_0+N\right)^2}{f_0^2}& =\frac{T+\Delta T}{T}\\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{\Delta T}{T}& =\frac{\left(f_0+N\right)^2}{f_0^2}-1=\left(\frac{f_0+N}{f_0}\right)^2-1
\end{aligned}
$

questions.q: A wire vibrates at a fundamental frequency of $500 \mathrm{ Hz}$. A second identical wire produces 5 beats per second with it when the tension in the first wire is slightly decreased. The ratio of the tension in the second wire to the tension in the first wire is approximately equal to
questions.solution:

Beat frequency, $f_b=5 \begin{aligned}& f_b=f_2-f_1 \\

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two non-reactive monoatomic ideal gases have their atomic masses in the ratio $3: 4.$ The ratio of their partial pressures when enclosed in a vessel kept at a constant temperature is $2: 3.$& The ratio of their densities is
questions.solution:
From ideal gas equation, we have $PV = nRT$
$⇒ PV = \dfrac{m}{M}RT$
$⇒ P = \dfrac{ρRT}{M}$

Taking the corresponding ration, we have
$⇒ \dfrac{PA}{PB} = \dfrac{{ρ}_{A}R{T}_{A}{M}_{A}}{{ρ}_{B}R{T}_{B}{M}_{B}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{PA}{PB} = \dfrac{ρA}{MA} \times \dfrac{MB}{ρB}, \left(∵ {T}_{A} = {T}_{B}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{ρA}{ρB} = \dfrac{PA}{PB} \times \dfrac{MA}{MB}$
$⇒ \dfrac{ρA}{ρB} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{2}{3} =0. 5$

questions.q: Consider an ideal gas in a closed container at $300K.$ The container is then heated so that the average velocity of& particles of the gas increases by a factor of $4.$& What would be the final temperature?
questions.solution:
We know the relation between absolute temperature and average speed of the molecule inside the container is,&

${v}_{avg} ∝ \sqrt{T}$, it means,

$\dfrac{\left({v}_{avg}\right)1}{\left({v}_{avg}\right)2} = \dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} ⇒ \dfrac{\left({v}_{avg}\right)1}{4\left({v}_{avg}\right)1} = \dfrac{300}{{T}_{2}} ⇒ {T}_{2} = 4800K$

Now use the relation between centigrade scale and Celsius scale,

$⇒ {T}_{2} = 4800 - 273 = 4527 ° C$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A diatomic gas of volume $2m^{3}$ at pressure $2 \times {10}^{5}Nm^{- 2}$ is compressed adiabatically to a volume $0. 5m^{3}.$ The work done in this process is,
[Use ${4}^{1. 4} = 6. 96$]
questions.solution:
In the adiabatic process, the formula of work done in terms of pressure and volume is, $W = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - {P}_{2}{V}_{2}}{\gamma - 1}$

For diatomic gas the value of $\gamma = 1. 4$

Here ${P}_{1} = 2 \times {10}^{5}Nm^{- 2}$, ${V}_{1} = 2m^{3}$ and ${V}_{2} = 0. 5m^{3}$

Put these values in the above formula,
$W = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - {P}_{2}{V}_{2}}{\gamma - 1}$

Here ${P}_{2}\left({V}_{2}\right)\gamma = {P}_{1}\left({V}_{1}\right)\gamma ⇒ {P}_{2} = \dfrac{{P}_{1}\left({V}_{1}\right)\gamma}{\left({V}_{2}\right)\gamma}$
$⇒ W = \dfrac{{P}_{1}{V}_{1} - \left(\dfrac{{P}_{1}\left({V}_{1}\right)\gamma}{\left({V}_{2}\right)\gamma}\right){V}_{2}}{\gamma - 1} = \dfrac{2 \times {10}^{5} \times 2 - \left(\dfrac{2 \times {10}^{5}\left(2\right)^{1}. 4}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{1}. 4}\right)\dfrac{1}{2}}{1. 4 - 1} ⇒ W = - 7. 4 \times {10}^{5}J$

&

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two trucks heading in opposite directions each with speed $0.1 u$, approach each other. The speed of the sound is $u$. The driver of first truck sounds his horn of frequency $495 \mathrm{ Hz}$. Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the frequencies heard by the driver of second truck, when the trucks approach each other and when the trucks have passed each other. The magnitude of $v_1-v_2$ is
questions.solution:
Given, frequency heard by first truck driver,
$v=495 \mathrm{ Hz}$
Velocity of sound, $v_s=u$
Velocity of trucks, $v_1=v_2=0.1 u$
In the first case, when two trucks are approaching each other:
The frequency heard by second truck driver,
$v_1=\left(\frac{v_s+v_2}{v_s-v_1}\right) v=\left(\frac{u+0.1 u}{u-0.1 u}\right) 495=\frac{1.1}{0.9} \times 495=605 \mathrm{ Hz}$
In the second case, when two trucks are receding each other:
The frequency heard by second truck driver,
$v_2=\left(\frac{v_s-v_2}{v_s+v_1}\right) v=\left(\frac{u-0.1 u}{u+0.1 u}\right) 495=\frac{0.9}{1.1} \times 495=405 \mathrm{ Hz}v_1-v_2=605-405=200 \mathrm{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The transverse displacement $y(x, t)$ of a wave on a string is given by $y(x, t)=e^{-\left(a x^2+b t^2+2 \sqrt{a b} x t\right)}$. This represents a
options: wave moving in negative $x$-direction with speed $\sqrt{\frac{b}{a}}$
wave moving in positive $x$-direction with speed $\sqrt{\frac{b}{a}}$
questions.solution:
Phase of given wave is
$\phi=a x^2+b t^2+2 \sqrt{a b} x t$
Differentiating with respect to time,
$\frac{d \phi}{d t}=0=2 a x \frac{d x}{d t}+2 b t+2 \sqrt{a b}\left(t \cdot \frac{d x}{d t}+x\right)\Rightarrow(2 a x+2 \sqrt{a b} t) \frac{d x}{d t}=-(2 \sqrt{a b} x+2 b t)$
So, wave velocity is
$v=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{-(2 \sqrt{a b} \cdot x+2 b t)}{(2 a x+2 \sqrt{a b} \cdot t)}=-\sqrt{\frac{b}{a}} \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$

questions.q: An engine sounding a whistle of frequency $2000 \mathrm{ Hz}$ is receding from the stationary observer at $72 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{h}$. What is the apparent frequency of the observer? The velocity of sound in air is $340 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Apparent frequency at observer, $f^{\prime}=f \left(\frac{v}{v+v_s}\right) where, $v=$ speed of sound $=340 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$ and v_s=72 $\mathrm{~km}$/ $\mathrm{h}=$72 $\times \frac{5}{18}=$20 $\mathrm{~ms}^{-1}\therefore \quad$f^{\prime}=2000 $\left(\frac{340}{340+20}\right)$ Hence, $\quad f^{\prime}=1889 \mathrm{~Hz}$

$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u}$

$\dfrac{1}{v1} = \dfrac{1}{f1} + \dfrac{1}{u1}$

$⇒ {v}_{1} = 15cm$, that means for the second lens objective distance ${u}_{2} = \left(15 - 5\right) = 10cm$

With respect to the ${3}^{rd}$ lens if incident rays are parallel we will get final image at focus which is at& ${f}_{3} = 30cm$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical sinusoidal waves are moving in the same direction along a stretched string, interfere with each other. The phase difference between them is $120^{{}^{\circ}}$. The amplitudes of both the waves are same. If the amplitude of the resultant wave due to interference is $2 \mathrm{ mm}$, the amplitude of each wave is
questions.solution:
Given, amplitude of each sinusoidal waves are
same.
i.e., $\quad a_1=a_2=a$
phase difference, $\phi=120^{{}^{\circ}}$
Resultant amplitude, A=2 $\mathrm{ mm}$\begin{aligned} \because \quad A & =\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+2 a_1 a_2 $\cos 120^{{}^{\circ}}}$ \\ 2 & =\sqrt{a^2+a^2+2 a^2$\left(-$$\frac{1}{2}$\right)$} \\ 2 & =\sqrt{a^2+a^2-a^2}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} 2 & =\sqrt{a^2} \\ 2 & =a \\ $$\text{ or }$$ \quad a & =2 $$\mathrm{ mm}$$\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A whistle of frequency $660 \mathrm{ Hz}$ moves in a circle of radius $1 \mathrm{ m}$ at an angular speed of $10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A string of length $100 \mathrm{ cm}$ has three resonant frequencies, $120 \mathrm{ Hz}, 200 \mathrm{ Hz}$ and $280 \mathrm{ Hz}$. If a node is formed at the end of the string, the speed of the transverse wave on this string is :
questions.solution:
Given, length of string, $l=100 \mathrm{~cm}=1 \mathrm{~m}$
Three resonant frequencies are given as $f_1=120 \mathrm{~Hz}, f_2=200 \mathrm{~Hz}, f_3=280 \mathrm{~Hz}\because$ Fundamental frequency $\left(f_0\right)$ is equal to the greatest common factor of $f_1, f_2 and f_3$.

$\therefore f_0=$ greatest common factor of $120 \mathrm{~Hz}, 200 \mathrm{~Hz} and 280 \mathrm{~Hz}$ i.e., $f_0=40 \mathrm{~Hz}$
Now, we know that, speed of transverse wave is given by $v=2 l f_0=2 \times 1 \times 40=80 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider two tuning forks with natural frequency $250 \mathrm{ Hz}$. One is moving away and another is moving towards a stationary observer at same speed. If the observer hears beats of frequency $5 \mathrm{ Hz}$, then the speed of the tuming fork is : (Given, speed of sound wave is $350 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$.)
questions.solution:
Given, speed of sound, $v=350 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$, actual frequency, $n_0=250 \mathrm{ Hz}$ and number of beats heared, $x=5$
As source is moving towards the observer therefore, the apparent frequency, n_1=n_0 $\cdot \frac{v}{v-v_s}$ Similarly, as source is moving away from the observer, therefore the apparent frequency, n_2=$\frac{n_0 v}{v+v_s}$ Beats heared by the observer, $x=n_1-n_2$
Hence, from the Eq. (i) and (ii), we get, $\begin{aligned} x= & n_0 v\left[\frac{1}{v-v_s}-\frac{1}{v+v_s}\right]\\
x= & n_0 v\left[\frac{v+v_s-v+v_s}{v^2-v_s^2}\right]\\
\Rightarrow \quad & x=n_0 v\left[\frac{2 v_s}{v^2-v_s^2}\right]\\
& x\left( v^2-v_s^2\right)=n_0 v\left(2 v_s\right)
\end{aligned} where, $ v_s=speed of $the tuning fork \Rightarrow v_s^2+\frac{2 n_0 v}{5} \cdot$ v_s-v²=0 Now, putting the values, in above Eqs. we get v_s^2+35000 v_s-122500=0 It is a quadratic equation, so the positive value of $ v_s$ is v_s=$\frac{7}{2}=3.5 \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$ Hence, the correct option is (2).

questions.q: A drone fitted with siren in flying directly away from the drone operator and towards a distant building at a speed of $15 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following equation represents a simple harmonic motion? (\omega$ is angular frequency, A is amplitude of oscillation and $i = $\sqrt{- 1})$
questions.solution:
Let the displacement equation of SHM is given by,

$x = Asin \left(\omegat +ϕ\right)

Differentiating above equation we get,

\dfrac{dx}{dt} =A\omegacos \left(\omegat +ϕ\right)

$⇒ $\dfrac{dx}{dt} =$=A\omega $\left(\sqrt{1 - {sin}^{2} \left(\omegat + ϕ\right)$} \right)

$∴ \dfrac{dx}{dt} ==$ A\$omega\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{x2}{A2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dx}{dt} =\omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dx}{dt} =\omega\sqrt{\left(- 1\right)}\sqrt{x^{2} - A^{2}}$

$∴ \dfrac{dx}{dt} ==$ i\$omega\sqrt{x^{2} - A^{2}}

$

questions.q: A highway truck has two horns $A$ and $B$. When sounded together, the driver records 50 beats in 10 seconds. With horn $B$ blowing and the truck moving towards a wall at a speed of $10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$, the driver noticed a beat frequency of $5 \mathrm{ Hz}$ with the echo. Here, Iet frequencies of hom A and B$ are $n_A and n_B$, respectively.
As given, \begin{aligned}& n_A-n_B=\frac{50}{10}\\
& n_A-n_B=5 \text{ beats }
\end{aligned}$ When, the hom $Bis blown while moving towards the wall the $apparent frequency, n_B^{\prime}=n_B$\frac{v+v_0}{v-v_s}$ Since, both the observer and source are moving with truck.
So, $\begin{aligned}& \text{ So, } \quad v_s=v_0=10 \mathrm{ m}/ \mathrm{s}\\
& n_B{ }^{\prime}=n_B\left(\frac{330+10}{330-10}\right)\\
& n_B{ }^{\prime}=n_B 1.0625 \\
&=\quad n_B{ }^{\prime}-n_B=0.0625 n_B
\end{aligned} As given, $ n_B^{\prime}-n_B=5 $\begin{aligned}0.0625 n_B & =5 \\
n_B & =80 \mathrm{ Hz}

So, \begin{aligned}& \therefore \quad n_A=n_B-5=80-5 \\

&

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The speed of sound in air at temperature $T$ and pressure $p$ is $v$. When the temperature is increased to $2 T$ and the pressure is reduced to $\frac{p}{2}$, then the speed is changed to
questions.solution:
Speed of sound in air does not depend on pressure, but directly proportional to the root of temperature, i.e. v \propto $\sqrt{T} \Rightarrow \frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}$ Given, $T_1=T and T_2=2 T$, $\begin{aligned}& v_1=v_1 v_2=? \\
& \frac{v_2}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{2 T}{T}} \Rightarrow v_2=\sqrt{2} v
\end{aligned}
$

questions.solution:
Resonant frequencies are 160,240 and $400 \mathrm{ Hz}$, so their simplest ratios are 160:240:400.
i.e. 2: 3: 5 Hence, 160 is second harmonic \Rightarrow \quad 160=$\frac{n v}{2} \text{, where }$ n=2 Substituting $n=2$ and $v=160 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, we get L=$\frac{2 \times 160}{2 \times 160}=1 \mathrm{ m}$ So, string length is $1 \mathrm{ m}=100 \mathrm{ cm}$.

questions.q: Calculate the minimum thickness of a soap film ( $n=1.33)$ that results in constructive interference in reflected light, if the film is illuminated with light whose wavelength in free space is $532 \mathrm{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
For constructive interference through a thin film in reflected light, thickness of film must be

t=$\left(m+\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{\lambda}{2 n_2}$ where, $m=0,1,2, \ldots$ and n_2= refractive index of medium (soap film)
With given values, we get

$\begin{aligned}t & =\frac{\lambda}{4 n_2} \quad\left(t_{\min } \text{ occurs$ with $}m=0\right) \\
& =\frac{532 \times 10^{-9}}{4 \times 1.33}=100 \mathrm{ nm}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An observer is standing $500 \mathrm{ m}$ away from a vertical hill. Starting between the observer and the hill, a police van sounding a siren of frequency $1000 \mathrm{ Hz}$ moves towards the hill with a uniform speed. If the frequency of the sound heard directly from the siren is $970 \mathrm{ Hz}$, the frequency of the sound heard after reflection from the hill (in Hz) is about, (velocity of sound $=330 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ ) :
questions.solution:
Sound heard directly
$f_1=f_o \left(\frac{v}{v+v_s}\right)\therefore \quad970=1000\left(\frac{330}{330+v_s}\right)
or $\quad v_s=10.2 $\mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}
The frequency of reflected sound is given by
$ f_2=f_o$\left(\frac{v}{v-v_s}\right)=1000\left(\frac{330}{330-10.2}\right)=\frac{1000 \times 330}{319.8}\approx1032  \mathrm{ Hz}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vehicle sounding a whistle of frequency $256 \mathrm{ Hz}$ is moving on a straight road, towards a hill with a velocity of $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. The number of beats per second observed by a person travelling in the vehicle is velocity of sound $=330 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
Apparent frequency heard by the observer,
$\begin{aligned}
n^{\prime} & =\left(\frac{v+v_s}{v-v_s}\right) \times n \\
& =\left(\frac{330+10}{330-10}\right) \times 256 \\
& =\frac{340}{320} \times 256=272 \mathrm{~Hz}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Number of beats heard by the observer
$=272-256=16$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A transverse wave propagating on a stretched string of linear density $3 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^{-1}$ is represented by the equation $y=0.2 \sin (15 x+60 t)$
where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The tension in the string (in newton) is
questions.solution:
Equation of wave, $y=0.2 \sin (1.5 x+60 t)$ Comparing with standard equation,
$\begin{aligned}
& y=A \sin (k x+\omega t) \\
& k=1.5, \omega=60 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Velocity of wave, $v=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac{60}{1.5}=40 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s} 
Velocity of wave in a stretched string,
$v=\sqrt{$\frac{T}{m}$}$
where $m=$ linear density
$T=$\text{ tension in$ the string }$
So,
\begin{aligned}
T & =v^2 m \\
& =(40)^2 \times 3 \times 10^{-4}=0.48
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An iron load of $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is suspended in air from the free end of a sonometer wire of length $1 \mathrm{ m}$. A tuning fork of frequency $256 \mathrm{ Hz}$, is in resonance with $\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ times the length of the sonometer wire. If the load is immensed in water, the length of the wire in metre that will be in resonance with the same tuning fork is $($ Specific gravity of iron $=8)$
questions.solution:
We know $I \propto \sqrt{T}
\therefore \quad \frac{I_{\text{air }}}{I_{\text{water }}}=\sqrt{\frac{T_{\text{air }}}{T_{\text{water }}}}\begin{array}{llrl}\text{ But specific gravity } 8 & =\frac{T_{\text{air }}}{T_{\text{air }}-T_{\text{water }}} \\ \Rightarrow & T_{\text{water }} =\frac{7}{8} T_{\text{air }} \\ \therefore & \frac{l_{\text{air }}}{l_{\text{water }}} =\sqrt{\frac{8}{7}} \\ \text{ But } & l_{\text{air }} =\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} l \text{ (given) } \\ \therefore & l_{\text{water }} =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}} l\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two uniform strings $A$ and $B$ made of steel are made to vibrate under the same tension. If the first overtone of $A$ is equal to the second overtone of $B$ and if the radius of $A$ is twice that of $B$, the ratio of the lengths of the strings is :
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency of string,
$n=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}$
where, $m=$ mass per unit length of the string
$=\pi r^2 \rho\therefore \quad n=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{\pi r^2 \rho}}$
For string $A$ first overtone,
$n_A=\frac{1}{l_1} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{m_1}}=\frac{1}{l_1} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{\pi r_1^2 \rho}}$
For string $B$ second overtone,
$n_B=\frac{3}{2 l_2} \sqrt{\frac{T_2}{\pi r_2^2 \rho_2}}$
According to question,
$n_A=n_B\frac{1}{l_1} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{\pi r_1^2 l_1}}=\frac{3}{2 l_2} \sqrt{\frac{T_2}{\pi r_2^2 l_2}}$
but $\quad T_1=T_2\therefore \quad \frac{2 l_2}{3 l_1}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi r_1^2 \rho}{\pi r_2^2 \rho}}\frac{4 l_2^2}{9 l_1^2}=\frac{r_1^2}{r_2^2}\left(\frac{l_1}{l_2}\right)^2=\frac{4 r_2^2}{9 r_1^2}\frac{2 l_2}{3 l_1}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}\frac{l_2}{l_1}=\frac{3 r_1}{2 r_2}\frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{2 r_2}{3 r_1}$
but $\quad r_1=2 r_2\therefore \quad \frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{2 r_2}{3\left(2 r_2\right)}l_1: l_2=1: 3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the length of a stretched string is shortened by $40 \%$ and the tension is increased by $44 \%$, then the ratio of the final and initial fundamental frequencies is :
questions.solution:
Fundamental frequency, $n=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}$
Initial frequency, $n_1=\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}$
New length, $l^{\prime}=l-\frac{l \times 40}{100}=0.6 l$
New tension, $T^{\prime}=T+\frac{T \times 44}{100}=1.44 \mathrm{ T}$
New frequency $n_2=\frac{1}{2 l^{\prime}} \sqrt{\frac{T^{\prime}}{m}}\therefore \quad \frac{n_2}{n_1}=\frac{\frac{1}{2 l^{\prime}} \sqrt{\frac{T^{\prime}}{m}}}{\frac{1}{2 l} \sqrt{\frac{T}{m}}}\frac{n_2}{n_1}=\frac{l}{l^{\prime}} \sqrt{\left(\frac{T^{\prime}}{T}\right)}=\frac{l}{0.6 l} \sqrt{\frac{1.44 T}{T}}=\frac{1}{0.6} \times 1.2=2\therefore \quad n_2: n_1=2: 1$

questions.q: In order to double the frequency of the fundamental note emitted by a stretched string, the length is reduced to $\frac{3}{4} th of the original length and the tension is changed. The factor by which the tension is to be changed is$
questions.solution:
Frequency of stretched string.
$\mathrm{n}=\frac{1}{2 l} \frac{\sqrt{T}}{m}\begin{aligned} & n \propto \frac{\sqrt{T}}{l} \\ & \frac{n_1}{n_2}=\frac{l_2}{I_1} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}} \Rightarrow \frac{n}{2 n}=\frac{\frac{3}{4}}{l} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}} \\ & \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\frac{T_1}{T_2}}=\frac{2}{3} \\ & \frac{T_1}{T_2}=\frac{4}{9} \Rightarrow T_2=\frac{9}{4} T_1\end{aligned}\therefore$ Tension should be changed by the factor $\frac{9}{4}$.

questions.q: A body thrown vertically upwards from the ground reaches a maximum height ' $h$ '. The ratio of the kinetic and potential energies of the body at a height $40 \%$ of $h$ from the ground is
questions.solution:
$In vertical upward projection,
\begin{aligned}

questions.q: A proton and an ' $\alpha$ ' particle are both accelerated from rest in a uniform electric field. The ratio of works done by the electric field on the proton and the $\alpha$-particle in a given time is
questions.solution:
Acceleration of charge particle in an electric field is
$a=\frac{q^E}{m} \therefore v=u+a t=\left(\frac{q^E}{m}\right) t \Rightarrow v \propto \frac{G}{m}\therefore$ Work done by electric field,
$\mathrm{W}=\Delta \mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mb}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{ W} \propto \mathrm{mv}^2 \propto \mathrm{ m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{m}}\right)^2\begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{W} \propto \frac{\mathrm{q}^2}{\mathrm{ m}} \\ & \therefore \frac{\mathbb{W}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{W}_\alpha}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{p}}}{q_\alpha}\right)^2\left(\frac{\mathrm{ m}_\alpha}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{p}}}\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)=1: 1\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A block of mass ' $m$ ' with an initial kinetic energy ' $E$ moves up an inclined plane of inclination ' $\theta$ '. If ' $\mu$ ' is the coefficient of friction between the plane and the body, the work done against friction before coming to rest is
questions.solution:
Let before coming to rest body slides up to distance s . $\mathrm{h}=\mathrm{s} \sin \theta$
From the work- energy theorem, $\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{W}_{\hat{\varepsilon}}+\Delta \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{mg}}=\Delta \mathrm{K} \\ & \Rightarrow-\mu \mathrm{mg}(\cos \theta) \mathrm{s}-\mathrm{mgs} \sin \theta=0-\mathrm{E} \\ & \Rightarrow \mu \mathrm{mgs} \cos \theta+\mathrm{mgs} \sin \theta=\mathrm{E} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{ s}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{mg}(\mu \cos \theta+\sin \theta)} \end{aligned}\therefore$ Work one by friction, $\Delta W_{\mathrm{f}}=-\mu \mathrm{mgs} \cos \theta=\frac{\mu \mathrm{E} \cos \theta}{\mu \cos \theta+\sin \theta}=\frac{\mu \mathrm{E} \cos \theta}{\sin \theta+\mu \cos \theta}$

& \Rightarrow $\mathrm{v}}_{1}=\frac{12 \times 4}{4}=12  \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}
\end{aligned}Kinetic energy is

\therefore \mathrm{KE}$}_{1}=$\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}}_{1}  \mathrm{v}$}_{1}^2=$\frac{1}{2} \times$4 $\times$144=288 $\mathrm{~J}$

The water exerts a constant drag force and the acceleration of the boat is constant. If the average power required by the boat is $45000 \mathrm{ W}$, then the magnitude of the drag force is
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{u}}{\mathrm{t}}=\frac{20-0}{5}=4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{\text{ Work done }}{\text{ time taken }}=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }} \times \mathrm{S}}{\mathrm{t}}$ Now, $\mathrm{S}=\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{a} \times 5^2=\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 5^2=50 \mathrm{ m} \begin{aligned}& \text{ So, }45000=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }} \times 50}{5}\\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }}=4500 \mathrm{ N}\\
& \text{ Now, } \mathrm{F}_{\text{net }}=\mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }}-\mathrm{F}_{\text{drag }}\\
& \Rightarrow \text{ ma }=\mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }}-\mathrm{F}_{\text{drag }}\\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\text{drag }}=\mathrm{F}_{\text{boat }}-\mathrm{ma}\\
& =4500-4000=500 \mathrm{ N}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Statement (I) : The slope of kinetic energy-displacement curve of a body in motion will be directly proportional to its acceleration. Statement (II) : From a height of $15 \mathrm{ m}$ a ball is projected vertically upwards with a velocity of $30 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. If the ball rises to the same height after hitting the ground, the loss of its energy on hitting the ground is $30 \%$.
Statement (III) : The velocity acquired by a body of mass ' $m$ ' after travelling a fixed distance from rest under the action of a constant force is directly proportional to mass ' $\mathrm{m}$ '. Which of the following is correct?
options: Statements I, II, III are true
Statements I, III are true, but statement II is false
Statement I is true, but statements II and III are false
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false
questions.solution:
We have $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mV}^2 \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dx}}(\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E})=\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{m} \times2 \mathrm{ V} \frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dx}}
\end{aligned}$ Slope of $($ K.E $-\mathrm{x})$ curve $=\mathrm{ma} \propto \mathrm{a}$
So, (I) is correct
When ball just strike the ground, then $\mathrm{V}=\sqrt{30^2+2 \times 10 \times 15}=\sqrt{1200} \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$ If ball reaches the same height after striking the ground then, velocity after collision $=30 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s} \begin{aligned}& \text{ So, } \Delta \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m}(1200-900) \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m} \times300 \\
& \frac{\Delta \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{E}} \times100=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m} \times 300}{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m} \times 1200} \times100=25 \%
\end{aligned} So, (II) is incorrect.
Now, equation of motion are independent of mass. So velocity will not depend on mass. So (III) is incorrect.$

questions.q: A solid spherical ball is rolled up an inclined plane of angle of inclination $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with an initial speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ at the bottom of the inclination. How far will the ball go up the plane. $\left(\right.$ Use $\left.g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text{ As P.E } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{i}}+(\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{i}}=(\mathrm{P} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}}+(\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E})_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 0+\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{m} \times 4^2+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2}{5} \mathrm{mR}^2\right) \times \frac{4^2}{\mathrm{R}^2}=\mathrm{mgh} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{4^2}{2}+\frac{1}{5} \times 4^2=10 \mathrm{ h} \Rightarrow 8+3.2=10 \mathrm{ h} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 1.12=\mathrm{h} \Rightarrow \mathrm{h}=1.12 \mathrm{ m} \\ & \text{ So, } \ell=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sin 30^{{}^{\circ}}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{1 / 2}=2 \mathrm{ h}=2.24 \mathrm{ m}=224 \mathrm{ cm}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body of mass $\mathrm{m}$ slides down along a frictionless inclined plane from height ' $h$ ' and just completes motion in a vertical circle of radius $2 \mathrm{~m}$ after reaching the bottom. What is the value of $h$ ?
[Use $\left.\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right]$
questions.solution:
To complete vertical circle, minimum velocity should be $\sqrt{5 \mathrm{Rg}}$, where $\mathrm{R}=$ Radius of circle

$\begin{aligned} & \text{ Now, } \mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{K}_1=\mathrm{P}_2+\mathrm{K}_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{mgh}+0=0+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m}(\sqrt{5 \mathrm{Rg}})^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{mgh}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ m} \times 5 \mathrm{Rg} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{h}=\frac{5 \mathrm{R}}{2}=\frac{5 \times 2}{2}=5 \mathrm{ m}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A ball of mass $1 \mathrm{ kg}$ moves in a straight line with velocity $v=c x^a$, where $c=1$ (SI unit) and $\alpha$ is a constant. If the work done by the net force during its displacement from $\mathrm{x}=0$ to $\mathrm{x}=4 \mathrm{ m}$ is $128 \mathrm{ J}$, then the $\alpha$ is

From work - Energy theorem
Work done $=$ Change in kinetic energy

$\begin{aligned}$128 & =$\frac{1}{2}$m v_2^2-$\frac{1}{2}$m v_1^2 \\
128 & =$\frac{1}{2}$v_2^2-$\frac{1}{2}$v_1^2
\end{aligned}

...(i) $(\because \mathrm{vm}=118)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force acts on a body of mass $15 \mathrm{ kg}$, initially at rest. If the instantaneous power due to the force at the end of the third second is $5 \mathrm{ W}$, then the instantaneous power (in W) at the end of the $4 \mathrm{ s}$ will be
questions.solution:
Mass of the body, $m=15 \mathrm{ kg}$
The instantaneous power due to the force $F$ at the end of 3s, $P=5 \mathrm{ W}$.
Acceleration, $a=\frac{F}{m}$
From kinematics, $v=u+a t \begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow \quad v=a t \quad(\because u=0) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad v=$\frac{F}{m}$ t \\
& =$\frac{3 F}{m} \quad(\because$ t=3 $\mathrm{ s})$\\
& \because $\text{ Power }=5 \mathrm{ W}=$ F $\cdot$ v=$\frac{3 F^2}{m}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad F²=$\frac{5 m}{3}=\frac{5 \times 15}{3}=25 \Rightarrow F=5 \mathrm{ N}$\\
&
\end{aligned} Let$ the instantaneous power at the end of 4 th second be P_1$ and velocity of body at the end of $4 \mathrm{ s}$ be $v^{\prime}$, then $\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad$ v^{\prime} & =u+a t=0+$\frac{F}{m}$ t \\
v^{\prime} & =$\frac{5}{15} \times4=\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s} \quad(\because$ t=4 $\mathrm{ s})$\\
P_1 & =$\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbfv^{\prime}$\\
& =5 $\times \frac{4}{3}=\frac{20}{3} \mathrm{ W}=6.67 \mathrm{ W}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is moving in $x y$-plane with a potential energy given as $U=(12 x+16 y) \mathrm{J}, x$ and $y$ being in metre. Assume the initial position of the ball at $t=0$ is at origin $(0,0)$ and it is moving with a velocity of $(15 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+20 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$. Then, identify the correct statement.
options: The path of the ball is parabolic.
The direction of motion of the ball initially at $t=0$ is parallel to the direction of acceleration.
The speed of the ball at $t=2 \mathrm{ s}$ is $5 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$.
The magnitude of acceleration of the ball is $8 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$.
questions.solution:
Mass of the ball, $m=2 \mathrm{ kg}
Patential energy, $U=(12 x+16 y) $\mathrm{J}$\therefore$ Force applied on it, \mathbf{F}=-\frac{d U}{d x}$ \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-$\frac{d U}{d y}$ \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}
\Rightarrow \quad $\mathbf{F}=$-12 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-16 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}

Initially $(a t t=0)$, the ball is at origin $(0,0)$ and is moving with velocity $\mathbf{v}_i=(15$ \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+20 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) $\mathrm{m}$ / $\mathrm{s}$

Now, $\mathbf{F}=m \mathbf{a}=m \frac{\mathbf{v}_f-\mathbf{v}_i}{t}$ (where $\mathbf{v}_f$ is the velocity of the ball after $t=2 \mathrm{ s} ) or

\frac{\mathbf{F} t}{m}=\mathbf{v}_$ f-$\mathbf{v}_i

Substituting$ the $given values in above equation, we get

\begin{aligned}$& \therefore \quad(-12 \hat{ $\mathbf{i}$ }-16 \hat{ $\mathbf{j}$ }) \times $\frac{t}{m}=\mathbf{v}_$ f-$\mathbf{v}_i \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(-12 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-16 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) $\times $\frac{2}{2}=\mathbf{v}_$ f-(15 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+20 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad $\mathbf{v}_f=15 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-12 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+20 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-16 \hat{\mathbf{j}} \\
& =(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{m}/ \mathrm{s}\\
& \therefore \quad\left|\mathbf{v}_$ f\right|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=$5 \mathrm{ m}/ \mathrm{s}$\\
&
\end{aligned}

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small disc of mass $1 \mathrm{ g}$ slides down a smooth hill of height $10 \mathrm{ m}$ from rest and gets on to a plank of mass $100 \mathrm{ g}$ as shown in the figure. Due to friction between the disc and the plank. The disc slows down and moves as one piece with the plank. The work done by the frictional force is approximately (Use, $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^2$ )
questions.solution:
The disc is at rest at the top of the hill. $\therefore$ Potential energy of the disc, $U=m g h$ Let the velocity of the sliding disc before the friction is $v$. $\therefore$ The kinetic energy, $K=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$
From energy conservation, $\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}$ m v² & =m g h \\ v & $=\sqrt{2 g h} \end{aligned} \Rightarrow \quad v=\sqrt{2 g h}$ The disc now gets onto the plank and slows down and moves as one piece with the plank. Let the velocity of the plank is $v^{\prime}$. From conservation of momentum, $\begin{aligned} m v \text{ and } =(m+M) v^{\prime} \\ \Rightarrow \quad v^{\prime} \text{ and } =\frac{m \sqrt{2 g h}}{(m+M)} \end{aligned}\therefore$ The kinetic energy of the plank, $\begin{aligned} K_2 \text{ and } =\frac{1}{2}(m+M) v^{\prime 2}=\frac{m^2 \times 2 g h}{2(M+m)}\\ \Rightarrow \quad K_2 \text{ and } =\frac{m^2 g h}{(m+M)} \end{aligned}\therefore$ The total work done by the frictional force is $\begin{aligned} W_f \text{ and } =K_1-K_2=m g h-\frac{m^2 g h}{m+M}\\ \text{ and } =\frac{M m g h}{m+M}\\ \Rightarrow \quad W_f \text{ and } =\frac{100 \times 10^{-3} \times 1 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 \times 10}{(100+1) \times 10^{-3}}\\ \Rightarrow \quad W_f \text{ and } =0.1 \mathrm{ J} \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the average terminal velocity of rain drop is $2 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$, then the energy transferred by rain to each square metre of the surface at a place which receives $100 \mathrm{ cm}$ of rain in a year is
questions.solution:
Given that,
Terminal velocity of rain, $v=2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$
Height, $h=100 \mathrm{ cm}=1 \mathrm{ m}$
Surface area, $A=1 \mathrm{ m}^2$
Volume, $V=A h=1 \mathrm{ m}^3$
Density of water, $\rho=10^3 \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ m}^{-3}$
Mass of water (rain), $m=V \rho=10^3 \mathrm{ kg}$
Now, energy transferred by rain per unit area $\begin{aligned}$& =$\frac{\text{ Kinetic energy }}{\text{ Area }}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} m v^2}{1}$\\
& =$\frac{1}{2}$ m v²=$\frac{1}{2} \times10^3 \times(2)^2 \\ \text{$ and $} =2 \times10^3 \mathrm{ J}$/ $\mathrm{m}^2
\end{aligned} Hence, energy transferred by rain$ to $each square metre is 2 \times 10^3 \mathrm{ J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A horizontal force $\mathbf{F}=\left(g-x^2\right) \hat{\mathbf{i}} \mathrm{N}$ acts on a wooden block resting on a horizontal smooth surface. The work done to move the block from $x=0$ to $x=3 \mathrm{ m}$ (in $\mathrm{J}$ ) is (Use $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Given that, force acting on wooden block

$\mathbf{F}=\left( g-x²\right) \hat{\mathbf{i}} \mathrm{N} Displacement, $d $\mathbf{x}= d x \hat{\mathbf{i}}$Work done by $\mathbf{F}$ for displacement fromx=0 to x=3 $\mathrm{ m} \begin{aligned}W & =\int_0^3  \mathbf{F} \cdot d \mathbf{x}=\int_0^3\left( g-x²\right) d x=\left[ g x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 \\
& =\left(3 g-\frac{27}{3}\right)-0=3 \times10-9 \\
& =30-9=21 \mathrm{ J}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object $A$ of mass $20$ kg and travelling at $20ms^{- 1}$ crashes into another object $B$ of mass $200$ kg and travelling at $10ms^{- 1},$ in the same direction. After the collision, object $A$ bounces back in opposite direction at a speed of $10ms^{- 1}$. The speed of the object $B$ after the collision is
questions.solution:
Since net force in collision on the system is zero, so from conservation of momentum, we have
${m}_{a}{u}_{a} + {m}_{b}{u}_{b} = {m}_{a}{v}_{a} + {m}_{b}{v}_{b}$
$⇒ 20 \times 20 + 200 \times 10 = 20 \times \left(- 10\right) + 200 \times {v}_{b}$
$⇒ 2400 = - 200 + 200 \times {v}_{b}$
$⇒ {v}_{b} = \dfrac{2600}{200} = 13ms^{- 1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of mass $0. 2kg$ moving with a speed of $20ms^{- 1}$ is brought to rest in $0. 1s.$& The average force applied to the ball is
questions.solution:
The mass is given of the ball is, $m = 0. 2kg$, now first calculate the retardation of the ball, using the first equation of the motion,

So the average force applied to the ball, $F = m\left|a\right| = 0. 2 \times 200 = 40N$

questions.q: System shown in the figure is in equilibrium and at rest. The spring and string are massless, now the string is cut. The acceleration of mass $2m$ and $m$ just after the string is cut will be
questions.solution:
Initially, both the blocks were under equilibrium, so& for mass $m$,
$T = mg$,

Now, after the string is cut, the tension in it becomes zero. Therefore,
for $m$,
$mg - 0 = ma ⇒ a = g$(downward)
and for $2m$,
$2mg + 0 - {F}_{s} = 2mb2mg + 0 - 3mg = 2mb ⇒ b = - \dfrac{g}{2}$
i.e., $\dfrac{g}{2}$& upward.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A constant force of $5N$ accelerates a stationary particle of mass $500gm$ through a displacement of $5m.The average power delivered is$
questions.solution:
Given, force, $F = 5N$

Mass, $m = 500g = 5 \times {10}^{- 1}kg$

Displacement, $s = 5m$

Work done is given by $W = \overset{→}{F} \cdot \overset{→}{s} = Fscos \left(\theta\right)

Let's assume$ the angle between force and displacement to be zero. Then work will be,

W = Fs = 5 $\times5 = 25J$

Let the time taken to travel the displacement of $5m$ be $ts$.
Applying Newton's second law of motion,

$F = ma$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{5}{5 \times {10}^{- 1}}$⇒ a = 10ms^{- 2}$

From the third equation of motion,

$s = ut + $\dfrac{1}{2} at^{2}$

$⇒ 5 = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times10t^{2}$, & & & & & $\left(\text{initial velocity,}u = 0\right)$

$⇒ t = 1s$

The average power is given by

${P}_{avg} = \dfrac{Total work}{total time taken} = \dfrac{25}{1} =25W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a small block sliding down an inclined plane of inclination $30 °$ with the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is $\mu = \dfrac{2}{3}x,$ where $x$ is the distance (in meter) through which the mass slides down. The distance covered by the mass before it stops is
questions.solution:
By equilibrium of block perpendicular to the incline, $N = mgcos \theta$. So kinetic friction is, ${f}_{k} = \muN = \mumgcos \theta$. Work done by constant force is given as, $W = FScos \theta$. Let distance covered by the mass is $x$ before coming at rest.

So,& ${W}_{g} = mg \times x \times cos\left(90 ° - \theta\right) = mgxsin \theta$

$⇒ {W}_{N} = Nxcos90 ° = 0$
Work done by the variable force is given as $W = {∫}_{x1}^{x2}Fdx$.
So, ${W}_{f} = {∫}_{0}^{x}{f}_{k}dx = - {∫}_{0}^{x}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}x mg cos \theta\right)dx$

$⇒ {W}_{f} = - mgcos \theta \left(\dfrac{x2}{2}\right) \times \dfrac{2}{3} = -$mgcos $\theta\left(\dfrac{x2}{3}\right)

By work-energy theorem

${W}_{g} + {W}_{N} + {W}_{f} = ∆ K. E.$
$mgxsin $\theta +$0 - mgcos $\theta\left(\dfrac{x2}{3}\right) =$0$
$⇒ x = 3tan$\theta =$3tan30 ° = $\sqrt{3}m$

Dimension of& $\sigmab^{4}$,$∴ \sigmab^{4} = \left[{ML}^{0}$ T^{- 3}K^{- 4}\right]$\left[$ L^{4}K^{4}\right]= [ {ML}^{4}T^{- 3} ]$.

questions.solution:
In the above question, all the forces are acted in the lower block and there is no force acting on the upper block, now the value friction force will be,&

Which is greater than, applied force so no blocks will move and no force will act in the upper block so the net friction force between the lower block and the upper block will be zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Identify the incorrect statement.
options: All conserved quantities are not necessarily scalars.
The law of conservation of energy is valid only in macroscopic domain.
Weak nuclear force operates in the range of $\sim 10^{-16} \mathrm{ m}$.
Laws of nature do not change with time.
questions.solution: The law of conservation of energy is valid both, macroscopic and microscopic domain. All conserved quantities are not necessarily scalars. e.g., conservation of linear momentum and angular momentum are vectors whereas conservation of energy is scalar.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force acts on a $30 \mathrm{ g}$ particle in such a way that the position of the particle as a function of time is given by $x=\alpha t^2$, where $x$ is in metre, $t$ is in seconds and $\alpha=1 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. The work done during the first $4 \mathrm{ s}$ is
questions.solution:
Given, mass of particle, $m=30 \mathrm{ g}=3 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{ kg}$ Displacement of the particle is given as
$x=\alpha t^2\therefore$ Velocity, $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t} \alpha t^2 \Rightarrow v=2 \alpha t$
Acceleration, $a=\frac{d v}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}(2 \alpha t) \Rightarrow a=2 \alpha\therefore$ Force on the particle,
$\begin{aligned}
F & =m a=3 \times 10^{-2} \times 2 \alpha & \\
& =6 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{ N} & {[\because \alpha=1] }
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Work done during first $4 \mathrm{ s}$,
$\begin{array}{rlrl}
W & =\int_0^4 F d x=\int_0^4 6 \times 10^{-2} d x & \\
& =6 \times 10^{-2} \int_0^4 d x=6 \times 10^{-2} \int_0^4 v d t \quad[\because d x=v d t] \\
& =6 \times 10^{-2} \int_0^4 2 \alpha t d t=6 \times 10^{-2} \times 2 \alpha \cdot\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^4 \\
& =12 \times 10^{-2} \times 8 & {[\because \alpha=1]} \\
& =0.96 \mathrm{ J}
\end{array}$

questions.q: Consider a particle is moving with a minimum speed $v$ at highest point of vertical circle of radius $R$. If the radius of the circle doubled the corresponding minimum speed will be
questions.solution:
When a particle moves along a vertical circle, then it has its minimum speed at the highest point of the vertical circle and $in this case it just
completes the loop. The minimum speed is
\begin{aligned} v_{\min } & =\sqrt{g R} \Rightarrow v_{\min } \propto \sqrt{R} \\ \text{ So, } \quad & \frac{\left(v_{\min }\right)_1}{\left(v_{\min }\right)_2}=\sqrt{\frac{R_1}{R_2}} \Rightarrow \frac{v}{\left(v_{\min }\right)_2}=\sqrt{\frac{R}{2 R}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \frac{v}{\left(v_{\min }\right)_2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Rightarrow\left(v_{\min }\right)_2=\sqrt{2} v\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two blocks of equal masses are connected with a massless spring of spring constant $2500 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ and length $10 \mathrm{ cm}$ at rest on the frictionless horizontal plane. If a constant horizontal force $10 \mathrm{ N}$ is applied as shown in the figure, find the maximum distance between the blocks.
questions.solution:
In the case of maximum elongation, whole system will be moving with a common acceleration a, so for the system
$F=(m+m) a \Rightarrow a=\frac{F}{2 m}$ The centre of mass of the system will also move with the same acceleration $a$. Let us suppose that both the masses elongate the spring by a distance $x_1 and x_2$, respectively. So, on taking the frame of centre of mass there will act a pseudo force equal to ma on the masses. On applying the work-energy theorem, taking the centre of mass as a reference point. $\begin{gathered} W_{\text{all forces }}=\Delta K \\ (F-m a) x_1+(m a) x_2-\frac{1}{2} K\left(x_1+x_2\right)^2=0 \\ {[\because \text{ w.r.t. centre of mass } \Delta K=0]} \\ \Rightarrow\left(F-m \times \frac{F}{2 m}\right) x_1+\left(m \times \frac{F}{2 m}\right) x_2 \\ \Rightarrow\left(F-\frac{F}{2}\right) x_1+\left(\frac{F}{2}\right) x_2-\frac{1}{2} K\left(x_1+x_2\right)^2=0 \\ \left.\Rightarrow \frac{F}{2} \times x_1+\frac{F}{2} \times x_2\right)^2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \frac{F}{2}\left(x_1+x_2\right)=\frac{1}{2} K\left(x_1+x_2\right)^2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad x_1+x_2=\frac{F}{K} \Rightarrow x_{\text{total }}=\frac{F}{K} \end{gathered}$ Here, $F=10 \mathrm{ N}, K=2500 \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2$ So, $\quad x_{\text{total }}=\frac{10}{2500} \mathrm{ m}=\frac{1}{250} \mathrm{ m}=\frac{100}{250} \mathrm{ cm}=0.4 \mathrm{ cm}$ So, the maximum distance between the blocks $\begin{aligned} \text{ will be }= & \text{ natural length }+x_{\text{total }} \\ = & 10 \mathrm{ cm}+0.4 \mathrm{ cm}=10.4 \mathrm{ cm} \\ & {[\because \text{ Natural length }=10 \mathrm{ cm}(\text{ given })] } \end{aligned}$

questions.q: The block starts from rest as shown in the figure. Find the work done by force of $10 \mathrm{I}$ and friction in the time 0 to $4 \mathrm{ s}$. [Take, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ ]
questions.solution:
Here, applied force, $F=10 \mathrm{ N}$
Friction force, $f=\mu N=0.2 \times m g=0.2 \times 2 \times 10=4 \mathrm{ N}$ Net force, $F_{\text{net }}=F-f=10-4=6 \mathrm{ N}\therefore$ Acceleration, $a=\frac{F_{\text{net }}}{m}=\frac{6}{2}=3 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ Distance covered in $4 \mathrm{ s}$, $s=0+\frac{1}{2} a t^2=\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times(4)^2=24 \mathrm{ m}$ Work done by applied force of $10 \mathrm{ N}$, $W_1=F s=10 \times 24=240 \mathrm{ J}$ Work done by friction force of $4 \mathrm{ N}$, $W_2=f s \cos 180^{{}^{\circ}}=-4 \times 24=-96 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.q: Under action of force, a $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ body moves such that its position $x$ as function of time $t$ is given by $x=\alpha t^2 / 2$, where $x$ is in metre, $t$ is in seconds and $\alpha=1 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. The work done by the force in the first two seconds is
questions.solution:
Given, $x=\frac{\alpha t^2}{2}$
As we know that, $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(\frac{\alpha t^2}{2}\right)=\alpha t\ldots(i)$
According to work-energy theorem Work done,
$W =\frac{1}{2} m v^2=\frac{1}{2} m(\alpha t)^2 \quad \text{ [using Eq. (i)] }frac{1}{2} m \alpha^2 t^2=\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times(1)^2 \times(2)^2=4 $$\mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force of $4 \mathrm{ N}$ acts on a $10 \mathrm{ kg}$ body initially at rest. Let $W_1$ is work done by force during $0 \leq t \leq$ ls. Likewise $W_2$ is the work done by force during ls $\leq t \leq 2 \mathrm{ s}$, where $t$ is time in second. The ratio $\frac{W_2}{W_1}$ is
questions.solution:
Mass of body, $m=10 \mathrm{ kg}$
Force, $\quad F=4 \mathrm{ N}$
Acceleration produced in the body due to applied force,
$a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{4}{10}=0.4 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$
For $0 \leq t \leq 1 \mathrm{ s}, t_1=1 \mathrm{ s}\therefore$ Distance travelled by the body is given as
$s_1=u t_1+\frac{1}{2} a t_1^2=0 \times 1+\frac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times 1^2=0.2 \mathrm{ m}\therefore$ Work done,
$W_1=F \times s_1=4 \times 0.2=0.8 \mathrm{ J}$
For $\mathrm{l} \leq t \leq 2 \mathrm{ s}, t_2=1 \mathrm{ s}$
Velocity of the body after $t_1=1 \mathrm{ s}$ is $v$, then
$v=0+a t_1=0+0.4 \times 1=0.4 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$
Distance travelled by the body in this situation is given as,
$s_2=v t_2+\frac{1}{2} a t_2^2=0.4 \times 1+\frac{1}{2} \times 0.4 \times 1^2=0.6 \mathrm{ m}\therefore$ Work done, $W_2=F s_2=4 \times 0.6=2.4 \mathrm{ J}\therefore \quad \frac{W_2}{W_1}=\frac{2.4}{0.8}=\frac{3}{1}=3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An elevator of mass $500 \mathrm{ kg}$ is ascending upwards with a constant acceleration $a=2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. What is the work done by the tension in the elevator cable during its climb by $12 \mathrm{ m}$ ? (Take, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Mass of elevator, $m=500 $$\mathrm{ kg}$$
Acceleration of elevator, $a=2 $\mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ (upward)
When elevator is going upward, then tension in the elevator cable,
$T=m(g+a)=500(10+2)=6000 \mathrm{ N}\therefore$ Work done by the tension force in the cable,
$W=T \times s=6000 \times 12[\because \text{ given } s=12 \mathrm{ m}]=72000 \mathrm{ J}=72 $$\mathrm{ kJ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force $\mathbf{F}=(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{N}$ is applied on an object of mass $M$. What is the work done by this force in moving the object horizontally along the $X$-axis by $3 \mathrm{ m}$ ?
questions.solution:
Displacement of object is along $X$-axis by $3 \mathrm{ m} ,  \mathbf{x}=3 \hat{ \mathbf{i}  m}\text{ Force }=2 \hat{ \mathbf{i} }+4 \hat{ \mathbf{j} } $$\mathrm{N}$$
Work done by force, $W=$\mathbf{F}$ \cdot $\mathbf{x}=$(2 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+4 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) \cdot 3 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}=6 $\mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of mass $m=1 \mathrm{ kg}$ is thrown from the top of a building with initial velocity $\mathbf{v}=(20 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(24 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ at time $t=0$. The change in the potential energy of the ball between $t=0$ and $t=6 \mathrm{ s}$, if the ball does not hit the ground, then (assume, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} \mathrm{ s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{u}=20 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+24 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$
To find change in PE, we have to consider only vertical motion of the ball. So, we have $u_y=24 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}, m=1 \mathrm{ kg}a_y=-10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2, t=6 \mathrm{ s}$ We take origin at point of projection, $h=u_y t-\frac{1}{2} g t^2=24 \times 6-\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 36=144-180=-36 \mathrm{ m}$ So, vertical displacement of the particle is $h=-36 \mathrm{ m}$ Hence, change in PE $=m g h=1 \times 10 \times-36=-360 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is hanging from a rope that is wrapped around a pulley of radius $25 \mathrm{ cm}$. The mass of pulley is $2 \mathrm{ kg}$. Find the acceleration of the object. (Assume, pulley to be a solid disk $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Let block falls through a height $h$, then loss of $\mathrm{PE}$ of block appears in form of KE of block and KE of rotation of pulley.
$\Rightarrow \underset{\text{ (block })}{m g h}=\underset{\text{ (block) }}{\frac{1}{2}} m v^2+\underset{\text{ (pulley) }}{\frac{1}{2}} I \omega^2\Rightarrow m g h=\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} \frac{M R^2}{2} \cdot \omega^2$
Here, $m=M=2 \mathrm{ kg}$,
So, $g h=\frac{v^2}{2}+\frac{R^2}{4} \omega^2$
As $v=R \omega, g h=\frac{3}{4} R^2 \omega^2$
Differentiating with respect to time,
$g \cdot \frac{d h}{d t}=\frac{3}{4} R^2 \cdot 2 \omega \cdot \frac{d \omega}{d t}g v=\frac{3}{4} R^2 \times 2 \times \frac{v}{R} \cdot \alpha\Rightarrow \quad g=\frac{6}{4} R \alpha \Rightarrow \frac{4 g}{6}=R \alpha \Rightarrow R \alpha=\frac{2 g}{3}$
But $R \alpha=a_t=$ tangential acceleration of pulley
$=$ acceleration of block
So, $a_t=R \alpha=\frac{2}{3} g=\frac{20}{3} \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

questions.q: A force acts on a body of mass $10 \mathrm{ kg}$, resulting in its displacement given as $x=\left(\frac{t^3}{25}\right) \mathrm{m}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. The work done by the force in $1 \mathrm{ s}$ is
questions.solution:
Given, displacement, $x=\frac{t^3}{25}$ So, velocity, $v=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{3 t^2}{25} \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ Acceleration, $a=\frac{d v}{d t}=\frac{6 t}{25} \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ Force $=$ Mass $\times$ Acceleration $F=10 \cdot\left(\frac{6 t}{25}\right)=\frac{12 t}{5} \mathrm{ N}$ Also, $\quad \frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{3 t^2}{25} \Rightarrow d x=\frac{3 t^2}{25} \cdot d t$ Work done in displacing object by displacement $d x$ is So, total work done by force in first $5 \mathrm{ s}$ is
So, total work done by force in first $5 \mathrm{ s}$ is
$=\frac{36}{5 \times 25} \times\left[\frac{t^4}{4}\right]_0^5=\frac{36 \times(5)^4}{5 \times 25 \times 4}=9 \times 5=45 \mathrm{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle having kinetic energy $K$ is projected at $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal. The kinetic energy at the highest point is
questions.solution:
The motion of projectile is as shown in figure,

Let initial velocity of projection is $u$, so initial kinetic energy is
$\mathrm{KE}_1=\frac{1}{2} m u^2$
At highest point, the vertical component of velocity is zero, while the horizontal component is $u \cos \theta$, which is non-zero. So, the kinetic energy at this point is
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE}_2 & =\frac{1}{2} m(u \cos \theta)^2=\frac{1}{2} m u^2 \cos ^2 \theta \\ =\mathrm{KE}_1 \cos ^2 60^{{}^{\circ}} & =\frac{K}{4}\left(\because \mathrm{KE}_1=K \text{ and } \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}}=1 / 2\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball of mass $2 \mathrm{ g}$ released from the top of an inclined plane describes a circular motion of radius $20 \mathrm{ cm}$ in the vertical plane upon reaching the bottom. The minimum height of the inclined plane is
questions.solution:
The motion of ball is as shown below
At bottom of incline (at $P$ ) the potential energy of ball is converted into kinetic energy i.e., $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} m v^2=m g h \\ & \Rightarrow \quad v=\sqrt{2 g h} \\ & \end{aligned}$ To complete the vertical circle, the velocity of ball should be at least $\sqrt{5 g R}$. $\Rightarrow \quad \begin{aligned} v & \geq \sqrt{5 g R} \\ \sqrt{2 g h} & \geq \sqrt{5 g R}\end{aligned}$ [From Eq. (i)] $\Rightarrow \quad h \geq \frac{5}{2} R$ or $h_{\min }=\frac{5}{2} \times 20=50 \mathrm{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal chain of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and length $90 \mathrm{~cm}$ over hangs a table with $60 \mathrm{~cm}$ on the table. How much work needs to be done to put the hanging part of the chain back on the table? $\left(\right.$ Let $\left.g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$
questions.solution:
Given, mass of metal chain, $m=2 \mathrm{ kg}$,
Total length of chain, $l=90 \mathrm{ cm}=0.9 \mathrm{ m}$, Hanging length of chain, $l^{\prime}=(90-60) \mathrm{cm}=30 \mathrm{ cm}=0.3 \mathrm{ m}$
The distance of centre of gravity of hanging length from the table,
$l_c=\frac{l^{\prime}}{2}=\frac{0.3}{2}=0.15 \mathrm{ m}$
Mass of the hanging part of chain,
$\begin{aligned} & m^{\prime}=\frac{0.30}{0.90} \times 2 \\ & m^{\prime}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{ kg}\end{aligned}\therefore$ Work needed to put hanging part of the chain back on the table,
$\begin{aligned} W & =m^{\prime} g l_c \\ & =\frac{2}{3} \times 10 \times 0.15=1 \mathrm{ J}\left(\because g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A light rigid wire of length $1 \mathrm{ m}$ is attached to a ball $A$ of mass $500 \mathrm{ g}$ to one end. The other end of the wire is fixed, so that the wire can rotate freely in the vertical plane about its fixed end. At the lowest point of the circular motion, the ball is given a horizontal velocity $6 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. Determined the radial component of the acceleration of the ball, when this rigid wire makes an angle $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the upward vertical. (Take, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Given, length of a rigid wire, $l=1 \mathrm{ m}$ mass of the ball, $m=500 \mathrm{ g}=0.5 \mathrm{ kg}$ velocity of ball at a point, $C=v \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$
Motion of body in vertical plane is shown in the figure. In $\triangle B O C$, $\begin{aligned} \cos60^{{}^{\circ}} & =\frac{O B}{O C}$\\ $\frac{1}{2}$& =$\frac{h}{1}$\\ h & =$\frac{1}{2}$ m \\ \therefore A B=A O+O B \quad & =l+h=1+$\frac{1}{2}$\\ A B & =$\frac{3}{2}$m \end{aligned} According$ to the laws of conservation of energy,(\mathrm{KE}+\mathrm{PE})$ at a point $A=(\mathrm{KE}+\mathrm{PE})$ at point $C \begin{aligned}$& $\frac{1}{2}$ m u²+0=$\frac{1}{2}$ m v²+m g(A B) \\ & u²=v²+2 g(A B) \\ & 6^2=v²+2 g $\cdot \frac{3}{2} \quad \text{ [From Eq. (i)] }$\\ & 6^2=v²+2 $\times10 \times \frac{3}{2}$\\ & v²=6 \end{aligned} $\therefore$ Radial component of acceleration of the ball a_C=$\frac{v^2}{l}=\frac{6}{l}=6 \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}^2 $

questions.q: A ball moves one-fourth $\left(\frac{1^{\text{th }}}{4}\right)$ of a circle of radius $R$ in time $T$. Let $v_1 and v_2$ be the magnitudes of mean speed and mean velocity vector. The ratio $\frac{v_1}{v_2}$ will be
questions.solution: Key idea Mean speed of a moving body, $v_{\mathrm{rms}$}=$\frac{\text{ total distance }}{\text{ total time taken }}$Mean velocity vector for a moving body, v_{w v}=$\frac{\text{ total displacement }}{\text{ total time taken }}$A ball moving in a circular arc is shown in the figure below, $$ \\ Here, $v_{\mathrm{rms}}=\frac{2 \pi R}{4} \times \frac{1}{T}=v_1$ Similarly, $v_{\mathrm{vv}}=\frac{\sqrt{2} R}{T}=v_2$ Hence, $\frac{v_1}{v_2}=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{2}}$ Option (4) is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Conservative forces are defined as the force for which,
options: work done depends only on the initial and final positions.
work done depends on the initial and final positions and also on the path taken.
work done depends only on the path taken.
work done depends only on the initial position.
questions.solution:
Conservative force is a force with the property that the total work done in moving a particle between two points is independent of the path followed but depends only on the initial and final positions.
So, the correct option is (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is projected vertically up from ground. Boy $' A '$ standing at the window of first floor of a nearby building observes that the time interval between the ball crossing him while going up and the ball crossing him while going down is $2s$. Another boy $B$ standing on the second floor notices the time interval between the ball passing him twice, during up and down motion is $1s$. Calculate the difference between the vertical positions of boy $B$ and boy $A$. (Assume $g = 10ms^{- 2}$)
questions.solution:
Let's assume ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are the speeds of the ball while crossing the Boy $A$ and $B$ respectively during its motion.

Applying the equation of motion, $S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$ for the motion of ball

while passing the Boy $A$ is

$⇒ 0 = {v}_{1}\left(2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(10\right)\left(2\right)^{2}$

$⇒ {v}_{1} = 10ms^{- 1}$.

while passing the Boy $B$ is

$⇒ 0 = {v}_{2}\left(1\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(10\right)\left(1\right)^{2}$

$⇒ {v}_{1} = 5ms^{- 1}$.

The difference between the vertical positions of the boys $A$ and $B$ is

${v}_{2}^{2} = {v}_{1}^{2} - 2gh$

$⇒ {5}^{2} = {10}^{2} - 2\left(10\right)h$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{100 - 25}{20} = 3. 75m$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is moving along a circle of radius $R$ such that its tangential acceleration~$\left({a}_{t}\right)$ varies with distance covered $\left(x\right)$ as ${a}_{t} = {αx}^{2}$, where $\alpha$ is a constant. The kinetic energy~$\left(K\right)$ of the particle varies with the distance as $K = \betax^{c}$, where $\beta$ and c are constants. The values of $\beta$ and c are
questions.solution:
Given,

Tangential acceleration, ${a}_{t} = \alphax^{2}$ and

Kinetic energy, $K = \betax^{c}$.

If $F$ is the tangential force acting on the particle then$F = m\alphax^{2}$

Now applying work energy theorem,

$W = ∆ KE$

$⇒ ∫ Fdx = K$

$⇒ ∫ m\alphax^{2}dx = K$

$⇒ K = \dfrac{m\alphax^{3}}{3} = \betax^{c}$

$∴ \beta = \dfrac{m\alpha}{3}; c = 3.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass of $2$ kg, initially at a height of $1. 2m$ above an uncompressed spring with spring constant $2 \times {10}^{4}Nm^{- 1},$ is released from rest to fall on the spring. Taking the acceleration due to gravity as $10ms^{- 2}$ and neglecting the air resistance, the compression of the spring in $mm$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

Mass, $m = 2\text{kg}$,

Spring constant, $k = 2 \times {10}^{4}Nm^{- 1}$

Acceleration due to gravity, $g = 10ms^{- 2}$.

Applying Law of conservation of mechanical energy,

$mg\left(h + x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$

$⇒ kx^{2} - 2mgx - 2mgh = 0$

$⇒ \left(2 \times {10}^{4}\right)x^{2} - 40x - 48 = 0$

Using Quadratic formula,

$⇒ x = \dfrac{40 \pm \sqrt{\left(- 40\right)^{2} - 4 \times 2 \times {10}^{4} \times \left(- 48\right)}}{2 \times 2 \times {10}^{4}}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{40 \pm 1960}{4 \times {10}^{4}}$

$x$ cannot be negative, thus

$x = \dfrac{40 + 1960}{4 \times {10}^{4}} = 50mm$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet of mass $1kg$ fired with a speed $2m{s}^{- 1}$ from $x = 0$ passes through a block of wood whose centre is kept at a distance of $10m$ from the origin as shown in figure. The retarding force $\left({F}_{r}\right)$ on the bullet within the wooden block is $- \dfrac{0 . 5}{x}$. The minimum length of the block (upto one decimal digit) required to completely stop the bullet is (Assume ${e}^{4} = 55$)
questions.solution:
Given

Mass of bullet $m = 1kg$

Velocity of bullet $v = 2m{s}^{- 1}$

The restoring force on the bullet within the block is $F = \dfrac{- 0 . 5}{x}$

Applying work energy theorem,

$W = ∆ KE$

$⇒ ∫ Fdx = - \dfrac{1}{2}m{u}^{2}$

$⇒ {∫}_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}Fdx = {∫}_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}\dfrac{- 0 . 5}{x}dx = - \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1 \times {2}^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{- 1}{2}\log_{e}^{\dfrac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}} = - 2$

$⇒ {e}^{4} = \dfrac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}} = \dfrac{\left(10 - L / 2\right)}{\left(10 + L / 2\right)} = 55$

$⇒ L = 19 . 3m$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A box of mass $3 \mathrm{ kg}$ moves on a horizontal frictionless table and collides with another box of mass $3 \mathrm{ kg}$ initially at rest on the edge of the table at height $1 \mathrm{ m}$. The speed of the moving box just before the collision is $4 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. The two boxes stick together and fall from the table. The kinetic energy just before the boxes strike the floor is (Assume, acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution: $\text{$ The given situation can be shown as below, } \\ According to law of conservation of momentum, total momentum before collision $=$ total momentum after collision. m_1 u_1+m_2 u_2=$\left(m_1+m_2\right) v Given, mass$ of boxes,\quad m_1=m_2=3$\mathrm{~kg}$ speed of the moving box, $\quad u_2=4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} and initial speed of second box, $u_2=0Putting the $given values, we get \Rightarrow \quad$\begin{aligned}$& 3 $\times$4+3 $\times$0=(3+3) v \\ & \quad v=\frac{12}{6}$=$2 \mathrm{~m}/ \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}Thus,$ the two bodies move with the velocity of2 $\mathrm{~m}$ / $\mathrm{s}$. Applying law of conservation of energy at height of $1 \mathrm{~m} and at the bottom of table. \mathrm{KE}_{2}+ \mathrm{PE}_{2}=\mathrm{KE}_{2}+\mathrm{PE}_{2} At the bottom just above the ground, the total energy is \mathrm{KE} as height is approximately equals to zero. $\begin{aligned}$& \frac{1}{2}\left(m_1+m_2\right)$ v²+$\left(m_1+m_2\right)$ g h=$\mathrm{KE}_{2}$ \\ & \Rightarrow \quad $\mathrm{KE}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ \times$6 $\times$4+6 $\times$10 $\times$1 \\ &=12+60=72 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}Hence,$ the kinetic energy just before the boxes strike the floor is72 $\mathrm{~J}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A ball of mass $2 \mathrm{ kg}$ is thrown from a tall building with velocity,
$\mathbf{v}=(20 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(24 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}) \hat{\mathbf{j}}$ at time $t=0 \mathrm{ s}$.
Change in the potential energy of the ball after, $t=8 \mathrm{ s}$ is (The ball is assumed to be in air during its motion between $0 \mathrm{ s}$ and $8 \mathrm{ s}, \hat{\mathbf{i}}$ is along the horizontal and $\hat{\mathbf{j}}$ is along the vertical direction (Take $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
Given, velocity of the ball, $\mathbf{v}=(20 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+24 \hat{\mathbf{j}}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ and mass of the ball, $m=2 \mathrm{ kg}$
From the equation of motion, when a ball is thrown,

$\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{g}t

Substituting the given values in $Eq. (i), we get

\begin{aligned}$\mathbf{v}$& =(20 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+24 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}-(10 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) 8 \\
& =20 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+24 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}-80 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}=20 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-56 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}
\end{aligned}

Fom$ the $law of conservation of energy, change in potential energy of the ball = change in kinetic energy of the ball

\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow\Delta$\mathrm{PE}$ & =$\frac{1}{2}$ m $\mathbf{u}^2-\frac{1}{2}$m $\mathbf{v}^2 \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m\left( \mathbf{u}^2-\mathbf{v}^2\right)$ \\
& =$\frac{2}{2}(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}$-$\mathbf{v}$ \cdot $\mathbf{v}$)\\
& =[(20 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+24 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) \cdot(20 \hat{\hat{$\mathrm{i}$ }}+24 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}) \\
& -[(20 \hat{\hat{$\mathrm{i}$}}-56 \hat{$\mathrm{j}$}) \cdot(20 \hat{$\mathrm{i}$ }-56 \hat{$\mathrm{j}$})] \\
& =(20)^2+(24)^2-(20)^2-(56)^2 \\
& =(24)^2-(56)^2=576-3136 \\
& =-2560=-2.56 $\mathrm{ kJ}$
\end{aligned}$ Hence, change in potential energy of the ball after $t=85 $\mathrm{ s}$ is $-2.56 \mathrm{KJ}.$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A small body of mass $500 \mathrm{ g}$ moves on a rough horizontal surface before finally stops. The initial velocity of the body is $2 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ and coefficient of friction is 0.3. Then, find absolute value of the average power developed by the frictional force during the time of motion. (Talse, $g=10 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution: As, retardation is constant, so average velocity v_{a v}=$\frac{\mathrm{k}+v}{2}=\frac{2+0}{2}=1 \mathrm{ m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$ Now, friction force, $f=\mu N=\mu m g$ Given, coefficient of friction, $\mu=0.3$ Mass of body, $m=500 \mathrm{ g}=0.5 \mathrm{ kg}\Rightarrow \quad f=0.3 \times 0.5 \times 10f=1.5 \mathrm{ N}$ Average power by friction, $\begin{aligned}& P_{a v}=f v_{a v} \\ & P_{a v}=1.5 \times1=1.5 \mathrm{ W} \end{aligned}$

W=$\frac{1}{2}$ K_{$\text{eq } } $\cdot \Delta$ t^2=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{k_2 k_2}{k_1+k_2}\right) \cdot \Delta$ l^2
